events.title: Guest Recital: How to See Know and Fall
events.description:
How to See Know and Fall is a collaboration between interdisciplinary percussionist/composer Brian Shankar Adler and electronic composer/software designer Jesse Stiles, combining intricate hybrid percussion with shimmering synth lines, ambient textures, and immersive visuals.

Live performances transform the stage into a dreamlike audiovisual environment where polyrhythms collide with live video, weaving data and performance into a visceral tapestry of sound and light. By bridging far-reaching rhythmic traditions, cutting-edge electronics, and critical explorations of emerging technologies, How to See Know and Fall offers audiences a revelatory experience at the cross-hairs of music, technology, and digital art.

BRIAN SHANKAR ADLER is a widely recognized percussionist and composer who blurs genre lines to create deeply expressive rhythmic landscapes. He has performed in settings ranging from glacial ice fields to Lincoln Center, showcasing his innovative approach to percussion around the globe. With commissions from chamber ensembles and collaborations in opera, dance, and beyond, Adler pursues a vision that intertwines technical precision with human connection.

JESSE STILES, formerly Associate Professor of Sound Media at the CMU School of Music, is an electronic composer, performer, and software designer whose immersive sonic environments have been presented at Carnegie Hall, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and beyond. As the Music Supervisor for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, he produced and performed in hundreds of concerts featuring the works of leading avant-garde composers. Currently an Associate Professor at the Penny W. Stamps School of Art & Design, Stiles continues to push the boundaries of interactive media and sound design.

events.title: Teaching Inclusively: Creating Trust in the Classroom
events.description:
A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

Do you trust your students, and do your students trust you? These questions are critical to building a supportive environment for learning in your classroom. In this seminar, we will review various ways to conceptualize trust in a learning environment and share research on why trust is essential to learning from K-12 to higher education. Finally, we will explore various actions instructors can take to build and show trust in their classrooms. Participants should expect to leave with a series of implementable “teaching moves” that foster and demonstrate trust in the classroom.

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: Halloween at Heinz Hall
events.description:
On Halloween, the Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic will perform a free concert for the Pittsburgh community at Heinz Hall. This 80-minute program, designed for families and audience members of all ages will be led by Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

The Halloween-themed event includes spooky standards like Modest Mussorgsky’s Night on Bald Mountain (conducted by CMU Philharmonic Associate Conductor, John William Brink) and Paul Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. The concert will also feature wizard of the keyboard, Tino Cardenes (current Music and Technology student of the School of Music and winner of the Philharmonic Soloist Competition, undergraduate division) performing Nikolai Kapustin’s jazzy Piano Concerto No. 2. The heart of the program is Manuel de Falla’s magical El Amor Brujo, which includes the famous “Ritual Fire Dance.” This performance will feature recent graduate of the School of Music, mezzo-soprano Isabelle Hoyou. Kids are encouraged to come in costume and arrive early for pre-concert fun in the lobby.

Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Jacob Joyce, guest conductor

John William Brink, associate conductor

Featured Artists:

Isabelle Hoyou, mezzo-soprano

Tino Cardenes, piano

Program:

Modest Mussorgsky – Night on Bald Mountain

Manuel de Falla – El Amor Brujo

Nikolai Kapustin – Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 14

Paul Dukas – The Sorcerer’s Apprentice

Cost:

FREE and open to the public. Tickets required.

events.title: Guest Lecture: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation
events.description:
Title: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation

Abstract:

Digital transformation in the built environment is increasingly defined not by technology adoption alone, but by the ability to demonstrate measurable value. AI, openBIM, VDC, digital twins, Lean practices, and performance metrics are becoming more closely connected as organizations seek better project, asset, and business outcomes.

Drawing on more than 30 years of experience in openBIM and digital innovation, including owner-focused initiatives across 30 countries, Dr. Calvin Kam will explore how governments, owners, and industry organizations can translate emerging technologies, open standards, and mandates into practical implementation strategies and measurable results.

Building on his work as Founder and CEO of Strategic Building Innovation, his work with buildingSMART International on Global openBIM Mandates and openBIM Business Value, and research associated with Stanford University’s Center for Integrated Facility Engineering (CIFE), the presentation will examine how frameworks such as the VDC Scorecard can help organizations connect information requirements, quality controls, technology adoption, KPIs, and performance with broader business value.

Looking forward, the session will explore how AI, openBIM, and VDC can increasingly enable digital twins, GIS, IoT, sustainability, and decarbonization - creating a stronger foundation for informed decision-making, smarter mandates, and improved whole-lifecycle performance across the built environment.

Bio:

Dr. Calvin Kam is Founder & CEO of Strategic Building Innovation and Strategic Green Innovation — the “GPS Navigator” for any enterprise charting a course for construction innovation while optimizing the value of built assets. Dr. Kam serves as the Chapter President of buildingSMART Chapter in the United States and an Executive of buildingSMART International’s Compliance Program. He received his Doctor of Philosophy degree from Stanford University in Design/Construction Integration and Construction Engineering & Management.

As an Adjunct Professor at Stanford University’s Center for Integrated Facility Engineering (CIFE) and a Co-Founder of GSA’s National BIM Program, Dr. Kam advises built asset owners globally on strategic innovation, including customized AI applications and digitalized construction management leveraging openBIM/GIS global standards. Dr. Kam has advised public agencies in APEC, Finland, Hong Kong China, Norway, UAE, U.K., U.S., and Singapore on AI, digitalization, innovation, open standards, productivity, value chain, and management science.

Elevated as a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects as well as buildingSMART International, Dr. Kam has given keynotes and lectures in over 30 countries and has been published in industry handbooks, APEC official publications, journals, and conference papers. He has been recognized through ENR’s “20 Under 40” and BD+C’s “40 Under 40” awards, and honored with fellowships by ASCE, SOM, and Stanford University.

Hosted by Professor Pingbo Tang

events.title: CEE Department Seminar: Burcin Becerik-Gerber
events.description:
The CEE department seminar series presents lectures from a diverse range of professors, industry leaders, and alumni, and covers topics discussed throughout CEE’s four core research areas. All members of the CMU community are welcome to attend CEE department seminars.

From Sensing to Adaptation: Human-Centered Intelligence in the Built Environment

The built environment is increasingly able to sense, learn, and respond, creating new opportunities to rethink how we design, construct, operate, and experience buildings and infrastructure. This talk presents our research toward human-centered intelligent built environments, from multimodal sensing and modeling of human experiences and interactions with buildings to AI-enabled simulation of human behavior and emergency response, adaptive building systems, and human–robot interaction and teleoperation in construction. Across these applications, a common question drives our work: how can we move beyond systems that simply collect data or automate predefined tasks toward environments and machines that understand context, anticipate human needs, and adapt their behavior accordingly? I will discuss recent advances and remaining challenges in creating built environments in which people, machines, and physical spaces can increasingly sense, learn from, and adapt to one another.

Bio: Dr. Burcin Becerik-Gerber is a Professor and Chair of the Sonny Astani Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Southern California and the Founder and Director of the USC Center for Intelligent Environments (CENTIENTS). Her research focuses on advanced sensing, data science, and artificial intelligence to support the design, construction, and operation of human-centered, adaptive buildings and infrastructure systems. She pioneered the field of Human-Building Interaction (HBI), which examines how human experience and behavior interact with intelligent, engineered systems in the built environment. Dr. Becerik-Gerber has authored over 200 peer-reviewed publications and has led more than $15 million in sponsored research funded by agencies including the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Transportation. Her work has received numerous honors, including MIT Technology Review TR35, the FIATECH Celebration of Engineering and Technology Innovation Award, ASCE’s Computing in Civil Engineering Award, the ASCE Henry L. Michel Award for Industry Advancement of Research, and the ASCE Peurifoy Construction Research Award. She is a member of the National Academy of Construction and serves on the National Academies Board on Infrastructure and the Constructed Environment.

events.title: CERCA Resilience & Adaptation Day
events.description:
Join CERCA for our inaugural Resilience and Adaptation Day on November 6th, as we shape priorities for CMU Miami’s grand challenge in Energy and Climate Resilience. Led by David Rounce and Costa Samaras, this workshop will explore how CMU’s cross-disciplinary strengths can address urgent priorities across South Florida and beyond.

In addition to technical sessions, part of the day will be dedicated to collaborative brainstorming, giving our community an opportunity to shape the research and educational framework of CMU Miami.

Program Highlights:

Geoscience & Physical Climate Impacts: A panel examining physical weather drivers, extreme storms, sea-level rise, and ecosystem impacts

Built Infrastructure & Decision Systems: Discussions on managing predictive uncertainty, electric grid operational planning, and human-AI digital twins to support adaptive community operations

Student STEM Slam Competition: Fast-paced pitches showcasing student concepts for climate adaptation and resilience solutions

CMU Miami Strategy: Dedicated time to craft recommendations for CMU Miami’s academic curriculum goals and interdisciplinary research framework

This event is for CMU affiliates only. Reach out to geenap@cmu.edu to inquire about registration.

events.title: CERCA Webinar with Orange Country Water District
events.description:
“Co-creating tomorrow: Community Driven Engineering for a Resilient Future” is a webinar series exploring the critical intersection of community wisdom and engineering expertise in the face of a changing climate. Organized by CERCA, CMU CEE’s Center for Engineering Resilience and Climate Adaptation, this series will foster a deeper understanding of how community engagement can enhance the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of climate adaptation initiatives.

The Orange County Water District (OCWD) manages the Orange County Groundwater Basin, which provides approximately 85% of the water supply for 2.5 million people. Maintaining a reliable groundwater supply in a highly urbanized coastal basin requires an integrated approach that includes seawater intrusion protection, water reuse, stormwater capture, and managed aquifer recharge (MAR).

Seawater intrusion has been a challenge in the Orange County Groundwater Basin since the 1920s. In response, OCWD constructed the Talbert Seawater Intrusion Barrier in the 1970s, creating a hydraulic barrier to protect the basin from further seawater intrusion. Today, OCWD continues to operate and improve its coastal barriers and is evaluating development of a new barrier in the Sunset Gap to address an additional potential pathway for seawater intrusion. Bill Leever, OCWD Principal Hydrogeologist, will discuss the history, operation, and future of OCWD’s seawater intrusion barrier program.

Adam Hutchinson, OCWD Recharge Planning Manager, will discuss how OCWD uses Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) and MAR to increase the capture and recharge of stormwater while maintaining flood-risk-management objectives. OCWD operates an extensive recharge system along the Santa Ana River and has worked with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for decades to temporarily store stormwater behind Prado Dam for subsequent release and groundwater recharge.

Together, the presentations will illustrate how a coastal groundwater basin can integrate seawater intrusion protection, flood management, stormwater capture, groundwater recharge, and recycled water as complementary elements of a resilient regional water-supply system.

events.title: PITT - PQI CCA: Tom Purdy (Pitt)
events.description:
Speaker: Tom Purdy (Pitt)

Title: Electro-Optic Quantum Sensors

Abstract: I will present recent experiments that connect quantum systems to each other and to the classical world with sufficient fidelity to harness their full potential as sensors and transducers. In the first part of my talk, I will consider how it might be possible to turn an electro-optic modulator, a workhorse of modern classical telecommunications systems for encoding microwave signals on laser light, into a transducer capable of efficiently moving quantum information between the optical and microwave domains. Our recent results show that bulk, resonant electro-optic devices are capable of transduction efficiency approaching unity, an over six-order-of-magnitude step-up from classical telecom devices. We are currently investigating how laser light in this system can be used to manipulate and measure microwave devices in analogy to laser cooling in atomic and optomechanical systems. We are also exploring how combining the best aspects of nanophotonic optical and bulk microwave devices can further improve performance. In the second part, I will survey some of the other projects in my lab that use high-quality-factor mechanical resonators for precision sensing and for quantum information storage. By studying how information is scattered and extracted in the interaction of mechanical resonators with free space light, we show how to reach and surpass the standard quantum limits of common optical measurement techniques such as optical lever detection and light-scattering position detection of small particles. I will also highlight some of the unexpected places where acoustic waves can replace their electromagnetic counterparts in quantum sensing, including mechanical quantum memories and the acoustic analog of blackbody radiation. In one such system, sound waves on a string cool the motion of a centimeter-scale object, an acoustic version of laser cooling.

events.title: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)
events.description:
Speaker: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)

Topic: Where do stars explode in the ISM? A new constraint on stellar feedback models

Abstract: In this talk, I will present the first set of direct observational constraints on where stars explode in the interstellar medium (ISM) from high-resolution surveys of nearby galaxies with JWST, HST, VLA, ALMA and VLT/MUSE. Explosions of stars, i.e. supernovae (SNe) are the main regulators of star-formation in galaxies. They achieve this most directly by launching winds, which remove cold star-forming gas from the ISM, and creating pressure in the ISM by supplying heat, turbulence and cosmic rays. The efficiency of these processes depend sensitively on the environments where SNe occur, particularly the correlation between SNe and dense gas clouds. While there is evidence of SN shocks interacting with molecular clouds, the ionizing radiation and stellar winds from massive stars can quickly unbind and disperse dense clouds before SNe occur. How these different feedback channels limit star-formation in molecular clouds and launch winds is one of the biggest open questions in galaxy evolution. I will discuss how we can address this topic with the novel method of observations of evolved massive stars and supernova remnants in the Local Volume, supplied by high-resolution multiwavelength surveys like PHANGS, LGLBS and SDSS. I will also show preliminary comparisons with hydrodynamical simulations of galaxies to show how these observations can serve as valuable checks on the underlying stellar feedback models.

events.title: CMU/Pitt Colloquium: Dan Baxter (Fermilab)
events.description:
Speaker: Daniel Baxter (Fermilab)

Topic: Harnessing Quantum Sensors to Search for Dark Matter

Abstract: The CosmiQuantum group at Fermilab is at the center of understanding the relationship between particle impacts in quantum processors and qubit errors. This research hopes to enable high-fidelity quantum computation by resolving the issue of phonon-mediated correlated errors following cosmic ray impacts in a superconducting qubit chip. Additionally, this challenge for quantum computing presents a unique opportunity for fundamental science, as the same errors that follow a particle impact can be used to search for low-energy signatures of new physics originating from dark matter or neutrino impacts. At Fermilab, we have two world-class underground facilities which are already being used to study this problem: NEXUS and QUIET. I will present results from operating superconducting qubits in each of these facilities, and the potential implications towards utilizing qubits as sensors of new physics.

events.title: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)
events.description:
Speaker: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)

Topic: Arch and Scaffold: Jordan’s statistical transformation theory and von Neumann’s Hilbert space formalism

Abstract: In early 1927, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, independently of one another, published their versions of a general formalism tying the various forms of the new quantum theory together and giving the theory’s statistical interpretation in full generality. This formalism has come to be known as the Dirac-Jordan (statistical) transformation theory. A few months later, in response to these publications, John von Neumann published his Hilbert space formalism for quantum mechanics. The relation between these two formalisms can be captured in terms of a metaphor for theory change in which one theory serves as the scaffold for the arch of another theory. What is unclear in this case is which formalism serves as the scaffold and which one as the arch. Did von Neumann build an arch on the scaffold built by Jordan? Or did von Neumann build a scaffold to prevent the arch built by Jordan from collapsing? Either way, the arch-and-scaffold metaphor is a promising alternative to Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm shifts for understanding theory change.

Note: Based on joint work with Anthony Duncan (University of Pittsburgh)

events.title: Formalization for Physics at ICARM
events.description:
https://icarm.io/events/2026/formalization-for-physics/

The Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM) at Carnegie Mellon is hosting a meeting, Formalization for Physics, organized by Sergey Cherkis, Michael Douglas, James Halverson, and Xi Yin on November 4-6. Local faculty and students are welcome to attend. Please register using the link below; you can join the participants’ discussion channel on the ICARM Zulip.

Register: https://icarm.io/join/0btzmSk86L5VdlJqNmQ7m1B6CQP6TKZ-7e1Vr-ZGYcw/

Zulip: https://icarm.zulipchat.com/join/pueyd62pbxstlmc43qeojl7q/

Description: Formal methods are becoming increasingly relevant to physics, not only as tools for checking completed arguments but also as instruments for clarifying definitions, exposing hidden assumptions, and organizing large bodies of technical knowledge. This workshop will bring together theoretical physicists, mathematical physicists, mathematicians, and proof-assistant practitioners to identify where machine-checked reasoning can be genuinely useful for physics research.

The proposal is not that formalization should replace physical intuition. The more realistic and scientifically useful goal is to understand how formalization can make precise which parts of an argument are rigorous, which parts depend on explicit mathematical assumptions, and which parts remain heuristic. This is especially relevant in theoretical and mathematical physics, where important arguments often involve several layers of definitions, conventions, and intermediate structures.

The timing is favorable because several communities are now converging. Proof assistants such as Lean, Coq, Isabelle, and Agda have reached the point where substantial parts of modern mathematics can be formalized. AI-assisted theorem proving and code generation are rapidly changing the cost profile of formalization. Physicists have recently completed several medium-size formalizations in quantum theory, on topics ranging from quantum information theory to constructive quantum field theory, and are starting to encounter the issues of coordination and organization which arose and were addressed in earlier large-scale projects.
events.summary: https://icarm.io/events/2026/formalization-for-physics/

This is especially relevant in theoretical and mathematical physics, where important arguments often involve several layers of definitions, conventions, and intermediate structures.

The timing is favorable because several communities are now converging. Proof assistants such as Lean, Coq, Isabelle, and Agda have reached the point where substantial parts of modern mathematics can be formalized. AI-assisted theorem proving and code generation are rapidly changing the cost profile of formalization. Physicists have recently completed several medium-size formalizations in quantum theory, on topics ranging from quantum information theory to constructive quantum field theory, and are starting to encounter the issues of coordination and organization which arose and were addressed in earlier large-scale projects.

events.title: CMU Theory Seminar: Rich Holman
events.description:
Speaker: Rich Holman

Title: Tensor Catalyzed Scalar Decoherence in Inflation

Abstract. We provide the first complete calculation of the leading contribution to the decoherence of primordial fluctuations in the scalar part of the metric fluctuations within simplest, single-clock, inflationary models, assuming decoherence comes from gravitational interactions with an environment made up of the other, unmeasured, short-wavelength scalar and tensor modes.

We include the contributions from all of the contributing interactions at leading order in powers of (H/Mp) and of the slow-roll parameter ϵ. Unlike all extant calculations in the literature we find a result that is not slow-roll suppressed (and so is the same order of magnitude as tensor-mode decoherence). The difference arises because the dominant decoherence comes from interactions that involve both the tensor and scalar environments simultaneously (and so are missed when they are examined separately). We verify that the leading contributions to decoherence are UV finite (as they must be). We confirm that the interactions driving decoherence become time-local and Gaussian in the deep super-Hubble inflationary regime and show how this can be used to reliably compute the evolution of the purity in the late-time regime relevant for observations (where naive perturbation theory is known to break down). The same derivation shows explicitly why the effects that undermine perturbation theory for decoherence do not also undermine the basic inflationary prediction for the amplitude of primordial fluctuations.

events.description:
Title: The Character of PRX: Editorial Insights from the First 15 Years and Beyond

Abstract: PRX is published by the American Physical Society, a nonprofit membership society of scientists. Its mission goal is to select around 250 *landmark* papers a year from all fields of physics and showcase them to a broad and multidisciplinary readership.

After 15 years, one might still wonder exactly what PRX is—or, asked differently, how PRX defines a “landmark” through the peer-review process. As an author or referee, you may be curious about how PRX editors actually select these papers. Furthermore, there is always the fair question: are these selections always accurate?

In this talk, I will discuss how we approach these questions. Many of these questions do not have a black-and-white answer in the case of a single paper. Instead, open-minded, reasoned, and constructive dialogue among authors, editors, and referees is key. Ultimately, we, at PRX, strive to navigate the editorial and peer-review process effectively to ensure that the experience is meaningful, productive, and - at times - even a pleasure for everyone involved.

events.title: CMU Theory Seminar: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)
events.description:
Speaker: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)

Title: Exploring non-equilibrium universality with Schwinger–Keldysh effective field theories

Abstract: Dissipation and noise arise throughout physics, from condensed matter to cosmology, whenever observable degrees of freedom interact with a medium. The Schwinger–Keldysh formalism provides a systematic framework for describing such dynamics. Building on techniques developed in fluctuating hydrodynamics, I will discuss how symmetry, locality and unitarity constrain the allowed interactions. I will then explain how dissipation and noise modify the EFT power counting compared with vacuum quantum field theory. Using a scalar theory with a Kardar–Parisi–Zhang interaction, I will finally explore the emergence of a non-equilibrium universality class and discuss whether cosmological expansion in de Sitter spacetime can make this new dynamical regime accessible in three spatial dimension.

events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

REGISTER HERE

Join us for an evening with artist Kearra Amaya Gopee as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

About the Artist

Kearra Amaya Gopee (born 1994, Miami, FL, raised in Carapichaima, Kairi (Trinidad and Tobago); lives on Lenape land in New York) is an anti-disciplinary artist and facilitator. Using video, sculpture, sound, and writing, they identify both violence and time as primary conditions that undergird the anti-Black world in which they work. Gopee has shown work at documenta 15, Kassel, Germany (2022), and The Kitchen, among other international film venues. They have participated in residencies at Skowhegan, the International Studio and Curatorial Program, Headlands Center for the Arts, and NLS Kingston. They have been awarded fellowships at MacDowell, the Leslie Lohman Museum, Queer|Art, and the Global Fund for Women. In 2024, Gopee was an Elaine G. Weitzen Fellow at the Whitney Museum Independent Study Program. They have lectured at Emory University, Rutgers University, and the Caltech-Huntington Program in Visual Culture. In 2025, Gopee was an artist in residence at MASS MoCA. They hold an MFA from University of California, Los Angeles, with a concentration in interdisciplinary studio and a BFA in photography and imaging from New York University.

Finding the Carnegie Museum of Art Theater

The theater is located on the ground floor of the Carnegie Museum of Art. From the main entrance of the museum, head down the stairs to the right of the reception desk and the theater will be at the end of the corridor. If you are entering from the parking lot at the rear of the museum, the theatre will be immediately to your right.

events.title: Jonathan González: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

REGISTER HERE

Join us for an evening with artist Jonathan González as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the work featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

The Strikebreakers

The Strikebreakers is a new site-specific, four-hour performance conceived for the Grand Staircase of Carnegie Museum of Art. Performed by five dancers over five consecutive days, the work unfolds as a slow transformation of bodies, relationships, and collective attention, using the museum’s architecture as both stage and collaborator.

Drawing its title from the complicated history of labor, industry, and Western Pennsylvania, The Strikebreakers does not seek to reenact a historical event. Instead, it approaches the figure of the worker as a choreographic proposition: a body shaped by repetition, endurance, care, fatigue, solidarity, and the continual negotiation between individual agency and collective responsibility. Historical archives surrounding labor movements and Black social life circulate throughout the work not as illustrations, but as conditions that quietly inform its movement, rhythm, and atmosphere.

The performance is less concerned with representing history than with asking how history continues to move through bodies in the present. The title also resonates with the legacy of the 1892 Homestead Strike and the histories of labor surrounding Andrew Carnegie’s industrial empire, while opening the work toward broader questions of collective action and social choreography.

About the Artist

Jonathan González (b. 1988, Queens, NY; lives in New York, NY) is an interdisciplinary artist whose work spans choreography, sound, image, writing, video, and collective practice. Their artistic research engages themes of memory, Black geographies, and African diasporic temporalities, often through site-specific and durational performance. By combining movement, sound, and image, González creates works that explore embodiment as both a record of history and a rehearsal for the future. González has presented work nationally at major institutions, including Spectral Dances (American Academy of Arts and Letters, 2024), a durational performance and sonic installation, and perejil (Crystal Bridges Museum of Art / The Momentary, 2022), a performance and video installation presented in the exhibition Entre / Between. Their writing extends their choreographic and visual investigations, with a forthcoming book, Ways to Move: Black Insurgent Grammars, to be published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2025. González is the recipient of major awards, including the Herb Alpert Award in the Arts (Dance, 2024), the MAP Fund (2024), and the Foundation for Contemporary Arts Grants to Artists (Performance Art / Theater, 2019). Their practice foregrounds hybridity and collaboration, positioning collective action as both an artistic method and a social intervention.

Finding Kresge Theatre

Kresge Theatre is located in the College of Fine Arts building on the south end of CMU’s campus (near the Hunt Library). To find the theatre, enter the College of Fine Arts building from the west (main) entrance closest to the College of Fine Arts Lawn. Street parking is available along Frew and Tech streets or in CMU’s East Campus Garage.

events.title: CaPS Global Connections: International Student Support Group
events.description:
The Global Connections group offers a welcoming and confidential space for students to connect around the shared and unique experiences of studying and living in the US.

This group provides an opportunity to explore challenges such as adjusting to the new culture, navigating language or communication differences, managing academic expectations, coping with homesickness, isolation, or visa-related stress, and balancing family and cultural values with life at CMU. Celebrating resilience, growth, and personal milestones will also be an important part of the group, with an emphasis on mutual support, understanding, and community. Our hope is that students will feel less alone and more empowered through shared reflection and connection.

A pre-group consultation is required. Contact Stella Yan for more information.

The CMU Choir, prepared by Director of Choirs, Mark Trawka, will combine forces with the Mendelssohn Choir of Pittsburgh, under the direction of Daniel Singer, and the Pittsburgh Youth Chorus, under the direction of Shawn Funk. The full Philharmonic will be onstage along with a chamber orchestra of instrumental soloists. Vocal soloists for this performance will be soprano Rochelle Bard, tenor Karim Sulayman, and baritone Daniel Okulitch.

events.title: Student Recital: Ziyu Cai
events.description:
Ziyu Cai, piano

Ziyu Cai is currently a piano performance student in the Advanced Music Studies program at Carnegie Mellon University, where he studies under Professor Sergey Schepkin. He previously earned a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence from Peking University and a Master of Science in Music Technology from Carnegie Mellon University.

Originally active as a pop musician, Ziyu discovered his love for classical music during his undergraduate years at Peking University. As president of PKU Piano, he soon became an active performer in the university’s classical music community. He made his concerto debut with the Peking University Symphony Orchestra, performing Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2 as the orchestra’s first piano soloist in recent years. He also presented a recital at Peking University Hall, featuring Chopin’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in collaboration with the Peking University String Quartet.

Ziyu has won numerous prizes in piano competitions. Over the past season, he won the Wenzhou Piano Competition, performing Beethoven Piano Concerto No. 3 with the Wenzhou Symphony Orchestra, as well as the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh Concerto Competition, performing Schumann Piano Concerto with the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh. He was also named the winner of the All University Orchestra Concerto Competition and is scheduled to perform Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with the orchestra in spring 2027.

Ziyu has previously studied with Luz Manríquez and Frédéric Chiu at Carnegie Mellon University. Alongside his piano studies, he works as a research assistant with Professor Roger Dannenberg, focusing on score following research.

Program

J.S. Bach – French Suite No. 5 in G Major, BWV 816

Ludwig van Beethoven – Piano Sonata No.2 in A Major, Op. 2 No. 2

Robert Schumann – Piano Sonata No.1 in F-sharp minor, Op.11

Cost: Free and open to the public, no tickets required.

events.title: Student Recital: Jason Wells
events.description:
“What do you NOT play?” is a quote said by those who’ve seen enough of J Wells to fully discover his obsession with orchestral winds and double reeds. J Wells proves that lifelong musicians do not have to start early. After taking up a hobby in the flute and soprano saxophone at age 17, he settled on the oboe and bassoon, having now played for four and three years respectively.

J Wells originally came to CMU for composition, but after experiencing the joys of performing in CMU’s All University Orchestra (AUO) and learning the bassoon within the Kiltie Band, decided to switch to a “Student Defined Major” encompassing the music education certification and the study of both double reeds. J Wells is director of the AUO Flute Choir and has a passion for working with ensembles. He also loves to double multiple woodwinds in the pit orchestra for student-run musicals and playing in the school’s bagpipe band.

Having grown up in Hong Kong, J Wells plans to return there after graduating to teach K-12 music and private double reed lessons.

Jason Wells, oboe

events.description:
Sergey Schepkin, piano

Thomas Barth, cello

SERGEY SCHEPKIN, piano

Praised by The Boston Globe for his “singular capability and

integrity,” Steinway Artist Sergey Schepkin has concertized

worldwide, from the United States to Europe to East Asia to New

Zealand. The US venues and series where he has performed

include New York’s Carnegie (Weill) Recital Hall, Alice Tully Hall,

and the Metropolitan Museum of Art; the Kennedy Center In Washington, D.C.;

Boston’s Symphony Hall, Jordan Hall, Gardner Museum, and Celebrity Series; the

LACMA and Maestro Foundation series in Los Angeles; and the Rockport and

Newport music festivals, among many others.

THOMAS BARTH, cello

Praised for his “expansive style” (Musical America)

and “superb phrasing” (Boston Musical Intelligencer),

cellist Thomas Barth enjoys a varied career as a

chamber and orchestral musician. He performs

frequently with groups including the Boston Symphony

Orchestra, the Handel and Haydn Society, A Far Cry,

Emmanuel Music, Skylark Vocal Ensemble, Boston

Baroque, and ChamberQUEER. In demand as a recording

artist of contemporary music, his work has been featured on the Albany, Parma,

and Sono Luminus labels. Mr. Barth is both at home performing at leading arts

venues and passionate about bringing thoughtful musical programming to wide

audiences through performances at schools, farms, and community centers

throughout North America and Europe. In 2022 he served as the cellist for the

critically acclaimed Broadway revival of “1776” and has performed in multiple world

premiere productions at the American Repertory Theater.

Program:

Nadia Boulanger - Pieces for Cello and Piano

Gabriel Fauré - Sonata No. 2 for Cello and Piano in G minor

Claude Debussy - Sonata for Cello and Piano in D minor

César Franck - Sonata for Cello and Piano in A major

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: A Night of Italian Opera
events.description:
Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Crystal Manich, Interim Director of Opera Studies

Matthew Kereama, director

On April 14th at Carnegie Music Hall, the philharmonic will team up with the School of Music’s opera department to present a gala-style concert of Italian opera. Conducted by Director of Orchestral Studies, Daniel Nesta Curtis, and directed by Matthew Kereama, the program will feature vocalists from the School of Music in select arias, ensembles, and scenes from famous operas. The first half will feature music from Gioachino Rossini’s Il Barbiere di Siviglia and L’Italiana in Algeri along with Gaetano Donizetti’s Don Pasquale and Lucia di Lammermoor. The second half will feature a condensed, 1-hour version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Boheme, focused on the opera’s 4 main characters.

Program:

Gioachino Rossini – Excerpts from Il Barbiere di Siviglia Overture

Gioachino Rossini – Act I Finale from L’italiana in Algeri

Gaetano Donizetti – Act III Duet: “Tornami a dir che m’ami” from Don Pasquale

Gaetano Donizetti – Excerpts from Lucia di Lammermoor

Giacomo Puccini – “BoheMedley”

Cost:

$10 Regular Admission

$5 Senior Citizen (65+) Admission

All students, along with CMU/Pitt faculty and staff, are free w/ valid ID

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: Halloween at Heinz Hall
events.description:
On Halloween, the Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic will perform a free concert for the Pittsburgh community at Heinz Hall. This 80-minute program, designed for families and audience members of all ages will be led by Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

The Halloween-themed event includes spooky standards like Modest Mussorgsky’s Night on Bald Mountain (conducted by CMU Philharmonic Associate Conductor, John William Brink) and Paul Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. The concert will also feature wizard of the keyboard, Tino Cardenes (current Music and Technology student of the School of Music and winner of the Philharmonic Soloist Competition, undergraduate division) performing Nikolai Kapustin’s jazzy Piano Concerto No. 2. The heart of the program is Manuel de Falla’s magical El Amor Brujo, which includes the famous “Ritual Fire Dance.” This performance will feature recent graduate of the School of Music, mezzo-soprano Isabelle Hoyou. Kids are encouraged to come in costume and arrive early for pre-concert fun in the lobby.

Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Jacob Joyce, guest conductor

John William Brink, associate conductor

Featured Artists:

Isabelle Hoyou, mezzo-soprano

Tino Cardenes, piano

Program:

Modest Mussorgsky – Night on Bald Mountain

Manuel de Falla – El Amor Brujo

Nikolai Kapustin – Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 14

Paul Dukas – The Sorcerer’s Apprentice

events.title: Masterclass: Mariam Adam, Valerie Coleman & Monica Ellis
events.description:
Mariam Adam, clarinet

Valerie Coleman, flute

Monica Ellis, bassoon

Mariam Adam, has performed with Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Paquito D’Rivera, Yo-Yo Ma, Eric le Sage, Claudio Bohorquez, Simon Shaheen, Kuss Quartet, Gil Kalish, Ann Marie-McDermott, the Zaide Quartet and in such venues and series as Carnegie Hall, Hollywood Bowl, Walt Disney Hall, Jordan Hall, Kennedy Center, San Francisco Performances, Wigmore Hall, Paris’ Cité de la Musique, Beijing Performing Arts Center, Bremen Musikfest, Jazz à Marciac, Colmar Festival and France’s pre-eminent Folle Journee.

A founding and former member of the multi Grammy-nominated woodwind quintet, Imani Winds, she maintained an active international touring schedule for over 18 years. In 2021 she reunited with members of the Imani Winds to premier Valerie Coleman’s “Phenomenal Women” in London with the Chineke! Orchestra which has led to reinvites on this and other works.

Mariam has been invited for solo recitals and chamber music concerts in such prestigious venues and festivals as Chamber Music Lincoln Center, Burlington’s Lane Series, Chamber Music Northwest, Skaneatles Festival, Chenango Festival, Fontana Arts, La Folle Journée Festival in Nantes, Théâtre de l’Archipel in Perpignan, Musica da Curitiba-Brazil, and various festivals and series in the United-States, Europe and South America. She has performed and toured with Orpheus Chamber Orchestra and France’s satire icon, Gaspard Proust. She has soloed with the Orchestre de Pau, Sacramento Symphony, the Monterey Symphony, the Singapore National Youth Orchestra, Prince George Philharmonic, the Appassionato Ensemble in France and the Prairie Winds Festival as well as a return special guest at the International Clarinet Association “ClarFest” opening concert.

Since 2016 she has been visiting principal clarinetist for the London-based Chineke! Ensemble and orchestra with return visits to BBC’s “Tune In” with Sean Rafferty.

Mariam Adam is an exclusive Selmer Paris Artist, Vandoren Artist and has served on the Executive Board for Chamber Music America as Vice President, the Chineke! board and Players Committee. She is faculty at the YOLA Institute with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Selmer Academy and is currently Assistant Clarinet Professor at the Blair School of Music at Vanderbilt University where she is a member of the Blair Wind Quintet and co-director of the Blair Colloquium Series.

Valerie Coleman is regarded by many as an iconic artist who continues to pave her own unique path as a composer, GRAMMY®-nominated flutist, and entrepreneur. Highlighted as one of the “Top 35 Women Composers” by The Washington Post, she was named Performance Today’s 2020 Classical Woman of the Year, an honor bestowed to an individual who has made a significant contribution to classical music as a performer, composer or educator. Her works have garnered awards such as the MAPFund, ASCAP Honors Award, Chamber Music America’s Classical Commissioning Program, Herb Alpert Ragdale Residency Award, and nominations from The American Academy of Arts and Letters and United States Artists. Umoja, Anthem for Unity was chosen by Chamber Music America as one of the “Top 101 Great American Ensemble Works” and is now a staple of woodwind literature.

Bassoonist Monica Ellis is a founding member of the Grammy nominated wind quintet, Imani Winds, who in their 23rd season, continue to make ground-breaking art while maintaining a vigorous international touring schedule.

Monica’s strong work ethic was instilled very early on from her mother and father, the late jazz saxophonist, Clarence Oden. As the administrative director & tour manager for Imani Winds, and Co-Artistic Director for the Imani Winds Chamber Music Festival, she maintains a fulfilling leadership role within group.

events.title: Guest Recital: How to See Know and Fall
events.description:
How to See Know and Fall is a collaboration between interdisciplinary percussionist/composer Brian Shankar Adler and electronic composer/software designer Jesse Stiles, combining intricate hybrid percussion with shimmering synth lines, ambient textures, and immersive visuals.

Live performances transform the stage into a dreamlike audiovisual environment where polyrhythms collide with live video, weaving data and performance into a visceral tapestry of sound and light. By bridging far-reaching rhythmic traditions, cutting-edge electronics, and critical explorations of emerging technologies, How to See Know and Fall offers audiences a revelatory experience at the cross-hairs of music, technology, and digital art.

BRIAN SHANKAR ADLER is a widely recognized percussionist and composer who blurs genre lines to create deeply expressive rhythmic landscapes. He has performed in settings ranging from glacial ice fields to Lincoln Center, showcasing his innovative approach to percussion around the globe. With commissions from chamber ensembles and collaborations in opera, dance, and beyond, Adler pursues a vision that intertwines technical precision with human connection.

JESSE STILES, formerly Associate Professor of Sound Media at the CMU School of Music, is an electronic composer, performer, and software designer whose immersive sonic environments have been presented at Carnegie Hall, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and beyond. As the Music Supervisor for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, he produced and performed in hundreds of concerts featuring the works of leading avant-garde composers. Currently an Associate Professor at the Penny W. Stamps School of Art & Design, Stiles continues to push the boundaries of interactive media and sound design.

events.description:
Tuesday, October 27, 2026 12:30 – 1:30 p.m. EST In Person: Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship, 3rd Level, Tepper Quad/Virtual Presenter: Bob Blattberg, Carnegie Mellon University Please note: The speaker for this talk will be virtual
Register
*This seminar is recommended for anyone participating in the McGinnis Venture Competition.
This workshop will explore how to understand the customer and then determine what the organization’s unique selling proposition (USP) is based on who the customer is. A critical source of failure of entrepreneurial enterprises is lack of understanding the customer. A second source of failure is not having a unique selling proposition, also called unique value proposition in the business model canvas. Topics to be covered include learning the customer is more than just the end user and often is what Bob calls the customer chain - the different layers including the end user and intermediate customers such as a retailer that also is involved in the purchase decision. Additionally Bob will describe the three criteria for determining if the product or service has a USP, what is the difference between a benefit and a feature and why is this critical in determining a USP along with examples from both for profit and non-profit firms of USP’s.

events.title: CONNECTS: Understanding the Customer and Creating a USP*
events.description:
Understanding the Customer and Creating a USP*
Tuesday, October 27, 2026
12:30 – 1:30 p.m. EST
In Person: Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship, 3rd Level, Tepper Quad/Virtual
Presenter: Bob Blattberg, Carnegie Mellon University
*Please note that this presenter will be virtual
Register
*This seminar is recommended for anyone participating in the McGinnis Venture Competition.
This workshop will explore how to understand the customer and then determine what the organization’s unique selling proposition (USP) is based on who the customer is. A critical source of failure of entrepreneurial enterprises is lack of understanding the customer. A second source of failure is not having a unique selling proposition, also called unique value proposition in the business model canvas. Topics to be covered include learning the customer is more than just the end user and often is what Bob calls the customer chain - the different layers including the end user and intermediate customers such as a retailer that also is involved in the purchase decision. Additionally Bob will describe the three criteria for determining if the product or service has a USP, what is the difference between a benefit and a feature and why is this critical in determining a USP along with examples from both for profit and non-profit firms of USP’s.

events.title: Jason Hirata: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

Join us for an evening with artist Jason Hirata as he shares an in-depth look at his practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

REGISTER NOW

About the Artist

Jason Hirata (born 1986, Seattle, WA; lives in New Jersey) performs an artistic ambiguity that parallels his personal comfort with indirectness, abstraction, and indeterminacy. Artistically, this invites interpretation. Psychologically, it might function as defense, avoidance of emotional exposure, and dissociation. Intentional ambiguity can foster reflection and collective engagement, but overuse of vagueness may impair clarity in personal relationships and professional collaboration. Role fluidity enables experimentation and boundary navigation, but identity fusion may scuttle the definition of self and direct assertiveness. Hirata has shown at Ulrik, New York; Fanta-MLN, Milan; CCS Hessel Museum of Art, Annandale-On-Hudson, New York; Fluentum, Berlin; Simian, Copenhagen; Paid, Seattle; Theta, New York; The Wig, Berlin; B. Beamesderfer Gallery, Highland Park, New Jersey; Billytown, The Hague; Artists Space, New York; 80WSE, New York; Svetlana, New York; Veronica, Seattle, and elsewhere.

Finding Kresge Theatre

Kresge Theatre is located in the College of Fine Arts building on the south end of CMU’s campus (near the Hunt Library). To find the theatre, enter the College of Fine Arts building from the west (main) entrance closest to the College of Fine Arts Lawn. Street parking is available along Frew and Tech streets or in CMU’s East Campus Garage.

About If the word we: 59th Carnegie International

On view May 2, 2026, through January 3, 2027

Organized every four years by Carnegie Museum of Art, the Carnegie International is the longest-running exhibition of international art in North America. The 59th edition is the most collaborative and far-reaching to date — a clear expression of the museum’s founding commitment to the art and artists of our time, at once grounded in our locality and extending globally. Titled If the word we, the 59th Carnegie International considers the first-person plural as an open and evolving proposition — one shaped by listening, translation, and transformation — bringing together artistic practices that engage shared experience, circulation, and worlds in transition. Drawing from a commissioned catalogue essay by writer Haytham el-Wardany, the exhibition approaches “we” not as a unified subject but as a complex and porous position, attentive to contradiction and change. Across a wide range of media, from painting, photography, and sculpture, to installation, video, performance, and theater, participating artists traverse cultural, political, intellectual, and spiritual geographies that extend beyond national boundaries. The projects emerge through everyday acts, materials, and environments, offering spatially expansive portraits of collective life in the present.

About the Visiting Artist Lecture Series

The Carnegie Mellon School of Art Lecture Series is made possible in part by Elizabeth (Thompson) and Thomas M. Cox (A’29) Distinguished Artists Funds, Robert L. Lepper Distinguished Lecture in Creative Inquiry, and Orville M. Winsand Lecture for Critical Studies. Carnegie Mellon makes every effort to provide accessible facilities and programs for individuals with disabilities. This publication can be made available in an alternate format upon request. For accommodations, contact the School of Art at schoolofart@cmu.edu or 412.268.2409. Lecture and event details are subject to change or cancellation.

SEE FULL SERIES

About the Artist

Weitzen Fellow at the Whitney Museum Independent Study Program. They have lectured at Emory University, Rutgers University, and the Caltech-Huntington Program in Visual Culture. In 2025, Gopee was an artist in residence at MASS MoCA. events.title: Jonathan González: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

Join us for an evening with artist Jonathan González as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the work featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

REGISTER NOW

The Strikebreakers

The Strikebreakers is a new site-specific, four-hour performance conceived for the Grand Staircase of Carnegie Museum of Art. Performed by five dancers over five consecutive days, the work unfolds as a slow transformation of bodies, relationships, and collective attention, using the museum’s architecture as both stage and collaborator.

Drawing its title from the complicated history of labor, industry, and Western Pennsylvania, The Strikebreakers does not seek to reenact a historical event. Instead, it approaches the figure of the worker as a choreographic proposition: a body shaped by repetition, endurance, care, fatigue, solidarity, and the continual negotiation between individual agency and collective responsibility. Historical archives surrounding labor movements and Black social life circulate throughout the work not as illustrations, but as conditions that quietly inform its movement, rhythm, and atmosphere.

The performance is less concerned with representing history than with asking how history continues to move through bodies in the present. The title also resonates with the legacy of the 1892 Homestead Strike and the histories of labor surrounding Andrew Carnegie’s industrial empire, while opening the work toward broader questions of collective action and social choreography.

About the Artist

Jonathan González (b. 1988, Queens, NY; lives in New York, NY) is an interdisciplinary artist whose work spans choreography, sound, image, writing, video, and collective practice. Their artistic research engages themes of memory, Black geographies, and African diasporic temporalities, often through site-specific and durational performance. By combining movement, sound, and image, González creates works that explore embodiment as both a record of history and a rehearsal for the future. González has presented work nationally at major institutions, including Spectral Dances (American Academy of Arts and Letters, 2024), a durational performance and sonic installation, and perejil (Crystal Bridges Museum of Art / The Momentary, 2022), a performance and video installation presented in the exhibition Entre / Between. Their writing extends their choreographic and visual investigations, with a forthcoming book, Ways to Move: Black Insurgent Grammars, to be published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2025. González is the recipient of major awards, including the Herb Alpert Award in the Arts (Dance, 2024), the MAP Fund (2024), and the Foundation for Contemporary Arts Grants to Artists (Performance Art / Theater, 2019). Their practice foregrounds hybridity and collaboration, positioning collective action as both an artistic method and a social intervention.

About the Artist

RJ Messineo (born 1980, Hartford, CT; lives in Greenfield, MA) makes paintings involving observation and abstraction. In the last six years, Messineo has developed an idiosyncratic device for making paintings that involves attaching thin wooden boards to the surfaces of their canvases with magnets. Messineo received an MFA from the University of California, Los Angeles (2009) and a BFA from Cornell University, Ithaca, NY (2002). They have participated in exhibitions at CANADA, New York, NY; Pace Gallery, New York; James Cohan Gallery, New York; Thomas Erben Gallery, New York; Ceysson & Bénétière, Koerich, Luxembourg; Night Gallery, Los Angeles; Artist Curated Projects, Los Angeles; Redling Fine Art, Los Angeles; and REDCAT, Los Angeles. Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

Rahm I. Emanuel most recently served as the United States Ambassador to Japan. As Ambassador, Emanuel helped deepen the U.S.-Japan alliance, including support for Japan's increased defense spending and expanded military cooperation. He promoted Japan's leadership in Indo-Pacific key security initiatives and participated in the historic trilateral summit at Camp David that reaffirmed that cooperation between the United States, Japan, and the Republic of Korea.

Previously, Emanuel was the 55th Mayor of the City of Chicago, a position he held until May 2019. During that time, he made the critical choices necessary to secure Chicago's future as a global capital. As Mayor, Emanuel added four years to a student’s education. He increased the school day by 75 minutes and added more than 200 hours to the school year, marking the largest single increase in educational time by any city and taking Chicago from having the least educational time of any large school district in the country to being on par with its peers. He implemented universal pre-kindergarten and full-day kindergarten for every Chicago child, and made Chicago the first city in America to provide free community college.

The Mayor's comprehensive public safety strategy focused on expanded prevention programs for at-risk youth, smarter policing strategies, and empowering parents and communities to reduce violence. The Ambassador made it a priority to bring global companies to the city, helping Chicago to lead the U.S. in corporate relocations and foreign direct investment for seven consecutive years. His administration invested in infrastructure, public transportation, open space, and cultural attractions. From the $8.5 billion O'Hare International Airport modernization program that is cementing Chicago's status as a global leader in travel, tourism, and trade to the development of the iconic 1.25-mile Chicago Riverwalk, the City's investments are creating thousands of good-paying jobs and making Chicago a better place to live, work, and play.
Prior to becoming Mayor, from November 2008 until October 2010, Emanuel served as President Barack Obama's Chief of Staff. In addition to being the President's top advisor, Emanuel helped the Obama administration secure the passage of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and the landmark Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.

Before serving as Chief of Staff, Emanuel was elected four times as a Member of the U.S. House of Representatives from Illinois's 5th Congressional District (2002-2008). As Chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, Emanuel helped pass legislation to raise the minimum wage and authored the Great Lakes Restoration Act.

From 1993 to 1998, Ambassador Emanuel was a key member of President Bill Clinton's administration, rising to serve as Senior Advisor to the President for Policy and Politics. During this time, Emanuel served as a legislative liaison to Congress and spearheaded efforts to pass several of President Clinton's signature achievements, most notably the Federal Assault Weapons Ban, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, and the historic Balanced Budget Act, which created the Children's Health Insurance Program that expanded health care coverage to 10 million children. Emanuel also worked closely with President Joseph R. Biden Jr., then a U.S. Senator, to shepherd the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 through Congress.

Emanuel graduated from Sarah Lawrence College in 1981 and received a Master's Degree in Speech and Communication from Northwestern University in 1985. He is married to Amy Rule, and they have three children.

events.description:
Google builds and operates a massive infrastructure in support of providing products and capabilities to its users and customers. The scale has dramatically increased as a result of the push for AI. While we benefit greatly from an integrated stack—from software down through specialized chips to optimized data center designs—we also need a way to coordinate all those efforts to avoid confusion, inefficiencies, and missed opportunities. —

Before this, he worked on cluster management for Google's compute infrastructure (Borg, Omega, Kubernetes). He is interested in far too many aspects of distributed systems, but a recurring theme has been technologies that allow systems to manage themselves.

He received a PhD in computer science from the University of Cambridge, joined HP Labs in 1982, and was elected an HP Fellow and an ACM Fellow in 2002 for his work on storage system design. He’s listed as an inventor on 50+ US patents, and has an adjunct faculty appointment at Carnegie-Mellon University. In his spare time he continues, stubbornly, trying to learn how to blow glass.

events.title: Database Seminar - Ippokratis Pandis
events.description:
Traditionally, data architectures maintain a strict division between high-throughput operational databases and large-scale analytical lakehouses. The general wisdom for organizations seeking low-latency real-time analytics is to copy data into dedicated serving layers, which creates data redundancy, stale insights, and fragmented governance.

In this talk, we explore how unifying operational and analytical workloads on open storage eliminates the need to copy data. In the first part, we present LakehouseRT, an analytical query engine designed to deliver millisecond-level query latency and high concurrency directly over open table formats in object stores governed by a unified catalog. In the second part, we show how Lakebase and its disaggregated compute and storage OLTP architecture not only provides best-in-class performance, elasticity, and availability for Postgres workloads, but also seamlessly enables low-latency analytics directly on live operational data without compromises.

—

Ippokratis Pandis:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/ippokratis-pandis-03b1402 is a Distinguished Engineer at Databricks working on data management systems. Previously, he spent a decade at AWS, where he served as Chief Architect of AWS Analytics and led the development of Amazon Redshift. Earlier, he contributed to Cloudera Impala and IBM DB2 BLU. He earned his Ph.D. from Carnegie Mellon University, where in the dungeons of Wean and Hamerschlag Halls, he worked on multicore transaction processing. He has authored numerous research papers and served the database community as General Chair of SIGMOD 2023 and President of HPTS.

This talk is part of the Whatever Andy Found Interesting While Out At Sea:

events.title: From Capturing People to Teaching Robots
events.description:
Abstract: Equipping AI and robotic systems with the ability to understand human behavior is essential for enabling them to assist people across a wide range of everyday applications. This need is more pressing than ever: the heaviest consumers of such knowledge are no longer perception systems alone, but robot policies that must learn to act in the physical world. Yet the high-quality 3D human motion data required to learn this knowledge remains extremely scarce.

In this talk, I will present our lab’s efforts to scale and enrich 3D human motion data by capturing everyday movements and natural human-object interactions, with the ultimate goal of teaching robots to move like humans.

I will first introduce our multi-year effort in building multi-camera capture systems, from Panoptic Studio to ParaHome, and most recently OmniRoboHome, a new system designed to capture human-object interactions in natural home environments. Next, I will present a complementary direction: learning everyday interactions and affordances from generative image and video models, which offer a scalable source of human behavior priors that capture systems alone cannot reach. Finally, I will discuss the missing pieces that vision and image models cannot provide, including physics, contact, and the gap across diverse embodiments, together with our recent efforts to fill them.

Before joining SNU, Hanbyul was a Research Scientist at Facebook AI Research (FAIR), Menlo Park. Hanbyul received his PhD from the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. He is a recipient of the Samsung Scholarship, the Okawa Foundation Research Grant, and the Best Student Paper Award at CVPR 2018.

events.title: Shaping the Body of Robots with Soft Skin and Muscles
events.description:
Abstract:

Just as skin and muscle give living creatures their ability to sense, move, and adapt, soft sensors and actuators are giving shape to a new kind of robot body. Built from flexible, compliant materials, soft robots can closely mimic the movements of biological systems, a significant step beyond conventional rigid machines. This talk explores recent technologies for designing and fabricating the two essential components of that body: artificial skin that lets robots feel their surroundings, and artificial muscles that let them move with natural, fluid motion. We will discuss how these components are engineered for responsiveness and reliability, how their signals can be interpreted despite the complex, nonlinear behavior of soft structures, and how sensing and actuation can be co-designed into a single integrated system. By integrating skin and muscle into a unified soft body, we can develop a new generation of robots capable of seamless and safe interaction in human environments.

Bio:

Yong-Lae Park (Member, IEEE) received the Ph.D. degree in mechanical engineering from Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA, in 2010.

He is currently a Professor with the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea. Prior to joining SNU, he was an Assistant Professor in the Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA (2013–2017) and a Technology Development Fellow in the Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA (2010–2013). His research interests include artificial skin sensors and muscle actuators, soft robots, wearable robots, rehabilitation robots, and medical robots.

Prof. Park is the recipient of the Best Conference Paper Award from the IEEE International Conference of Soft Robotics (2019), the Best Application Paper Award from the IEEE Transactions on Haptics (2019), and the Best Paper Award from the IEEE Sensors Journal (2013). He is currently serving as a Senior Editor in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, an Associate Editor in Soft Robotics and npj Robotics.

events.title: Structured Learning for Fast Physical Prediction
events.description:
Abstract:

Physical simulation is essential for robotics and engineering design, but remains computationally expensive, especially for complex geometries and long time horizons. Learning-based approaches offer faster predictions, but often lack the mathematical structure needed for reliable simulation.

In this talk, I will present three approaches that combine learning with mathematical structure: continuous reduced-order representations for generalization across shapes, geometric lifting for handling discontinuities, and Koopman-based linear operators for efficient long-horizon prediction. Together, these methods demonstrate how structured learning can enable faster, more expressive, and more reliable physical simulation.

Biography:

Chang Yue is a Ph.D. student in Computer Science at the University of Toronto, advised by Prof. Eitan Grinspun. Her research focuses on mathematically structured learning for fast and generalizable physical simulation. Her work has received the SIGGRAPH 2025 Best Paper Award and Best Paper Award Honorable Mention. She was also recognized as a WiGRAPH Rising Star in 2026.

events.title: “Lawless Progress on Wicked Problems”: Shifting the Roles of Humans in Human-AI Systems
events.description:
Abstract: AI is rapidly changing the roles that humans play as developers and users of new technology. In this talk, I will discuss three of those shifting roles and how my group addresses them through technical innovation and interdisciplinary design. Across these projects, understanding human roles is central to determining what systems should optimize, what data they need, and how they can be trusted.

Humans as objective functions: Many real-world applications involve optimizing user-specific objectives, but users’ descriptions of those objectives can be vague, inconsistent, or even self-contradictory. I will discuss our work on Interactive Explainable Ranking (Best Paper, CHI 2026), which combines optimization, AI, and interaction design to help users identify and resolve contradictions in how they evaluate different items—from open-ended course projects to purchasing options or contestants in a competition to find the best cat.

Humans as a source of data: AI is only effective if we have the right data, and many important applications depend on specific or individualized data that needs to be captured in uncontrolled settings. Multiple projects in my group focus on designing systems that help humans capture such data using mobile devices. This work connects capture guidance, sampling theory, computational imaging, and interaction design to support downstream learning, with applications spanning remote healthcare, infrastructure, and agriculture.

Humans as adversaries: Some advances in AI also carry significant potential for harm, which calls for designing new approaches to protect against adversarial use. One problem that AI has made particularly challenging is video forensics. I will discuss my group’s work on designing coded illumination systems to add near-imperceptible watermarks to lighting in high-stakes environments. These watermarks make it easier to detect manipulation in recorded videos without requiring access to or control over recording cameras.

Bio: Abe Davis is an assistant professor in the Computer Science Department at Cornell University, where his group works at the intersection of human-AI systems and visual computing. He earned his Ph.D. in EECS at MIT. His dissertation received the Sprowls Award for Best PhD Thesis in Computer Science at MIT, as well as the ACM SIGGRAPH Outstanding Doctoral Dissertation Honorable Mention Award. He has received the NSF CAREER Award and a Sloan Research Fellowship, and has published award-winning papers in venues across visual computing and HCI. He has also been recognized in Forbes’ “30 Under 30” and Business Insider’s “50 Scientists Who Are Changing the World.”

Title: MaintainingUnderstanding in the Age of AI
Speaker: Margaret-AnneStorey, Professor of Computer Science, University of Victoria
Abstract: AI is changingsoftware development faster than our engineering practices are evolving, andyet many developers feel the pressure to adopt AI and deliver features at afrantic pace. Although AI can improve speed, emerging evidence highlightsconsiderable variability in outcomes and reveals new challenges incoordination, comprehension, and cognitive fatigue. These shifts raiseimportant questions about how teams maintain shared understanding of complexsystems, and how they remain in control as they become increasingly reliant onAI agents. As we delegate more work and decisions to agents, how do we makesure humans still understand what is happening and retain the ability toquestion, steer, and intervene when necessary?
In thistalk, I’ll explore new approaches for helping humans and AI maintainunderstanding as software systems evolve: understanding how the system works,why it was built in a certain way, and whether it still meets the intended usergoals and design constraints. I’ll share some emerging ideas for measuring andmitigating losses of technical, cognitive and intentional understanding, andconsider how we might design tools and practices that allow humans and AIagents to work together without reducing human judgement and control.
Bio: Margaret-Anne Storeyis a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Victoria and a CanadaResearch Chair in Human and Social Aspects of Software Engineering. She isco-author of the SPACE framework and a leading researcher in DeveloperExperience (DevEx). Her research focuses on how developers and teams understandcomplex software systems, and how tools, AI, and collaborative practices shapethat understanding. Her recent work examines how generative AI is transforming softwareengineering by changing how understanding is created, shared, and maintained.She collaborates with industry partners including Microsoft and DX. She holdsan honorary doctorate from Lund University.

Description "Behind the Toolkits: Confessions, Compromises, and Contradictions in Ethics-Focused Design"What does it really mean to design methods for ethical design practice? And what happens when the work of designing for ethics becomes an ethical challenge in itself? In this talk, I offer an insider's account of the messy, uncertain, and often contradictory work of designing ethics-focused methods for design practitioners and students. Drawing on my experience surveying existing ethics-focused design methods and developing my own, including Anti-Heroes and Value Lanes, I will share the questions, doubts, fears, and tensions that have shaped my own perception of what this artifact called an “ethics-focused method” could mean, look like, or even achieve.Rather than presenting perfected solutions, I will open up the process behind these methods, sharing the experiments, compromises, and lessons that rarely make it into the final toolkit. I will introduce my AAA philosophy—Awareness, Action, and Agency/Advocacy—as a way of making sense of my experiences as a method designer and understanding how different methods invite ethical reflection, support action, and empower advocacy. The talk will offer practical resources for method designers, educators, practitioners, and students who are also trying to make ethics matter in design.

Speaker's Bio
Sai Shruthi Chivukula is an Assistant Professor in Information Experience Design Program, School of Information at Pratt Institute, New York. She directs Translate, a research group conducting translational work and investigating ethics in technology and design practice. Her research lies at the intersection of HCI and UX, design practice, ethics and values in design, design education, and critical qualitative research. She investigates how designers and HCI practitioners navigate ethical decision-making in everyday practice, including how they recognize ethical concerns, negotiate competing values and responsibilities, and translate ethical awareness into action. Her work develops practical, open-access methods and pedagogical resources that support ethical reflection and decision-making in design education and professional practice. A new strand of her research is exploring Regulation-Informed Design, examining how emerging technology regulations and policy can inform design methods, processes, and professional decision-making. In 2025, she co-authored her first book Universal Methods of Ethical Design, a practical guide to integrating ethical reflection and decision-making into everyday design practice. At Pratt, she teaches courses related to UX design, Conversational UX, Service Design, and Deceptive Design. She loves weaving together her research and teaching, while making art, experimenting with new recipes, and finding creative expression in everyday life.
