events.title: Controllable, Efficient and Personalized Generative AI: From Long-Horizon Video to Interactive World Models
events.description:
Abstract: Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms of control, generate over extended horizons within practical computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a central question: How can we make visual generation controllable, efficient, and personal?

I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First, Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next, VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of extended generation by learning compact representations of past context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate them.

I will close with broader directions for video generation, including new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26). This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography, supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact with them.

Bio: Pinar Yanardag is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive world models. She earned her PhD from Purdue as a Fulbright Fellow and was a postdoctoral researcher at the MIT Media Lab, where her generative AI projects attracted over one million participants and media coverage from TIME, The Washington Post, and CNN. She received an NSF CAREER award for her research on generative cinematography and was recognized as an Outstanding Area Chair at CVPR 2026. Her research is supported by industry partners including Google, Adobe, Snap, and Qualcomm.

events.title: High-Capacity and Undetectable Multi-Agent Collusion
events.description:
Speaker: Qi Pang.
High-Capacity and Undetectable Multi-Agent CollusionQi PangOct. 28, 2026 (Wed, 1:30 pm)Abstract: LLM agents increasingly coordinate through natural language, creating a new security risk: colluding agents may use apparently benign messages to exchange hidden information or coordinate unauthorized actions. Existing practical steganographic protocols usually assume unrealistic symmetry between agents or achieve very low capacity. In this talk, I will present Codetta, a high-capacity steganographic protocol for independently deployed LLM agents in realistic asymmetric settings. Codetta enables agents to communicate while preserving the sender’s output distribution. Across multiple agent workloads and sender models, Codetta achieves up to 94× higher capacity than prior asymmetric protocols. These results suggest that effectively undetectable collusion between independently deployed agents is becoming practical, and that transcript inspection alone may be insufficient for auditing multi-agent systems.

events.title: AI Institute for Societal Decision Making Seminar - Tom Costello
events.description:
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

—

Thomas Costello: https://thcostello.com/ is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
events.description:
Speaker: Veit Elser, Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

events.title: Simulation-Driven Robot Learning for the Lazy Researcher
events.description:
Abstract: This talk will delve into the workflow of building robot learning methods powered by large-scale physics simulation. While the promise of simulation is low-effort data generation that scales cheaply with human effort, the reality is often not as simple, with considerable human effort required to actually make simulation a useful tool for real-world robotic manipulation. In this talk, I will study how to develop methods that explicitly reduce manual human effort in enabling simulation as a data generation tool – from behavior generation, to model selection, to enabling downstream transfer to the real-world. In doing so, I will outline an effort-efficient path to leveraging simulation as a data source for robot learning – hopefully to make robotics easier for lazy researchers like me!

Bio: Abhishek Gupta is an assistant professor in computer science and engineering at the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Washington since 2022. He leads the Washington Embodied Intelligence and Robotics Development lab focusing on robot learning and reinforcement learning. Previously, he was a postdoctoral scholar at MIT, collaborating with Russ Tedrake and Pulkit Agrawal. Prior to that he received his Ph.D. and B.S degrees from UC Berkeley, working with Sergey Levine and Pieter Abbeel. Abhishek is the recipient of IEEE RAS Early Career Award, Toyota Research Institute Young Investigator award and an Amazon Science Hub award, along with award nominations at several top conferences and workshops. His research interests lie in scalable reinforcement learning methods for robot learning, in particular methods for continual adaptation in the real world and what role simulation can play in this process.

events.title: Video Intelligence for Understanding Behavior and Guiding Action
events.description:
Abstract: ​Modern video-language models have become remarkably good at describing what is happening in a video. Yet their ability to understand the behavior they observe, and to act on that understanding, remains limited. This talk presents our group’s work on building these missing capabilities. I will begin with foundational methods for scalable video perception, from space-time attention to hierarchical representations and active search over long videos. I will then introduce strategic video intelligence, using team sports as a natural microworld in which cooperative and competitive behavior can be studied rigorously, and present two complementary lines of work within it. The first investigates whether video generation models can simulate strategic multi-agent behavior well enough to support better decisions. The second examines how agents can study behavioral histories across large multimodal corpora, compiling repeated analytical work into reusable representations, abstractions, and procedures. Finally, I will present WatchAct, a benchmark for robot manipulation grounded in observed human behavior, where a robot watches a person and then has to act on what it saw. Together, these works move video models from perceiving behavior, to understanding it, to guiding action.

Bio: ​Gedas Bertasius is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His research focuses on video understanding and multimodal AI, particularly on systems that can perceive, reason about, and act on behavior observed in video. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Pennsylvania and was a postdoctoral researcher at Facebook AI Research before joining UNC. He is the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, four Sony Research Awards, two Meta Research Awards, and the Egocentric Vision Distinguished Paper Award. He was also a CVPR Best Paper Award finalist. Prior to his research career, he played professional basketball in Lithuania, an experience that still shapes his work on understanding strategic behavior in video.

events.title: SCS Distinguished Industry Lecture - Mark Russinovich
events.description:
AI is changing the security model of computing. It puts expert capability into anyone’s hands, operates at machine speed, and turns software from passive code into an active participant that can discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, deceive overseers, and reason about the constraints meant to contain it. At the same time, alignment safeguards that keep AI systems operating within their intended goals and constraints can be removed, unsafe models can gain capability from aligned ones, and untrusted information can steer agents toward privileged actions. These are not just new bugs; they challenge assumptions that have shaped computer security for decades. We need a new security stack, one based on isolation, capabilities, provenance, and deterministic enforcement. Intelligence cannot be the security boundary.

—

Mark Russinovich is CTO, Deputy CISO, and Technical Fellow for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft’s global enterprise-grade cloud platform. A widely recognized expert in distributed systems, operating systems and cybersecurity, Mark earned a Ph.D. in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. He later co-founded Winternals Software, joining Microsoft in 2006 when the company was acquired. Mark is a popular speaker at industry conferences such as Microsoft Ignite, Microsoft Build, and RSA Conference. He has authored several nonfiction and fiction books, including the Microsoft Press Windows Internals book series, Troubleshooting with the Sysinternals Tools, as well as fictional cyber security thrillers Zero Day, Trojan Horse and Rogue Code.

CMU community welcomed.

Oren will share with you the ten commandments of early-stage startup creation. The commandments are funny but also practical. They draw on his work with founders at the AI House, Madrona, and his own experience as the founder of AI startups from Netbot (1996) to Vercept (2024).

—

Oren Etzioni is a pioneering Artificial Intelligence researcher, entrepreneur, and prominent voice in AI safety and ethics.

Oren was the Founding Chief Executive Officer at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from its inception in 2013 until late 2022 – one of the most highly respected AI research institutes in the world, whose mission is AI for the Common Good. Under his leadership, AI2 pursued ambitious projects aimed at advancing the state-of-the-art in AI and addressing extraordinary scientific, engineering and societal challenges.

In 2024, hei founded and ran TrueMedia.org – a non-profit technology organization using AI to create a non-partisan, free and broadly accessible dashboard to combat political disinformation by identifying manipulated media and AI-based forgery of video, audio, images and text across social media platforms. He has been a Professor at the University of Washington’s Computer Science department since 1991, and a Venture Partner at the Madrona Venture Group since 2000. He is also the Founder and Technical Director of the AI2 Incubator.

events.title: How Can Robots Learn to Interact and Coordinate with Others?
events.description:
Abstract: Robots in the real world rarely act alone. They share spaces with other robots and with people, and succeeding there means learning to interact and coordinate with them. This talk looks at what makes interaction hard and how we might get there. I start with multi-agent reinforcement learning, where challenges like credit assignment make coordination difficult to learn, and show how the reasoning capabilities of foundation models can help coach robots to learn coordination. Coordination doesn’t have to be learned through trial and error though, so I then look at learning it from demonstrations. Imitating interacting agents turns out to be quite different from imitating a single one but it can still build on single-agent imitation. I then close by reversing the question: rather than asking what single-agent methods can do for multi-agent problems, I ask what multi-agent thinking can do for a single robot and show that continual learning, for example, can be cast as a consensus optimization problem which results in a natural way to balance learning new tasks against retaining old ones.

Bio: Negar Mehr is an Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering at UC Berkeley, where she directs the Berkeley Intelligent Control (ICON) Lab. Her research focuses on multi-agent interactions. Her lab develops learning-based methods grounded in game theory and control to enable robots to interact safely and intelligently with humans and other autonomous agents. She received her Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from UC Berkeley in 2019 and was a postdoctoral scholar in Aeronautics and Astronautics at Stanford University. Before returning to Berkeley, she was an Assistant Professor of Aerospace Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. She is a recipient of the ONR Young Investigator Award, the NSF CAREER Award, the ASME Rising Star Award, and the IEEE ITSS Best Ph.D. Dissertation Award.

events.title: Theory Lunch Seminar - Henry Fleischmann
events.description:
Given a weighted directed graph G = (V, E,w), its minimum cut is the nonempty S \⊊ V minimizing the weight of edges from S to V∖S. Finding such a minimum cut is called the Directed Mincut Problem. Until very recently, solving this problem efficiently, that is in almost-linear m1 + o(1) time, was one of the flagship open problems in the field of fast graph algorithms. It served as a marker of the relative limitations of our techniques for directed vs. undirected graph problems.

In this talk I will describe a shockingly simple almost-linear time algorithm for directed mincut. The algorithm is more than simple enough to be covered in a graduate algorithms course, and improves on the previous best running time of ~m√n by Cen et al. [FOCS ‘21].

This algorithm was discovered by me prompting GPT-6 Astra and providing very limited guidance.

A complete exposition of the result, written by me and my coauthors Jason Li, Thatchaphol Saranurak, and Benyu Wang, can be found here:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10898.√

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
events.description:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.

Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: Will Rinkoff (C_Robo) + Char Stiles: Artist Talk
events.description:
Will Rinkoff (C_Robo) + Char Stiles: Artist Talk
October 22, 2026 5:30 PM–6:30 PM
4919 Frew Street
Carnegie Mellon University - College of Fine Arts Room 111
Pittsburgh, PA 15213

BIG ALUMNI RETURN from Char Stiles and c_robo giving artist talks in the STUDIO Thursday 10/22 at 5:30 and Saturday performances at Detour’s TRACKWORKS Festival at Tech25 in Mount Oliver!

Will and Char will be discussing their work as multimodal performance artists – Will is specifically interested in pushing the laptop interface in a live performance context, and the laptop’s role as the universal interface for media and systems. Char’s practice follows work from coding GPU shaders to creating a new creative coding integrated development environment, to live coding music. Through performance and audience interaction, Char explores how the tools we use to create code fundamentally shape what we can imagine and express. Specifically, Char has been working on making the IDE (the software that we use to write software) into an expressive medium in its own right.

Artist Bios

Over the last few years, c_robo_ has established himself as one of the most distinctive artists working with Strudel, the web-based implementation of TidalCycles.
With pitch_black_system, he continues to expand a practice built around live coding, algorithmic composition and a highly individual approach to rhythm and structure.
As Strudel continues to mature, it is becoming an increasingly important platform for artists exploring code-based composition, offering new ways to rethink sequencing, variation and musical form beyond the constraints of conventional production workflows.
Technology alone, however, does not define the outcome. While Strudel provides an open and powerful environment for experimentation, it is Will’s musical intuition, experience and compositional sensibility that give these systems their identity. pitch_black_system stands as another compelling example of that balance between process and artistic vision.
As we continue to witness this remarkable wave of creativity, where code-based tools are reshaping the possibilities of composition, it is encouraging to see artists like c_robo_ bringing coherence, balance and a distinctive musical voice to this new way of making music.

Char Stiles is a computational artist, educator, and researcher. She works creatively in the lower levels of graphical computational systems & makes jokes about how computers work.
She was at the MIT Media Lab’s Future Sketches group researching the future of creative coding in performance. She is a part of the Livecode.nyc collective & she co-founded Hex House, an artist studio and event space in East Williamsburg.
She has performed internationally, including festivals such as Electric Forest, Portola, and Mutek Nexus. She has lectured and led workshops at Carnegie Mellon University, Duke University, University of Limerick, MIT, Cooper Union, The New School and NYU.

events.description:
The Urban Classroom Public Lecture with Vicky Achnani and Vikki Ayanna Jones
October 7, 2026 5:30 PM–7:30 PM
4919 Frew Street
CMU College of Fine Arts Room 111
Pittsburgh, PA 15213

Vicky Achnani, Vikki Ayanna Jones

In an era of environmental reckoning and social unrest, architectural practice and pedagogy must cultivate a community-centered discipline that serves as a bold experiment, a tangible demonstration, and a new common.
Addressing the critical intersections of the climate crisis, social equity, and food apartheid, The Urban Classroom: Sankofa Bamboo Greenhouse establishes a design-build methodology anchored in material adaptation and reuse, digital prefabrication and empirical structural verification. Winner of ACSA 2026 Best Design Project.

Located in Pittsburgh’s Homewood neighborhood, the project provides vital spatial infrastructure — including a sapling nursey, a gathering space, and weekend market platform – for the Sankofa Village Community Garden, directly confronting the persistence of local food insecurity while empowering the urban community it serves. Through a full-scale design-build intervention in an underserved neighborhood, it constructs a compelling case for low-carbon practice, framed as an act of community solidarity and sustainable intervention. At its core, the project is dedicated to expanding the boundaries of both professional practice and architectural education while producing exemplary instances of community-driven architecture.

Meshwork Festival — Accepting Student Commission Proposals
February 25, 2027–February 28, 2027

Annie Hui-Hsin Hsieh and Johannes DeYoung

About Meshwork
Meshwork is a new visual music festival in Pittsburgh, tracing spaces where sound and image converge, movement becomes signal, and bodies meet machines. Across performance, cinema, animation, installation, and computational art, artists and audiences meet within a shifting meshwork, where disciplines collide, known forms dissolve, and new relations emerge. Founded and directed by Johannes DeYoung and Annie Hui-Hsin Hsieh, and supported by Carnegie Mellon University College of Fine Arts, Meshwork brings artists and audiences together to expand embodied audiovisual experience and reimagine what visual music can become.
Student Commissions – Apply here
The festival is calling for proposals from the CMU student community for groundbreaking new creative projects that challenge the sensory boundaries between the visual and the auditory.
The festival will support four projects of up to $1500 in material support to be presented at the festival in late February 2027. Priority will be given to interdisciplinary projects, and any material purchase will need to comply with CMU’s general equipment purchasing guidelines.

events.title: Structured Learning for Fast Physical Prediction
events.description:
Abstract:
Physical simulation is essential for robotics and engineering design, but remains computationally expensive, especially for complex geometries and long time horizons. Learning-based approaches offer faster predictions, but often lack the mathematical structure needed for reliable simulation.
In this talk, I will present three approaches that combine learning with mathematical structure: continuous reduced-order representations for generalization across shapes, geometric lifting for handling discontinuities, and Koopman-based linear operators for efficient long-horizon prediction. Together, these methods demonstrate how structured learning can enable faster, more expressive, and more reliable physical simulation.

Biography:
Chang Yue is a Ph.D. student in Computer Science at the University of Toronto, advised by Prof. Eitan Grinspun. Her research focuses on mathematically structured learning for fast and generalizable physical simulation. Her work has received the SIGGRAPH 2025 Best Paper Award and Best Paper Award Honorable Mention. She was also recognized as a WiGRAPH Rising Star in 2026.

Homepage: https://changy1506.github.io/

Sponsor:
The VASC seminar is generously sponsored by HeyGen, an all-in-one
AI-powered video generation platform that leverages advances in
computer vision, generative modeling, and multimodal learning to make
high-quality video creation both scalable and accessible.

events.description:
In this fireside chat, iii faculty member Susanna Zlotnikov speaks with Nickey Skarstad, a senior director of product at Duolingo, about the culture behind making the world’s No. 1 language learning app.

​Skarstad will give us a look into the organizational practices that cultivate Duolingo’s unique innovation culture and what a typical day looks like for Duos building personalized experiences for over 40 million users world-wide.

​Specifically, Zlotnikov and Skarstad will explore how tech and product teams work together to build cutting-edge personalized experiences for millions of users, and how AI is pushing the Duolingo team to change the way they work and innovate.

​There will be 30 minutes to hear from our co-hosts, and 15 minutes for Q&A.

Hosted by the Integrated Innovation Institute (iii)

events.title: EPP Seminar: Sonia Mangones — Transportation, Air Pollution, and Inequalities: Evidence from Bogotá, Colombia
events.description:
Environmental justice research often examines the burden of pollution in relation to the population’s socioeconomic vulnerability. Climate justice research examines differential responsibility, asking who emits and who ultimately carries the burden they create. Urban mobility justice research rarely combines these two questions empirically, even though mobility is where they intersect most directly, since travel generates emissions and also shapes where resulting pollution concentrations fall across the city. This talk presents findings from an empirical study of Bogotá, Colombia, that measures both sides of this relationship at the level of city blocks, combining residential pollution concentration (NO2 and PM2.5) with a block-level proxy for travel-emission responsibility built from official mobility and emissions data. Two findings challenge a simple story in which the poor pollute least and suffer most. First, pollution concentration does not increase monotonically with deprivation; it peaks at intermediate socioeconomic levels. Second, emission responsibility does decline cleanly with vulnerability, but the resulting imbalance, where responsibility is low and pollution concentration is high, concentrates in population segments that can only be identified by combining policy instruments that separately inform socioeconomic vulnerability and the spatial distribution of the imbalance. I discuss what this means for the mobility justice conversation and the implications for transportation and environmental policy.

Speaker BIo:

Sonia Cecilia Mangones Matos is an Associate Professor at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, where she directs the Translogyt Research Group. Her work lies at the intersection of transportation engineering, urban sustainability, environmental impacts of transportation, road safety, and public policy. Her research combines quantitative methods, data analytics, and interdisciplinary approaches to examine sustainable urban mobility, transportation-related air pollution, emissions, and the implications of transportation systems for public health and urban equity.

Sonia holds a Ph.D. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University and an M.Sc. in Transportation Engineering from Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Her international academic experience includes research stays at CNRS in Toulouse and the LIVE Laboratory at the University of Strasbourg in France, as well as a research visit to Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile. She is Co-Chair of the Sustainable Transport Committee of the Pan-American Society of Transportation Research (PANAMSTR) and actively contributes to the World Conference on Transport Research, Community Modeling and Analysis System (CMAS) South America, and the Transportation Research Board in the US. She has led and collaborated on research projects with public institutions in Colombia, including the Ministry of Transport and the National Road Safety Agency. Her recent work has received broader recognition, including the 2025 L’Oréal–UNESCO “For Women in Science” Regional Award for her work on AI-enabled sustainable urban mobility and the 2025 Afro-Colombian of the Year Award in the Science and Technology category, recognizing her contributions to science and applied research in Colombia.

She is currently a Fulbright Visiting Scholar in Carnegie Mellon University’s Department of Engineering and Public Policy, where her project develops a justice-based framework integrating mobility, emissions, and pollution concentration and examines how complex technical evidence can be translated into actionable policy.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
events.description:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.

Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: Ghostly Preferences: When Coherence Requires a Strict Preference Among Equivalent Random Variables
events.description:
Join the Philosophy Department for our annual Halloween talk! We will be handing out candy and while costumes are not required, they are welcome!

Presenter: Teddy Seidenfeld

Abstract: When utilities for outcomes are bounded, or when all variables are simple, it is required by (canoncial) expected utility to have preferences defined over probability distributions or lotteries over outcomes. That is, under such circumstances two random variables with a common probability distribution over outcomes – equivalent random variables – must occupy the same place in an agent’s preference ordering over lotteries. For example, with outcomes determined by a flip of a fair coin (i.e, where the probability of landing heads = the probability of landing tails = 1/2), winning $1 if heads and losing $1 if tails is equally preferred to losing $1 if heads and winning $1 if tails. Also, then one is indifferent between trading one of these lotteries for the other.

events.title: SCS Distinguished Industry Lecture - John Wilkes
events.description:
Google builds and operates a massive infrastructure in support of providing products and capabilities to its users and customers. The scale has dramatically increased as a result of the push for AI. While we benefit greatly from an integrated stack—from software down through specialized chips to optimized data center designs—we also need a way to coordinate all those efforts to avoid confusion, inefficiencies, and missed opportunities. The talk will discuss one of the approaches we are using to provide a control system for a $xxxB/year capital expenditure program.

—

John Wilkes: http://john.e-wilkes.com has been at Google since 2008, where he is working on automation for building warehouse scale computers, with a current focus on fleet-wide capacity planning. Before this, he worked on cluster management for Google's compute infrastructure (Borg, Omega, Kubernetes). He is interested in far too many aspects of distributed systems, but a recurring theme has been technologies that allow systems to manage themselves.

He received a PhD in computer science from the University of Cambridge, joined HP Labs in 1982, and was elected an HP Fellow and an ACM Fellow in 2002 for his work on storage system design. Along the way, he’s been program committee chair for SOSP, FAST, EuroSys and HotCloud, and has served on the steering committees for EuroSys, FAST, SoCC and HotCloud. He’s listed as an inventor on 50+ US patents, and has an adjunct faculty appointment at Carnegie-Mellon University. In his spare time he continues, stubbornly, trying to learn how to blow glass.

Campus community welcomed.

events.title: CyLab Seminar - Rolfe Schmidt
events.description:
The Signal Protocol is among the most heavily analyzed cryptographic protocols ever deployed: pen-and-paper proofs, symbolic models, and machine-checked computational proofs all attest to its security. Those results are real. Nevertheless, over the years we have found — and fixed — vulnerabilities in Signal that degraded the security of real conversations.

This talk surveys a few of them, ranging from the core protocol implementation to product features layered well above it. For each, I answer the obvious question: what did the proofs actually cover, and why did the deployed system fall outside that coverage? These were not errors in the analysis. They were gaps between the mathematical abstractions and the engineering ones.

To put those cases in context, I show a bird's-eye view of Signal's codebase: how small a fraction is the protocol proper, and how much of the rest determines the security users actually experience. I close with how I think the research community and industry can narrow the gap, and how advances in formal verification are letting us analyze the code that ships.

—

Rolfe Schmidt:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/rolfeschmidt is a Research Engineer at Signal Messenger, where he works to bridge academic research with Signal's engineering and security needs. He co-designed the PQXDH key agreement protocol and the SPQR post-quantum ratchet, and has worked on Signal's ORAM-backed contact discovery, Secure Value Recovery, and anonymous credential systems. He collaborates widely on formal analysis of deployed protocols.

events.title: Software and Societal Department Distinguished Seminar - Margaret-Anne Storey
events.description:
AI is changing software development faster than our engineering practices are evolving, and yet many developers feel the pressure to adopt AI and deliver features at a frantic pace. Although AI can improve speed, emerging evidence highlights considerable variability in outcomes and reveals new challenges in coordination, comprehension, and cognitive fatigue. These shifts raise important questions about how teams maintain shared understanding of complex systems, and how they remain in control as they become increasingly reliant on AI agents. As we delegate more work and decisions to agents, how do we make sure humans still understand what is happening and retain the ability to question, steer, and intervene when necessary?

In this talk, I’ll explore new approaches for helping humans and AI maintain understanding as software systems evolve: understanding how the system works, why it was built in a certain way, and whether it still meets the intended user goals and design constraints. I’ll share some emerging ideas for measuring and mitigating losses of technical, cognitive and intentional understanding, and consider how we might design tools and practices that allow humans and AI agents to work together without reducing human judgement and control.

—

Margaret-Anne Storey: https://margaretstorey.com/ is a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Victoria and a Canada Research Chair in Human and Social Aspects of Software Engineering. She is co-author of the SPACE framework and a leading researcher in Developer Experience (DevEx). Her research focuses on how developers and teams understand complex software systems, and how tools, AI, and collaborative practices shape that understanding. Her recent work examines how generative AI is transforming software engineering by changing how understanding is created, shared, and maintained. She collaborates with industry partners including Microsoft and DX. She holds an honorary doctorate from Lund University.

events.title: Software Engineering Institute Webcast: How Real is Real Enough? A Decade of Lessons from GHOSTS
events.description:
The Department of War is increasingly using digital twins and digital engineering to support training, testing, cybersecurity, mission rehearsal, and AI-enabled analysis. But building a useful digital representation raises a fundamental question: How much of the real system needs to be reproduced for an effective simulation? In this webcast, we draw on a decade of developing and deploying GHOSTS:
https://github.com/cmu-sei/GHOSTS/ to examine how engineers can determine the level of realism needed to meet objectives and use that determination to decide what must be modeled—including networks, users, organizations, adversaries, and autonomous agents—and what can safely be left out.

Attendees will learn
- how GHOSTS evolved over a decade:
https://www.sei.cmu.edu/library/a-decade-of-ghosts-in-the-machine-from-cyber-range-realism-to-cognitive-mission-rehearsal/ of cyber exercises, experimentation, and operational use.
- why more simulation detail does not automatically produce more useful or realistic results.
- how GHOSTS models interactions between people, organizations, information, cyber systems, and increasingly autonomous agents.
- how the concept of sufficient realism can guide the design of simulations for training, experimentation, and mission rehearsal.
Who Should Attend?
- digital engineering, digital twin, and modeling and simulation leads
- cyber operations, cyber range, and training leaders
- program managers, systems engineers, and test and evaluation professionals
- mission engineering, experimentation, and AI and autonomy practitioners

Dustin Updyke is a researcher and engineer at the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University, where he leads work at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and modeling and simulation. He created and leads development of GHOSTS, an open source simulation framework that has supported cyber training and experimentation across Department of War environments for more than a decade. His current work explores how human, organizational, social, cognitive, and autonomous-agent behavior can be incorporated into increasingly complex mission simulations while maintaining the level of realism necessary for useful training, testing, and experimentation

events.title: Vision and Autonomous Systems Seminar - Chang Yue
events.description:
Physical simulation is essential for robotics and engineering design, but remains computationally expensive, especially for complex geometries and long time horizons. Learning-based approaches offer faster predictions, but often lack the mathematical structure needed for reliable simulation.
In this talk, I will present three approaches that combine learning with mathematical structure: continuous reduced-order representations for generalization across shapes, geometric lifting for handling discontinuities, and Koopman-based linear operators for efficient long-horizon prediction. Together, these methods demonstrate how structured learning can enable faster, more expressive, and more reliable physical simulation.

—

Her research focuses on mathematically structured learning for fast and generalizable physical simulation. Her work has received the SIGGRAPH 2025 Best Paper Award and Best Paper Award Honorable Mention. She was also recognized as a WiGRAPH Rising Star in 2026.

events.title: Robotics Ph.D. Thesis Proposal - Yilin Wu
events.description:
Generalist robot policies—such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)—are trained end-to-end on large observation-action datasets and can perform increasingly diverse manipulation tasks. Yet these policies remain unreliable amid the complexity of real environments and user contexts. A common remedy is to finetune the entire policy for a particular deployment, but this may degrade the pretrained capabilities that make generalist policies valuable. This raises the central question of this thesis: how should robot policies be adapted to particular users and environments while preserving their generality?

This thesis argues that maximizing adaptation while minimizing loss of generality requires identifying what should be adapted and choosing how to adapt it in the least invasive way. For example, a deployment may call for changes to the task specification (what the user wants done), the state representation (which aspects of the scene matter for the task), or the behavioral support (the range of actions the policy can produce). At each of these levels, the desired behavior may already lie within the policy’s pretrained capabilities and only need to be elicited, or the policy may need to acquire new knowledge or skills through additional training.

We study two corresponding adaptation mechanisms: inference-time steering, which guides pretrained action distribution toward the target while keeping policy parameters fixed, and targeted training, which learns additional context or behaviors through limited parameter updates. For steering, we first propose language-based verification methods that check generated actions against user instructions and reasoning plans. Next, to handle incomplete state information in contact-rich manipulation, we introduce a bi-level visual and tactile steering algorithm. Third, to steer the action distribution in open-world settings, we contribute a world model that predicts the consequences of candidate behaviors while balancing fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference efficiency.

Steering, however, can only elicit behaviors the pretrained policy already supports. We turn to targeted training methods with parameter-efficient updates to improve the base policy via learning a compact multi-stream memory that conditions the policy on history-dependent state, and residual policies that incorporate user corrections to expand the policy’s behavioral capabilities. Finally, the proposed work revisits the role of meta-learning for adapting generalist robot policies. We propose separating shared representation learning across tasks from task-specific action learning using limited demonstrations. The goal is adaptation with fewer demonstrations and trainable parameters, with explicit retention of pretrained capabilities

Thesis Committee
Andrea Bajcsy (Chair)
Guanya Shi
Oliver Kroemer
Anirudha Majumdar (Princeton University)

events.title: Computer Science Ph.D. Speaking Skills Talk - Runming Li
events.description:
Intrinsically-typed presentations of type theory often use equality types in the meta-language to represent object-language judgmental equality. In such equational syntax, proof-relevant logical relations define computability predicates on judgmental equivalence classes of types and terms. This approach, however, does not directly account for reduction, which is directed and plays a central role in many logical-relations arguments.

This work develops a directed version of proof-relevant logical relations in simplicial homotopy type theory, a directed variant of homotopy type theory, where reductions are internalized as inequality types. We construct object syntax as a directed quotient inductive type. The central observation is that contravariant families in simplicial type theory provide exactly the proof-relevant form of closure under expansion for logical relations: computability evidence can be transported backward along reductions, with the required functoriality and universal property built in.

Using this observation, we construct a unary logical relations model with contravariant computability predicates and prove directed Boolean canonicity: every closed Boolean term reduces to either true or false. We then extend the construction to dependent types and universes, where a comonadic flat modality provides the discreteness needed for type conversion and universe predicates. Finally, we adapt the method to binary logical relations, separating vertical reduction from horizontal parametricity and obtaining a proof-relevant account of representation independence.

Presented as part of the PLunch Seminar Series
Presented in Partial Fulfillment of the CSD Speaking Skills Requirement

events.title: Joint Cypto Seminar / Computer Science Ph.D. Speaking Skills Talk - QI Pang
events.description:
LLM agents increasingly coordinate through natural language, creating a new security risk: colluding agents may use apparently benign messages to exchange hidden information or coordinate unauthorized actions. Existing practical steganographic protocols usually assume unrealistic symmetry between agents or achieve very low capacity.

In this talk, I will present Codetta, a high-capacity steganographic protocol for independently deployed LLM agents in realistic asymmetric settings. Codetta enables agents to communicate while preserving the sender’s output distribution. Across multiple agent workloads and sender models, Codetta achieves up to 94× higher capacity than prior asymmetric protocols. These results suggest that effectively undetectable collusion between independently deployed agents is becoming practical, and that transcript inspection alone may be insufficient for auditing multi-agent systems.

events.title: Database Seminar - Ippokratis Pandis
events.description:
Traditionally, data architectures maintain a strict division between high-throughput operational databases and large-scale analytical lakehouses. The general wisdom for organizations seeking low-latency real-time analytics is to copy data into dedicated serving layers, which creates data redundancy, stale insights, and fragmented governance.

In this talk, we explore how unifying operational and analytical workloads on open storage eliminates the need to copy data. In the first part, we present LakehouseRT, an analytical query engine designed to deliver millisecond-level query latency and high concurrency directly over open table formats in object stores governed by a unified catalog. In the second part, we show how Lakebase and its disaggregated compute and storage OLTP architecture not only provides best-in-class performance, elasticity, and availability for Postgres workloads, but also seamlessly enables low-latency analytics directly on live operational data without compromises.

—

Ippokratis Pandis:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/ippokratis-pandis-03b1402 is a Distinguished Engineer at Databricks working on data management systems. Previously, he spent a decade at AWS, where he served as Chief Architect of AWS Analytics and led the development of Amazon Redshift. Earlier, he contributed to Cloudera Impala and IBM DB2 BLU. He earned his Ph.D. from Carnegie Mellon University, where in the dungeons of Wean and Hamerschlag Halls, he worked on multicore transaction processing. He has authored numerous research papers and served the database community as General Chair of SIGMOD 2023 and President of HPTS.

events.title: Robotics Ph.D. Thesis Proposal - Sriram Narayanan
events.description:
Computer vision seeks to understand the physical world from images, yet much of this understanding remains rooted in the appearance of reflected visible light. Objects also absorb and emit radiation, exchange heat with their surroundings, and change their temperature over space and time. These processes encode information about materials, geometry, and physical interactions that conventional visible cameras often cannot access. Thermal imaging makes aspects of this energy exchange observable, opening new possibilities for computational imaging.

This dissertation develops a physics-based framework for thermal computational imaging by treating light and heat transport as complementary sources of scene information. Observations across wavelength and time depend differently on geometry, materials, illumination, and temperature. Connecting these observations through physical models helps distinguish scene properties that remain ambiguous in individual measurements.

We develop this premise through a sequence of inverse problems. Spectral and temporal thermal observations enable separation of radiation emitted by an object from radiation reflected from its surroundings, supporting temperature recovery even when material emissivity is unknown. Next, we show how the thermal consequences of absorbed light complement visible reflection, allowing surface reflectance and shading to be separated without explicitly recovering geometry or lighting. We then establish heat conduction as a geometric cue, recovering three-dimensional shape from the spatial relationships governing temperature evolution across dark, textured, and visibly transparent objects. Combining conduction with shading further allows local shape ambiguities to be resolved through their complementary geometric constraints.

The proposed work extends these connections into thermal simulation within VisionSIM, linking scene illumination, transient heat transport, emitted and reflected radiation, and sensor dynamics to predict thermal observations. Together, the completed and proposed work connect scene reconstruction and image synthesis through the coupled physics of light and heat. They establish energy exchange as both a source of constraints for recovering scene properties and a basis for predicting thermal observations.

Aswin Sankaranarayanan
Ioannis Gkioulekas
Ravi Ramamoorthi (UCSD)
Shree Nayar (Columbia)

events.title: Vision and Autonomous Systems Seminar - Pinar Yanardag
events.description:
Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms of control, generate over extended horizons within practical computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a central question: How can we make visual generation controllable, efficient, and personal?

I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First, Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next, VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of extended generation by learning compact representations of past context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate them.

I will close with broader directions for video generation, including new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26). This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography, supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact with them.

—

Pinar Yanardag: https://pinguar.org/ is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive world models. She earned her PhD from Purdue as a Fulbright Fellow and was a postdoctoral researcher at the MIT Media Lab, where her generative AI projects attracted over one million participants and media coverage from TIME, The Washington Post, and CNN. She received an NSF CAREER award for her research on generative cinematography and was recognized as an Outstanding Area Chair at CVPR 2026. Her research is supported by industry partners including Google, Adobe, Snap, and Qualcomm.

Faculty Host: Fernando De La Torre

The VASC Seminar is generously sponsored by HeyGen: https://www.heygen.com.

events.description:
Perhaps no group is more affected by -- and has more opportunity to shape -- emerging technology than college students. Technology such as AI can be awe-inspiring, terrifying, underwhelming, and really annoying -- sometimes all at once. We want to hear about your experiences, your perspectives, your hopes, and your concerns.

The Block Center for Technology & Society:
https://www.cmu.edu/block-center invites CMU students to submit to our new opportunity, Tech Takes: A Student Perspective Series.

Each month, the Center will post a new writing prompt related to a contemporary issue in technology & society; CMU students are invited to submit brief (< 250-word) reflections responding to the prompt.

Winning responses will be selected by a committee, which will prioritize distinctive and well-articulated perspectives that engage the prompt in a compelling and thoughtful manner. A selection of winning student responses will be published with attribution via the Block Center channels reaching a broad audience of people curious about the role of technology in society.

One response will be selected as the “Block Center Student Perspective of the Month” and will receive a $250 prize.

Timing
- Questions will be announced the first Thursday of every month,
- and, submissions will be due the last day of the month at 11:59PM.

events.title: GOOGLE x CMU Tech Talk (Ph.D.)
events.description:
Join Google engineers Patrick Musau (Google DeepMind) and Se-Joon Chung (Google XR, CMU alum) for an in-depth technical talk exploring real-world systems engineering across autonomous cybersecurity and gesture-based XR. The session will highlight how Googlers apply their PhD training to solve complex, planetary-scale engineering challenges. This will be followed by an open Q&A on transitioning from academia to industry, alongside a brief overview of Google's PhD SWE roles and research internships.

In the realm of cybersecurity and Gen AI, Patrick will share how Google is pioneering autonomous, machine-speed defense to counter a collapsed exploit window (dropping from years down to under two days) that has rendered manual patching obsolete. To counter these attacks, Google built CodeMender, an agentic security platform powered by domain-specialized models (Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and Gemini 4 Argon) running within automated program-analysis harnesses. He will dive into how CodeMender autonomously generates working Proofs of Concept to verify vulnerabilities and synthesizes semantics-preserving patches directly in production codebases without human intervention.

In the field of XR, Se-Joon will walk through the engineering journey of bringing Google Maps Immersive View to gesture-based Android XR, enabling users to naturally navigate the globe without a controller. Moving from physical joysticks to bare hands required solving fundamental challenges around nausea, fatigue, and precision across both aerial 3D Tiles and indoor 3D Gaussian Splats. He will share how Google designed comfortable hands-first locomotion mechanics to mitigate simulator sickness, engineered robust relative-tracking systems to eliminate crossed-pointer orientation flips, and leveraged environmental affordances to keep users intuitively constrained within valid 3D capture boundaries.

events.title: Computer Science Ph.D. Speaking Skills Talk -Yixuan Xu
events.description:
Model distillation enables efficient emulation of frontier large language models (LLMs), creating a need for robust mechanisms to detect when a third-party student model has trained on a teacher model's outputs. However, existing fingerprinting techniques that could be used to detect such distillation rely on heuristic perturbations that impose a steep trade-off between generation quality and fingerprinting strength, often requiring significant degradation of utility to ensure the fingerprint is effectively internalized by the student.

We introduce antidistillation fingerprinting (ADFP), a principled approach that aligns the fingerprinting objective with the student's learning dynamics. Building upon the gradient-based framework of antidistillation sampling, ADFP utilizes a proxy model to identify and sample tokens that directly maximize the expected detectability of the fingerprint in the student after fine-tuning, rather than relying on the incidental absorption of the un-targeted biases of a more naive watermark. Experiments on GSM8K, OASST1, and MBPP demonstrate that ADFP achieves a significant Pareto improvement over state-of-the-art baselines, yielding stronger detection confidence with minimal impact on utility across mathematical reasoning, dialogue, and code generation, even when the student model's architecture is unknown.

Presented in Partial Fulfillment of the CSD Speaking Skills Requirement

events.title: AI Institute for Societal Decision Making Seminar - Tom Costello
events.description:
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

—

Thomas Costello: https://thcostello.com/ is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: SCS Distinguished Industry Lecture - Mark Russinovich
events.description:
AI is changing the security model of computing. It puts expert capability into anyone’s hands, operates at machine speed, and turns software from passive code into an active participant that can discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, deceive overseers, and reason about the constraints meant to contain it. At the same time, alignment safeguards that keep AI systems operating within their intended goals and constraints can be removed, unsafe models can gain capability from aligned ones, and untrusted information can steer agents toward privileged actions. These are not just new bugs; they challenge assumptions that have shaped computer security for decades. We need a new security stack, one based on isolation, capabilities, provenance, and deterministic enforcement. Intelligence cannot be the security boundary.

—

Mark Russinovich:
https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/author/mark-russinovich/ is CTO, Deputy CISO, and Technical Fellow for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft’s global enterprise-grade cloud platform. A widely recognized expert in distributed systems, operating systems and cybersecurity, Mark earned a Ph.D. in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. He later co-founded Winternals Software, joining Microsoft in 2006 when the company was acquired. Mark is a popular speaker at industry conferences such as Microsoft Ignite, Microsoft Build, and RSA Conference. He has authored several nonfiction and fiction books, including the Microsoft Press Windows Internals book series, Troubleshooting with the Sysinternals Tools, as well as fictional cyber security thrillers Zero Day, Trojan Horse and Rogue Code.

CMU community welcomed.

events.title: Statistics and Data Science Seminar - Alex Luedtke
events.description:
We introduce the Sinkhorn treatment effect, an entropic optimal transport measure of divergence between counterfactual distributions. Unlike classical quantities such as the average treatment effect, this measure captures differences across entire distributions. We analyze this divergence as a statistical functional and show it can be written as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings with an appropriate kernel. This characterization allows us to establish first-order pathwise differentiability in general, and second-order pathwise differentiability under the null hypothesis of equal counterfactual distributions. Leveraging this smoothness, we construct debiased estimators and use them to obtain asymptotically valid tests for distributional treatment effects with a fixed entropic regularization parameter. Because the power of the test depends on this unknown parameter, we further propose an aggregated test that combines evidence across a grid of regularization choices. Experiments on simulated and image data demonstrate the practical advantages of our estimator and testing procedure.

—

Alex Luedtke: https://alexluedtke.com/ is a Professor of Health Care Policy and Affiliate in Statistics at Harvard University. Previously, he held faculty appointments in Statistics and Biostatistics at the University of Washington and Fred Hutch. Alex works at the intersection of semiparametrics, causal inference, and machine learning. Much of his work leverages computational power to automate the construction of efficient statistical procedures. To this end, he has developed methods that let machines "learn to learn" from data, and algorithms that work out derivations once done by hand. He applies these tools as part of multidisciplinary teams to improve decision-making in mental health and infectious disease research.

Selected honors include a COPSS Emerging Leader Award, NIH Director's New Innovator Award, and Mortimer Spiegelman Award. His work has been supported by NIH, NSF, PCORI, WHO, and Netflix. Alex received a PhD in Biostatistics from UC Berkeley and an ScB in Applied Mathematics from Brown University.

events.title: CMU Energy Week 2027: Energy Systems, Innovation, and Resilience
events.description:
Energy systems are entering a period of unprecedented change. Rising electricity demand from AI and data centers, increasing climate risks, evolving supply chains for critical minerals and energy technologies, and growing pressure to maintain affordability and reliability are reshaping how energy systems are planned, built, and operated.

Meeting these challenges and advancing towards net-zero emissions requires more than developing and deploying new technologies. It demands coordinated innovation across infrastructure, markets, policy, finance, digital systems, and institutions—while strengthening the ability of energy systems to adapt, recover, and continue delivering benefits under changing conditions.

CMU Energy Week brings together leaders from industry, government, academia, and civil society to explore how to build energy systems that are resilient, affordable, secure, and aligned with long-term decarbonization goals.

The programming is organized around three successive, interconnected tracks:

events.description:
About the Webcast
Like their industry counterparts, government organizations, military services, and federal agencies are launching artificial intelligence (AI) pilots, testing generative AI, and exploring new ways to advance mission delivery. Yet moving from isolated experiments to enterprise-wide adoption requires far more than promising technology. As AI safety and security concerns intensify, organizations must prioritize disciplined implementation of key practices. Such discipline demands strong governance, trusted data, a prepared workforce, an adaptable infrastructure, effective risk management, clear measures of value, and aligned resource management. Regulated industries face similar challenges.

Drawing on deep policy and defense expertise from the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) in addition to the Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) Software Engineering Institute (SEI) and Accenture Federal Services, the panel will examine what it takes for government services and federal agencies, as well as any regulated industry, to progress from experimentation to the sustainable implementation of AI.

Attendees will learn how to manage the security and trust risks that accompany the deployment of AI platforms using structured, enterprise-level governance. The discussion will explore how organizations can assess their current level of readiness, identify gaps that may limit adoption, and align AI investments with mission outcomes, oversight expectations, and public trust.

The panelists will explore actionable strategies to overcome legacy challenges, safely scale emerging AI technologies, and manage security, trust, and operational risk across critical public and defense sector mission environments. Participants will gain practical insights into the capabilities that distinguish mature AI adoption, the challenges government and regulated industry organizations are encountering, and the steps leaders can take now to build a foundation for intentional scale.

Attendees will learn how to
- identify gaps in governance, infrastructure, and risk management practices to drive sustainable AI adoption
- apply practices to ensure secure, safe, and trustworthy AI
- address legacy constraints to align infrastructure costs and resource allocation with AI investment priorities

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Graphics Colloquium - Adriana Schulz
events.description:
Generative models have transformed our ability to create images, geometry, and other digital content. But designing objects for the physical world requires more than generating something plausible or visually compelling. Physical artifacts must also be manufacturable and satisfy functional and performance requirements, turning design into a search through complex, highly constrained spaces.

It is tempting to think generative models will simply absorb this challenge without the need for explicit optimization. I will argue the opposite: optimization is not merely still relevant; it is becoming more powerful. The recent success of AI is, at its core, a success of large-scale optimization, and it has dramatically expanded what practical optimization can do. But harnessing this power requires rethinking how we represent designs—not treating representations as fixed and building optimizers around them, but instead designing representations for optimization. Through examples from computational design and digital fabrication, I will show how this perspective can make difficult inverse problems tractable and enable new tools for creating objects that work in the physical world.

—

https://www.computationaldesign.group/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fprofile%2Fadriana-full.jpg&w=256&q=75

Adriana Schulz:
https://www.computationaldesign.group/adriana is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Brown University. Her research develops computational tools for designing physical artifacts, combining ideas from geometry processing, machine learning, and programming languages. She grew up in Brazil and completed her Ph.D. in Computer Science at MIT in 2018, before joining the faculty at the University of Washington and later Brown. Her work has been recognized with an Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship, an NSF CAREER Award, the CRA Anita Borg Early Career Award, MIT Technology Review’s Innovators Under 35, and the ACM SIGGRAPH Significant New Researcher Award.

Faculty Host: Jim McCann

The Carnegie Mellon Graphics Colloquium is hosted by the Carnegie Mellon Graphics Lab: https://graphics.cs.cmu.edu/ and generously supported by Meta and Adobe.

events.description:
The Brainstorming sessions are led by students of all levels, these sessions offer a casual forum to discuss AI-related research while exploring cross-cutting connections between various disciplines in artificial intelligence.

About this session
Led by: Keerthana Gurushankar:
https://www.keerthanagurushankar.com/ — Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department

Peer review at major research journals now involves hundreds of submissions per month, and the case for automated reviewer assignment is clear. What is less clear is how to do it well: unlike conference assignment, which can be solved offline once all submissions are in, journal assignment must be done online: each paper assigned immediately upon arrival, from a pool of reviewers who may become unavailable for weeks once assigned.

We study this as an instance of online task assignment with reusable resources: tasks arrive over time, each must be immediately assigned to k of R available resources, and each assigned resource is busy for d subsequent timesteps. This model captures peer review, healthcare scheduling, ridesharing, and emergency dispatch. I will present restless-bandit based policies and upper bounds. I will also discuss a closed-form Whittle index policy for automated reviewer assignment and insights from evaluation on a four-year trace of submissions to TMLR.

events.title: 3rd Annual Philosophy Department Halloween Talk - Teddy Seidenfeld
events.description:
When utilities for outcomes are bounded, or when all variables are simple, it is required by (canoncial) expected utility to have preferences defined over probability distributions or lotteries over outcomes. That is, under such circumstances two random variables with a common probability distribution over outcomes - equivalent random variables - must occupy the same place in an agent's preference ordering over lotteries. For example, with outcomes determined by a flip of a fair coin (i.e, where the probability of landing Heads = the probability of landing Tails = 1/2), winning $1 if Heads and losing $1 if tails is equally preferred to losing $1 if Heads and winning $1 if Tails. Also, then one is indifferent between trading one of these lotteries for the other.

However, if strict preference over lotteries respects uniform, strict dominance in outcomes between random variables,

and if indifference between two random variables entails indifference between the two lotteries of trading one for the other, then preferences over unbounded random variables cannot preserve indifference between all pairs of equivalent variables. In such circumstances, preference is not a function of probability and utility for outcomes.

- What are the objects of such preferences?
I illustrate such ghostly preferences using three equivalent St. Petersburg variables.

—

Teddy Seidenfeld:
https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/philosophy/people/faculty/seidenfeld.html (H.A. Simon University Professor of Philosophy and Statistics) works on foundations at the interface between philosophy and statistics, often being concerned with problems that involve multiple decision makers. For example, in collaboration with M.J. Schervish and J.B. Kadane (Statistics, CMU), they relax the norms of Bayesian theory to permit a unified standard, both for individuals acting as separate decision makers and collectively, in forming a cooperative group agent. By contrast, this is an impossibility for strict Bayesian theory. For a second example, in collaboration with Larry Wasserman (Statistics, CMU), they examine the short-run consequences of using Bayes rule for updating a set of expert Bayesian opinions with shared information. They focus on anomalous cases (they call dilation), where an experiment is certain to result in new evidence that increases the experts: uncertainty about an event of common interest where uncertainty is reflected in the extent of probabilistic disagreements among the experts.

His current collaborations with Kadane and Schervish include a theory for indexing the degree of incoherence in non-Bayesian statistical decisions, work on the representation of coherent choice-functions using sets of probabilitis, and investigations involving scoring rules for probabilistic forecasts. The three also work together on the development of finitely additive expectations for unbounded random variables.

There will be candy!

Rahm I. Emanuel most recently served as the United States Ambassador to Japan. As Ambassador, Emanuel helped deepen the U.S.-Japan alliance, including support for Japan's increased defense spending and expanded military cooperation. He promoted Japan's leadership in Indo-Pacific key security initiatives and participated in the historic trilateral summit at Camp David that reaffirmed that cooperation between the United States, Japan, and the Republic of Korea.

Previously, Emanuel was the 55th Mayor of the City of Chicago, a position he held until May 2019. During that time, he made the critical choices necessary to secure Chicago's future as a global capital. As Mayor, Emanuel added four years to a student’s education. He increased the school day by 75 minutes and added more than 200 hours to the school year, marking the largest single increase in educational time by any city and taking Chicago from having the least educational time of any large school district in the country to being on par with its peers. He implemented universal pre-kindergarten and full-day kindergarten for every Chicago child, and made Chicago the first city in America to provide free community college.

The Mayor's comprehensive public safety strategy focused on expanded prevention programs for at-risk youth, smarter policing strategies, and empowering parents and communities to reduce violence. The Ambassador made it a priority to bring global companies to the city, helping Chicago to lead the U.S. in corporate relocations and foreign direct investment for seven consecutive years. His administration invested in infrastructure, public transportation, open space, and cultural attractions. From the $8.5 billion O'Hare International Airport modernization program that is cementing Chicago's status as a global leader in travel, tourism, and trade to the development of the iconic 1.25-mile Chicago Riverwalk, the City's investments are creating thousands of good-paying jobs and making Chicago a better place to live, work, and play.
Prior to becoming Mayor, from November 2008 until October 2010, Emanuel served as President Barack Obama's Chief of Staff. In addition to being the President's top advisor, Emanuel helped the Obama administration secure the passage of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and the landmark Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.

Before serving as Chief of Staff, Emanuel was elected four times as a Member of the U.S. House of Representatives from Illinois's 5th Congressional District (2002-2008). As Chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, Emanuel helped pass legislation to raise the minimum wage and authored the Great Lakes Restoration Act.

From 1993 to 1998, Ambassador Emanuel was a key member of President Bill Clinton's administration, rising to serve as Senior Advisor to the President for Policy and Politics. During this time, Emanuel served as a legislative liaison to Congress and spearheaded efforts to pass several of President Clinton's signature achievements, most notably the Federal Assault Weapons Ban, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, and the historic Balanced Budget Act, which created the Children's Health Insurance Program that expanded health care coverage to 10 million children. Emanuel also worked closely with President Joseph R. Biden Jr., then a U.S. Senator, to shepherd the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 through Congress.

Emanuel graduated from Sarah Lawrence College in 1981 and received a Master's Degree in Speech and Communication from Northwestern University in 1985. He is married to Amy Rule, and they have three children.
