events.title: Theory Lunch Seminar - Henry Fleischmann
events.description:
Given a weighted directed graph G = (V, E,w), its minimum cut is the nonempty S \⊊ V minimizing the weight of edges from S to V∖S. Finding such a minimum cut is called the Directed Mincut Problem. Until very recently, solving this problem efficiently, that is in almost-linear m1 + o(1) time, was one of the flagship open problems in the field of fast graph algorithms. It served as a marker of the relative limitations of our techniques for directed vs. undirected graph problems.

In this talk I will describe a shockingly simple almost-linear time algorithm for directed mincut. The algorithm is more than simple enough to be covered in a graduate algorithms course, and improves on the previous best running time of ~m√n by Cen et al. [FOCS ‘21].

This algorithm was discovered by me prompting GPT-6 Astra and providing very limited guidance.

A complete exposition of the result, written by me and my coauthors Jason Li, Thatchaphol Saranurak, and Benyu Wang, can be found here:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10898.√

Talk title coming soon

Bio:
Praneeth Vepakomma is currently a Visiting Assistant Professor at MIT in IDSS and is an Assistant Professor at MBZUAI. He previously obtained his PhD at MIT in and works on trustworthy/responsible computation that includes a sub-focus on distributed (resource-efficient) and private computation in statistics, ML and data science at large. He has extensive industrial experience across Meta, Apple, Amazon, Motorola Solutions, Corning and several startups. His research focuses on developing algorithms for distributed computation in statistics & machine learning under constraints of privacy, & efficiency.

He won the Meta PhD research fellowship in Applied Statistics, two SERC Scholarships (for Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing) from MIT’s Schwarzman college of computing. He co-founded a research based non-profit (Integrity Distributed) that won the Financial Times Digital Innovation Award. He won a Best Student Paper Award at FL-IJCAI, a Baidu Best Paper Award at NeurIPS-SpicyFL and a Best Paper Runner Up Award at FG-2021. His technical work is inspired by foundations of non-asymptotic statistics, randomized algorithms, learning augmented algorithms, combinatorics, and at times just by systems design. He was Interviewed in the book, ‘Data Scientist: The Definitive Guide to Becoming a Data Scientist’ and has organized several workshops at ICLR, ICML, IJCAI, CVPR and NeurIPS.

Bio:

Andrew Ilyas is an assistant professor at CMU. events.title: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)
events.description:
Speaker: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)

Topic: Where do stars explode in the ISM? A new constraint on stellar feedback models

Abstract: In this talk, I will present the first set of direct observational constraints on where stars explode in the interstellar medium (ISM) from high-resolution surveys of nearby galaxies with JWST, HST, VLA, ALMA and VLT/MUSE. Explosions of stars, i.e. supernovae (SNe) are the main regulators of star-formation in galaxies. They achieve this most directly by launching winds, which remove cold star-forming gas from the ISM, and creating pressure in the ISM by supplying heat, turbulence and cosmic rays. The efficiency of these processes depend sensitively on the environments where SNe occur, particularly the correlation between SNe and dense gas clouds. While there is evidence of SN shocks interacting with molecular clouds, the ionizing radiation and stellar winds from massive stars can quickly unbind and disperse dense clouds before SNe occur. How these different feedback channels limit star-formation in molecular clouds and launch winds is one of the biggest open questions in galaxy evolution. I will discuss how we can address this topic with the novel method of observations of evolved massive stars and supernova remnants in the Local Volume, supplied by high-resolution multiwavelength surveys like PHANGS, LGLBS and SDSS. I will also show preliminary comparisons with hydrodynamical simulations of galaxies to show how these observations can serve as valuable checks on the underlying stellar feedback models.

events.title: Fall Sophomore Open House
events.description:
Did you know that there is a CMU alumni network you can start tapping into while you’re still on campus? Come find out how to make connections now and keep building those relationships long after graduation.

Stop by the Fall Sophomore Open House anytime between 5:30 and 7 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29 to learn more.

Here’s what you can expect:

- Tips for connecting with alumni, whether you’re just getting started or exploring what’s next
- Fall-themed treats and refreshments, music and lawn games (no tricks, just treats!)
- A free CMU Alumni Association-sponsored giveaway for every attendee (free swag, anyone?)
- PLUS, a chance to win a Personal Brand Boost: a professional photo session, social media pro tips and a mini-session with an executive communication and networking coach

Questions? Contact CMUevents@andrew.cmu.edu.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)
---

events.title: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress
events.description:
This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

events.description:
A year-long, cohort-based leadership development program for new and returning department heads, associate deans and other academic leaders.

In today’s higher education environment, effective leadership is critical. Academic leaders must navigate complex administrative demands while fostering trust, managing conflict, and leading teams with agility and empathy.

Learn more about the program and meet the cohort.

Diana Dumitru, Ion Ratiu Professor

Hiding Patterns: Evasion and

Postwar Justice between Romania

and the Soviet Union

As Soviet forces returned to Bessarabia in 1944, many Holocaust

perpetrators sought to evade postwar accountability through flight,

concealment, or crossing the Romanian border. This paper follows forty

perpetrators implicated in the July 1941 massacre of over 300 Jews in a

Bessarabian village, who were split between Romanian and Soviet

jurisdictions by the postwar border. What determined whether evasion

succeeded: citizenship, mobility, local ties, or the structures of the pursuing

states? One crime, one cohort, divided by a single border. What accounted

for their radically different fates?

Why did ordinary young women from interwar Poland leave everything

behind to fight for Republican Spain? Through interconnected biographies, this

paper examines how class, gender, education, and ethnicity shaped women’s

paths toward political radicalization, socialism, and communism. Some

encountered radical politics through universities, travel, and intellectual

circles; others through hospitals, factories, poverty, and prison. Despite varied

trajectories, their paths converged in Spain, where commitments to socialism,

communism, and above all anti-fascism gave political meaning to experiences

shaped by inequality, care, and social change.

events.title: Student Recital: Ziyu Cai
events.description:
Ziyu Cai, piano

Program

J.S. Bach – French Suite No. 5 in G Major, BWV 816

Ludwig van Beethoven – Piano Sonata No.2 in A Major, Op. 2 No. 2

Robert Schumann – Piano Sonata No.1 in F-sharp minor, Op.11

Cost: Free and open to the public, no tickets required.

Ziyu Cai is currently a piano performance student in the Advanced Music Studies program at Carnegie Mellon University, where he studies under Professor Sergey Schepkin. He previously earned a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence from Peking University and a Master of Science in Music Technology from Carnegie Mellon University.

Originally active as a pop musician, Ziyu discovered his love for classical music during his undergraduate years at Peking University. As president of PKU Piano, he soon became an active performer in the university’s classical music community. He made his concerto debut with the Peking University Symphony Orchestra, performing Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2 as the orchestra’s first piano soloist in recent years. He also presented a recital at Peking University Hall, featuring Chopin’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in collaboration with the Peking University String Quartet.

Ziyu has won numerous prizes in piano competitions. Over the past season, he won the Wenzhou Piano Competition, performing Beethoven Piano Concerto No. 3 with the Wenzhou Symphony Orchestra, as well as the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh Concerto Competition, performing Schumann Piano Concerto with the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh. He was also named the winner of the All University Orchestra Concerto Competition and is scheduled to perform Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with the orchestra in spring 2027.

Ziyu has previously studied with Luz Manriquez and Frederic Chiu at Carnegie Mellon University. Alongside his piano studies, he works as a research assistant with Professor Roger Dannenberg, focusing on score-following research.

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: A Night of Italian Opera
events.description:
Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Crystal Manich, Interim Director of Opera Studies

Matthew Kereama, director

On April 14th at Carnegie Music Hall, the philharmonic will team up with the School of Music’s opera department to present a gala-style concert of Italian opera. Conducted by Director of Orchestral Studies, Daniel Nesta Curtis, and directed by Matthew Kereama, the program will feature vocalists from the School of Music in select arias, ensembles, and scenes from famous operas. The first half will feature music from Gioachino Rossini’s Il Barbiere di Siviglia and L’Italiana in Algeri along with Gaetano Donizetti’s Don Pasquale and Lucia di Lammermoor. The second half will feature a condensed, 1-hour version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Boheme, focused on the opera’s 4 main characters.

Program:

Gioachino Rossini – Excerpts from Il Barbiere di Siviglia Overture

Gioachino Rossini – Act I Finale from L’italiana in Algeri

Gaetano Donizetti – Act III Duet: “Tornami a dir che m’ami” from Don Pasquale

Gaetano Donizetti – Excerpts from Lucia di Lammermoor

Giacomo Puccini – “BoheMedley”

$10 Regular Admission

$5 Senior Citizen (65+) Admission

All students, along with CMU/Pitt faculty and staff, are free w/ valid ID

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: Halloween at Heinz Hall
events.description:
On Halloween, the Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic will perform a free concert for the Pittsburgh community at Heinz Hall. This 80-minute program, designed for families and audience members of all ages will be led by Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

The Halloween-themed event includes spooky standards like Modest Mussorgsky’s Night on Bald Mountain (conducted by CMU Philharmonic Associate Conductor, John William Brink) and Paul Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. The concert will also feature wizard of the keyboard, Tino Cardenes (current Music and Technology student of the School of Music and winner of the Philharmonic Soloist Competition, undergraduate division) performing Nikolai Kapustin’s jazzy Piano Concerto No. 2. The heart of the program is Manuel de Falla’s magical El Amor Brujo, which includes the famous “Ritual Fire Dance.” This performance will feature recent graduate of the School of Music, mezzo-soprano Isabelle Hoyou. Kids are encouraged to come in costume and arrive early for pre-concert fun in the lobby.

Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

John William Brink, associate conductor

Tino Cardenes, piano

events.title: Masterclass: Valerie Coleman & Monica Ellis
events.description:
Valerie Coleman, flute

Monica Ellis, bassoon

Valerie Coleman is regarded by many as an iconic artist who continues to pave her own unique path as a composer, GRAMMY®-nominated flutist, and entrepreneur. Highlighted as one of the “Top 35 Women Composers” by The Washington Post, she was named Performance Today’s 2020 Classical Woman of the Year, an honor bestowed to an individual who has made a significant contribution to classical music as a performer, composer or educator. Her works have garnered awards such as the MAPFund, ASCAP Honors Award, Chamber Music America’s Classical Commissioning Program, Herb Alpert Ragdale Residency Award, and nominations from The American Academy of Arts and Letters and United States Artists. Umoja, Anthem for Unity was chosen by Chamber Music America as one of the “Top 101 Great American Ensemble Works” and is now a staple of woodwind literature.

Bassoonist Monica Ellis is a founding member of the Grammy nominated wind quintet, Imani Winds, who in their 23rd season, continue to make ground-breaking art while maintaining a vigorous international touring schedule.

Monica’s strong work ethic was instilled very early on from her mother and father, the late jazz saxophonist, Clarence Oden. As the administrative director & tour manager for Imani Winds, and Co-Artistic Director for the Imani Winds Chamber Music Festival, she maintains a fulfilling leadership role within group.

events.description:

Matilda Kaul, violin

Jessica Thompson, viola

Angela Park, cello

Praised by The New Yorker as “a fresh and vital young participant in what is a golden age of American string quartets,” the Daedalus Quartet has established itself as a leader among the new generation of string ensembles. Since winning the top prize in the Banff International String Quartet Competition, they have performed in many of the world’s leading musical venues including Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center, the Library of Congress, the Gardner Museum, and abroad at Vienna’s Musikverein, the Salzburg Mozarteum, the Concertgebouw, the Cité de la Musique in Paris, as well as in leading venues in Japan.

The Daedalus Quartet has won plaudits for its adventurous exploration of contemporary music including commissions of Fred Lerdahl’s Third String Quartet and Chaconne, Joan Tower’s White Water, Huck Hodge’s The Topography of Desire, David Horne’s Flight from the Labyrinth, and Vivian Fung’s Frenetic Memories.

Since 2006, the Daedalus Quartet has served as Quartet-in-Residence at the University of Pennsylvania where they are recognized for their innovative programming and interdisciplinary collaborations, particularly in their Beethoven Quartet cycle, Music and Migration, Hearing Women’s Voices and Bartok’s Monster projects.

events.title: Guest Recital: How to See Know and Fall
events.description:
How to See Know and Fall is a collaboration between interdisciplinary percussionist/composer Brian Shankar Adler and electronic composer/software designer Jesse Stiles, combining intricate hybrid percussion with shimmering synth lines, ambient textures, and immersive visuals.

Live performances transform the stage into a dreamlike audiovisual environment where polyrhythms collide with live video, weaving data and performance into a visceral tapestry of sound and light. By bridging far-reaching rhythmic traditions, cutting-edge electronics, and critical explorations of emerging technologies, How to See Know and Fall offers audiences a revelatory experience at the cross-hairs of music, technology, and digital art.

BRIAN SHANKAR ADLER is a widely recognized percussionist and composer who blurs genre lines to create deeply expressive rhythmic landscapes. He has performed in settings ranging from glacial ice fields to Lincoln Center, showcasing his innovative approach to percussion around the globe. With commissions from chamber ensembles and collaborations in opera, dance, and beyond, Adler pursues a vision that intertwines technical precision with human connection.

JESSE STILES, formerly Associate Professor of Sound Media at the CMU School of Music, is an electronic composer, performer, and software designer whose immersive sonic environments have been presented at Carnegie Hall, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and beyond. As the Music Supervisor for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, he produced and performed in hundreds of concerts featuring the works of leading avant-garde composers. Currently an Associate Professor at the Penny W. Stamps School of Art & Design, Stiles continues to push the boundaries of interactive media and sound design.

events.title: Jason Hirata: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

Join us for an evening with artist Jason Hirata as he shares an in-depth look at his practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

REGISTER NOW

About the Artist

Jason Hirata (born 1986, Seattle, WA; lives in New Jersey) performs an artistic ambiguity that parallels his personal comfort with indirectness, abstraction, and indeterminacy. Artistically, this invites interpretation. Psychologically, it might function as defense, avoidance of emotional exposure, and dissociation. Intentional ambiguity can foster reflection and collective engagement, but overuse of vagueness may impair clarity in personal relationships and professional collaboration. Role fluidity enables experimentation and boundary navigation, but identity fusion may scuttle the definition of self and direct assertiveness. Hirata has shown at Ulrik, New York; Fanta-MLN, Milan; CCS Hessel Museum of Art, Annandale-On-Hudson, New York; Fluentum, Berlin; Simian, Copenhagen; Paid, Seattle; Theta, New York; The Wig, Berlin; B. Beamesderfer Gallery, Highland Park, New Jersey; Billytown, The Hague; Artists Space, New York; 80WSE, New York; Svetlana, New York; Veronica, Seattle, and elsewhere.

Finding Kresge Theatre

Kresge Theatre is located in the College of Fine Arts building on the south end of CMU’s campus (near the Hunt Library). To find the theatre, enter the College of Fine Arts building from the west (main) entrance closest to the College of Fine Arts Lawn. Street parking is available along Frew and Tech streets or in CMU’s East Campus Garage.

About If the word we: 59th Carnegie International

On view May 2, 2026, through January 3, 2027

Organized every four years by Carnegie Museum of Art, the Carnegie International is the longest-running exhibition of international art in North America. events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

Join us for an evening with artist Jonathan González as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the work featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

The Strikebreakers

The Strikebreakers is a new site-specific, four-hour performance conceived for the Grand Staircase of Carnegie Museum of Art. Performed by five dancers over five consecutive days, the work unfolds as a slow transformation of bodies, relationships, and collective attention, using the museum’s architecture as both stage and collaborator.

Drawing its title from the complicated history of labor, industry, and Western Pennsylvania, The Strikebreakers does not seek to reenact a historical event. Instead, it approaches the figure of the worker as a choreographic proposition: a body shaped by repetition, endurance, care, fatigue, solidarity, and the continual negotiation between individual agency and collective responsibility. Historical archives surrounding labor movements and Black social life circulate throughout the work not as illustrations, but as conditions that quietly inform its movement, rhythm, and atmosphere.

The performance is less concerned with representing history than with asking how history continues to move through bodies in the present. The title also resonates with the legacy of the 1892 Homestead Strike and the histories of labor surrounding Andrew Carnegie’s industrial empire, while opening the work toward broader questions of collective action and social choreography.

About the Artist

Jonathan González (b. 1988, Queens, NY; lives in New York, NY) is an interdisciplinary artist whose work spans choreography, sound, image, writing, video, and collective practice. Their artistic research engages themes of memory, Black geographies, and African diasporic temporalities, often through site-specific and durational performance. By combining movement, sound, and image, González creates works that explore embodiment as both a record of history and a rehearsal for the future. González has presented work nationally at major institutions, including Spectral Dances (American Academy of Arts and Letters, 2024), a durational performance and sonic installation, and perejil (Crystal Bridges Museum of Art / The Momentary, 2022), a performance and video installation presented in the exhibition Entre / Between. Their writing extends their choreographic and visual investigations, with a forthcoming book, Ways to Move: Black Insurgent Grammars, to be published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2025. González is the recipient of major awards, including the Herb Alpert Award in the Arts (Dance, 2024), the MAP Fund (2024), and the Foundation for Contemporary Arts Grants to Artists (Performance Art / Theater, 2019). Their practice foregrounds hybridity and collaboration, positioning collective action as both an artistic method and a social intervention.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal - Yilin Wu
events.description:
Date: October 26, 2026
Time: 10:00-11:30 AM ET
Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal
Zoom Link
Location: NSH 4305
Title: Reconciling Adaptation and Generality in Robot Policies

Who: Yilin Wu
Abstract:

Generalist robot policies—such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)—are trained end-to-end on large observation-action datasets and can perform increasingly diverse manipulation tasks. Yet these policies remain unreliable amid the complexity of real environments and user contexts. A common remedy is to finetune the entire policy for a particular deployment, but this may degrade the pretrained capabilities that make generalist policies valuable. This raises the central question of this thesis: how should robot policies be adapted to particular users and environments while preserving their generality?

This thesis argues that maximizing adaptation while minimizing loss of generality requires identifying what should be adapted and choosing how to adapt it in the least invasive way. For example, a deployment may call for changes to the task specification (what the user wants done), the state representation (which aspects of the scene matter for the task), or the behavioral support (the range of actions the policy can produce). At each of these levels, the desired behavior may already lie within the policy’s pretrained capabilities and only need to be elicited, or the policy may need to acquire new knowledge or skills through additional training.

We study two corresponding adaptation mechanisms: inference-time steering, which guides pretrained action distribution toward the target while keeping policy parameters fixed, and targeted training, which learns additional context or behaviors through limited parameter updates. For steering, we first propose language-based verification methods that check generated actions against user instructions and reasoning plans. Next, to handle incomplete state information in contact-rich manipulation, we introduce a bi-level visual and tactile steering algorithm. Third, to steer the action distribution in open-world settings, we contribute a world model that predicts the consequences of candidate behaviors while balancing fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference efficiency.

Steering, however, can only elicit behaviors the pretrained policy already supports. We turn to targeted training methods with parameter-efficient updates to improve the base policy via learning a compact multi-stream memory that conditions the policy on history-dependent state, and residual policies that incorporate user corrections to expand the policy’s behavioral capabilities. Finally, the proposed work revisits the role of meta-learning for adapting generalist robot policies. We propose separating shared representation learning across tasks from task-specific action learning using limited demonstrations. The goal is adaptation with fewer demonstrations and trainable parameters, with explicit retention of pretrained capabilities

Andrea Bajcsy (Chair)
Guanya Shi
Oliver Kroemer

events.title: Controllable, Efficient and Personalized Generative AI: From Long-Horizon Video to Interactive World Models
events.description:
Abstract: Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms of control, generate over extended horizons within practical computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a central question: How can we make visual generation controllable, efficient, and personal?
I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First, Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next, VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of extended generation by learning compact representations of past context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate them.
I will close with broader directions for video generation, including new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26). This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography, supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact with them.

Bio: Pinar Yanardag is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive world models. She earned her PhD from Purdue as a Fulbright Fellow and was a postdoctoral researcher at the MIT Media Lab, where her generative AI projects attracted over one million participants and media coverage from TIME, The Washington Post, and CNN. She received an NSF CAREER award for her research on generative cinematography and was recognized as an Outstanding Area Chair at CVPR 2026. Her research is supported by industry partners including Google, Adobe, Snap, and Qualcomm.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal - Chen Wu
events.description:
Date: October 28, 2026
Time: 11:00 AM -12:30 PM ET
Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal
Zoom Link
Location: NSH 3305
Title: Learning to Explore and Learning from Exploration for Language Models
Who: Chen Wu
Abstract:

Learning from experience offers a way for language models to improve beyond the solutions available in their training data. Instead of relying only on demonstrations, a model can attempt problems, receive feedback, and learn from the outcomes. This process takes many forms, such as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, search at test time, training via self-improvement, and the integration of knowledge that arrives after training. In all of these scenarios, two capabilities matter: (1) exploring a broad range of solutions, and (2) learning from exploration to improve future performance. In practice, both still remain challenging — models often repeat similar attempts even when they fail, and learning from their outcomes is difficult when feedback is unreliable or when updates degrade existing capabilities. This thesis develops methods to address both challenges.
For learning to explore, we study why language models generate a narrow range of solutions and how to encourage broader exploration. We first examine the role of training objectives in simple algorithmic tasks, finding that next-token prediction is myopic, while multi-token objectives and input-side randomness produce more diverse and original outputs. We then study the effect of post-training, which concentrates a model’s reasoning into a small number of modes. We introduce mode-conditioning (ModC), which makes these modes controllable and allocates test-time samples across them.
For learning from exploration, we study how models can provide useful feedback to themselves when exploring and can incorporate new experience without losing existing capabilities. We first introduce self-trained verification (STV), which teaches a model to identify errors in its own solutions. The resulting verifier improves reasoning through iterative refinement, especially on hard problems. We then address the problem of forgetting when learning from new experience. We show that the degradation caused by off-policy training is not inherent to the data, but depends on how the update is applied. We therefore introduce grafting, which learns the update on an earlier checkpoint and transfers it to the post-trained model while masking the directions to which the post-trained model is most sensitive. Grafting outperforms more complex and expensive baselines on both new and old tasks.
Building on these results, the proposed work continues under the two directions. For learning to explore, I will study how to guide exploration on problems beyond a model’s current ability, with hints, reference solutions, and verifier feedback, without the model depending on or exploiting the guidance. For learning from exploration, I will study how new experience can be integrated with pretrained knowledge so that the two compose, and how a model can learn more from less experience by learning how to learn.

events.description:
Who: Sriram Narayanan
Type: RI Thesis Proposal
Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026
Time: 02:00PM – 03:30PM (ET)
Location: NSH 4305
Zoom link: Here
Title: Thermal Computational Imaging through Light and Heat Transport
Abstract:
Computer vision seeks to understand the physical world from images, yet much of this understanding remains rooted in the appearance of reflected visible light. Objects also absorb and emit radiation, exchange heat with their surroundings, and change their temperature over space and time. These processes encode information about materials, geometry, and physical interactions that conventional visible cameras often cannot access. Thermal imaging makes aspects of this energy exchange observable, opening new possibilities for computational imaging.
This dissertation develops a physics-based framework for thermal computational imaging by treating light and heat transport as complementary sources of scene information.
Observations across wavelength and time depend differently on geometry, materials, illumination, and temperature. Connecting these observations through physical models helps distinguish scene properties that remain ambiguous in individual measurements.
We develop this premise through a sequence of inverse problems. Spectral and temporal thermal observations enable separation of radiation emitted by an object from radiation reflected from its surroundings, supporting temperature recovery even when material emissivity is unknown. Next, we show how the thermal consequences of absorbed light complement visible reflection, allowing surface reflectance and shading to be separated without explicitly recovering geometry or lighting. We then establish heat conduction as a geometric cue, recovering three-dimensional shape from the spatial relationships governing temperature evolution across dark, textured, and visibly transparent objects. Combining conduction with shading further allows local shape ambiguities to be resolved through their complementary geometric constraints.
The proposed work extends these connections into thermal simulation within VisionSIM, linking scene illumination, transient heat transport, emitted and reflected radiation, and sensor dynamics to predict thermal observations. Together, the completed and proposed work connect scene reconstruction and image synthesis through the coupled physics of light and heat. They establish energy exchange as both a source of constraints for recovering scene properties and a basis for predicting thermal observations.

Aswin Sankaranarayanan
Ioannis Gkioulekas

events.description:
In this fireside chat, iii faculty member Susanna Zlotnikov speaks with Nickey Skarstad, a senior director of product at Duolingo, about the culture behind making the world’s No. 1 language learning app.

​Skarstad will give us a look into the organizational practices that cultivate Duolingo’s unique innovation culture and what a typical day looks like for Duos building personalized experiences for over 40 million users world-wide.

​There will be 30 minutes to hear from our co-hosts, and 15 minutes for Q&A.

events.title: Teaching Inclusively: Creating Trust in the Classroom
events.description:
A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

Do you trust your students, and do your students trust you? These questions are critical to building a supportive environment for learning in your classroom. In this seminar, we will review various ways to conceptualize trust in a learning environment and share research on why trust is essential to learning from K-12 to higher education. Finally, we will explore various actions instructors can take to build and show trust in their classrooms. Participants should expect to leave with a series of implementable “teaching moves” that foster and demonstrate trust in the classroom.
events.summary: A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

events.title: Faculty Insights with Joe DeCarolis
events.description:
Please join us for CMU Engineering’s virtual program, “Faculty Insights: A 20 Minute Briefing.” In this series, faculty will share insights into their research, its impact, and provide perspective for the future of the field. Following the presentation, attendees will have an opportunity to direct questions and comments to the speaker.

“Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions”

Rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers could substantially increase U.S. power sector emissions and electricity costs by 2030, with particularly large impacts in regions such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Using a detailed energy model covering 26 interconnected U.S. power regions, we evaluate how demand growth, fuel prices, and federal policies affect electricity generation, infrastructure investment, and costs. Data centers could push U.S. power sector carbon emissions up by as much as 28% and spike regional electricity costs by up to 57% by 2030.
events.summary: Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions

Graduate school can demand a lot of you—but becoming a more effective student doesn’t require completely reinventing how you study. In this practical workshop, you’ll learn how small, consistent changes can lead to meaningful improvements in your academic habits and productivity.

We’ll explore strategies including habit stacking, reflection routines, weekly reviews, tiny improvements to your study practices, and consistency over intensity. You’ll have the opportunity to identify what’s working, pinpoint one area you’d like to improve, and create a simple plan for a small change you can put into practice immediately.

Learning Objectives:

Discover practical strategies for building sustainable study habits.

Create a simple weekly reflection and review routine.

Learn how to make your existing study practices more efficient.

Learn how to practice consistency over intensity.

Personalize “on small change” for immediate implementation.

This is an in-person workshop.

events.title: Slow Looking: A Photo Walk and Journaling Session in Schenley Park
events.description:
Slow down, look closely, and discover what you might otherwise walk past.

Join Wellness & Meaning-Making Programs and the CMU Sustainability Initiative for Slow Looking: a photo walk and journaling session in Schenley Park. Together, we’ll explore how paying attention to the natural world can create opportunities for reflection, connection, and care for ourselves and our surroundings.

This guided outdoor walk combines contemplative practice with photography and written reflection. You’ll take a small number of photos of things that catch your attention or evoke an emotional response, then write a short introspective caption for each. Photos will be printed on site.

All are welcome. No prior mindfulness, photography, or journaling experience is needed.

Please RSVP through our Google Form: https://forms.gle/4HCzjaRkrWGKBLUf7

Registration is collected only through this form.

Wear comfortable walking shoes and dress for the weather.

Questions or access needs? Contact Michael Tumminia at mtummini@andrew.cmu.edu or Imama Zahoor at izahoor@andrew.cmu.edu.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)
---

events.title: Ghosting Adobe: Open Source Alternatives in Desktop Design and Publishing
events.description:
Worried about paying for an Adobe subscription when you lose your student license? Or just looking to pick up some basic techniques for digital multimedia work?

This workshop will introduce students to some of the most widely used, professional-grade open source alternatives to Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign. We will discuss interoperability and go over primary features of each tool. After a crash course in suggested workflows, students will have the opportunity to test out the tools with a design activity.

If you would like to follow along on your own machine and participate in the charrette, please bring your laptop. We will be reviewing Gimp, Inkscape, and Scribus. All three programs are available for free download for Linux, Windows, and Mac operating systems; please review install requirements and make sure you have enough available space.

No previous experience with Adobe (or non-Adobe) software is required for this workshop.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Using AI-supported tools for literature searching
events.description:
Are you using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT to find scholarly articles? Join us for this workshop to discover AI-powered research tools available through the library that are designed specifically for scholarly research.

Learn how tools such as Consensus, Keenious, Scite.ai and Scopus AI can help you avoid hallucinated citations while connecting you directly to real scholarly literature. Built on the same powerful large language model technology as general-purpose AI assistants, these tools operate within trusted scholarly databases and integrate more seamlessly with library subscriptions, making it easier to access full-text articles. You'll also see how these tools use citation networks to uncover connections between papers, helping you identify influential research and discover related studies. Advanced filtering options—including publication date, citation count, journal impact, and more—make it easier to find the most relevant and authoritative sources for your research.

----

events.title: Rescheduled: AI Literacy Workshop
events.description:
Are you interested in better understanding the opportunities and hazards of using AI to solve problems in the world? This workshop will introduce you to frameworks for how to apply AI responsibly and effectively. We will cover understanding users, finding AI applications that deliver value, considering data in AI systems and its impact on outputs, and risks/safety of AI applications.

Hosted by Dr. Nikolas Martelaro (HCII) and Dr. Emma Slayton (CMU Libraries), this workshop does not require you to have built AI before. However, you should be aware of some AI, and have used some of it (from using computer vision to ChatGPT). We will be working hands-on with some AI during the workshop, please bring your computers.

The workshop will take place between 5 pm and 7 pm on Wednesday October 21st.

Participants will receive a certificate for completion.

events.title: "Choose your own adventure!": Introduction to nonlinear storytelling games with Twine
events.description:
This workshop will introduce students to Twine—a free and open source tool for designing and making interactive stories. Through visual mapping and a text-based editor, users can craft stories that respond to user input as well as randomized and timing-based behavior for memorable, customized story experiences. Useful both for creating full interactive experiences as well as for preliminary design stages—such as storyboarding more complex stories or as proof of concept for larger games—Twine is an essential tool for those interested in interactive games and stories.

In this workshop, students will learn the basics of using Harlowe, Twine’s default story format and the most beginner-friendly. Students will learn how to form interactive fiction through features like dynamic hypertext and conditional syntax (if/else…then…) to shape their unique interactive storytelling experience.

No coding experience required; all skill levels are welcome!

events.title: Conducting Scoping Reviews to Understand the Research Landscape
events.description:
How can we find and synthesize all of the existing research on a topic when there is so much information out there? Scoping reviews are a popular research synthesis method for systematically describing the existing literature on a topic. They are more reproducible and comprehensive than a traditional literature review and can help us to understand the scope of research in an area, identify existing gaps, and surface trends and key concepts. If you are considering developing a research synthesis project for your field, or are curious about such methods and how they apply in your discipline, please join us! You'll be provided with guidance and next steps for starting a scoping review at the end of the session. This session is aimed at graduate students, staff and faculty researchers, but anyone is welcome to join.

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

Learners should bring a laptop and should already have installed R and RStudio on their computer. Installation and set-up instructions and workshop slides can be found on the workshop website.

Describe the different panes in the RStudio environment and how they are used when coding in R.
Run lines of R code from a script file to the console.
Create and store new objects in R.
Find help information for functions.
Use functions in R with appropriate syntax and arguments.
Define, create and manipulate vectors in R.

events.title: "He sat like a Senegalese": Acclimatizing Michel Adanson (1727-1806), a French Botanist in West Africa 1749-1753
events.description:
The French naturalist Michel Adanson (1727–1806) traveled to Senegal with the French West India Company in 1749, where he lived among the Wolof, learned their language, and studied their cultural practices. He also adopted their way of sitting, a posture he continued to practice after his 1753 return to Paris. His experience shaped his approach to natural history: he adopted African plant names, developed a phonetic French system influenced by his Wolof dictionary, and proposed a “natural” taxonomy based on numerous characteristics of plants and animals, including humans, rather than Linnaeus’s simpler binomial system. This talk explores how Adanson’s engagement with the Senegalese influenced the reception of his ideas in France during the Age of Revolutions.

Dr. Caulkins teaches at Central Washington University and is writing a history of eighteenth-century botanical conservatories.

RSVP

The lecture is free and open to all.
Please RSVP so we can plan for seating and catering.

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

events.description: Generative AI tools are rapidly transforming the research landscape, offering powerful capabilities alongside significant risks of bias, hallucination, and inaccuracy. Designed for researchers, academics, and students, this workshop demystifies how GenAI models operate at a high level and provides a structured approach to evaluating data source, capabilities, and outputs of AI tools. Using specialized AI-powered literature search tools subscribed by the University Libraries as examples, participants will learn about their advantages over general-purpose chatbots, explore their core strengths and limitations, apply a practical framework to examine their credibility, and discuss how to apply the framework to real-world examples. By the end of the session, you will possess the critical skills needed to assess when, where, and how to integrate GenAI responsibly into your research workflow.

events.title: GIS Day 2026: GIS for All
events.description:
Join us for a GIS Day celebration on Friday, November 13th, 2026. We are getting a head start on GIS Day, which is traditionally celebrated on the 3rd Wednesday of November as an international forum for users of GIS technology to demonstrate real-world applications that are making a difference in society and for people to learn more about Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and its benefits. This in-person, all-day event will be hosted in Carnegie Mellon University’s Cohon University Center.

The event is a day-long symposium with talks, a roundtable, map and research gallery, open house, and more. Our theme this year is GIS for All, and as always we welcome participation from a wide variety of disciplines and workplaces. We would love for you to share your work at GIS Day! We especially want students across the region to participate.

Suggested topics for talks, maps and posters include but are not limited to:

Cartographic or Interactive Application Accessibility

Community Engagement or Non-Technical Audiences

Environmental or Social Justice

Crowd Sourced Data

Spatial Tools

Personal Mapping

Transportation, Navigation, & Wayfinding

Historical or Fictional Mapping

Emergency Mapping

Digital Twins

Indoor GIS

GeoAI (including Machine Learning and Imagery Analysis)

GIS in Education

Infrastructure

Spatial Data Governance

Non-Traditional Uses of GIS (ie. Using GIS in hobbies, like crocheting maps)

Other

This event and our workshops are open to all. We hope this event is a day for people to mingle and learn. Submissions are open to anyone in the Western PA region.

We are accepting submissions for the following:

Tabling at Open House (1.5 hours in the afternoon) Organizations, companies, informal groups or people with research demonstrations can set up a table at the open house to share your services, swag or research.

Lightning talks (3-5 minutes) Short 3-5 minute talk about something you’ve been working on or think people should know.

Maps (displayed in a gallery) A map that you created. Maps should have a Title, Legend, and Cartographer credits. Please submit a final version that could be printed for the event. Screenshots of web maps will not be accepted. Recommended size: 30 inches x 40 inches (either portrait or landscape).

Research Posters (displayed in a gallery) A poster describing a research project that includes some spatial question or involves mapping or spatial analysis. Recommended size: 30 inches x 40 inches (either portrait or landscape).

Submit your work for participation by October 20th - Deadline extended to October 26th

If you have questions about submitting, we will be hosting several Office Hours in October via Zoom leading up to the submission deadline.

Notification of acceptance: October 30th

Thank you, and we look forward to getting to know you and seeing what you have been working on!

events.description:
CMUQ-Library invites you to read The Thing Around Your Neck with us for our next Book Club meeting.

The Thing Around Your Neck is a collection of short stories by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, a MacArthur "Genius Grant" recipient widely recognized as one of the most influential feminist voices in contemporary literature.

The anthology features 12 short stories collected while Adichie was completing her MacArthur fellowship and Hodder fellowship from Princeton University. In her own words, the intention behind the work was to "peel apart the layers of losses and gains that immigrants face.” Drawing on the experiences of Adichie’s own family and friends, the stories move between Lagos, Nigeria and the U.S, following characters navigating family, marriage, class, and what it means to belong, both at home and abroad.

Join us for an hour of conversation, good company, and even better food. Only 2 chapters needed!

When: Sunday, October 25th, 1-2 pm

Where: Room 1160

Chapters to Read:

Chapter 1: Cell One
Chapter 8: The American Embassy

Register now and pick up your personal copy in the library.

events.title: Getting Started with R and R Studio Part 2
events.description:
This two-part introductory workshop aims to teach basic concepts, skills, and tools for working with data in R so that you can get more done in less time, and apply concepts of reproducibility to your research. This is an introduction to R designed for participants with no R programming experience. Part 1 of the workshop covers basic information about R syntax and the RStudio interface, including installing packages and working with vectors. Part 2 will cover importing CSV files, working with dataframes, how to deal with categorical variables, how to add/remove rows and columns using the popular dplyr package, and how to calculate summary statistics from a dataframe. Taking Part 1 and Part 2 is encouraged, but optional

Learners should bring a laptop and should already have installed R and RStudio on their computer. Installation and set-up instructions and workshop slides can be found on the workshop website.

Learning objectives for Part 2:

Install packages and load libraries in R.
Import a dataset and use tidyverse functions to explore dataset attributes.
Create subsets of dataframes.
Work with categorical variables in R.
Use the dplyr package to select columns and filter rows.
Use the dplyr package to perform various operations on a dataframe such as creating new variables, splitting and combining data, and summarizing data.
Use pipes in R to string together a series of steps.
Export a data set from R Studio.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Text mining the scholarly literature
events.description:
Text and data mining (TDM) of scholarly literature can support tasks such as screening abstracts for a systematic review and analyzing how a field evolves over time. However, getting from a research question to a usable corpus can be intimidating. In this workshop, we’ll introduce scholarly APIs and how to query them, comparing open sources like OpenAlex and arXiv with publisher platforms. From there, we’ll walk through the basics of assembling a corpus, providing tips for full-text retrieval and an overview of licensing restrictions (including how to avoid common mistakes that can lead to blocked access!). Finally, we’ll demonstrate a text analysis workflow and provide you with resources that you can adapt to your own project.

events.description:
Working with the Command Line Interface

Session 3 of 5 — Code & Data Management Pt 2

Curious about that dark screen with the blinking cursor? This is your chance to get comfortable with one of the most useful and transferable skills in research computing. The command line gives you real control over your files, your data, and your time, and it works the same way whether you're in physics, biology, the humanities, or anywhere in between.

This series runs as a playground. You'll learn by doing, trying things out, making mistakes, and building confidence along the way. Every question is welcome, especially the ones you think are too basic, we are all learning together!

Who should come: students, faculty, and staff from any discipline. If you work with research data, scripts, or files, you'll get something out of this.

What you need: the only requirement is familiarity with the content from the previous workshops in this series. Having attended the earlier sessions is ideal, since each one builds on the last. (Session 1 has no prerequisites, so it's the perfect place to jump in.)

The full series (5 sessions):

Introduction to the Command Line
Code & Data Management (Part 1)
Code & Data Management (Part 2)
Automating Workflows
Using LLMs with the Command Line

Bring a laptop and come ready to practice. We'll share the slides afterward so you can focus on doing rather than taking notes. Come have fun and think about how these skills fit into your own work

events.title: Introduction to Primary Source Research with the University Archives
events.description:
Interested in using primary sources in your research? This beginner-friendly workshop introduces the Carnegie Mellon University Archives and the resources available to support archival research. Participants will learn how to identify relevant archival collections both in the University Archives and at outside institutions, search finding aids and digital collections, and use databases to locate primary sources. We'll also talk through what to expect when you actually come in for a research visit.

Not familiar with primary resources? Primary resources are records that provide first-hand account or evidence of an event, action, topic, or time period. They include materials such as letters, photographs, meeting minutes, institutional records, manuscripts, oral histories, and more.

After this workshop, you will be able to:

Identify primary sources relevant to your research topic.
Search the Carnegie Mellon University Archives finding aids and digital collections.
Use archival discovery tools such as ArchivesGrid, Historic Pittsburgh, and the Digital Public Library of America to locate physical and digital collections at other institutions.
Prepare for an archival research visit and request materials.

This workshop is intended for students with little or no experience using archives. Participants are encouraged to bring a laptop to follow along with the demonstrations and practice searching archival finding aids.

events.title: Managing and semi-automating collaborative literature reviews with Sysrev
events.description:
Are you working on or planning to conduct a document or literature review project with collaborators or students? Are you starting a solo literature review and looking to take a more systematic and transparent approach? Do you want to use large language models to speed up your review but aren't sure where to start and don't want to turn over the whole process to AI?

We'll cover all of these scenarios in this workshop using Sysrev, a highly customizable document review platform that facilitates the selection of studies and extraction of data from journal articles and other types of documents, and allows teams of any size to work together. We will recommend workflows within Sysrev and using other tools that can support a rigorous, transparent and publishable literature review project. We'll cover Sysrev's integrated LLM auto-labelling feature and other features that can help streamline and improve efficiency for large-scale literature reviews like systematic and scoping reviews, without compromising the rigor and reliability of your review.

Note that this event will not be recorded.

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

This workshop’s goal is to equip participants with the knowledge and tools necessary to write efficient, scalable code and establish maintenance practices that ensure the long-term viability of their research software projects.

Specifically participants will:

Identify the primary performance constraint (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O) limiting their current code
Use basic profiling tools to pinpoint code bottlenecks
Identify and apply appropriate strategies for versioning research datasets alongside code

No coding experience is needed. If participants have a project that they are working on, we can use that throughout the workshop. Otherwise, example projects will be provided for participants to practice these skills.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal – Chen Wu
events.description:
Date: October 28, 2026

Time: 11:00 AM -12:30 PM ET

Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal

Zoom Link

Location: NSH 3305

Title: Learning to Explore and Learning from Exploration for Language Models

Who: Chen Wu

Abstract:

Learning from experience offers a way for language models to improve beyond the solutions available in their training data. Instead of relying only on demonstrations, a model can attempt problems, receive feedback, and learn from the outcomes. This process takes many forms, such as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, search at test time, training via self-improvement, and the integration of knowledge that arrives after training. In all of these scenarios, two capabilities matter: (1) exploring a broad range of solutions, and (2) learning from exploration to improve future performance. In practice, both still remain challenging — models often repeat similar attempts even when they fail, and learning from their outcomes is difficult when feedback is unreliable or when updates degrade existing capabilities. This thesis develops methods to address both challenges.

For learning to explore, we study why language models generate a narrow range of solutions and how to encourage broader exploration. We first examine the role of training objectives in simple algorithmic tasks, finding that next-token prediction is myopic, while multi-token objectives and input-side randomness produce more diverse and original outputs. We then study the effect of post-training, which concentrates a model’s reasoning into a small number of modes. We introduce mode-conditioning (ModC), which makes these modes controllable and allocates test-time samples across them.

For learning from exploration, we study how models can provide useful feedback to themselves when exploring and can incorporate new experience without losing existing capabilities. We first introduce self-trained verification (STV), which teaches a model to identify errors in its own solutions. The resulting verifier improves reasoning through iterative refinement, especially on hard problems. We then address the problem of forgetting when learning from new experience. We show that the degradation caused by off-policy training is not inherent to the data, but depends on how the update is applied. We therefore introduce grafting, which learns the update on an earlier checkpoint and transfers it to the post-trained model while masking the directions to which the post-trained model is most sensitive. Grafting outperforms more complex and expensive baselines on both new and old tasks.

Building on these results, the proposed work continues under the two directions. For learning to explore, I will study how to guide exploration on problems beyond a model’s current ability, with hints, reference solutions, and verifier feedback, without the model depending on or exploiting the guidance. For learning from exploration, I will study how new experience can be integrated with pretrained knowledge so that the two compose, and how a model can learn more from less experience by learning how to learn.

COMMITTEE MEMBERS

Aditi Raghunathan, Chair

Jeff Schneider

Max Simchowitz

Ruslan Salakhutdinov

Yejin Choi, Stanford University

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal – Sriram Narayanan
events.description:
Who: Sriram Narayanan

Type: RI Thesis Proposal

Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

Time: 02:00PM – 03:30PM (ET)

Location: NSH 4305

Zoom link: Here

Title: Thermal Computational Imaging through Light and Heat Transport

Abstract:

Computer vision seeks to understand the physical world from images, yet much of this understanding remains rooted in the appearance of reflected visible light. Objects also absorb and emit radiation, exchange heat with their surroundings, and change their temperature over space and time. These processes encode information about materials, geometry, and physical interactions that conventional visible cameras often cannot access. Thermal imaging makes aspects of this energy exchange observable, opening new possibilities for computational imaging.

This dissertation develops a physics-based framework for thermal computational imaging by treating light and heat transport as complementary sources of scene information.

Observations across wavelength and time depend differently on geometry, materials, illumination, and temperature. Connecting these observations through physical models helps distinguish scene properties that remain ambiguous in individual measurements.

We develop this premise through a sequence of inverse problems. Spectral and temporal thermal observations enable separation of radiation emitted by an object from radiation reflected from its surroundings, supporting temperature recovery even when material emissivity is unknown. Next, we show how the thermal consequences of absorbed light complement visible reflection, allowing surface reflectance and shading to be separated without explicitly recovering geometry or lighting. We then establish heat conduction as a geometric cue, recovering three-dimensional shape from the spatial relationships governing temperature evolution across dark, textured, and visibly transparent objects. Combining conduction with shading further allows local shape ambiguities to be resolved through their complementary geometric constraints.

The proposed work extends these connections into thermal simulation within VisionSIM, linking scene illumination, transient heat transport, emitted and reflected radiation, and sensor dynamics to predict thermal observations. Together, the completed and proposed work connect scene reconstruction and image synthesis through the coupled physics of light and heat. They establish energy exchange as both a source of constraints for recovering scene properties and a basis for predicting thermal observations.

Thesis Committee Members:

Srinivasa Narasimhan (Chair)

Aswin Sankaranarayanan

Ioannis Gkioulekas

Ravi Ramamoorthi (UCSD)

Shree Nayar (Columbia)

events.title: Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing
events.description:
This Next Manufacturing seminar features a talk by Dr. Amaranth Karra, Postdoctoral Researcher, University of North Texas.

Abstract

The anisotropy of the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V additively manufactured (AM) via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) is increased by the long and textured columnar prior beta grains that typically occur despite the high cooling rates (105–107 K/s). Additionally, both AM and conventionally fabricated Ti-6Al-4V exhibit dwell-fatigue sensitivity at room-temperature, resulting in premature failure in the low-cycle fatigue regime. This work explores the design and printing of yttria dispersion-hardened Ti-6Al-4V with minimal powder feedstock preparation. A uniformly dispersed yttria with a mean particle size of∼100 nm in the Ti-6Al-4V matrix decreases the transverse size of the prior beta grains. Furthermore, STEM bright-field micrographs reveal dispersoid pinning of dislocations, and STEM EDS confirms that the dispersoids are yttria as expected. A modest increase in room-temperature microhardness is observed, and room-temperature nanoindentation creep results show a∼64% lower mean creep rate compared to standard PBF-LB Ti-6Al-4V. Additionally, a room-temperature compression test was performed to determine the respective yield strengths to study cold creep, and its implications are discussed. At normalized stresses, ODS Ti-6Al-4V exhibits substantially lower long-term creep rates, albeit with greater initial deformation. This work successfully demonstrates the use of PBF-LB to fabricate oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) Ti-6Al-4V, enabling refinement of the prior beta grains and improved long-term time-dependent deformation at normalized stresses.

Bio

Amaranth Karra is a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of North Texas. He received his Ph.D. and M.S. in Materials Science and Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on process metallurgy, additive manufacturing, and process–structure–property relationships in advanced metallic materials. His work spans laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition of refractory alloys, titanium alloys, and oxide dispersion-strengthened materials, with an emphasis on understanding defect formation, phase evolution, and process optimization using advanced characterization techniques, including in situ synchrotron X-ray imaging and diffraction. His current research investigates the additive manufacturing of dispersion-strengthened Ti–6Al–4V alloys, while his doctoral research focused on additive manufacturing of tungsten and tungsten-based alloys for extreme-environment applications.

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.

events.description:
Restored Version of the 1948 film, often described as the “Mother of all Holocaust Films.”

Director Wanda Jakubowska survived Auschwitz. She set and filmed the movie in Auschwitz and used survivors and locals in the cast. This film influenced a generation of filmmakers but then was forgotten, and surviving negatives began to decay.

This restoration from 2020 makes the film available for new generations. The pandemic limited its distribution, but now we are welcoming you to join us for the Pittsburgh premiere.

events.title: Workshop: Why We Build Worlds, by Liam Young (Unknown Fields) (After Digitalism sub-theme)
events.description:
Image

Planet City. Designer and Director: Liam Young; Costume Producer: Ane Crabtree

We have always learned the future through imaginary worlds. Long before science and simulations, before satellites traced the earth or models calculated climates, we have rehearsed the future in fictions. We have immersed ourselves in imaginary worlds to wrestle with the unbearable questions of our own making, to carry thoughts too heavy to hold alone.Fiction is not ornament, it is infrastructure, It is how meaning survives time, how it moves across centuries and cultures, how it speaks what cannot be drawn or measured. Speculative future worlds are often mistaken for prophecy. They are not crystal balls, they are rehearsal rooms, they do not help us predict the future, they prepare us for it, places where we practice becoming something else. Within their imagined streets and speculative landscapes, we test new ways of living, new relationships between humans and machines, between cities and the living Earth, between extinction and survival. We glimpse the beliefs that build worlds and those that end them. These worlds hold both our brightest hopes and our darkest fears. They are not escapes, they are confrontations that allow us to feel the weight of choices not yet made and think out loud about who we are, what we fear, and what we might yet become. In this sense, Imaginary Worlds are both born from culture and yet also give birth to it. In this workshop we explore how the worlds we imagine do not stay on the page or the screen, they leak outward, into design studios, policy documents, engineering labs, and political dreams.

events.title: Book Talk: Concrete Colonialism: Architecture, Urbanism, and the US Imperial Project in the Philippines (2025), by Diana Jean S. Martinez (After Speed / After Time sub-theme)
events.description:
Image

Concrete Colonialism traces how reinforced concrete became a material instrument of the U.S. colonial project in the Philippines, linking construction to ideas of modernization, progress, permanence, and futurity. The book reveals how architecture can impose particular temporalities by materializing a vision of the future while displacing existing ways of building and inhabiting. In relation to After Speed / After Time, Martinez’s work asks whose futures architecture constructs, whose temporalities it privileges, and how ideas of technological progress become embedded in material and spatial practices. The book invites us to reconsider architecture’s relationship to time beyond speed, efficiency, and linear notions of progress.

events.title: Live Cinema Event: New Planetary Imaginaries, by Liam Young (Unknown Fields) (After Digitalism sub-theme)
events.description:
Image

The Great Endeavour. Designer and Director: Liam Young; VFX Supervisor: Alexy Marfin

Following centuries of colonization, globalization, and never-ending economic extraction, we have remade the world from the scale of the cell to the tectonic plate. Science fiction dystopias, once read as speculative cautionary tales, are now the stage sets of the everyday, as many of us live out a disaster film in real time. In this seemingly futureless moment, New Planetary Imaginaries ventures beyond the familiar horizons of catastrophe to ask what other stories might be written into the fabric of the Earth. A sci-fi safari through possible tomorrows, the journey moves across imagined planets and speculative civilizations, cities that gather billions into a single landscape, machines that draw carbon from the atmosphere, oceans cultivated as forests, abandoned infrastructures returned to wildness, and new forms of energy, ecology and planetary engineering. Each world is a fiction, but each begins with a question that belongs to the present. What if we could remake the systems that have remade us? What might a different relationship with the Earth look like? What new urban forms, myths and infrastructures might emerge from the ruins of the old?Presented as a live cinema event, the stories unfold through a collision of live narration, moving image and sound, carrying the audience between documentary and dream, evidence and prophecy, the world we have inherited and the worlds we might yet build.

events.title: Public lecture: Smaller Architecture, by Michael Meredith (After Bigness sub-theme)
events.description:
Image

Dome with Four Occuli

Through Small Architecture, Meredith proposes a critical alternative to the monumental scale, concentration of capital, and spectacular urban ambitions associated with architectural “Bigness.” Rather than treating scale as synonymous with significance, Meredith considers an architecture that is more local, concentrated, inclusive, attentive, and deliberate. The lecture will examine what becomes possible when architecture moves away from limitless growth and the production of ever-larger objects and systems. At the same time, it will consider how emerging infrastructures such as AI data centers complicate any simple return to smallness, revealing new forms of immense scale hidden behind seemingly immaterial technologies.

events.title: "x-change" Book Launch: "2025-26: infrastructures of x-change"
events.description:
Image

Carnegie Mellon Architecture, "2025–26: infrastructures of x-change." Designed by Studio Elana Schlenker and Jordi Ng, and edited by Tuliza Sindi and Meredith Marsh.

Carnegie Mellon Architecture invites you to the "x-change" Book Launch Celebration on Friday, October 30, 2026, from 12:30-1:50pm in the CFA Great Hall.We invite you to join us as we celebrate a special 10-year anniversary of Carnegie Mellon Architecture's "x-change," our annual publication showcasing work from first-year students to Ph.D. candidates. Inaugurated in 2017 as "EX-CHANGE," the publication has since evolved into "x-change" to more pointedly reflect its role as a platform for critical discourse and reflection.Pick up your copy of "x-change," take a look back at all nine previous issues, explore past exhibitions, play the 2021 video game, and enjoy light refreshments with friends and colleagues!The 2026 "x-change" book is available in both print and digital editions. To request a printed copy by mail, please complete this form. Please only use this form if you are off campus and need to have the book mailed to you. The book is available free of charge, while copies last.About the "x-change" PublicationEach year, the publication looks critically at the ideas, methods and pedagogical frameworks that shape CM—A's programs, to position student work within broader disciplinary conversations around architectural research and practice.The publication becomes a platform for articulating the range of questions that CM—A is both framing and engaging with, as it captures its sociocultural climate while acting as a record of the depth and breadth of student work produced each year.The book was designed by Studio Elana Schlenker and Jordi Ng, and co-edited by Tuliza Sindi and Meredith Marsh. The "x-change" exhibition of work, "What's for Lunch? discursive dining around three grand challenges," was on view in the College of Fine Arts Great Hall from August 24 to September 4, 2026.2025-26 Theme: "infrastructures of x-change"For the publication's 10th anniversary, "x-change" returns in a reflexive state regarding what it has become: an infrastructure of assembly and a critical scaffold for gathering. Across its 10 years, the publication has operated less as a curated argument than as a recurring system that's part archive, part interface, and part conversation, in which diverse and sometimes conflicting practices are placed into proximity, allowing difference to exist alongside one another, toward unearthing wonderfully contradictory questions and dispositions. This volume embodies 10 years of what it's taken to stabilize infrastructural conditions of assembly across editorial shifts, material evolutions, institutional memory, collective labor, and love, and leads an optimistic path to its future.Book Team: "2025-26: infrastructures of x-change"Cover and book design: Studio Elana Schlenker, Jordi Ng; Co-editors: Tuliza Sindi, Meredith Marsh; Student team: Sanjana Bandaru, Abby Feldmann, Gabby Ferrari, Mikayla Gee, Boone Lewis, Sydney Mansavage, Sarah Molina, Ana Oliveira Furtado, Ashanti Ramirez; Staff acknowledgements: Alycia Barney, David KoltasSpecial ThanksPublication of this book has been generously aided by the EX-CHANGE Fund. Carnegie Mellon Architecture gratefully acknowledges Mark Ferguson (CFA'78) and Natalie Jacobs (CFA'79), and Desmone (Gold Sponsorship), for their generous sponsorship of this publication. Additional thanks to our individual donors: Julio C. Ascencios (P’CFA'27), Lauren A. Marx-Ascencios (P'CFA'27), Elizabeth Beryl Hager (CFA'26), Andrew Yoon (CFA'25).Published by in otherwards, the Imprint of Carnegie Mellon University School of Architecture.

events.title: Advancing the Science of AI Agent Evaluation Workshop
events.description:
Advancing the Science of AI Agent Evaluation Workshop
A Cross-Sector Workshop hosted by CMU AIMSEC and Microsoft Research

The Evaluation Gap for AI Agents
As AI agents move from research prototypes into systems that act on people’s behalf, our ability to evaluate them has not kept pace. Rigorous, shared measurement science is the foundation of accountability, and it is currently one of the field’s most significant gaps.
On October 22–23, 2026, Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University’s AI Measurement Science & Engineering Center (AIMSEC) will convene 150+ key leaders across academia, industry, civil society, and government to define shared standards and measurement science for evaluating and governing AI agents.
The program combines keynote presentations, lightning talks, panel discussions, and hands-on working groups addressing AI agent evaluation frameworks, tooling, and domain-specific challenges. Attendees will participate directly in breakout discussions that will inform open public synthesis reports for the field.
