events.title: Tepper San Francisco: Leading in an Agentic World: How AI Will Reshape Strategy, Innovation, and Competitive Advantage
events.description:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from a tool that assists humans to a network of intelligent agents capable of reasoning, planning, coordinating, and taking action. As organizations begin to adopt agent-based systems at scale, leaders face important questions: How will competitive advantage change? What new business models emerge when AI can act as well as analyze? How should companies balance human judgment, organizational design, and autonomous decision-making?

Join Tepper School of Business professor Param Singh and Coy Ross (MBA 2007), Senior Director of AI Planning & Strategy at Microsoft, for a dynamic conversation exploring the future of leadership in an agentic world. Drawing from cutting-edge research and real-world enterprise experience, they will discuss how AI is transforming strategy, innovation, product development, workforce design, and customer engagement.

Together, they will explore:

The evolution from generative AI to agentic AI

How organizations are redesigning workflows around intelligent agents

New opportunities for innovation, productivity, and growth

The leadership capabilities that will matter most in the coming decade

What executives, founders, and investors should be doing today to prepare for what comes next

Attendees will leave with a clearer understanding of how AI is reshaping business and practical insights for leading through the next wave of technological change.

Light refreshments will be served.

Attire: Business casual

Please register online by Monday, October 26, 2026, 5 pm PDT

Event Agenda:

6:30-7:15 pm - Check-in/Networking Reception

7:30 pm - Fireside Chat

7:45 pm - Q&A

8:30-9 pm - Networking Reception

Space is limited — we hope to see you there!

In this fireside chat, iii faculty member Susanna Zlotnikov speaks with Nickey Skarstad, a senior director of product at Duolingo, about the culture behind making the world’s No. 1 language learning app.

​There will be 30 minutes to hear from our co-hosts, and 15 minutes for Q&A.

events.title: Inside the Cyber Threat Landscape with FBI Pittsburgh
events.description:
Patrick Myers, Supervisory Special Agent with the FBI Pittsburgh Field Office, will offer a front-line perspective on today’s evolving cyber threats, sharing insights into how cybercriminals and nation-state actors operate—and how these risks increasingly intersect with everyday digital behaviors, at work and at home. Learn about current threat trends and how individuals and organizations can become targets.

Supervisory Special Agent Patrick Myers has been with the FBI since 2015. He is currently assigned to the FBI’s Pittsburgh Division, where he supervises a National Security Cyber squad focusing on state-sponsored cyber actors. As a special agent, SSA Myers has conducted investigations into hackers with Russia’s Military Intelligence, the GRU. SSA Myers’ work has led him to participate in investigations and in the defense of computer systems, including election networks worldwide, the Olympic Games, and U.S. critical infrastructure. SSA Myers is a member of the FBI’s Cyber Action Team (CAT), the FBI Cyber Division’s rapid response force, on call to deploy globally to bring in-depth cyber intrusion expertise and specialized investigative skills to bear in response to significant cyber events.

events.title: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Iain Cheeseman
events.description:
Research Area: analyzing the process by which cells duplicate, focusing on how the molecular machinery that segregates the chromosomes is rewired across diverse physiological contexts.

Guest Speaker: Iain Cheeseman, PhD

Professor of Biology at MIT

Core Member, Whitehead Institute

Title: “Unlocking the Hidden Proteome”

Our lab is fascinated by the molecular machinery that directs core cellular processes, and in particular how these processes are modulated and rewired across different physiological contexts. Our work has focused on the proteins that direct chromosome segregation and cell division, including the macromolecular kinetochore structure that mediates chromosome-microtubule interactions. Although cell division is an essential cellular process, this machinery is remarkably flexible in its composition and properties, which can vary dramatically between species and are even modulated within the same organism — over the cell cycle, during development, and across diverse physiological situations. To define the basis by which the kinetochore and other core cellular structures are rewired to adapt to diverse situations and functional requirements, we are currently investigating diverse transcriptional, translational, and post-translational mechanisms that act to generate proteomic variability both within individual cells and across tissues, cell state, development, and disease.

Student Invited Seminar Speaker

events.title: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Joshua Weinstein
events.description:
Research area: programming DNA to encode molecular organization

Guest Speaker: Joshua Weinstein, PhD

Assistant Professor of Medicine

University of Chicago

Title: TBA

Joshua Weinstein is a biophysicist and molecular technologist. He works on developing DNA-based technologies for high-throughput encoding and decoding of biological information with a view toward applications in biology and medicine. He has previously worked on applying massively parallel DNA sequencing to the study of immune receptor repertoires. Recently, he invented DNA microscopy, an imaging modality that uses DNA rather than light as an imaging medium in order to generate detailed pictures of how genetic diversity distributes spatially across biological specimens.

Departmental Host: Professor Kaplow

The Ask a CMU Student Webinar is an online Q&A panel series where prospective students can explore student life at Carnegie Mellon University.

Each Tartan Talk will feature our Tartan Ambassadors talking about their student involvement within academics, activities, research, the city of Pittsburgh and more. Bring your questions, and our Tartan Ambassadors will be ready to answer!

Register Now
events.summary: The Ask a CMU Student Webinar is an online Q&A panel series where prospective students can explore student life at Carnegie Mellon University.

events.title: Campus Visit (Info Session + Campus Tour)
events.description:
Join us in Pittsburgh for an Information Session and Campus Tour to learn more about academics, campus life and more at Carnegie Mellon!

Register now.

Please note the following information:

Registration is required, and be sure to complete your registration before making travel plans to ensure spots are not filled.

All times are listed in Eastern Standard Time, and registration closes 48 hours before the scheduled event.

Admission Counseling Sessions are available as an add-on to your visit, giving you an opportunity to speak directly with an admission counselor and ask questions one-on-one. Spots are limited; if available, simply select a time slot at the bottom of the registration form, and ensure that it falls before or after your scheduled Information Session and Campus Tour.

events.title: Coulter Welcome Center Closed
events.description:
The Coulter Welcome Center is closed on Wednesdays. On these days, campus tours are unavailable, and visitors will be unable to pick up campus maps or informational materials in-person.

If you plan to visit on a Wednesday when the Coulter Welcome Center is closed and there are no campus visits, Admission counselors are available in the office or by phone from 8:30 to 4:30 p.m. (Eastern Time).

Simply drop by the Office of Undergraduate Admission on the second floor of Warner Hall, or call 412-268-2082. Visitors can collect informational material and campus maps during walk-ins.

Jeannette Sutton, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the College of Emergency Preparedness, Homeland Security, and Cybersecurity at the University at Albany, SUNY. events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
events.description:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.

Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: Global Entrepreneurship Week
events.description:
Global Entrepreneurship Week (GEW) is a global movement that celebrates and supports entrepreneurship by creating opportunities for people to learn, connect, share ideas, and take action. At Carnegie Mellon University Africa (CMU-Africa), GEW provides an opportunity to bring together students, founders, alumni, industry, investors, ecosystem partners, and the wider university community around entrepreneurship, innovation, and technology. Through the Innovation Hub, CMU-Africa supports students and entrepreneurs through business incubation, mentorship, technical talent, industry connections, and opportunities to develop and test solutions to real-world challenges. GEW 2026 will build on these efforts by creating a week that brings the CMU-Africa entrepreneurship community together to explore ideas, build capabilities, connect with opportunities, and showcase what is being created.

This year’s theme “Entrepreneurs Thrive Here” reflects CMU-Africa’s ambition to create an environment where students and founders can explore entrepreneurship, develop their ideas, access the resources and networks they need, and turn ideas into meaningful solutions. It recognises that entrepreneurs thrive when they have access not only to knowledge and technology, but also to people, mentorship, opportunities, and a supportive community.

events.title: Open Source in Energy Access Symposium (OSEAS)
events.description:
The Open Source in Energy Access Symposium (OSEAS) is the first global event dedicated to harnessing Open Source technologies to accelerate universal energy access. Co-organized by EnAccess and WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, OSEAS has quickly become a flagship global gathering for open innovation in the energy sector.

The first edition took place in 2024 in Abuja, Nigeria, marking a groundbreaking moment in uniting global stakeholders.

The second edition, hosted in 2025 in Nairobi, Kenya, which drew even greater momentum.

Due to overwhelming demand from participants and partners, OSEAS is now set to become an annual event. The third edition will take place on October 26-27, 2026 in Kigali, Rwanda.

OSEAS 2026 will once again unite global policymakers, entrepreneurs, industry leaders, tech innovators and the Open Source Community to explore challenges, seize opportunities and create synergies. Based on your valued feedback, we’ve enhanced this year’s program with:

Expanded working group sessions

Dedicated poster exhibition space

Product fair

A donor roundtable

An improved hackathon experience

Site visit

Open Source technology and tools have been transforming the Energy Access landscape - enhancing interoperability, boosting cost efficiency, and ensuring high quality. However, it’s only recently that their full potential has started to shine through. By accelerating collaboration and dialogue, OSEAS 2025 aims to push us closer to universal energy access.

events.title: Department Colloquium: Dr. David Badre
events.description:
Title: The organization of neural representations for control

Abstract: Cognitive control allows us to think and behave flexibly based on our context and goals. Most theories of cognitive control propose a control representation that enables the same input to produce different outputs contingent on contextual factors. However, the computational features of these control representations that enable this flexible mapping remain unknown. In this talk, I will focus on the geometry of neural control representations that enable cognitive control. I will present evidence from fMRI and EEG showing how these representations are organized and change as a function of different task structures, over the course of a trial, and over the course of practice; and I will discuss how these changes relate to efficient behavioral control.

Takes place in rm 336B in Baker Hall. Zoom link available if you are not able to make it in person.

This focus on group reflection and discussion sets the stage for collaboratively unlearning harmful biases that might negatively impact our ability to help loved ones or community members experiencing dating, domestic violence, and sexual assault.

events.title: UVA - Darden at Virginia Investing Challenge (DVIC) Stock Pitch Competition
events.description:
We are excited to announce that Darden Capital Management will be hosting the 15th Annual Darden at Virginia Investing Challenge (DVIC) on Thursday, November 12th, 2026. This premier stock pitch competition brings together top MBA programs from across the country to compete for cash prizes and recognition.

DVIC participants are also invited to attend the networking reception on the evening of November 12th. Last year, the competition featured teams from twelve top-tier business schools, and we look forward to maintaining and exceeding that level of excellence again this year.

This year DVIC will be held at UVA Darden DC Metro at the Sands Family Grounds. Sands Family Grounds is conveniently located 30 mins from Dulles International Airport and 8 mins from Reagan National Airport in Arlington, Virginia just across the river from Washington D.C.

Tentative Schedule:
Wednesday, November 11th – Arrival at Washington DC
Thursday, November 12th – Lunch, DVIC Competition (preliminary & final rounds), and networking reception
Friday, November 13th – Departure from Washington DC

We’ll follow up again soon with additional details regarding travel, accommodations, and registration logistics. In the meantime, we kindly ask that you save the date and begin confirming interest in your MBA program.
Dress Code: Business Formal
---

events.title: UCLA - Anderson 2026 Fink Credit Pitch Competition
events.description:
The one-day event includes opportunities for students and firms to network and participate in recruiting activities in addition to the competition.

This is the premier competition for any MBAs interested in pursuing a career in credit research. All teams will have an opportunity to hone their craft, receive valuable feedback from the judges, and compete to take home a portion of the $6,000 prize pool split across the top 3 teams.

Below you’ll find a brief description of the event. You may also view the event website, and this highlight video for more information.

Who Should Apply: Teams should consist of 3-4 MBA students, with a majority of the students being first-years. We encourage diverse teams, and require that at least one team member be a woman.

What: Teams will be pitching one credit or credit-based security to a panel of distinguished judges. Last year’s participating firms included: BlackRock, Capital Group, Columbia Threadneedle, DoubleLine, Oaktree, PIMCO, Sagard | HalseyPoint, TCW, and Western Asset. Student resumes will be distributed to participating firms.

Application Deadline: 11:59 PM PT on October 16th, 2026.
Competition Date: November 6th, 2026 – A detailed agenda will be provided closer to the event.
Where: UCLA Anderson School of Management
---

events.description:
We want to offer a fun meditation session for our members to help you start the second half of the semester off right. Maybe even open your third eye. A sound bath is a guided relaxation experience in which participants rest comfortably while listening to soothing sounds and vibrations created by instruments such as singing bowls. No prior experience is needed, just an open mind and willingness to take a break. More information on what to expect will be provided before the session begins.

We have mats and other comfort supplies available for up to 17 people. If attendance exceeds 17, additional participants will need to bring their own mat, blanket, or anything else that will help them feel comfortable during the session. We also encourage attendees to wear comfortable clothing and bring a water bottle.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)

Come with the problems that tripped you up, the concepts you're still unsure about, or just the feeling that something isn't clicking yet. Work through practice problems with classmates, get your questions answered by tutors, and leave feeling ready for the final.

events.title: [ECTC] Site Visit to Optimus Technologies
events.description:
Visit Optimus Technologies, a Pittsburgh-based clean transportation company developing technology to decarbonize heavy-duty trucking. Optimus’ patented Vector System enables existing diesel vehicles to operate on 100% biodiesel (B100), reducing lifecycle CO₂ emissions without requiring fleets to replace their trucks or build new charging infrastructure.

We’ll get an inside look at how Optimus combines engineering, software, and alternative fuels to tackle one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonize. The visit will provide an opportunity to see the technology firsthand, hear about the company’s growth and commercialization strategy, and ask questions about careers and the future of low-carbon transportation.

A $5 deposit is required and will be fully refunded upon attendance. The facility is accessible by public transit. The visit starts at 10:00am - please arrive 15 minutes early.

Agenda: TBD
Dress Code: Business Casual

events.title: Immigration and the American Economy: Growth, Fiscal Impact, and Trade-Offs
events.description:
Join the Adam Smith Society for a talk with Daniel Di Martino, a fellow at the Manhattan Institute, on the economics of U.S. immigration policy. Drawing on his research, Di Martino will unpack how different immigrant groups — by education, age, and legal status — affect GDP, government budgets, and long-term economic growth, and what trade-offs different policy proposals involve.

In keeping with our mission of bringing together students and professionals to discuss and debate free-market ideas, this talk won't argue for a single "right" answer. Instead, it's designed to surface the genuine tensions at play: fiscal cost versus economic contribution, short-term versus long-term effects, and who bears the gains and costs of different labor market outcomes. The session closes with open Q&A and discussion — we want to hear where you push back.

When: Wednesday, September 30, 2026, 1:00 PM
Where: TEP 2111, Tepper School of Business
Hosted by: The Adam Smith Society, with support from the Manhattan Institute and YAF

Open to all students interested in the competition of ideas — no background in economics required.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)
---

events.title: Cornell - MBA Women in Investing Conference
events.description:
The Cornell MBA Women in Investing (WIN) Conference is designed to educate MBA students about careers in the asset management industry, where women are vastly underrepresented in investment management roles, and facilitate networking and recruiting opportunities with sponsoring firms.

Resume books of all participants will be distributed to representatives of sponsoring firms, who are hoping to identify talent for recruitment pipelines at this forum. Interested/selected students will have the opportunity to pitch a stock to judges and recruiters from sponsoring firms and to interview with firms for summer internships if selected.

More than 60 MBA students from 10-12 universities and representatives from approximately 20 top-tier investment management firms are expected to attend.

Eligibility: The WIN Conference is designed primarily for first-year MBA students graduating in 2028 who are interested in exploring careers in investment management though second years may also apply and attend. Up to 4 students can participate in the stock pitching team. WIN is an inclusive event and interested students of any sex are welcome to apply.

Apply by October 9th at 11:59 PM EST: https://cvent.me/qgdqPl

events.title: Biophilic Design Club - intro meeting
events.description:
My name is Sola Nishimura. I am founding a club called "Biophilic Design Club".

Join the first intro meeting on October 1st 5:30pm @ Posner 152.

I believe this climate crisis, at its core, is a cultural problem layered underneath an economic one. People don't love nature enough, desire a change, or know that a better life could exist, which is being fueled by the lack of financial investments into sustainable solutions. So then, what if we can make nature and sustainability something so visually and emotionally irresistible, yet something that can be so effortlessly AND practically be integrated into the daily texture of our life, so that they can begin to HOPE, and DESIRE these changes? Then, using the concept of "demand-driven market creation" (the idea that the market doesn't just satisfy pre-existing wants, it can be reshaped by creating new wants, which then drive supply side investment"), can we somehow convince society that sustainable products/solutions can very well be economically sound?

These are some activities I am thinking of for this club:
- Creating Nature Booth @ Carnival: walls covered in grass, moss, vines. Solar panels and wind turbine on the roof.
- Green fashion @ Lunar Gala?
- Starting a Green Cafe?
- Monthly "Nature time" at Schenley Park: We bring music, free tea, bubbles, blankets to lay on, drawing materials, balloons, sports activities, peace, rest, and joy
- Increase social media presence
- Creating short film about "Biophilia" and what we do as a club
- Make music that matches our vibe
- Compete in business cases
- Talk to our Government
---

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Text Mining the Scholarly Literature
events.description:
Text and data mining (TDM) of scholarly literature can support tasks such as screening abstracts for a systematic review and analyzing how a field evolves over time. However, getting from a research question to a usable corpus can be intimidating. In this workshop, we’ll introduce scholarly APIs and how to query them, comparing open sources like OpenAlex and arXiv with publisher platforms. From there, we’ll walk through the basics of assembling a corpus, providing tips for full-text retrieval and an overview of licensing restrictions (including how to avoid common mistakes that can lead to blocked access!). Finally, we’ll demonstrate a text analysis workflow and provide you with resources that you can adapt to your own project.

Tartan Tuesday participants have the chance to win prizes, like more CMU apparel, by visiting the Alumni House (5017 Forbes Ave.) Tuesdays from noon to 5 p.m. and spinning the Tartan Wheel. Note: Tartan Tuesday does not occur during fall or spring breaks.

events.title: Slow Looking: A Photo Walk and Journaling Session in Schenley Park
events.description:
Slow down, look closely, and discover what you might otherwise walk past.

Join Wellness & Meaning-Making Programs and the CMU Sustainability Initiative for Slow Looking: a photo walk and journaling session in Schenley Park. Together, we’ll explore how paying attention to the natural world can create opportunities for reflection, connection, and care for ourselves and our surroundings.

This guided outdoor walk combines contemplative practice with photography and written reflection. You’ll take a small number of photos of things that catch your attention or evoke an emotional response, then write a short introspective caption for each. Photos will be printed on site.

All are welcome. No prior mindfulness, photography, or journaling experience is needed.

Please RSVP through our Google Form: https://forms.gle/4HCzjaRkrWGKBLUf7

Registration is collected only through this form.

Wear comfortable walking shoes and dress for the weather.

Questions or access needs? Contact Michael Tumminia at mtummini@andrew.cmu.edu or Imama Zahoor at izahoor@andrew.cmu.edu.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)
---

events.title: Cookies & Conversation with Former Rep. Brian Sims
events.description:
Stop by for cookies and a relaxed, personal conversation with Brian Sims, current Vanderbilt University professor, former Pennsylvania State Representative, and the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to the Pennsylvania General Assembly. This informal hour is built for students who care about LGBTQ+ rights but aren't sure what to do next.

Are you worried about the state of LGBTQ+ rights? Want to help but don't know where to start? Curious about queer advocacy and activism? Looking for personalized advice from a queer leader? Bring those questions.

Sims has spent his career at the center of this work. He is a civil rights attorney and five-term legislator whose floor remarks on marriage equality drew national attention. He later served as CEO of Agenda PAC and led government affairs and public policy at Out Leadership. He has spoken at more than 150 colleges and universities and has twice been named to the Out 100.

There is no formal presentation and no expertise required. Come as you are, grab a cookie, and ask about getting involved, finding your lane in advocacy, balancing activism with a career, or anything else on your mind. Students from every program and background are welcome, allies included.

Thursday, October 22, 2026, 4:00-5:00 PM, CUC 335. Organized by CMQ+ with sponsorship from the Heinz Student Experience and Engagement Office.

events.title: [GBA] Finals Group Study Session - Probability & Statistics, R & Python
events.description:
What are the odds you walk into your Prob and Stats final feeling completely confident? If you're not sure, you're not alone. Somewhere between conditional probability, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and that one line of R or Python code that just won't run, almost every Tepper student has found themselves wondering what the question is even asking.

This session is here to change those odds. Our tutors were in your seat last year, puzzling over the same p‑values, distributions, regression outputs, and error messages. They figured it out, and now they're here to help you do the same, one problem at a time.

Bring the practice questions that stumped you, the formulas you keep mixing up, the code that isn't giving you the output you expect, or just the sense that something hasn't quite clicked yet. Work through problems with classmates, get your questions answered by tutors, and leave with a clearer picture of what's coming on the final.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)

events.title: Policy Analysis & Action in the Age of AI
events.description:
UPDATE: We are currently at capacity for our space. Please join us for programming later in the day if you are able to.

Join former Pennsylvania State Representative Brian Sims for a policy-focused conversation on what it takes to analyze, shape, and advise on policy, both inside and after public office. Sims is a civil rights attorney and five-term legislator who, in 2012, became the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to the Pennsylvania General Assembly, representing Philadelphia's 182nd District for a decade. His work spanned civil rights, healthcare access, reproductive rights, and government reform.

This session is geared toward students in the School of Public Policy & Management and anyone curious about policy analysis and consulting.

Sims will reflect on how legislative decisions actually get made, how analysis informs advocacy, and how his path from the statehouse to Out Leadership, Agenda PAC, and academia reveals the many roles a policy professional can play. He will also discuss how AI and emerging technologies are changing policy and advocacy work. As CEO of Agenda PAC, he directed an AI-driven research operation tracking anti-LGBTQ+ elected officials in all fifty states, a case study relevant to all students studying AI's real-world use cases.

Expect candid insight, real-world examples, and time for questions about careers at the intersection of data, technology, and public service.

Thursday, October 22, 2026, 12:30-1:50 PM, HBH 1005. Organized by CMQ+ with support from the Heinz Consulting Club and sponsored by the Heinz Student Experience and Engagement Office.

Lunch provided to registrants.

events.title: Oktoberfest with Brewmeisters
events.description:
Oktoberfest started on October 12, 1810 in celebration of the marriage of the crown prince of Bavaria, who later became King Louis I, to Princess Therese von Sachsen-Hildburghausen and concluded five days later with a horse race held in an open area that came to be called Theresienwiese (“Therese’s green”). Present day Oktoberfest has grown into a multi-week celebration in Munich and become the largest annual festival in the world, drawing millions of people every year. Many other cities around the world have created their own Oktoberfest celebrations, including Pittsburgh!

Join Brewmeisters on 10/3 from 12-2 PM at Eleventh Hour Brewery in Lawrenceville to celebrate Oktoberfest at their German Village! Event admission covers two beer tickets and two pretzels. No Horns Pizza will also have a food truck on site. From Lawrenceville we'll travel to Market Square for the larger Prostburgh celebration (more information below). Prost!

events.title: You Matter: A Community Conversation on LGBTQIA+ Health Equity
events.description:
Admiral Rachel Levine has spent her career on the distance between the care people need and the care they receive. She trained as a pediatrician and specialized in adolescent medicine. She served as Pennsylvania's Physician General and then Secretary of Health. She was confirmed as the 17th Assistant Secretary for Health at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, where she led the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps.

Her remarks will explore how health systems can better serve LGBTQIA+ patients, and what meaningful equity looks like in everyday practice. She will also address how these pressures show up outside of healthcare settings, including on college campuses.

The evening opens with brief remarks from Admiral Levine, followed by a moderated discussion and audience questions.

This event is offered alongside the Combating Hate Series from the Office of the Vice Provost for Community, Culture and Engagement.
Dress Code: Casual (jeans ok)

events.description:
Culturally Responsive Bystander (CuRB) Training empowers participants to respond to dating violence, stalking, and sexual assault while providing culturally responsive and person-centered support through open discussion, scenario exercises, and actionable tools. CuRB explores how identity, power, and privilege impacts our role as bystanders and provides space to explore how we arrive at our understandings and perceptions of others. This focus on group reflection and discussion sets the stage for collaboratively unlearning harmful biases that might negatively impact our ability to help loved ones or community members experiencing dating, domestic violence, and sexual assault.

At Carnegie Mellon, we are committed to ensuring that every community member feels safe and protected. This focus on group reflection and discussion sets the stage for collaboratively unlearning harmful biases that might negatively impact our ability to help loved ones or community members experiencing sexual assault, domestic violence, and stalking. Learn more about CuRB training.

events.title: [O&A] ANNUAL PINK PARTY (21+) | PINK PANTHER EDITION
events.description:
💖🪩 Grab your glitter, fluff up those feather boas, and get ready to boogie 🪩💖

This year’s Pink Party is going PINK PANTHER! Think sleek, playful, mysterious, and unapologetically pink. Whether you’re serving classic Pink Panther, glamorous spy-movie chic, head-to-toe hot pink, or your own fabulous interpretation of the theme, come ready for a night of dancing, celebration, and queer joy with the Out & Allied community.

🌸 About the Pink Party
The Pink Party is Out & Allied’s signature annual celebration, a night rooted in LGBTQ+ history and powered by community joy. The color pink has long been a symbol of both queer resistance and self-expression, from the reclamation of the pink triangle as a symbol of pride to its place in today’s unapologetically vibrant queer culture. Over time, Pink Parties have become spaces where LGBTQ+ folks and allies come together to celebrate authenticity, build community, and dance the night away in solidarity and joy.

🪩 What to Expect
This year’s party will be bigger and bolder than ever:
✨ Drag Queens bringing the glamour and show-stopping energy
🍽 Food and drinks to keep the vibes flowing (Vegan, Vegetarian, GF options)
🎶 Great music to get everyone on the dance floor
📸 Photo-worthy moments all night long
💖 A night celebrating queer joy, friendship, and community

💗 Theme: Pink Panther
🎟 Dress Code: Pink, panther, anything that makes you feel fabulous
🌈 Hosted by: Out & Allied

🏳️‍🌈 💖 PARTY WITH A PURPOSE: SUPPORTING PROUD HAVEN 💖 🏳️‍🌈

This year, Out & Allied is proud to support Proud Haven, a Pittsburgh-based nonprofit that provides safe spaces, resources, and support for LGBTQIA+ youth and young adults experiencing homelessness or housing instability.

Proud Haven works to ensure that LGBTQIA+ young people have access to affirming environments, essential resources, and a community where they can feel safe, supported, and celebrated.

We're especially excited to bring our Tepper and broader Pittsburgh communities together to raise awareness and funds for this incredible organization!

Throughout the evening, we'll be sharing ways to donate directly to Proud Haven. Whether you give a little or a lot, every contribution helps support their mission of creating a safer, more inclusive future for LGBTQIA+ youth.

Come for the party, stay for the purpose, and help us turn queer joy into community impact!

🐆 💖 WHY PINK PANTHER? 💖 🐆

This year’s Pink Party theme, Pink Panthers, is inspired by the Pink Panthers Patrol, a queer community safety group formed in New York City in 1990 in response to rising anti-LGBTQ+ violence. The group became known for visibly standing up for and protecting the queer community when traditional institutions often failed to do so. Our theme celebrates that history of courage, solidarity, visibility, and looking out for one another. Pink Panthers gives us a fun, bold theme for the night while also honoring the strength and resilience of the LGBTQ+ community.

events.title: [B&T] Silicon Valley Trek 2026
events.description:
Join your fellow Tepper students for an immersive exploration of the heart of the tech industry! This October during fall break, the Business & Technology Club is organizing a career trek to Silicon Valley, where you'll get unparalleled access to some of the world's most innovative companies.

What You'll Experience
Company Visits: Get an inside look at the companies you may want to work at
Real Connections: Meet with Tepper alumni and industry professionals who can share insights about their career journeys and the realities of working in tech
Industry Insights: Learn firsthand about organizational structures, company cultures, and the diverse career paths available in Silicon Valley
Career Exploration: Gain valuable perspective that will help inform your future career decisions

Why This Trek Matters
Whether you're exploring your post-graduation career options or looking to deepen your understanding of the tech landscape, this trek offers something you can’t get from a website or recruiting presentation—authentic, personal exposure to the companies and people that define Silicon Valley. You'll return to campus with a deeper understanding of the industry and meaningful connections that could shape your career path.

Key Details
When: October 12-14, 2026 (Fall Break)
Where: Silicon Valley, California
Who: Open to MBA (FT & PT) and MSPM students
Format: In-person company visits and networking events

Deposit Policy
A $300 deposit is required to secure your spot on the trek. The deposit is fully refundable at the end of the trek if you attend all scheduled company visits on time.
If you are late by up to 10 minutes for any visit, you will forfeit 50% of your deposit for that visit.
If you are late by more than 10 minutes, you will forfeit 100% of your deposit for that visit.
If you cancel or miss a corporate visit entirely, you will forfeit 100% of your deposit for that visit.
This policy ensures fairness to companies generously hosting us and to fellow classmates who depend on everyone’s professionalism.
More information about additional company visits, registration details, and logistics will be shared soon. This is your chance to explore one of the world's most dynamic business ecosystems alongside your Tepper classmates.
Dress Code: Business Casual

Featuring Tomas Chess on oud and ney, Dariush Saghafi on santur, Siamak Salavatian on tombak, and Mohammad Reza Moradi on vocals, this concert brings together the sounds of plucked and hammered strings, flute, percussion and voice.

Date: Saturday, November 14, 2026
Time: 7:30 PM
Location: McConomy Auditorium, first floor of the Cohon University Center, Carnegie Mellon University

Members of the CMU community and guests beyond campus are welcome to join us for this evening of Persian music.

General admission: $20
Student admission: $5 cash at the door

Online tickets are available through Eventbrite with additional fees:
https://www.eventbrite.com/e/iranian-maqami-dastgahi-music-concert-tickets-2002594274383?aff=oddtdtcreator

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Using AI-supported tools for literature searching
events.description:
Are you using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT to find scholarly articles? Join us for this workshop to discover AI-powered research tools available through the library that are designed specifically for scholarly research.

Learn how tools such as Consensus, Keenious, Scite.ai and Scopus AI can help you avoid hallucinated citations while connecting you directly to real scholarly literature. Built on the same powerful large language model technology as general-purpose AI assistants, these tools operate within trusted scholarly databases and integrate more seamlessly with library subscriptions, making it easier to access full-text articles. You'll also see how these tools use citation networks to uncover connections between papers, helping you identify influential research and discover related studies. Advanced filtering options—including publication date, citation count, journal impact, and more—make it easier to find the most relevant and authoritative sources for your research.
---

events.description:
The Cornell MBA Women in Investing (WIN) Conference is designed to educate MBA students about careers in the asset management industry, where women are vastly underrepresented in investment management roles, and facilitate networking and recruiting opportunities with sponsoring firms.

Resume books of all participants will be distributed to representatives of sponsoring firms, who are hoping to identify talent for recruitment pipelines at this forum. Interested/selected students will have the opportunity to pitch a stock to judges and recruiters from sponsoring firms and to interview with firms for summer internships if selected.

More than 60 MBA students from 10-12 universities and representatives from approximately 20 top-tier investment management firms are expected to attend.

Eligibility: The WIN Conference is designed primarily for first-year MBA students graduating in 2028 who are interested in exploring careers in investment management though second years may also apply and attend. Up to 4 students can participate in the stock pitching team. WIN is an inclusive event and interested students of any sex are welcome to apply.

events.title: At the Intersection of Leadership & Allyship: How to Show Up, Even When You Don’t Know How
events.description:
Join Brian Sims, former Pennsylvania State Representative, for an evening conversation, At the Intersection of Leadership and Allyship: How to Show Up, Even When You Don't Know How. Open to the whole campus community, this session explores what effective, everyday allyship looks like and how leaders can act with courage and humility, even without a perfect script.

Sims is a civil rights attorney and the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to the Pennsylvania General Assembly, where he served five terms. He has since led government affairs and public policy for Out Leadership, directed Agenda PAC as CEO, and teaches culture, advocacy, and leadership as adjunct faculty at Vanderbilt University NYC. Drawing on that experience, he will share lessons on showing up for LGBTQ+ colleagues, classmates, and communities, whether you are a student leader, a future manager, or someone simply wanting to do better.

Expect an open, candid discussion rather than a lecture, with room for audience questions. Everyone, from longtime advocates to those just beginning, is welcome.

A reception for graduate students will follow off campus, offering a chance to continue the conversation and meet peers across programs. Please note that *only* students 21 and older can attend this reception, in conjunction with the needs of Tepper Out&Allied.

Thursday, October 22, 2026, 6:30-7:45 PM, HBH A301. Organized by CMQ+ in coordination with Tepper Out&Allied, with sponsorship from the Heinz Student Experience and Engagement Office.

Dinner will be provided to attendees

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal - Yilin Wu
events.description:
Date: October 26, 2026
Time: 10:00-11:30 AM ET
Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal
Zoom Link
Location: NSH 4305
Title: Reconciling Adaptation and Generality in Robot Policies

Who: Yilin Wu
Abstract:

Generalist robot policies—such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)—are trained end-to-end on large observation-action datasets and can perform increasingly diverse manipulation tasks. Yet these policies remain unreliable amid the complexity of real environments and user contexts. A common remedy is to finetune the entire policy for a particular deployment, but this may degrade the pretrained capabilities that make generalist policies valuable. This raises the central question of this thesis: how should robot policies be adapted to particular users and environments while preserving their generality?

This thesis argues that maximizing adaptation while minimizing loss of generality requires identifying what should be adapted and choosing how to adapt it in the least invasive way. For example, a deployment may call for changes to the task specification (what the user wants done), the state representation (which aspects of the scene matter for the task), or the behavioral support (the range of actions the policy can produce). At each of these levels, the desired behavior may already lie within the policy’s pretrained capabilities and only need to be elicited, or the policy may need to acquire new knowledge or skills through additional training.

We study two corresponding adaptation mechanisms: inference-time steering, which guides pretrained action distribution toward the target while keeping policy parameters fixed, and targeted training, which learns additional context or behaviors through limited parameter updates. For steering, we first propose language-based verification methods that check generated actions against user instructions and reasoning plans. Next, to handle incomplete state information in contact-rich manipulation, we introduce a bi-level visual and tactile steering algorithm. Third, to steer the action distribution in open-world settings, we contribute a world model that predicts the consequences of candidate behaviors while balancing fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference efficiency.

Steering, however, can only elicit behaviors the pretrained policy already supports. We turn to targeted training methods with parameter-efficient updates to improve the base policy via learning a compact multi-stream memory that conditions the policy on history-dependent state, and residual policies that incorporate user corrections to expand the policy’s behavioral capabilities. Finally, the proposed work revisits the role of meta-learning for adapting generalist robot policies. We propose separating shared representation learning across tasks from task-specific action learning using limited demonstrations. The goal is adaptation with fewer demonstrations and trainable parameters, with explicit retention of pretrained capabilities
COMMITTEE MEMBERS
Andrea Bajcsy (Chair)
Guanya Shi
Oliver Kroemer
Anirudha Majumdar, Princeton University

events.title: Controllable, Efficient and Personalized Generative AI: From Long-Horizon Video to Interactive World Models
events.description:
Abstract: Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms of control, generate over extended horizons within practical computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a central question: How can we make visual generation controllable, efficient, and personal?
I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First, Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next, VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of extended generation by learning compact representations of past context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate them.
I will close with broader directions for video generation, including new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26). This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography, supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact with them.

Bio: Pinar Yanardag is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive world models. She earned her PhD from Purdue as a Fulbright Fellow and was a postdoctoral researcher at the MIT Media Lab, where her generative AI projects attracted over one million participants and media coverage from TIME, The Washington Post, and CNN. She received an NSF CAREER award for her research on generative cinematography and was recognized as an Outstanding Area Chair at CVPR 2026. Her research is supported by industry partners including Google, Adobe, Snap, and Qualcomm.

Homepage: https://pinguar.org

AI-powered video generation platform that leverages advances in
computer vision, generative modeling, and multimodal learning to make
high-quality video creation both scalable and accessible.

Title: Learning to Explore and Learning from Exploration for Language Models

Abstract:

Learning from experience offers a way for language models to improve beyond the solutions available in their training data. Instead of relying only on demonstrations, a model can attempt problems, receive feedback, and learn from the outcomes. This process takes many forms, such as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, search at test time, training via self-improvement, and the integration of knowledge that arrives after training. In all of these scenarios, two capabilities matter: (1) exploring a broad range of solutions, and (2) learning from exploration to improve future performance. In practice, both still remain challenging — models often repeat similar attempts even when they fail, and learning from their outcomes is difficult when feedback is unreliable or when updates degrade existing capabilities. This thesis develops methods to address both challenges.
For learning to explore, we study why language models generate a narrow range of solutions and how to encourage broader exploration. We first examine the role of training objectives in simple algorithmic tasks, finding that next-token prediction is myopic, while multi-token objectives and input-side randomness produce more diverse and original outputs. We then study the effect of post-training, which concentrates a model’s reasoning into a small number of modes. We introduce mode-conditioning (ModC), which makes these modes controllable and allocates test-time samples across them.
For learning from exploration, we study how models can provide useful feedback to themselves when exploring and can incorporate new experience without losing existing capabilities. We first introduce self-trained verification (STV), which teaches a model to identify errors in its own solutions. The resulting verifier improves reasoning through iterative refinement, especially on hard problems. We then address the problem of forgetting when learning from new experience. We show that the degradation caused by off-policy training is not inherent to the data, but depends on how the update is applied. We therefore introduce grafting, which learns the update on an earlier checkpoint and transfers it to the post-trained model while masking the directions to which the post-trained model is most sensitive. Grafting outperforms more complex and expensive baselines on both new and old tasks.
Building on these results, the proposed work continues under the two directions. For learning to explore, I will study how to guide exploration on problems beyond a model’s current ability, with hints, reference solutions, and verifier feedback, without the model depending on or exploiting the guidance. For learning from exploration, I will study how new experience can be integrated with pretrained knowledge so that the two compose, and how a model can learn more from less experience by learning how to learn.

Type: RI Thesis Proposal
Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026
Time: 02:00PM – 03:30PM (ET)
Location: NSH 4305
Zoom link: Here
Title: Thermal Computational Imaging through Light and Heat Transport
Abstract:
Computer vision seeks to understand the physical world from images, yet much of this understanding remains rooted in the appearance of reflected visible light. Objects also absorb and emit radiation, exchange heat with their surroundings, and change their temperature over space and time. These processes encode information about materials, geometry, and physical interactions that conventional visible cameras often cannot access. Thermal imaging makes aspects of this energy exchange observable, opening new possibilities for computational imaging.
This dissertation develops a physics-based framework for thermal computational imaging by treating light and heat transport as complementary sources of scene information.
Observations across wavelength and time depend differently on geometry, materials, illumination, and temperature. Connecting these observations through physical models helps distinguish scene properties that remain ambiguous in individual measurements.
We develop this premise through a sequence of inverse problems. Spectral and temporal thermal observations enable separation of radiation emitted by an object from radiation reflected from its surroundings, supporting temperature recovery even when material emissivity is unknown. Next, we show how the thermal consequences of absorbed light complement visible reflection, allowing surface reflectance and shading to be separated without explicitly recovering geometry or lighting. We then establish heat conduction as a geometric cue, recovering three-dimensional shape from the spatial relationships governing temperature evolution across dark, textured, and visibly transparent objects. Combining conduction with shading further allows local shape ambiguities to be resolved through their complementary geometric constraints.
The proposed work extends these connections into thermal simulation within VisionSIM, linking scene illumination, transient heat transport, emitted and reflected radiation, and sensor dynamics to predict thermal observations. Together, the completed and proposed work connect scene reconstruction and image synthesis through the coupled physics of light and heat. They establish energy exchange as both a source of constraints for recovering scene properties and a basis for predicting thermal observations.

events.title: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford)
events.description:
Please note the unusual time.

Quantitative estimates for almost harmonic maps

Abstract: A fundamental question in the analysis of variational problems is whether functions that almost minimise a given energy, or almost solve its Euler-Lagrange equations, provide good approximations of true minimisers or critical points. In practice, one would like to understand this question not only at a qualitative level, but to obtain precise quantitative control on the distance of almost solutions to exact solutions in terms of the size of the error.

A major challenge in such a quantitative analysis of geometric variational problems is that the classical approach breaks down in the presence of singularities or changes of topology.

In this talk, we will discuss these issues for the Dirichlet energy of maps from surfaces into Riemannian manifolds for which the concentration of energy on small domains leads to a loss of compactness and the formation of a so-called bubble tree.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
events.description:
Speaker: Veit Elser, Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

events.title: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University)
events.description:
An Adaptive Variational Dual Scheme for equation solving

Abstract: I will describe a scheme for converting the question of solving a given system of equations and associated side-conditions into a variational problem whose formal Euler-Lagrange system recovers the given system and side-conditions using a change-of-variables generated by the scheme. The variational principle is convex, and the method uses a string of such convex variational principles to seek a solution of the original question as an interior minimizer of the last variational problem of the string. Weak coercivity of a variational problem in the string endows its minimizer the status of a weaker `variational dual solution’ to the original, possibly non-variational problem. This last point of view is directly related to Y. Brenier’s Hidden Convexity approach to nonlinear PDE.

Due to the inherent convexity of the scheme, it allows for obtaining `unstable’ solutions of the original, primal system of equations in a `stable’ manner. A ChatGPT-enabled exploration of the scheme in the context of approximation of the mixed curvature isometric embedding problem from R^2 to R^3 will be discussed, as well as the problem of finding deformations of a membrane with prescribed principal stretch fields. This last problem is practically important for questions of sensing and actuation.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: GSPS: Yulei Xu
events.description:
A Converse to Burke’s Theorem for a Queueing Map

Abstract: Burke’s theorem is a classical result in queueing theory, describing the preservation of Poisson departure processes in an exponential queue. We investigate a converse question motivated by the corner growth model: if a queueing transformation preserves an i.i.d. sequence of interarrival times, must the underlying distributions be exponential?

We show that, under strict stability and a natural support assumption, the answer is yes, even without assuming that the initial sojourn time is stationary. The main challenge is to recover independence between the hidden sojourn time and the observed interdeparture time solely from the process-level fixed-point property. Our approach combines a pathwise conservation identity, exponential tilting, and coupling to extract this independence from long blocks of future departures.

I will introduce the queueing map, explain the main probabilistic mechanism, and discuss its connection to stationary last-passage percolation and possible extensions beyond i.i.d. inputs.

Abstract: A seminal result of Dvoretzky-Milman asserts that every n-dimensional normed space contains an almost Euclidean subspace of at least logarithmic dimension. The exact interdependence between the subspace dimension and the distortion (i.e quantification of “almost Euclidean”) has remained unsettled for several decades. A recent AI-assisted paper of Klartag and Moshe has produced a resolution of the problem, using remarkably elementary arguments. I will present a proof of their result. If there is time left, I will talk about another recent AI-assisted breakthrough.

events.title: CNA seminar: Alpar Meszaros (Durham University)
events.description:
Equilibria and quantitative convergence for Mean Field Games of Controls

Abstract: We study equilibria in large-population stochastic differential games with interactions through both states and controls, within the framework of Mean Field Games. Focusing on general nonseparable Hamiltonians under displacement monotonicity assumptions, we investigate the existence, uniqueness, and quantitative convergence of different notions of Nash equilibria, including open-loop, closed-loop, and distributed equilibria.

A central challenge in this setting is the analysis of nontrivial consistency relations on the space of probability measures, whose structure depends on the equilibrium concept. We discuss how a careful study of these relations, combined with suitable a priori estimates, yields well-posedness and quantitative convergence results as the number of players tends to infinity. The results cover both stochastic and deterministic models, including some settings with common noise. The talk will be based on two recent works in collaboration with J. Jackson (University of Chicago) and H.J. Lam (University of Durham), respectively.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
events.description:
This exhibition inaugurates University Libraries’ newly renovated Posner Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning.

The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only. Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Public open hours will resume the first full week of the fall 2026 semester as follows:

Monday, closed

Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. (Reading Room & Exhibitions)

Thursday, 3-7 p.m. (Exhibitions only)

Learn more about University Libraries Special Collections.

events.title: Artificial Intelligence and Precision Medicine: From Traditional Machine Learning to AI?
events.description:
Precision medicine has evolved significantly alongside advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence, moving from foundational statistical models to today’s deep-learning-driven and foundation-model diagnostic tools. This talk traces that progression, examining how AI enables large-scale analysis of complex medical data to support more personalized disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Beyond the technical advances, the talk considers the broader implications of this shift—including questions of regulation, interpretability, cost, and responsibility—as AI-based tools move from research settings into everyday clinical practice.
The talk will outline how AI relates to precision medicine, introduce the core concepts underlying AI and machine learning, present how these methods are being applied in real diagnostic and clinical settings, and close with a discussion of their broader impact on health and policy.

events.title: Privacy Seminar @ HBH 1002 or Zoom
events.description:

events.title: S3D Distinguished Speakers Series: Margaret-Anne Storey
events.description:
S3D Distinguished SpeakersSeries – Joint with MSE
Wednesday, October 28, 2026
12:00 p.m. – 1:15 p.m.
In person at TCS 358
Overflow/watch room: TCS 360
Or online via Zoom: https://cmu.zoom.us/j/98473836934?pwd=Sm1ZK0dzamF4eEZHNmlGbFFYK0RmQT09
pizza provided starting at 11:45
Title: MaintainingUnderstanding in the Age of AI
Speaker: Margaret-AnneStorey, Professor of Computer Science, University of Victoria
Abstract: AI is changingsoftware development faster than our engineering practices are evolving, andyet many developers feel the pressure to adopt AI and deliver features at afrantic pace. Although AI can improve speed, emerging evidence highlightsconsiderable variability in outcomes and reveals new challenges incoordination, comprehension, and cognitive fatigue. These shifts raiseimportant questions about how teams maintain shared understanding of complexsystems, and how they remain in control as they become increasingly reliant onAI agents. As we delegate more work and decisions to agents, how do we makesure humans still understand what is happening and retain the ability toquestion, steer, and intervene when necessary?
In thistalk, I’ll explore new approaches for helping humans and AI maintainunderstanding as software systems evolve: understanding how the system works,why it was built in a certain way, and whether it still meets the intended usergoals and design constraints. I’ll share some emerging ideas for measuring andmitigating losses of technical, cognitive and intentional understanding, andconsider how we might design tools and practices that allow humans and AIagents to work together without reducing human judgement and control.
Bio: Margaret-Anne Storeyis a Professor of Computer Science at the University of Victoria and a CanadaResearch Chair in Human and Social Aspects of Software Engineering. She isco-author of the SPACE framework and a leading researcher in DeveloperExperience (DevEx). Her research focuses on how developers and teams understandcomplex software systems, and how tools, AI, and collaborative practices shapethat understanding. Her recent work examines how generative AI is transforming softwareengineering by changing how understanding is created, shared, and maintained.She collaborates with industry partners including Microsoft and DX. She holdsan honorary doctorate from Lund University.

events.title: Privacy Seminar @ HBH 1002 or Zoom
events.description:
Join weekly conversations with the architects of modern privacy—from Meta's data privacy engineers to Microsoft Research partners, from Google's cloud privacy leaders to Princeton's AI ethics pioneers. Our Current Topics in Privacy Seminar brings together the field's most influential voices, including former Big Tech privacy chiefs, DARPA researchers, and founders of privacy startups. Recent speakers include danah boyd (Cornell University), Daniel J. Solove (GW Law/TeachPrivacy CEO), and Arvind Narayanan (Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy). Whether you're exploring our program or already working in privacy, access these cutting-edge discussions in person at CMU Pittsburgh or virtually via Zoom. This isn't just a course—it's your direct connection to the privacy leaders defining tomorrow's standards.
Members of the CMU community interested in receiving notifications about the seminars each week should contact the course instructor to request to be added to the email list.
Instructor: Hana Habib
Time and location: Tuesdays, 12:30-1:50 PM. All seminars will be held in Hamburg Hall, 1002 or via Zoom: https://cmu.zoom.us/j/97389172852?pwd=Q2Q5MEE2b29TaS9VeDQ4VHVXckV2dz09

events.title: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford)
events.description:
Please note the unusual time.

Quantitative estimates for almost harmonic maps

Abstract: A fundamental question in the analysis of variational problems is whether functions that almost minimise a given energy, or almost solve its Euler-Lagrange equations, provide good approximations of true minimisers or critical points. In practice, one would like to understand this question not only at a qualitative level, but to obtain precise quantitative control on the distance of almost solutions to exact solutions in terms of the size of the error.

A major challenge in such a quantitative analysis of geometric variational problems is that the classical approach breaks down in the presence of singularities or changes of topology.

In this talk, we will discuss these issues for the Dirichlet energy of maps from surfaces into Riemannian manifolds for which the concentration of energy on small domains leads to a loss of compactness and the formation of a so-called bubble tree.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
events.description:
Speaker: Veit Elser, Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

events.title: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University)
events.description:
An Adaptive Variational Dual Scheme for equation solving

Abstract: I will describe a scheme for converting the question of solving a given system of equations and associated side-conditions into a variational problem whose formal Euler-Lagrange system recovers the given system and side-conditions using a change-of-variables generated by the scheme. The variational principle is convex, and the method uses a string of such convex variational principles to seek a solution of the original question as an interior minimizer of the last variational problem of the string. Weak coercivity of a variational problem in the string endows its minimizer the status of a weaker `variational dual solution’ to the original, possibly non-variational problem. This last point of view is directly related to Y. Brenier’s Hidden Convexity approach to nonlinear PDE.

Due to the inherent convexity of the scheme, it allows for obtaining `unstable’ solutions of the original, primal system of equations in a `stable’ manner. A ChatGPT-enabled exploration of the scheme in the context of approximation of the mixed curvature isometric embedding problem from R^2 to R^3 will be discussed, as well as the problem of finding deformations of a membrane with prescribed principal stretch fields. This last problem is practically important for questions of sensing and actuation.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: GSPS: Yulei Xu
events.description:
A Converse to Burke’s Theorem for a Queueing Map

Abstract: Burke’s theorem is a classical result in queueing theory, describing the preservation of Poisson departure processes in an exponential queue. We investigate a converse question motivated by the corner growth model: if a queueing transformation preserves an i.i.d. sequence of interarrival times, must the underlying distributions be exponential?

We show that, under strict stability and a natural support assumption, the answer is yes, even without assuming that the initial sojourn time is stationary. The main challenge is to recover independence between the hidden sojourn time and the observed interdeparture time solely from the process-level fixed-point property. Our approach combines a pathwise conservation identity, exponential tilting, and coupling to extract this independence from long blocks of future departures.

I will introduce the queueing map, explain the main probabilistic mechanism, and discuss its connection to stationary last-passage percolation and possible extensions beyond i.i.d. inputs.

events.title: PCG Reading Group: Konstantin Tikhomirov
events.description:
On the optimal dependence on distortion in Dvoretzky’s theorem

Abstract: A seminal result of Dvoretzky-Milman asserts that every n-dimensional normed space contains an almost Euclidean subspace of at least logarithmic dimension. The exact interdependence between the subspace dimension and the distortion (i.e quantification of “almost Euclidean”) has remained unsettled for several decades. A recent AI-assisted paper of Klartag and Moshe has produced a resolution of the problem, using remarkably elementary arguments. I will present a proof of their result. If there is time left, I will talk about another recent AI-assisted breakthrough.

events.title: CNA seminar: Alpar Meszaros (Durham University)
events.description:
Equilibria and quantitative convergence for Mean Field Games of Controls

Abstract: We study equilibria in large-population stochastic differential games with interactions through both states and controls, within the framework of Mean Field Games. Focusing on general nonseparable Hamiltonians under displacement monotonicity assumptions, we investigate the existence, uniqueness, and quantitative convergence of different notions of Nash equilibria, including open-loop, closed-loop, and distributed equilibria.

A central challenge in this setting is the analysis of nontrivial consistency relations on the space of probability measures, whose structure depends on the equilibrium concept. We discuss how a careful study of these relations, combined with suitable a priori estimates, yields well-posedness and quantitative convergence results as the number of players tends to infinity. The results cover both stochastic and deterministic models, including some settings with common noise. The talk will be based on two recent works in collaboration with J. Jackson (University of Chicago) and H.J. Lam (University of Durham), respectively.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Using AI-supported tools for literature searching
events.description:
Are you using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT to find scholarly articles? Join us for this workshop to discover AI-powered research tools available through the library that are designed specifically for scholarly research.

Learn how tools such as Consensus, Keenious, Scite.ai and Scopus AI can help you avoid hallucinated citations while connecting you directly to real scholarly literature. Built on the same powerful large language model technology as general-purpose AI assistants, these tools operate within trusted scholarly databases and integrate more seamlessly with library subscriptions, making it easier to access full-text articles. You'll also see how these tools use citation networks to uncover connections between papers, helping you identify influential research and discover related studies. Advanced filtering options—including publication date, citation count, journal impact, and more—make it easier to find the most relevant and authoritative sources for your research.

----

The workshop will take place between 5 pm and 7 pm on Wednesday October 21st.

Participants will receive a certificate for completion.

events.title: "Choose your own adventure!": Introduction to nonlinear storytelling games with Twine
events.description:
This workshop will introduce students to Twine—a free and open source tool for designing and making interactive stories. Through visual mapping and a text-based editor, users can craft stories that respond to user input as well as randomized and timing-based behavior for memorable, customized story experiences. Useful both for creating full interactive experiences as well as for preliminary design stages—such as storyboarding more complex stories or as proof of concept for larger games—Twine is an essential tool for those interested in interactive games and stories.

In this workshop, students will learn the basics of using Harlowe, Twine’s default story format and the most beginner-friendly. Students will learn how to form interactive fiction through features like dynamic hypertext and conditional syntax (if/else…then…) to shape their unique interactive storytelling experience.

No coding experience required; all skill levels are welcome!

events.title: Conducting Scoping Reviews to Understand the Research Landscape
events.description:
How can we find and synthesize all of the existing research on a topic when there is so much information out there? Scoping reviews are a popular research synthesis method for systematically describing the existing literature on a topic. They are more reproducible and comprehensive than a traditional literature review and can help us to understand the scope of research in an area, identify existing gaps, and surface trends and key concepts. If you are considering developing a research synthesis project for your field, or are curious about such methods and how they apply in your discipline, please join us! You'll be provided with guidance and next steps for starting a scoping review at the end of the session. This session is aimed at graduate students, staff and faculty researchers, but anyone is welcome to join.

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

events.title: Research Software Engineering: Documentation for Sustainability
events.description:
This is the fourth in a series of workshops designed to teach best practices for research software engineering to ensure reproducibility and sustainability of code developed at CMU.

Attendance at every workshop session is not necessary.

This workshop’s goal is to equip participants with the essential skills and tools to document their research software effectively and ensure that their analysis is fully reproducible by others (and their future selves).

Specifically participants will:

Design a comprehensive README that serves as the single source of truth for software setup including config.yaml, contributing.md, and requirements.txt
Implement simple practices to integrate documentation and coding standards (FAIR) into their workflow
Understand and utilize environment encapsulation tools (e.g., Docker) to manage dependencies reliably
Differentiate between user guides, tutorials, and interactive documentation, and know when to use each

No coding experience is needed. If participants have a project that they are working on, we can use that throughout the workshop. Otherwise, example projects will be provided for participants to practice these skills.
