events.title: Getting Started with R and RStudio Part 1
events.description:
This two-part introductory workshop aims to teach basic concepts, skills, and tools for working with data in R so that you can get more done in less time, and apply concepts of reproducibility to your research. This is an introduction to R designed for participants with no R programming experience. Part 1 of the workshop covers basic information about R syntax and the RStudio interface, including installing packages and working with vectors. Part 2 will cover importing CSV files, working with dataframes, how to deal with categorical variables, how to add/remove rows and columns using the popular dplyr package, and how to calculate summary statistics from a dataframe. Taking Part 1 and Part 2 is encouraged, but optional.

Learners should bring a laptop and should already have installed R and RStudio on their computer. Installation and set-up instructions and workshop slides can be found on the workshop website.

Learning objectives for Part 1:

Describe the different panes in the RStudio environment and how they are used when coding in R.
Run lines of R code from a script file to the console.
Create and store new objects in R.
Find help information for functions.
Use functions in R with appropriate syntax and arguments.
Define, create and manipulate vectors in R.

This is Part 1 of a two-part series. If you're interested in signing up for Part 2, register here!

events.title: Wrangling and managing data for large-scale literature reviews
events.description:
The amount of scholarly publishing is growing rapidly. Conducting comprehensive and rigorous literature reviews means working with large amounts of sometimes messy data from many sources. In this workshop, we'll provide some tips, tricks and techniques to help you efficiently clean and manage bibliographic data, and thoroughly document your review process, to support rigorous methods, transparency and reproducibility in the literature review process. We'll get into some advanced features of Zotero, an open source citation manager, that will help streamline aspects of literature review including running custom scripts to batch-edit metadata and auto-populate missing abstracts (no coding experience required!).

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

Note that this workshop will not be recorded.

events.title: Working with the Command Line Interface (Using LLMs with the Command Line)
events.description:
Working with the Command Line Interface

Session 5 of 5 — Using LLMs with the Command Line

Curious about that dark screen with the blinking cursor? This is your chance to get comfortable with one of the most useful and transferable skills in research computing. The command line gives you real control over your files, your data, and your time, and it works the same way whether you're in physics, biology, the humanities, or anywhere in between.

This series runs as a playground. You'll learn by doing, trying things out, making mistakes, and building confidence along the way. Every question is welcome, especially the ones you think are too basic, we are all learning together!

Who should come: students, faculty, and staff from any discipline. If you work with research data, scripts, or files, you'll get something out of this.

What you need: the only requirement is familiarity with the content from the previous workshops in this series. Having attended the earlier sessions is ideal, since each one builds on the last. (Session 1 has no prerequisites, so it's the perfect place to jump in.)

The full series (5 sessions):

Introduction to the Command Line
Code & Data Management (Part 1)
Code & Data Management (Part 2)
Automating Workflows
Using LLMs with the Command Line

Bring a laptop and come ready to practice. We'll share the slides afterward so you can focus on doing rather than taking notes. Come have fun and think about how these skills fit into your own work

events.description: Generative AI tools are rapidly transforming the research landscape, offering powerful capabilities alongside significant risks of bias, hallucination, and inaccuracy. Designed for researchers, academics, and students, this workshop demystifies how GenAI models operate at a high level and provides a structured approach to evaluating data source, capabilities, and outputs of AI tools. Using specialized AI-powered literature search tools subscribed by the University Libraries as examples, participants will learn about their advantages over general-purpose chatbots, explore their core strengths and limitations, apply a practical framework to examine their credibility, and discuss how to apply the framework to real-world examples. By the end of the session, you will possess the critical skills needed to assess when, where, and how to integrate GenAI responsibly into your research workflow.

events.description:
This two-part introductory workshop aims to teach basic concepts, skills, and tools for working with data in R so that you can get more done in less time, and apply concepts of reproducibility to your research. This is an introduction to R designed for participants with no R programming experience. Part 1 of the workshop covers basic information about R syntax and the RStudio interface, including installing packages and working with vectors. Part 2 will cover importing CSV files, working with dataframes, how to deal with categorical variables, how to add/remove rows and columns using the popular dplyr package, and how to calculate summary statistics from a dataframe. Taking Part 1 and Part 2 is encouraged, but optional

Learners should bring a laptop and should already have installed R and RStudio on their computer. Installation and set-up instructions and workshop slides can be found on the workshop website.

Learning objectives for Part 2:

Install packages and load libraries in R.
Import a dataset and use tidyverse functions to explore dataset attributes.
Create subsets of dataframes.
Work with categorical variables in R.
Use the dplyr package to select columns and filter rows.
Use the dplyr package to perform various operations on a dataframe such as creating new variables, splitting and combining data, and summarizing data.
Use pipes in R to string together a series of steps.
Export a data set from R Studio.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Text mining the scholarly literature
events.description:
Text and data mining (TDM) of scholarly literature can support tasks such as screening abstracts for a systematic review and analyzing how a field evolves over time. However, getting from a research question to a usable corpus can be intimidating. In this workshop, we’ll introduce scholarly APIs and how to query them, comparing open sources like OpenAlex and arXiv with publisher platforms. From there, we’ll walk through the basics of assembling a corpus, providing tips for full-text retrieval and an overview of licensing restrictions (including how to avoid common mistakes that can lead to blocked access!). Finally, we’ll demonstrate a text analysis workflow and provide you with resources that you can adapt to your own project.

Not familiar with primary resources? Primary resources are records that provide first-hand account or evidence of an event, action, topic, or time period. They include materials such as letters, photographs, meeting minutes, institutional records, manuscripts, oral histories, and more.

After this workshop, you will be able to:

Identify primary sources relevant to your research topic.
Search the Carnegie Mellon University Archives finding aids and digital collections.
Use archival discovery tools such as ArchivesGrid, Historic Pittsburgh, and the Digital Public Library of America to locate physical and digital collections at other institutions.
Prepare for an archival research visit and request materials.

This workshop is intended for students with little or no experience using archives. Participants are encouraged to bring a laptop to follow along with the demonstrations and practice searching archival finding aids.

When working with data, the ways in which we communicate about or discuss analysis is as important as the act of research itself. In this workshop, we will go over strategies to develop research questions tied to specific data sets, identify core elements of data that may lead to successful and fruitful analysis, as well as how to use both data and results from analysis to communicate ideas to academic and public audiences.

This workshop is a part of CMU Libraries’ Communicating Data. For other workshops in the series, please see the links below at CMU Libraries website:

Data Visualization Best Practices | September 16

Data Visualization in R | September 23

Data Visualization in Tableau | September 30

Data Visualization for Power BI | October 7

Data Storytelling | October 28

events.title: Managing and semi-automating collaborative literature reviews with Sysrev
events.description:
Are you working on or planning to conduct a document or literature review project with collaborators or students? Are you starting a solo literature review and looking to take a more systematic and transparent approach? Do you want to use large language models to speed up your review but aren't sure where to start and don't want to turn over the whole process to AI?

We'll cover all of these scenarios in this workshop using Sysrev, a highly customizable document review platform that facilitates the selection of studies and extraction of data from journal articles and other types of documents, and allows teams of any size to work together. We will recommend workflows within Sysrev and using other tools that can support a rigorous, transparent and publishable literature review project. We'll cover Sysrev's integrated LLM auto-labelling feature and other features that can help streamline and improve efficiency for large-scale literature reviews like systematic and scoping reviews, without compromising the rigor and reliability of your review.

Note that this event will not be recorded.

This workshop is part of the Advanced and Systematic Literature Review Series.

events.title: Research Software Engineering: Maintenance Practices for Sustainable, Open-source Code
events.description:
This is the final session in a series of workshops designed to teach best practices for research software engineering to ensure reproducibility and sustainability of code developed at CMU.

Attendance at all workshop sessions is not necessary.

This workshop’s goal is to equip participants with the knowledge and tools necessary to write efficient, scalable code and establish maintenance practices that ensure the long-term viability of their research software projects.

Specifically participants will:

Identify the primary performance constraint (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O) limiting their current code
Use basic profiling tools to pinpoint code bottlenecks
Identify and apply appropriate strategies for versioning research datasets alongside code

No coding experience is needed. If participants have a project that they are working on, we can use that throughout the workshop. Otherwise, example projects will be provided for participants to practice these skills.

Join us for a captivating afternoon celebrating the work of Tony nominee and two time Pulitzer Prize finalist – Sarah Ruhl. Experience a dynamic selection of scenes and monologues from Ruhl’s poetic catalogue, brought to life by the Carnegie Mellon School of Drama’s Acting Ensemble (Class of 2027) with the playwright in attendance!

Tickets are $20 general admission, $10 for full-time students and available to reserve here or by calling 412-431-2489.

Don’t miss this unique opportunity to witness the next generation of performers engage with one of the most exciting voices in contemporary theater. Thanks to Simon & Schuster, signed scripts and books will be available in the lobby for purchase via check, cash, or online donation.

The evening is directed by Ausar Stewart & Bria Walker-Rhoze and presented by the Center for New Work with support from the Richard King Mellon Foundation. The Center for New Work connects the Carnegie Mellon School of Drama and Pittsburgh’s established theaters to generate new work initiatives, creating a collaborative hub between higher education and regional theaters to sustain new live theatrical performance. Whether it be readings, workshops, masterclasses, or productions, the Center provides students for-credit and extracurricular learning opportunities to engage with leading theatremakers as they develop their latest creations. Local partners include City Theatre Company, Confluence Theater of Pittsburgh, Kelly Strayhorn Theater, New Hazlett Theater, and the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust.

Sarah Ruhl
Pulitzer Prize Finalist, 2006 MacArthur Fellow, Playwright, Essayist, & Poet

Sarah Ruhl is an award winning playwright, essayist, and poet. She has written fifteen plays including In the Next Room (or the Vibrator Play), The Clean House, and Eurydice. Her plays have been produced on- and off-Broadway, around the country, internationally, and have been translated into many languages.

Her most recent book, Lessons from My Teacher, is an extraordinary collection of essays that testify to the singular impact of teachers across every stage of our lives. Elizabeth Strout calls it “Pristine, perfect [with] multitudes of truthful lessons for anyone who is wondering about Life—and how to move through it.” Sarah Ruhl is also the author of The Dreams I’ll Dream Tonight, Smile: A Memoir (longlisted for the Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence), 100 Essays I Don’t Have Time to Write (a New York Times Notable Book), Letters from Max (with Max Ritvo), and 44 Poems for You.

She has been a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist, a Tony Award nominee, and the recipient of the MacArthur Fellowship. Sarah Ruhl has received the Steinberg Playwright Award, the Samuel French Award, the Feminist Press Under 40 Award, the National Theater Conference Person of the Year Award, the Susan Smith Blackburn Prize, a Whiting Award, a Lily Award, and a PEN/Laura Pels International Foundation for Theater Award.

Sarah Ruhl teaches at the Yale School of Drama, and lives in Brooklyn with her husband, Tony Charuvastra, who is a child psychiatrist, and their three children.

Join us for an unforgettable evening of music featuring Carnegie Mellon School of Drama’s Music Theater Ensemble (Class of 2028) performing the songbook of two-time Tony Award winner & Pulitzer finalist Jeanine Tesori, who will be in attendance!

Tickets are $75-110* and available to reserve here or by calling 412-456-6666.

The Music Theater Songbook Cabaret has been a tradition since 2010, giving third-year students the opportunity to work with the industry’s leading songwriters & artistic leaders. The one-night only event has become a coveted ticket, filling up the Greer Cabaret in downtown Pittsburgh for an evening of unforgettable songs and performances. This year, the Cabaret will feature the music of renowned composer Jeanine Tesori whose catalogue is one of the most diverse – spanning across Broadway, opera, film, and television.

*VIP table seats come with a special School of Drama swag bag and signed poster.

The Music Theater Songbook Cabaret is directed by Rick Edinger & Michael McKelvey and produced by the CMU Center for New Work with support from the CMU School of Drama, the Richard King Mellon Foundation, and the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust. The Center for New Work connects the Carnegie Mellon School of Drama and Pittsburgh’s established theaters to generate new work initiatives, creating a collaborative hub between higher education and regional theaters to sustain new live theatrical performance. Whether it be readings, workshops, masterclasses, or productions, the Center provides students for-credit and extracurricular learning opportunities to engage with leading theatremakers as they develop their latest creations.

Jeanine Tesori
Tony Award Winner, Pulitzer Prize Finalist

Jeanine Tesori is a composer of musical theatre, opera and film. Her musicals include Kimberly Akimbo; Soft Power; Fun Home; Shrek The Musical; Caroline, or Change; Thoroughly Modern Millie; and Violet. She is a two-time recipient of the Tony Award for Best Score and a two-time Finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Her operas include A Blizzard on Marblehead Neck; The Lion, The Unicorn and Me; and Blue, which received the MCANA Award for Best New Opera. For her opera Grounded, she became one of the first two women to be commissioned by The Metropolitan Opera. Tesori served as Supervising Vocal Producer on Steven Spielberg’s West Side Story.

She is the Founding Artistic Director of New York City Center’s Encores! Off-Center series and a lecturer in music at Yale University.

Description "Behind the Toolkits: Confessions, Compromises, and Contradictions in Ethics-Focused Design"What does it really mean to design methods for ethical design practice? And what happens when the work of designing for ethics becomes an ethical challenge in itself? In this talk, I offer an insider's account of the messy, uncertain, and often contradictory work of designing ethics-focused methods for design practitioners and students. Drawing on my experience surveying existing ethics-focused design methods and developing my own, including Anti-Heroes and Value Lanes, I will share the questions, doubts, fears, and tensions that have shaped my own perception of what this artifact called an “ethics-focused method” could mean, look like, or even achieve.Rather than presenting perfected solutions, I will open up the process behind these methods, sharing the experiments, compromises, and lessons that rarely make it into the final toolkit. I will introduce my AAA philosophy—Awareness, Action, and Agency/Advocacy—as a way of making sense of my experiences as a method designer and understanding how different methods invite ethical reflection, support action, and empower advocacy. The talk will offer practical resources for method designers, educators, practitioners, and students who are also trying to make ethics matter in design.

Speaker's Bio
Sai Shruthi Chivukula is an Assistant Professor in Information Experience Design Program, School of Information at Pratt Institute, New York. She directs Translate, a research group conducting translational work and investigating ethics in technology and design practice. Her research lies at the intersection of HCI and UX, design practice, ethics and values in design, design education, and critical qualitative research. She investigates how designers and HCI practitioners navigate ethical decision-making in everyday practice, including how they recognize ethical concerns, negotiate competing values and responsibilities, and translate ethical awareness into action. Her work develops practical, open-access methods and pedagogical resources that support ethical reflection and decision-making in design education and professional practice. A new strand of her research is exploring Regulation-Informed Design, examining how emerging technology regulations and policy can inform design methods, processes, and professional decision-making. In 2025, she co-authored her first book Universal Methods of Ethical Design, a practical guide to integrating ethical reflection and decision-making into everyday design practice. At Pratt, she teaches courses related to UX design, Conversational UX, Service Design, and Deceptive Design. She loves weaving together her research and teaching, while making art, experimenting with new recipes, and finding creative expression in everyday life.

events.description:
Title: The Character of PRX: Editorial Insights from the First 15 Years and Beyond

Abstract: PRX is published by the American Physical Society, a nonprofit membership society of scientists. Its mission goal is to select around 250 *landmark* papers a year from all fields of physics and showcase them to a broad and multidisciplinary readership.

After 15 years, one might still wonder exactly what PRX is—or, asked differently, how PRX defines a “landmark” through the peer-review process. As an author or referee, you may be curious about how PRX editors actually select these papers. Furthermore, there is always the fair question: are these selections always accurate?

In this talk, I will discuss how we approach these questions. Many of these questions do not have a black-and-white answer in the case of a single paper. Instead, open-minded, reasoned, and constructive dialogue among authors, editors, and referees is key. Ultimately, we, at PRX, strive to navigate the editorial and peer-review process effectively to ensure that the experience is meaningful, productive, and - at times - even a pleasure for everyone involved.

events.title: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford)
events.description:
Please note the unusual time.

Quantitative estimates for almost harmonic maps

Abstract: A fundamental question in the analysis of variational problems is whether functions that almost minimise a given energy, or almost solve its Euler-Lagrange equations, provide good approximations of true minimisers or critical points. In practice, one would like to understand this question not only at a qualitative level, but to obtain precise quantitative control on the distance of almost solutions to exact solutions in terms of the size of the error.

A major challenge in such a quantitative analysis of geometric variational problems is that the classical approach breaks down in the presence of singularities or changes of topology.

In this talk, we will discuss these issues for the Dirichlet energy of maps from surfaces into Riemannian manifolds for which the concentration of energy on small domains leads to a loss of compactness and the formation of a so-called bubble tree.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University)
events.description:
An Adaptive Variational Dual Scheme for equation solving

Abstract: I will describe a scheme for converting the question of solving a given system of equations and associated side-conditions into a variational problem whose formal Euler-Lagrange system recovers the given system and side-conditions using a change-of-variables generated by the scheme. The variational principle is convex, and the method uses a string of such convex variational principles to seek a solution of the original question as an interior minimizer of the last variational problem of the string. Weak coercivity of a variational problem in the string endows its minimizer the status of a weaker `variational dual solution’ to the original, possibly non-variational problem. This last point of view is directly related to Y. Brenier’s Hidden Convexity approach to nonlinear PDE.

Due to the inherent convexity of the scheme, it allows for obtaining `unstable’ solutions of the original, primal system of equations in a `stable’ manner. A ChatGPT-enabled exploration of the scheme in the context of approximation of the mixed curvature isometric embedding problem from R^2 to R^3 will be discussed, as well as the problem of finding deformations of a membrane with prescribed principal stretch fields. This last problem is practically important for questions of sensing and actuation.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
events.description:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.

Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: Bystander Intervention Training
events.description:
Culturally Responsive Bystander (CuRB) Training empowers participants to respond to dating violence, stalking, and sexual assault while providing culturally responsive and person-centered support through open discussion, scenario exercises, and actionable tools. CuRB explores how identity, power, and privilege impacts our role as bystanders and provides space to explore how we arrive at our understandings and perceptions of others. This focus on group reflection and discussion sets the stage for collaboratively unlearning harmful biases that might negatively impact our ability to help loved ones or community members experiencing dating, domestic violence, and sexual assault.

At Carnegie Mellon, we are committed to ensuring that every community member feels safe and protected. This focus on group reflection and discussion sets the stage for collaboratively unlearning harmful biases that might negatively impact our ability to help loved ones or community members experiencing sexual assault, domestic violence, and stalking. Learn more about CuRB training.

events.title: GSPS: Yulei Xu
events.description:
A Converse to Burke’s Theorem for a Queueing Map

Abstract: Burke’s theorem is a classical result in queueing theory, describing the preservation of Poisson departure processes in an exponential queue. We investigate a converse question motivated by the corner growth model: if a queueing transformation preserves an i.i.d. sequence of interarrival times, must the underlying distributions be exponential?

We show that, under strict stability and a natural support assumption, the answer is yes, even without assuming that the initial sojourn time is stationary. The main challenge is to recover independence between the hidden sojourn time and the observed interdeparture time solely from the process-level fixed-point property. Our approach combines a pathwise conservation identity, exponential tilting, and coupling to extract this independence from long blocks of future departures.

I will introduce the queueing map, explain the main probabilistic mechanism, and discuss its connection to stationary last-passage percolation and possible extensions beyond i.i.d. inputs.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Introduction to Prompt Engineering
events.description:
Learn to harness the full potential of AI language models through effective prompt design. events.title: AI Fluency Week: Text Mining the Scholarly Literature
events.description:
Text and data mining (TDM) of scholarly literature can support tasks such as screening abstracts for a systematic review and analyzing how a field evolves over time. However, getting from a research question to a usable corpus can be intimidating. In this workshop, we’ll introduce scholarly APIs and how to query them, comparing open sources like OpenAlex and arXiv with publisher platforms. From there, we’ll walk through the basics of assembling a corpus, providing tips for full-text retrieval and an overview of licensing restrictions (including how to avoid common mistakes that can lead to blocked access!). Finally, we’ll demonstrate a text analysis workflow and provide you with resources that you can adapt to your own project.

events.title: AI Fluency Week: Using AI-supported tools for literature searching
events.description:
Are you using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT to find scholarly articles? Join us for this workshop to discover AI-powered research tools available through the library that are designed specifically for scholarly research.

Learn how tools such as Consensus, Keenious, Scite.ai and Scopus AI can help you avoid hallucinated citations while connecting you directly to real scholarly literature. Built on the same powerful large language model technology as general-purpose AI assistants, these tools operate within trusted scholarly databases and integrate more seamlessly with library subscriptions, making it easier to access full-text articles. You'll also see how these tools use citation networks to uncover connections between papers, helping you identify influential research and discover related studies. Advanced filtering options—including publication date, citation count, journal impact, and more—make it easier to find the most relevant and authoritative sources for your research.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello - Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues
events.description: Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

events.title: CBDR Seminar - "Buy Now, Pain Less: The Impact of Adding a Financing Option to Affordable Purchases"
events.description:
With the rise of Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) financing, consumers increasingly encounter financing options at checkout, even when they do not need financing to complete their purchases. This research investigates how the mere presence of a financing option influences consumers who intend to pay outright. A field dataset capturing Instacart grocery shoppers' online purchase behavior before and after the implementation of BNPL financing (N = 6,952) as well as a series
of controlled shopping simulation studies (combined N = 6,435) find that the presence of a financing option, even when not used, increases purchase completion intentions by enhancing the subjective affordability of one-time payment purchases. When financing
options are available, the preference to pay outright is interpreted as a sign of higher social status, elevating the subjective status of consumers who prefer such payment. This effect is attenuated among consumers who already perceive themselves as having
high social status or in contexts where the association between financing and lower status is less pronounced. By identifying how the mere presence of financing affects consumers uninterested in using it, we advance theory and practice on payment methods,
subjective affordability, and cart abandonment.

events.title: AMES: Elio Nimier-David, "Colleges, Business Dynamism, and Local Growth"
events.description: Can new colleges transform a local economy? This article studies the largest higher-education expansion in French history, a policy that opened hundreds of teaching-oriented colleges across 145 cities in the 1990s. Exploiting the staggered timing of openings, I find a persistent 17% increase in the share of college graduates. The policy induced creative destruction: firm creation rose by 16% while incumbent firms contracted. Entry was concentrated in skill-intensive and in tradable industries, led by experienced entrepreneurs. On net, value added grew by 5% and productivity by 6%. These gains were unevenly distributed: skilled employment rose among younger workers, while older, less-educated workers experienced lasting losses. Twenty-five years later, cohorts of enrollment age when the colleges opened have more education, higher employment rates, and more-skilled jobs. Overall, local effects were larger in initially less-developed areas, contributing to a narrowing of spatial disparities.

events.title: Finance - "Mixology: Order flow segmentation design"
events.description: I analyze the welfare consequences of segmentation in financial markets. Venues vary in their mixture of information-motivated versus liquidity-motivated order flow. In a simple model, I consider the combinations of information-motivated investor welfare and liquidity-motivated investor welfare that can be achieved by some segmentation. This set’s Pareto frontier can (under certain conditions) be implemented by a simple class of segmentations, in which a fraction of information-motivated flow is segregated, while the remainder pools with liquidity-motivated flow. These results call into question the wisdom of the current regulatory framework as it applies to segmentation, e.g., in U.S. equities. Keywords: adverse selection, cream-skimming, segmentation, third-degree price discrimination

events.title: MFRS: Shane Greenstein, "Where the Cloud Rests: The Economic Geography of Data Centers"
events.description: This study provides an analysis of the entry strategies of third-party data centers in the United States. We examine the market prior to the pandemic, in 2018 and 2019, when supply and demand for data services were relatively stable geographically. We compare these patterns with the entry strategies of major cloud-based data centers for services on demand, which include those known as cloud services. We conclude that third-party firms and cloud providers have different entry strategies for this digital infrastructure. The former favors urban settings more and appears sensitive to buyer demand for proximity. They trade off costs of supply, which vary with density, and economies of scale, which cannot be achieved without large volumes of demand. We also find that data center firms providing specialized services display an urban bias. Cloud providers tend to display a lower propensity for locating in urban areas, concentrating their buildings in a small number of locations. We see little evidence to suggest cloud providers will spread their data centers to any but a small number of low-density locations. Our findings support speculation about the likely direction of changes as demand shifts to the cloud, and the location decisions begin to concentrate in the hands of cloud providers.

events.title: Rules in the Face of Complexity (with Kirby Nielsen)
events.description: We show that complexity can affect how people approach decision environments (the “extensive margin”), and also can affect choices conditional on a given approach (the “intensive margin”). On the extensive margin, we hypothesize that individuals resort to “rules”—simplified choice processes that we measure as being easier to describe to another person—as the complexity of the decision environment increases. We test our hypothesis using an experiment by exogenously varying the complexity of the decision environment and measuring how well another individual can replicate the decision-maker’s choices given the decision-maker’s description of how they chose. We find that individuals’ choice processes are more describable in complex choice environments, which we interpret as evidence that decision-making becomes more rule-like as complexity increases. Additional secondary evidence suggests that rule-based decision- making is a choice simplification that reduces the cognitive costs of decision-making. On the intensive margin, when we exogenously fix the choice process, we find that complexity leads to more decision noise

events.title: Applied Microeconomics - "Intergenerational Time Transfers: Altruism and Strategic Motives within the Family" (with Chao Fu and Chamna Yoon)
events.description: Extended families provide a large share of both childcare for young children and long-term care (LTC) for elderly parents, yet these activities are typically studied in isolation. We examine whether intergenerational time transfers are linked across stages of the life cycle and whether they are driven by altruistic or strategic motives. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study and plausibly exogenous variation in childcare costs, we document evidence consistent with implicit family contracts in which early childcare assistance is later reciprocated through elderly care. To interpret these patterns, we develop and estimate a dynamic model of intergenerational care provision that incorporates both altruistic preferences and strategic motives, including reciprocity and bequest incentives. Exploiting the dynamic structure of the model and exogenous variation in childcare costs, we separately identify these mechanisms. The estimated model shows that strategic motives play an important role in shaping the intertemporal link between childcare and LTC. Counterfactual policy analysis reveals substantial spillovers across care sectors. Childcare subsidies crowd out grandparental childcare and reduce the future LTC provided by adult children, whereas policies that condition old-age benefits on past childcare provision strengthen family-based care in both stages. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for dynamic family incentives for optimal policy designs.

events.title: Return or Rebuild Abroad? Expectations and Family Decisions among Ukrainian Refugees
events.description: How do refugees decide whether to return home or build a life abroad when the duration and outcome of war remain uncertain? These decisions shape both the prospects for reconstruction in their home countries and integration in receiving countries. Drawing on two joint papers using a longitudinal survey of Ukrainian refugees across Europe, this talk examines how expectations, local violence, and children’s future opportunities relate to return plans and subsequent behavior. Stated intentions strongly predict actual return: 42 percent of respondents who planned to return soon in 2022 had returned by 2026, compared with just 1 percent of those planning to settle abroad. Local violence reduces return to refugees’ home municipalities, while increasingly pessimistic expectations about the war are associated with declining intentions to return. The second paper examines how children’s return prospects shape decisions for the whole family. During the study period, Ukraine’s restrictions on men leaving the country meant that returning teenage sons could lose the option to leave again upon turning 18. As hopes of a short war receded, families with teenage boys became less likely to return than otherwise similar families without teenage boys. Parents also became more likely to work in their host countries, without corresponding increases in language learning. Together, the studies illuminate how families revise consequential plans under prolonged uncertainty and how constraints facing children reshape parents’ choices.

events.title: Economics Micro Theory - “Optimal Project Management,” joint with Doruk Cetemen and Juuso Toikka
events.description: We study optimal dynamic contracts for long-term projects where a risk-averse agent exerts hidden effort to increase the drift of a Brownian process toward a com- pletion threshold. Relative to the first best, the optimal contract slows progress, makes success less likely, induces earlier termination, and narrows project scope. Allowing for costly project resets generates further distortions: resets may be excessive or insufficient depending on the residual effort required afterwards. With endogenous risk taking, optimal incentives introduce penalties for failure and reduce rewards for effort above a critical progress level, resulting in discontinuous and nonmonotonic effort in progress. In the baseline model, the optimal contract can be implemented with linear spot contracts that require no long-term commitment.

events.title: Temporal Bracketing of Performance Incentives: Quasi-Experimental. Evidence from Last-Mile Delivery Operations
events.description: Last-mile logistics firms face recurring capacity challenges during temporary demand surges. We study temporal bracketing of performance incentives, which we refer to as the division of a performance horizon into evaluation intervals (e.g., weekly vs. monthly), with targets and bonuses scaled proportionally, as a lever for expanding throughput via the existing workforce. We conducted a quasi-experimental field study with a major logistics provider that shifted from monthly to weekly incentive evaluation and feedback. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate that agents handled 23.4% more parcels and successfully delivered 20.7% more, while delivery success rates reduced by two percentage points. The proportion of agents earning at least one week of incentive increased from 10.9% to 46.5%; a counterfactual decomposition attributes approximately 74% of this increase to more frequent evaluation structurally, with the remainder reflecting behavioral responses and their interaction with narrower windows. Despite higher bonus expenditure, estimated operating cost savings reached 1.51%. An effort-choice model with stochastic output and threshold-based bonuses highlights statistical averaging as the mechanism linking evaluation horizons to marginal effort incentives. Broader brackets reduce output uncertainty and strengthen incentives near targets; narrower brackets strengthen incentives sufficiently far below or above targets. With tiered bonuses, narrower brackets can sustain effort toward higher tiers after lower targets are attained. The model also separates structural changes in expected bonuses from behavioral responses and bounds additional bonus expenditure. Temporal bracketing can expand peak-period capacity without additional headcount, but shorter evaluation windows are not universally preferable. Managers should align evaluation frequency with agents’ proximity to targets and the incentive tier structure, balancing productivity gains against higher compensation costs and potential service-quality losses. Distinguishing structural increases in bonus access from behavioral improvements is essential for evaluating incentive effectiveness.

events.title: Applied Microeconomics - "Economics of Property Insurance"
events.description: We study the economics of homeowners’ property insurance by examining how contract design balances the trade-off between incentive alignment and risk sharing. Using granular contract-level property insurance data merged with property-level disaster risk for millions of U.S. households, we develop and structurally estimate a model in which insurers optimally determine contract terms given property risk and household risk preferences. The estimates provide, to our knowledge, the first large-scale contract-level structural measures of risk aversion, risk premia, and the cost of moral hazard, allowing us to quantify how disaster risk is allocated between insurers and households. We find that the cost of moral hazard is small, yet the very mechanism used to mitigate it substantially increases households’ exposure to disaster risk: contract design leaves policyholders exposed to roughly 29 percent of total expected losses. This residual exposure is most pronounced for low-FICO households and for properties with the greatest tail risk. Counterfactuals indicate that mandating full insurance would lead to substantial market exit, increasing household vulnerability. We further show that insurers’ financial constraints are systematically correlated with the riskiness of underwritten properties and with household characteristics.

events.title: AIDE: Lynn Wu, "Large Language Models Polarize Ideologically but Moderate Affectively in Online Political Discourse"
events.description: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how people engage in political discourse online. We examine how the release of ChatGPT altered ideological and emotional patterns in Reddit's largest political forum. Analysis of millions of comments shows that ChatGPT intensified ideological polarization: liberal-leaning authors posted increasingly liberal comments, while conservative-leaning authors posted increasingly conservative comments. Multiple falsification tests suggest that these findings are unlikely to be driven by contemporaneous events, such as the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, or by broader platformwide trends in political polarization. Mechanism tests show that this shift does not stem from the creation of more persuasive or ideologically extreme original content using LLM. Instead, it originates from the tendency of LLM-assisted comments to echo and reinforce the original post's viewpoint, a pattern consistent with algorithmic sycophancy. Yet, despite growing ideological divides, affective polarization, measured by hostility and toxicity, declined. These findings reveal that LLMs can simultaneously deepen ideological separation and foster more civil exchanges, challenging the long-standing assumption in literature that extremity and incivility necessarily move together.

events.title: Finance Seminar - "The Limits of Voluntary Transparency in Competitive Markets"
events.description: Many financial assets trade infrequently and are difficult to value. Can price transparency arise voluntarily among competitors, or must it be mandated? In collateralized loan obligation markets, dealers publicly share attributed, nonbinding price estimates, known as price talks, before competing in sealed-bid auctions. We model price talk as costly revelation of a common-value signal before idiosyncratic values are realized. We show that dealers with unfavorable information talk because their chance of winning is low and revealing private information raises it. Dealers with favorable information stay silent because revelation would dissipate their bidding advantage. In 53,000 auctions with 430,000 price talks, the talk consensus predicts transaction prices, yet silent dealers win the majority of auctions, and prices are further above the consensus when nontalkers win, a “silence premium.” Voluntary transparency produces informative public valuations while maintaining competition among silent dealers. In counterfactuals, mandating disclosure would mainly redistribute surplus from dealers to sellers and not improve price informativeness. Key words. Over-the-counter markets, dealer intermediation, pre-trade disclosure, transparency, auctions, CLOs

events.title: Labor & Development Seminar at Pitt -- “You may use AI”: How explicit permission affects AI adoption and work quality
events.description: Generative AI raises individual productivity in experiments, yet many workers do not use it on the task in front of them. We test whether ambiguity about whether AI use is permitted is itself a barrier. In a preregistered 2 × 2 experiment, 3,026 US and 572 German white-collar workers completed an incentivized writing task under a platform default that discourages AI use. Participants were randomized to receive a one-sentence statement explicitly permitting AI use, a one-paragraph summary of scientific evidence on AI’s productivity benefits, both, or neither. Explicit permission raised task-level AI use by 39 percentage points in both countries, cut completion time by 0.4 standard deviations in the US (0.6 in Germany), and improved writing clarity by 0.4 standard deviations in both countries, an effect that is stable across four automated raters and an incentivized panel of 234 human raters blind to treatment. Gains in depth, creativity, and use of examples were smaller. Productivity information alone had more muted effects. Even when explicitly permitted, roughly half of workers did not use AI, citing a preference for producing their own work rather than rules. Permission left demographic adoption gaps unchanged but widened the gap by prior attitudes toward AI from 7 to 31 percentage points, a pattern that replicated in Germany. Explicit task-level permission is a low-cost organizational lever for AI adoption, but its effects are strongly conditioned by workers’ prior attitudes.

events.title: Applied Microeconomics - “Interdependent Values in Matching Markets: Evidence from Medical Programs in Denmark”
events.description: This paper presents the first empirical analysis of interdependent values in a two-sided matching market. We study admissions to medical programs in Denmark, which are assigned through a centralized mechanism. We build a novel equilibrium model of this market with a flexible information structure. The model yields formal predictions under the dominant assumption in existing theory and applied design work: private values. Leveraging unique administrative data and an admission reform, we test and strongly reject the private value hypothesis: students and competing programs hold private information that, if available to each program, would enable them to admit students more likely to enroll and less likely to drop out. Programs respond to these sources of interdependent values by favoring local applicants. We estimate the model and show that sharing information would significantly increase student persistence and program payoffs, but strategic behavior can limit the effectiveness of feasible policy interventions. Attempts to elicit students’ private information via a multi-round admission process can backfire by inducing strategic misreporting, but programs’ sharing information via a common exam could produce substantial improvements.

events.title: On the fragility of AI Agent collusion
events.description: Problem Definition: Recent work shows that pricing with symmetric LLM agents leads to algorithmic collusion. Yet real deployments are messier: firms adopt models that have different capabilities, different algorithms, proprietary prompts, varying update frequencies, and asymmetric information sets. This raises a central question for competition policy: does LLM-mediated algorithmic collusion survive the heterogeneity typical of real-world deployments, and if variation disrupts collusion, which dimensions matter most? Methodology/results: We show that collusion is fragile under the heterogeneity typical of real deployments. In a stylized repeated-pricing model, heterogeneity in patience or data access reduces the set of collusive equilibria. Experiments with open-source LLM agents (totaling over 2,000 compute hours) align with these predictions: patience heterogeneity reduces price lift from 22% to 10% above competitive levels; asymmetric data access, to 7%. Increasing the number of competing LLMs breaks up collusion; so does cross-algorithm heterogeneity, that is, setting LLMs against Q-learning agents. But model-size differences (e.g., 32B vs. 14B weights) do not; they generate leader-follower dynamics that stabilize collusion. Managerial implications: Our results inform antitrust and AI governance: enforcement actions restriction data-sharing and policies promoting algorithmic diversity can curb coordination, while capability asymmetries should not be assumed to disrupt collusion and may instead stabilize it through leader-follower roles.

events.title: Economics Micro Theory - "Monopoly Theory with Price-Increase Aversion, with Yuval Salant"
events.description:
A consumer is averse to price increases if increasing the price of a good reduces the consumer's willingness to pay for it. We study the optimal dynamic pricing strategy of a monopolist firm in a market with price-increase averse consumers and demand shocks. The strategy is countercyclical at the bottom in the sense that the firm charges the highest prices when demand is weak. The strategy also exhibits downward price stickiness: when demand is such that current profit considerations entail a small price decrease,
the firm refrains from doing so and keeps prices constant. Despite higher expected prices, consumer welfare in a market with strong price-increase aversion is larger than in a market without price-increase aversion. We then generalize these observations to
a model of reference-dependent pricing, where the price history determines the reference price. This introduces a novel trade-off for the firm between profiting today and manipulating tomorrow's reference price.

events.title: Finance Seminar - "Less Duration, More Durable: The Case for Using Floating-Rate Debt to Reduce Treasury Borrowing Costs"
events.description: The U.S. government pays over $1 trillion in interest expenses in 2026 on a national debt of over $40 trillion. Managing this interest burden is critical for the sustainability of U.S. fiscal conditions and the long-term health of the U.S. Treasury market. Building on a dynamic model of interest rates, and adjusting for the liquidity premium and discounts of various types of Treasury securities, we show that greater issuance of floating-rate notes (FRNs) during periods of elevated interest rate risk premium can meaningfully reduce the U.S. government’s interest expense. Such saving overweighs the illiquidity discount in the market price of existing Treasury FRNs. The savings are also greater if the FRNs are linked to shorter-maturity T-bills.

events.title: Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke
events.description:
Sinkhorn Treatment Effects: A Causal Optimal Transport Measure

Abstract: We introduce the Sinkhorn treatment effect, an entropic optimal transport measure of divergence between counterfactual distributions. Unlike classical quantities such as the average treatment effect, this measure captures differences across entire distributions. We analyze this divergence as a statistical functional and show it can be written as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings with an appropriate kernel. This characterization allows us to establish first-order pathwise differentiability in general, and second-order pathwise differentiability under the null hypothesis of equal counterfactual distributions. Leveraging this smoothness, we construct debiased estimators and use them to obtain asymptotically valid tests for distributional treatment effects with a fixed entropic regularization parameter. Because the power of the test depends on this unknown parameter, we further propose an aggregated test that combines evidence across a grid of regularization choices. Experiments on simulated and image data demonstrate the practical advantages of our estimator and testing procedure.

Bio: Alex Luedtke is a Professor of Health Care Policy and Affiliate in Statistics at Harvard University. Previously, he held faculty appointments in Statistics and Biostatistics at the University of Washington and Fred Hutch.

Alex works at the intersection of semiparametrics, causal inference, and machine learning. Much of his work leverages computational power to automate the construction of efficient statistical procedures. To this end, he has developed methods that let machines “learn to learn” from data, and algorithms that work out derivations once done by hand. He applies these tools as part of multidisciplinary teams to improve decision-making in mental health and infectious disease research.

Selected honors include a COPSS Emerging Leader Award, NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, and Mortimer Spiegelman Award. His work has been supported by NIH, NSF, PCORI, WHO, and Netflix.

Alex received a Ph.D. in Biostatistics from UC Berkeley and an ScB in Applied Mathematics from Brown University.

In this installment of the CyLab Seminar Series, Praneeth Vepakomma of MIT will share his latest research.

Speaker:
Praneeth Vepakomma

Visiting Professor

MIT

Talk Title:
Talk title coming soon

Abstract:
Abstract coming soon

Bio:
Praneeth Vepakomma is currently a Visiting Assistant Professor at MIT in IDSS and is an Assistant Professor at MBZUAI. He previously obtained his PhD at MIT in and works on trustworthy/responsible computation that includes a sub-focus on distributed (resource-efficient) and private computation in statistics, ML and data science at large. He has extensive industrial experience across Meta, Apple, Amazon, Motorola Solutions, Corning and several startups. His research focuses on developing algorithms for distributed computation in statistics & machine learning under constraints of privacy, & efficiency.

He won the Meta PhD research fellowship in Applied Statistics, two SERC Scholarships (for Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing) from MIT’s Schwarzman college of computing. He co-founded a research based non-profit (Integrity Distributed) that won the Financial Times Digital Innovation Award. He won a Best Student Paper Award at FL-IJCAI, a Baidu Best Paper Award at NeurIPS-SpicyFL and a Best Paper Runner Up Award at FG-2021. His technical work is inspired by foundations of non-asymptotic statistics, randomized algorithms, learning augmented algorithms, combinatorics, and at times just by systems design. He was Interviewed in the book, ‘Data Scientist: The Definitive Guide to Becoming a Data Scientist’ and has organized several workshops at ICLR, ICML, IJCAI, CVPR and NeurIPS.

Bio:
Franziska Roesner is a professor in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, where her research focuses on computer security and privacy. Her interests are broad within that domain, identifying and addressing security and privacy challenges faced by end users of existing and emerging technologies. Roesner co-directs the Security and Privacy Research Lab.

She is the recipient of an NSF CAREER Award (2017), an Emerging Leader Alumni Award from the UT Austin College of Natural Sciences (2017), an MIT Technology Review Innovators Under 35 Award (2017), a Google Security and Privacy Research Award (2017), an Undergraduate Research Mentor Award (2020), a Consumer Reports Digital Lab Fellowship (2021), and a Google Research Scholar Award (2022).

Bio:

Andrew Ilyas is an assistant professor at CMU. Previously, he was a Stein Fellow at Stanford Statistics and a Ph.D. student MIT, where he was fortunate to be advised by Costis DaskalakisOpens in new window and Aleksander MadryOpens in new window and supported by an Open Philanthropy AI FellowshipOpens in new window. Ilyas attended MIT for undergrad, majoring in CS and in Math. Outside of research, I enjoy playing soccer and table tennis.

Ilyas’s goal is to uncover general principles that describe and predict the behavior of ML systems—ideally enabling predictably reliable future systems. This goal entails combining statistical tools with large-scale experiments to precisely understand the ML “pipeline,” from training data (and the way we collect it), to learning algorithms, to deployment. He also likes thinking broadly about (human) trust in AI systems.

events.title: Five Lessons on Caregiving from Wilderness Survival
events.description:
Five Lessons on Caregiving from Wilderness Survival
In 2015, after a violent attack on her beloved partner, Virginia Eubanks suddenly became a family caregiver. In the weeks, months, and years that followed, she and her partner struggled to stay afloat as they faced wave upon wave of setbacks, including a serious case of post-traumatic stress disorder. Then, a second case. Eubanks developed “collateral” PTSD, a condition common among caregivers but rarely discussed.
An old lifesaving manual provided unexpected help. Inspired by its lessons, Eubanks studied wilderness first aid, kayak self-rescue, winter survival, bushwhacking, and lifeguarding. She interviewed experts and everyday heroes—from neuroscientists to monks to forest rangers. Join Eubanks to discover what it takes to build communities of care that can sustain us in uncertain times.
Event Details

Location

The Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry (CFA 111)

Date

Wednesday, October 28, 2026

Time

5:00-7:00 pm

About the Speaker
Virginia Eubanks, PhD. Associate Professor. Department of Political Science. University of Albany, SUNY
Virginia Eubanks is a longform investigative reporter, essayist, memoirist, and Associate Professor of Political Science at the University at Albany, SUNY. She is the author of A Guide to Open Water Lifesaving: Lessons on Love and Survival (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, August 2026). She is also the author of Automating Inequality: How High-Tech Tools Profile, Police, and Punish the Poor; Digital Dead End: Fighting for Social Justice in the Information Age; and co-editor, with Alethia Jones, of Ain’t Gonna Let Nobody Turn Me Around: Forty Years of Movement Building with Barbara Smith. Her investigative reporting and personal essays have appeared in The New York Times Magazine, Scientific American, The Nation, Harper’s, and Nature. With Andrea Quijada, she is the co-editor of a forthcoming collection of oral histories, Not a Number: Global Stories from the Automated Welfare State. She has been a fellow or resident at MacDowell, Edward Albee, New America, Carey Institute for Global Good, and Blue Mountain Center.
When not sleeping in her truck in the Adirondacks, she lives in Troy, NY.

events.title: The Screen Novel: Storytelling Through Digital Interfaces
events.description:
The Screen Novel: Storytelling Through Digital Interfaces

About the Workshop
Join a bilingual (English/Arabic) creative writing workshop that explores the Screen Novel, where everyday screens become the story itself.
In this introductory bilingual creative-writing workshop, participants will explore the possibilities of the Screen Novel through examples, discussion, and a guided writing exercise. No prior experience in digital design, programming, or creative writing is required.

Event Details

Location

Danforth Lounge, 2nd Floor, CUC

Date

Wednesday, October 21, 2026

Time

5:30-7:00 pm

A Note on the Screen Novel
The Screen Novel is an experimental form of digital storytelling that reimagines the epistolary novel for the age of smartphones, platforms, and personal digital archives. It does not use screenshots or digital images merely as illustrations accompanying a conventional narrative. Rather, it treats digital interfaces themselves—text messages, notifications, emails, maps, call logs, search histories, social-media feeds, and lock screens—as the primary surface of narration.
In a Screen Novel, readers encounter a story through fragments: an unanswered message, a deleted conversation, a location pin, an online profile, a notification appearing at an unexpected moment, or the silence created by the absence of a reply. Plot, character, time, and emotional experience emerge gradually from these partial traces. The reader is therefore not only a recipient of the narrative but also an active participant in reconstructing its missing connections.
The form is especially attentive to the ways contemporary life is shaped by screens. Our friendships, desires, conflicts, memories, migrations, and losses increasingly unfold through digital devices and platforms. The Screen Novel seeks to explore this reality aesthetically and critically, asking how digital interfaces alter our sense of intimacy, privacy, memory, presence, absence, and storytelling itself.
The Screen Novel should not be confused with the interactive novel, the cinematic novel, or the comics novel. Its central concern is not reader choice, filmic technique, or sequential illustration. Instead, it recognizes the screen as a narrative environment: a space where language, image, time, emotion, and social relations meet. By bringing Arabic and English materials, multilingual communication, and cross-cultural digital archives into dialogue, the form also opens new possibilities for writing across languages, borders, and media.

About the Speaker
Mukhtar Saad Shehata (مختار سعد شحاته), Writer and Researcher, Department of Languages, Cultures, and Applied Linguistics, Carnegie Mellon University
Mukhtar Saad Shehata is an Egyptian writer and researcher in the Department of Languages, Cultures, and Applied Languages at Carnegie Mellon University. He is the recipient of the 2019 Ibn Battuta Prize for Travel Writing for An Arab’s Diary in the Land of Samba and the author of more than fifteen books spanning fiction, short stories, literary criticism, and anthropological research. His best-known works include Macaques of Africa, forthcoming in English translation in the United States; Shared Margins, co-authored with Samuli Schielke, on the conditions of creativity and writing; and Semi-Cities, a study of social, spatial, and digital transformations in the Egyptian countryside, particularly the northern Nile Delta. His work develops the concepts of the “Screen Novel,” “semi-city,” and “electronic masculinity,” exploring the intersections of storytelling, digital media, and everyday social life.

events.title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
events.description:
Speaker: Veit Elser, Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Jingjing Tang
events.description:
Title: Reliable Epidemic Intelligence from Delayed and Revised Public Health Surveillance Data

Committee:
Roni Rosenfeld, Chair, CMU
Bryan Wilder, Co-chair, CMU
Harry Hochheiser, PITT
Cecile Viboud, NIH

GHC 6501
Zoom link in email invitation

Abstract:
Epidemic situational awareness depends on timely and accurate information about ongoing transmission. In practice, recent surveillance observations are incomplete because of reporting and administrative delays, while even finalized records remain delayed and noisy measurements of underlying epidemic activity. This thesis examines how these limitations shape epidemic inference, from forecasting incomplete surveillance records to characterizing the information they ultimately contain.

We first develop Delphi-RF, a nonparametric revision-forecasting framework that captures reporting and revision dynamics through designed features and generates distributional forecasts of mature surveillance values. The framework accommodates different data types, reporting frequencies, and diseases. We then extend this framework to AutoDelphiRF, which automates revision forecasting through pre-forecast diagnosis, adaptive pooling of location–lag tasks with similar revision behavior, and post-forecast calibration and reliability assessment, without requiring dataset-specific exploratory analysis.

Even after revisions have resolved, epidemiological delays constrain inference about latent epidemic dynamics. We characterize these inferential limits through a spectral analysis of observation-level identifiability, showing how delays attenuate temporal variation. We further characterize how this attenuation, together with observation noise, affects the distinguishability of short-timescale epidemic trajectories and epidemiologically relevant features such as short-term growth and the magnitude and duration of transient events.

Together, these contributions provide practical and efficient methods for real-time revision forecasting from incomplete surveillance data while characterizing the limits on what epidemic dynamics can be reliably inferred from delayed and noisy observations.

events.title: Sazan Mahbub - Thesis Proposal
events.description:
Title: Principled Generative Modeling for Biology: Learned Priors, Context-Aware Generation, and Phenotype-Guided Design

Committee:
Eric P. Xing, Carnegie Mellon University (Chair)
Jose Lugo-Martinez, Carnegie Mellon University
David Koes, University of Pittsburgh
Le Song, GenBio AI / Mohamed Bin Zayed University of AI (External Member)

Zoom: In email

Abstract: Generative modeling for biology requires learning across heterogeneous modalities, including DNA, RNA, protein sequences, molecular structures, and cellular images. Foundation models acquire powerful priors over these modalities, but biological generation also requires principled mechanisms for incorporating context and uncertainty. Structural constraints, target-specific molecular evidence, and cellular context influence which outputs are biologically plausible and relevant. This thesis develops machine learning methods that connect probabilistic formulations with efficient algorithm design, progressing from scalable biological representations and generative priors to context-aware generation and phenotype-guided biomolecular design.
Aim 1 develops foundation models for DNA, RNA, and proteins, examining pretraining data, model capacity, and sparse computation, and advances conditional sequence generation through discrete diffusion and uncertainty-aware refinement. Aim 2 develops context-aware generation through fine-grained multimodal retrieval and reusable memory composition. Its central study retrieves residue-level structure–sequence evidence for protein inverse folding, while supporting studies investigate context-dependent composition and probabilistic synthesis of interpretable model parameters. Aim 3 develops a microscopy-image generative model conditioned on protein sequence and cellular morphology, and integrates it with molecular priors for multimodal generation and phenotype-guided protein design. The framework distinguishes the spatial and semantic roles of cellular and molecular information and investigates whether and how phenotype distributions guide protein generation beyond sequence priors and structural conditioning. Computational experiments examine fold-preserving sequence diversification and joint sequence-structure diversification, with independent evaluation of localization, structural compatibility, diversity, and cost.
Together, these aims connect theoretical foundations, practical algorithm development, and empirical evaluation to advance generative modeling across molecular and cellular scales and investigate how reusable biological priors and context can support biomolecular design.

events.title: ICSD Talk, Hannah Rubin
events.description:
Statistical Biases in Evaluation
Gesiel da Silva and Hannah Rubin
Statistical biases significantly impact the fairness of decision processes, though their influence is often difficult to spot. Rather than affecting accuracy of individual outcomes, statistical biases result solely by virtue of statistical differences in groups being evaluated, e.g., the frequency of false positives or negatives. For example, while some contend that algorithms used to assess risk of recidivism are not biased due to their predicting individuals' risks accurately and meeting certain fairness criteria, it has been shown that these algorithms lead to disparate impact due to unequal error rates across groups (Chouldechova, 2017). In this work, we build on work by Heesen and Romeijn (2019) to examine how statistical biases shape evaluation processes - such as editorial or grant peer review, loan approvals, and immigration decisions - and how mechanisms such as familiarity‑driven feedback loops, prevalence effects, and algorithmic homogenization can magnify and intensify these impacts.

events.title: ICSD Talk, Tyler Marghetis
events.description:
Title: The Revolutionary Species
Abstract: What makes us human? Are we toolmakers? Storytellers? Rational animals? Sure, maybe. But I argue for a different answer: humans are revolutionaries. Revolutions depend on stable traditions and sudden transformation, and humans are prodigious at both. We develop shared patterns of thought and behavior that persist, often stubbornly. But we also reconfigure those patterns, often rapidly, sometimes radically. This dynamic recurs across scales, from moments to millennia, from individuals to entire societies. I will illustrate my argument with computational analyses of several forms of human revolution: creative breakthroughs among artists, musicians, and mathematicians; the emergence and collapse of large-scale cooperation; and the recorded history of global philosophy. Across these very different domains, I find shared principles of stability and transformation. To be human is to live on the edge of revolution.

--
Tyler Marghetis, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor, Cognitive & Information Sciences
University of California, Merced

Carnegie Mellon University
Social & Decision Sciences Seminar Announcement

Gonzalo Arrieta (University of Zurich)

Title: Rules in the Face of Complexity (with Kirby Nielsen)
Date: Tuesday, October 27

Time: 12:30 p.m.
Location: Porter Hall 223D (Lunch will be served)
Faculty interested in meeting with Gonzalo or joining him for dinner, as well as graduate students and postdocs interested in joining him for lunch, are encouraged to sign up here.

Abstract:

We show that complexity can affect how people approach decision environments (the “extensive margin”), and also can affect choices conditional on a given approach (the “intensive margin”). On the extensive margin, we hypothesize that individuals resort to “rules”—simplified choice processes that we measure as being easier to describe to another person—as the complexity of the decision environment increases. We test our hypothesis using an experiment by exogenously varying the complexity of the decision environment and measuring how well another individual can replicate the decision-maker’s choices given the decision-maker’s description of how they chose. We find that individuals’ choice processes are more describable in complex choice environments, which we interpret as evidence that decision-making becomes more rule-like as complexity increases. Additional secondary evidence suggests that rule-based decision-making is a choice simplification that reduces the cognitive costs of decision-making. On the intensive margin, when we exogenously fix the choice process, we find that complexity leads to more decision noise.

Best,

Philosophy Colloquium, Hannah Rubin
events.description:
Citation Norms and Citation Gaps
Beck Apicello and Hannah Rubin

Citation gaps – systematic undercitation of women and minoritized scholars – are both an ethical and epistemic concern for scientific communities. We argue that these gaps emerge from field‑level norms about how much to read, how much to cite, and whether to prioritize relevance or prestige. We develop an agent-based model to analyze how these factors interact with demographic representation and homophily to create citation gaps. We also introduce an evolutionary model to examine how citation gaps change as representation increases over time and show that whether gaps diminish depends on a field’s relationship to the past: communities that weight recent work more heavily tend to see gaps shrink, while those anchored in canonical literature may sustain them even as representation grows. The analysis clarifies how local norms and long‑term dynamics jointly structure citation inequality.

events.title: Halloween Talk - Teddy Seidenfeld
events.description:
Presenter: Teddy Seidenfeld
Location: Baker Hall A51 (Giant Eagle Auditorium)
Day/Time: Monday, October 26, 5:00-6:30pm
***We will be handing out candy***

Title: Ghostly Preferences -- When coherence requires a strict preference among equivalent random variables.

Abstract: When utilities for outcomes are bounded, or when all variables are simple, it is required by (canoncial) expected utility to have preferences defined over probability distributions or lotteries over outcomes. That is, under such circumstances two random variables with a common probability distribution over outcomes – equivalent random variables – must occupy the same place in an agent's preference ordering over lotteries. For example, with outcomes determined by a flip of a fair coin (i.e, where the probability of landing Heads = the probability of landing Tails = 1/2), winning $1 if Heads and losing $1 if tails is equally preferred to losing $1 if Heads and winning $1 if Tails. Also, then one is indifferent between trading one of these lotteries for the other.

However, if strict preference over lotteries respects uniform, strict dominance in outcomes between random variables,
and if indifference between two random variables entails indifference between the two lotteries of trading one for the other, then preferences over unbounded random variables cannot preserve indifference between all pairs of equivalent variables. In such circumstances, preference is not a function of probability and utility for outcomes.

What are the objects of such preferences?

I illustrate such ghostly preferences using three equivalent St. Petersburg variables.
