events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“Harnessing Light, Color, Ions and Electrons: from Electrochromics to Artificial Retina,” presented by Jianguo Mei

Abstract: The Mei Research Group at Zhejiang University bridges fundamental discovery and real-world innovation by integrating chemistry, materials science, engineering and medicine. We develop organic semiconductors and conductors with transformative potential for printed electronics, bioelectronics, and living electronics, pursuing both technological impact and fundamental scientific frontiers.

In this seminar, I will highlight two complementary research directions: Electrochromic Technologies and Living Electronics. Both are rooted in the precise control of light, color, ions, and electrons, yet extend these principles toward very different applications. Through Ambilight Inc., our discoveries in flexible electrochromic thin films have been translated into roll-to-roll manufacturing and commercialized for applications ranging from electric vehicles to consumer electronics. These examples illustrate how fundamental discoveries made in an academic laboratory can evolve into market-ready technologies.

Our second direction, Living Electronics, asks a more fundamental question: Can electronics become part of living systems rather than being implanted into them? Inspired by biological vision, our work on Organic Eyes seeks to emulate the sensing and processing functions of the human visual system. In parallel, we are exploring electronics that can grow within the brain, creating electronic materials that form and function directly within living neural tissue. While these goals remain at the frontier of science, they point toward a fundamentally different relationship between synthetic materials and biology.

To illustrate the broader philosophy behind our research, I will discuss the journey of n-doped poly(benzodifurandione) (n-PBDF)-from an unexpected polymer discovery and scalable synthesis to applications in flexible electronics and bioelectronics. This case study captures our approach: coupling curiosity-driven discovery with mission-driven innovation. By connecting fundamental chemistry to real-world needs while pursuing ambitious scientific frontiers, we seek to turn new molecular concepts into technologies that can ultimately benefit society.

Refs: M. Chen, D. Wang, Y. Zou, et al., J. Mei, “Long-range extended chains arising from polymerization-driven spontaneous assembly,” Science 393, 172 (2026); S. Samal, S. Xiao, S. Nelson, et al., J. Mei, “Blood-catalyzed n-doped polymers for reversible optical neural control,” Science 392, eadu5500 (2026); K. Chen, H. Hu, I. Song, et al., J. Mei, “Organic optoelectronic synapse based on photon-modulated electrochemical doping,” Nature Photonics 17, 629–637 (2023); I. Song, W.-J. Lee, Z. Ke, et al., J. Mei, “An n-doped capacitive transparent conductor for all-polymer electrochromic displays,” Nature Electronics 7, 1158–1169 (2024).

Jianguo Mei is a Qiushi Chair Professor at Zhejiang University, where he is establishing research programs in organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, printed electronics, and living electronics and leading the Center for Living Electronics and Adaptive Neurotherapeutics (CLEAN). He previously spent 12 years at Purdue University, where he served as Richard and Judith Wien Professor of Chemistry and Department Head. He has authored more than 150 peer-reviewed publications, holds 39 granted U.S. patents, and has received more than 22,000 citations. He is also a co-founder of Ambilight Inc., which pioneered the roll-to-roll manufacturing of flexible electrochromic films for smart windows and other applications.

events.description:
The CEE department seminar series presents lectures from a diverse range of professors, industry leaders, and alumni, and covers topics discussed throughout CEE’s four core research areas. All members of the CMU community are welcome to attend CEE department seminars.

From Sensing to Adaptation: Human-Centered Intelligence in the Built Environment

The built environment is increasingly able to sense, learn, and respond, creating new opportunities to rethink how we design, construct, operate, and experience buildings and infrastructure. This talk presents our research toward human-centered intelligent built environments, from multimodal sensing and modeling of human experiences and interactions with buildings to AI-enabled simulation of human behavior and emergency response, adaptive building systems, and human–robot interaction and teleoperation in construction. Across these applications, a common question drives our work: how can we move beyond systems that simply collect data or automate predefined tasks toward environments and machines that understand context, anticipate human needs, and adapt their behavior accordingly? I will discuss recent advances and remaining challenges in creating built environments in which people, machines, and physical spaces can increasingly sense, learn from, and adapt to one another.

Bio: Dr. Burcin Becerik-Gerber is a Professor and Chair of the Sonny Astani Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Southern California and the Founder and Director of the USC Center for Intelligent Environments (CENTIENTS). Her research focuses on advanced sensing, data science, and artificial intelligence to support the design, construction, and operation of human-centered, adaptive buildings and infrastructure systems. She pioneered the field of Human-Building Interaction (HBI), which examines how human experience and behavior interact with intelligent, engineered systems in the built environment. Dr. Becerik-Gerber has authored over 200 peer-reviewed publications and has led more than $15 million in sponsored research funded by agencies including the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Transportation. Her work has received numerous honors, including MIT Technology Review TR35, the FIATECH Celebration of Engineering and Technology Innovation Award, ASCE’s Computing in Civil Engineering Award, the ASCE Henry L. Michel Award for Industry Advancement of Research, and the ASCE Peurifoy Construction Research Award. She is a member of the National Academy of Construction and serves on the National Academies Board on Infrastructure and the Constructed Environment.

events.title: Theory Lunch Seminar - Taha Ameen
events.description:
Speaker: TAHA AMEEN, Postdoctoral Fellow, Computer Science Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Recent progress in alignment and testing of multiple
correlated random graphs

Graph alignment, also called graph matching, is the problem of
recovering the hidden correspondence between the vertices of two or
more graphs from their correlated edges. In the standard random model,
each graph retains every edge of a common Erdős–Rényi graph
independently with some probability, and the vertices of each graph
are relabeled by an unknown, uniformly random permutation. The problem
is thus an average-case, noisy version of graph isomorphism, with
applications to de-anonymizing social networks and object tracking in
computer vision. Finding the best alignment of two arbitrary graphs is
an instance of the quadratic assignment problem, which is NP-hard in
the worst case. For two random graphs, however, the past decade has
produced sharp information-theoretic thresholds for recovering the
alignment and for detecting whether the graphs are correlated at all,
as well as polynomial-time algorithms that succeed at constant
correlation.

This talk focuses on what changes when more than two graphs are
observed. For m correlated graphs, we determine sharp thresholds for
exact recovery of all correspondences, and identify a regime in which
no pair of graphs can be aligned on its own but all m graphs can be
aligned jointly. For the Gaussian analog of this problem, we
characterize the detection threshold. I will close with recent
progress on polynomial-time algorithms and open problems on whether
efficient methods can benefit from additional graphs.

Based on joint work with Bruce Hajek.

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Qi Pang
events.description:
Speaker: QI PANG, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department, Carnegie
Mellon University

Talk Title: High-Capacity and Undetectable Multi-Agent Collusion

LLM agents increasingly coordinate through natural language, creating
a new security risk: colluding agents may use apparently benign
messages to exchange hidden information or coordinate unauthorized
actions. Existing practical steganographic protocols usually assume
unrealistic symmetry between agents or achieve very low capacity.

In this talk, I will present Codetta, a high-capacity steganographic
protocol for independently deployed LLM agents in realistic asymmetric
settings. Codetta enables agents to communicate while preserving the
sender’s output distribution. Across multiple agent workloads and
sender models, Codetta achieves up to 94× higher capacity than prior
asymmetric protocols. These results suggest that effectively
undetectable collusion between independently deployed agents is
becoming practical, and that transcript inspection alone may be
insufficient for auditing multi-agent systems.

Presented as part of the Crypto Seminar Series

events.title: VASC Seminar - Gedas Bertasius
events.description:
Speaker: GEDAS BERTASIUS, Assistant Professor, Department of Computer
Science, University of North Carolina

Talk Title: Video Intelligence for Understanding Behavior and Guiding
Action

Modern video-language models have become remarkably good at describing
what is happening in a video. Yet their ability to understand the
behavior they observe, and to act on that understanding, remains
limited. This talk presents our group's work on building these missing
capabilities. I will begin with foundational methods for scalable
video perception, from space-time attention to hierarchical
representations and active search over long videos. I will then
introduce strategic video intelligence, using team sports as a natural
microworld in which cooperative and competitive behavior can be
studied rigorously, and present two complementary lines of work within
it. The first investigates whether video generation models can
simulate strategic multi-agent behavior well enough to support better
decisions. The second examines how agents can study behavioral
histories across large multimodal corpora, compiling repeated
analytical work into reusable representations, abstractions, and
procedures. Finally, I will present WatchAct, a benchmark for robot
manipulation grounded in observed human behavior, where a robot
watches a person and then has to act on what it saw. Together, these
works move video models from perceiving behavior, to understanding it,
to guiding action.

—

Gedas Bertasius is an Assistant Professor in the Department of
Computer Science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
His research focuses on video understanding and multimodal AI,
particularly on systems that can perceive, reason about, and act on
behavior observed in video. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science
from the University of Pennsylvania and was a postdoctoral researcher
at Facebook AI Research before joining UNC. He is the recipient of the
NSF CAREER Award, four Sony Research Awards, two Meta Research Awards,
and the Egocentric Vision Distinguished Paper Award. He was also a
CVPR Best Paper Award finalist. Prior to his research career, he
played professional basketball in Lithuania, an experience that still
shapes his work on understanding strategic behavior in video.

events.title: CyLab Seminar - Florian Schaub
events.description:
Speaker: FLORIAN SCHAUB, Associate Professor of Information, School of
Information,and Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and
Computer Science, College of Engineering University of Mighigan

Talk Title: The Policy–Practice Gap in Privacy: Why Legal
Protections Fall Short and How to Make Them More Effective

Around the world, data protection and privacy laws are proliferating
as policymakers seek to protect consumers from harms arising in a data
ecosystem fueled by the extensive collection, use, and sale of
personal information. Yet these laws often fail to produce meaningful
improvements in consumers' privacy in practice.

Dr. Schaub’s research investigates how public policy and legal
requirements affect consumers’ privacy in practice. His empirical
findings show that privacy notices rarely provide meaningful
transparency into companies’ data practices; cookie banners do not
support informed consent; despite the availability of privacy rights
and controls, consumers often permit more data collection and
third-party sharing than they expect; and effective identity-theft
protections, such as credit freezes, continue to have low adoption
rates.

In this talk, Dr. Schaub will discuss his group’s empirical research
on these issues and identify factors that create and sustain the
privacy policy–practice gap. He will also discuss how human-centered
privacy design and research-informed policymaking can help turn formal
rights and requirements into effective protections for consumers.

—

Dr. Florian Schaub is an associate professor of information and of
electrical engineering and computer science at the University of
Michigan. His interdisciplinary research spans privacy, human-computer
interaction, emerging technologies, and public policy. He studies
people’s privacy decision-making and behavior, investigates the
privacy implications of emerging technologies, and develops
human-centered privacy and security solutions that help people better
manage their privacy. Dr. Schaub holds a PhD in computer science from
Ulm University and was a postdoctoral fellow in Carnegie Mellon
University’s School of Computer Science. His research has been
recognized with the 2019 Caspar Bowden Award for Outstanding Research
in Privacy Enhancing Technologies and with best paper awards at
leading conferences in human-computer interaction and cybersecurity,
including ACM CHI, USENIX Security, ACM CCS, and SOUPS. He is an ACM
Distinguished Member and a DARPA Young Faculty Award recipient. His
research has influenced industry practice and public policy, including
rulemaking for the California Consumer Privacy Act.

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Wayne Chi
events.description:
Speaker: WAYNE CHI, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Interaction-as-a-Judge

Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive
applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While
humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM
evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This
mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately
apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an
evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact
with an application.

We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation
and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect
and release two complementary datasets: 6, 858 pairs of applications
with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and 222
applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to
standard non-interactive approaches, we find that
Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting
human preferences (65.6% → 69.1%) and requirement verification
(77.0% → 81.6%).

We also observe scaling benefits—across both preference alignment
and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve
performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time
experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also
improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time,
Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs 75.5% of broken requirements within
five attempts, compared to 55.4% for code-only self-feedback. At
training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal
improves win-rate over the base model by 6.7pp while reducing both
code length bias by 35.7% and build failure rates by 7.2pp compared to
a code-only reward signal.

Requirement

events.title: VASC Seminar - Pinar Yanardag
events.description:
Speaker: PINAR YANARDAG, Assistant Professor of Computer Science,
Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

Talk Title: Controllable, Efficient and Personalized Generative AI:
From Long-Horizon Video to Interactive World Models

Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet
building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize
remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms
of control, generate over extended horizons within practical
computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and
preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a
central question: How can we make visual generation controllable,
efficient, and personal?

I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First,
Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models
represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and
responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next,
VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of
extended generation by learning compact representations of past
context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving
generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces
personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to
bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate
them.

I will close with broader directions for video generation, including
new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical
plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with
desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26).
This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography,
supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that
remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact
with them.

—

Pinar Yanardag is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at
Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her
research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized
generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive

events.title: Principles of Programing Seminar (PoP) - Simon Gregersen
events.description:
Speaker: SIMON ODDERSHEDE GREGERSEN, Faculty Member,CISPA Helmholtz
Center for Information Security, Saarbrücken

Talk Title: Cryptographic Protocol Security through Effect Handlers
and Probabilistic Relational Separation Logic

Cryptographic protocols combine randomized computation, distributed
interaction, and adversarial behavior, which makes machine-checked,
end-to-end security proofs difficult. Cryptographers have a
well-established methodology for such proofs, Universal Composability
(UC), in which a protocol is shown secure by proving it
indistinguishable from an idealized specification to any adversary.
However, existing verification tools either abstract away the
probabilistic reasoning or offer limited support for the interactive
control flow that UC modeling relies on.

In this talk, I will present ongoing work showing that algebraic
effects and handlers are a natural fit for this setting. Protocols,
ideal functionalities, and adversaries become effect handlers, and
UC-style security statements become approximate equivalences between
handler-based programs. To prove such equivalences, we develop
ClutchEff, a probabilistic relational separation logic for effectful
programs that combines relational reasoning about handlers with
approximate probabilistic couplings. On top of ClutchEff, we build a
relational logical-relations model of an affine type-and-effect
system, which lets us reason about arbitrary well-typed adversaries. I
will illustrate the approach with case studies including
Diffie–Hellman key exchange and the PVW oblivious transfer protocol.

Faculty Host: Stephanie Balzer

—

Simon Oddershede Gregersen is a tenure-track faculty member at the
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security in Saarbrücken,
Germany. His research focuses on programming languages and formal
verification, with the goal of making it practical to prove strong
guarantees about distributed and randomized programs. To that end, he
develops foundational, machine-checked reasoning techniques based on
separation logic, logical relations, and interactive theorem proving.
He co-leads the Clutch project on program logics for higher-order
probabilistic programs. Before joining CISPA, he was a postdoctoral
fellow at New York University with Joseph Tassarotti, supported by an
Internationalization Fellowship from the Carlsberg Foundation. He
received his PhD from Aarhus University, supervised by Amin Timany and
Lars Birkedal.

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Yixuan Xu
events.description:
Speaker: YIXUAN XU, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Antidistillation Fingerprinting

Model distillation enables efficient emulation of frontier large
language models (LLMs), creating a need for robust mechanisms to
detect when a third-party student model has trained on a teacher
model's outputs. However, existing fingerprinting techniques that
could be used to detect such distillation rely on heuristic
perturbations that impose a steep trade-off between generation quality
and fingerprinting strength, often requiring significant degradation
of utility to ensure the fingerprint is effectively internalized by
the student.

We introduce antidistillation fingerprinting (ADFP), a principled
approach that aligns the fingerprinting objective with the student's
learning dynamics. Building upon the gradient-based framework of
antidistillation sampling, ADFP utilizes a proxy model to identify and
sample tokens that directly maximize the expected detectability of the
fingerprint in the student after fine-tuning, rather than relying on
the incidental absorption of the un-targeted biases of a more naive
watermark. Experiments on GSM8K, OASST1, and MBPP demonstrate that
ADFP achieves a significant Pareto improvement over state-of-the-art
baselines, yielding stronger detection confidence with minimal impact
on utility across mathematical reasoning, dialogue, and code
generation, even when the student model's architecture is unknown.

Presented in Partial Fulfillment of the CSD Speaking Skills
Requirement

events.title: Theory Seminar - Emily Diana
events.description:
Speaker: EMILY DIANA, Assistant Professor, Operations Research Group,
Tepper School of Business, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Learning in Strategic Environments: Fair Classification
and Algorithmic Pricing

Algorithms are increasingly deployed in settings where the individuals
or firms interacting with them behave strategically. In this talk, I
will discuss two problems in which this strategic behavior changes the
learning problem and the outcomes that can be guaranteed.

First, I will consider strategic classification, where agents
manipulate their features, at a cost, to receive a positive
classification from a learner’s classifier, and the learner aims to
learn a classifier robust to these strategic manipulations. We study
learning objectives with minimax group fairness guarantees in a
population consisting of several groups, where each group may have its
own cost function. For separable costs and a small number of groups,
we give an efficient algorithm for learning an approximately optimal
deterministic classifier. For general cost functions, we give
oracle-efficient algorithms for learning approximately optimal
randomized classifiers when the hypothesis class has finite strategic
VC dimension.

I will then turn to algorithmic pricing. Here, firms repeatedly choose
prices using online learning algorithms, and we study when regret
guarantees are sufficient to rule out algorithmic collusion. We
characterize how the regret notion and the structure of the pricing
game affect the possibility of supra-competitive prices. In
particular, we give conditions under which coarse correlated or
correlated equilibria collapse to the unique Nash equilibrium,
identify settings in which no external regret alone guarantees
competitive prices, and study price correctors that modify algorithmic
price recommendations so that expected transaction prices converge to
competitive levels while firms cannot gain much by reverting to their
original recommendations.

events.title: VASC Seminar - Abe Davis
events.description:
Speaker: ABE DAVIS, Assistant Professor
Computer Science Department
Cornell University

Talk Title: Lawless Progress on Wicked Problems: Shifting the Roles of
Humans in Human-AI Systems

AI is rapidly changing the roles that humans play as developers and
users of new technology. In this talk, I will discuss three of those
shifting roles and how my group addresses them through technical
innovation and interdisciplinary design. Across these projects,
understanding human roles is central to determining what systems
should optimize, what data they need, and how they can be trusted.

Humans as objective functions: Many real-world applications involve
optimizing user-specific objectives, but users’ descriptions of
those objectives can be vague, inconsistent, or even
self-contradictory. I will discuss our work on Interactive Explainable
Ranking (Best Paper, CHI 2026), which combines optimization, AI, and
interaction design to help users identify and resolve contradictions
in how they evaluate different items—from open-ended course projects
to purchasing options or contestants in a competition to find the best
cat.

Humans as a source of data: AI is only effective if we have the right
data, and many important applications depend on specific or
individualized data that needs to be captured in uncontrolled
settings. Multiple projects in my group focus on designing systems
that help humans capture such data using mobile devices. This work
connects capture guidance, sampling theory, computational imaging, and
interaction design to support downstream learning, with applications
spanning remote healthcare, infrastructure, and agriculture.

Humans as adversaries: Some advances in AI also carry significant
potential for harm, which calls for designing new approaches to
protect against adversarial use. One problem that AI has made
particularly challenging is video forensics. I will discuss my
group’s work on designing coded illumination systems to add
near-imperceptible watermarks to lighting in high-stakes environments.
These watermarks make it easier to detect manipulation in recorded
videos without requiring access to or control over recording cameras.

—

Abe Davis is an assistant professor in the Computer Science Department
at Cornell University, where his group works at the intersection of
human-AI systems and visual computing. He earned his Ph.D. in EECS at
MIT. His dissertation received the Sprowls Award for Best PhD Thesis
in Computer Science at MIT, as well as the ACM

SIGGRAPH Outstanding Doctoral Dissertation Honorable Mention Award. He
has received the NSF CAREER Award and a Sloan Research Fellowship, and
has published award-winning papers in venues across visual computing

and HCI. He has also been recognized in Forbes’ “30 Under 30”
and Business Insider’s “50 Scientists Who Are Changing the
World.”

events.description:
Speaker: MARK RUSSINOVICH, Chief Technical Officer
Deputy Chief Information Security Officer, and Technical Fellow
Microsoft Azure

Talk Title: Intelligence Is Not a Security Boundary: Building Controls
Before AI Agents Outrun ThemMonday, October 26, 2026, 5 – 6:30pm
AI is changing the security model of computing. It puts expert
capability into anyone’s hands, operates at machine speed, and turns
software from passive code into an active participant that can
discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, deceive overseers, and
reason about the constraints meant to contain it. At the same time,
alignment safeguards that keep AI systems operating within their
intended goals and constraints can be removed, unsafe models can gain
capability from aligned ones, and untrusted information can steer
agents toward privileged actions. These are not just new bugs; they
challenge assumptions that have shaped computer security for decades.
We need a new security stack, one based on isolation, capabilities,
provenance, and deterministic enforcement. Intelligence cannot be the
security boundary.—Mark Russinovich is CTO, Deputy CISO, and
Technical Fellow for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft’s global
enterprise-grade cloud platform. A widely recognized expert in
distributed systems, operating systems and cybersecurity, Mark earned
a Ph.D. in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. He
later co-founded Winternals Software, joining Microsoft in 2006 when
the company was acquired. Mark is a popular speaker at industry
conferences such as Microsoft Ignite, Microsoft Build, and RSA
Conference. He has authored several nonfiction and fiction books,
including the Microsoft Press Windows Internals book series,
Troubleshooting with the Sysinternals Tools, as well as fictional
cyber security thrillers Zero Day, Trojan Horse and Rogue Code.CMU

events.description:
Speaker: RIKU ARAKAWA, Ph.D. Student, Human-Computer Interaction
Institute, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Sensing and Human-AI Interaction for Reliable, Proactive
Care Over Time

Context-aware proactive systems can move beyond today’s reactive,
chatbot-style interactions by sensing users’ activities and states
and providing support at appropriate moments. Such capabilities are
particularly promising for health and well-being, where AI assistants
could serve as companions that understand users’ conditions and
evolving needs in everyday life. However, real-world sensing is
inherently uncertain: sensor data are noisy, human behavior is
ambiguous, and the meaning of an observed activity varies across
individuals and contexts. As a result, simple sensing-and-intervention
pipelines can trigger inappropriate interventions, frustrate users,
and undermine trust. My research investigates how to build proactive
systems that remain reliable under sensing uncertainty through three
complementary directions: (1) understanding and mitigating sensing
uncertainty, (2) designing uncertainty-aware Human-AI interactions,
and (3) enabling adaptation through everyday interactions. In this
talk, I will illustrate this research trajectory through several
interactive assistants for health and well-being. Drawing on
deployments involving more than 300 patients, I will share lessons
from translating these systems into real-world settings and discuss
future directions toward reliable, adaptive AI companions for everyday
care.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar - Tom Costello
events.description:
Speaker: TOM COSTELLO, Assistant Professor, Department of Social and
Decision Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in
conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant
to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social
and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways.
When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they
are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk
I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and
what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending
this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview
first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored
arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the
most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage
persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results
imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for
information.

—

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision
Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as
Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at
Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s
Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology,
political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our
viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why
they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial
intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: Theory Seminar
events.description:
Speaker: MOR HARCHOL-BALTER, Bruce J. Nelson Professor of Computer
Science Department of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: The Joys of Stochastic Scheduling

Scheduling is the primary tool we have for improving system
performance without purchasing additional resources. By simply
changing the order in which we run jobs, we can dramatically improve
response time (both mean response time and the tail of response
time). Scheduling is particularly effective in the case of
heavy-tailed job size distributions, which are omnipresent and can
result in very high response times. In this talk we focus on the
heavy-tailed job size setting.

We will start by reviewing optimal scheduling for the single-server
queue (the M/G/1), both for the mean and asymptotic tail of response
time. This is well understood. We then turn to multi-server
systems (the M/G/n), where almost nothing is understood on optimal
scheduling. We present our new results on the first scheduling
algorithms for the M/G/n which are asymptotically strongly tail
optimal.

We finish by discussing newer job models, like the multi-server job
model, which is representative of today’s datacenter jobs. Here we
present some recent algorithms for optimal scheduling under heavy
traffic.

Throughout, our emphasis will be on intuition and lessons learned.

Joint work with primarily Zhouzi Li and Alan Scheller-Wolf.

⇢ This talk is meant as a practice talk for the Markov Lecture
keynote which I'm giving next month at INFORMS APS

events.title: VASC Seminar - Hanbyul Joo
events.description:
Speaker: HANBYUL JOO, Associate Professor, Department of Computer
Science and Engineering, Seoul University

Talk Title: From Capturing People to Teaching Robots

Equipping AI and robotic systems with the ability to understand human
behavior is essential for enabling them to assist people across a wide
range of everyday applications. This need is more pressing than ever:
the heaviest consumers of such knowledge are no longer perception
systems alone, but robot policies that must learn to act in the
physical world. Yet the high-quality 3D human motion data required to
learn this knowledge remains extremely scarce.

In this talk, I will present our lab's efforts to scale and enrich 3D
human motion data by capturing everyday movements and natural
human-object interactions, with the ultimate goal of teaching robots
to move like humans.

I will first introduce our multi-year effort in building multi-camera
capture systems, from Panoptic Studio to ParaHome, and most recently
OmniRoboHome, a new system designed to capture human-object
interactions in natural home environments. Next, I will present a
complementary direction: learning everyday interactions and
affordances from generative image and video models, which offer a
scalable source of human behavior priors that capture systems alone
cannot reach. Finally, I will discuss the missing pieces that vision
and image models cannot provide, including physics, contact, and the
gap across diverse embodiments, together with our recent efforts to
fill them.

—

Hanbyul Joo is an associate professor at Seoul National University
(SNU) in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering. Before
joining SNU, Hanbyul was a Research Scientist at Facebook AI Research
(FAIR), Menlo Park. Hanbyul received his PhD from the Robotics
Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. He is a recipient of the
Samsung Scholarship, the Okawa Foundation Research Grant, and the Best
Student Paper Award at CVPR 2018.

events.title: Crypto Seminar - William Wang
events.description:
Speaker: WILLIAM WANG, Ph.D. Student, Courant Institute, New York
University

Talk Title: The Cost of Rewinding for Succinct Arguments: Strict-Time
Barriers and Expected-Time Security

Succinct arguments are central cryptographic objects, underlying
applications such as blockchains, image authentication, and, more
recently, AI safety. Almost all succinct arguments used in practice
follow the commit-and-open paradigm introduced by Kilian (STOC 1992).
Decades of work have generalized and optimized this paradigm, yet the
security it provably achieves in the standard model remains unclear.

Existing analyses proceed by rewinding and leave a gap: strict-time
analyses lose an inverse-polynomial factor, while the sharper
expected-time analyses apply only to a special case of the paradigm.
In this talk, we close this gap, giving matching upper and lower
bounds on the security of commit-and-open succinct arguments.

Based on joint work with Alessandro Chiesa, Ziyi Guan, and Yuetian Wu.

Ziyi Guan will also be present.

events.title: Database Seminar - Marco Primi
events.description:
Speaker: MARCO PRIMITalk Title: Everything Has Bugs. Here’s How
Antithesis Catches Them.

Programs used to run on a single computer start to end. Today nearly
all software is part of a larger distributed system. Databases were
among the earliest to undergo this transition at the turn of the
century, replication, fault-tolerance, consensus, scalability were the
hot topics of the early cloud era, and they are still relevant today
more than ever.

The shift to distributed-everything has been bumpy, to say the least.
Testing techniques developed during the program's age have proven
themselves ineffective on systems that need to deal with
interleavings, message delays, partial failures, and mind-numbing vast
state spaces.

Over the past decade, new testing techniques have emerged to confront
these new challenges. We will review some of these techniques such as
property-based testing, deterministic simulation testing, chaos
testing, guided fuzzing, mutation testing, differential testing, and
more.

I’ll introduce Antithesis, a platform designed to put these powerful
techniques at your fingertips, allowing you to catch even the most
insidious and rare bugs in minutes. As an example, we’ll review bugs
Antithesis found in Raft implementation, which represents the heart of
numerous databases and storage systems upon which our world relies.

—

Marco Primi identifies as a database and a systems dependability nerd.
After graduating with a Master in Dependable Distributed Systems,
Marco spent the last 15 years working on large and complex systems in
places like Apple and Netflix. Marco's primary area of interest is
leveraging distributed system theory and formal methods to build
high-performance, scalable, reliable distributed systems. With special
focus on replication and consensus.

This talk is part of the Whatever Andy Found Interesting While Out At
Sea.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar - Tomer Ullman
events.description:
Speaker: TOMER D. ULLMAN, Morris Kahn Associate Professor of
Psychology, Department of Psychology, Harvard University

Talk Title: The Bare Stage Before the Mind’s Eye

NOTE: This event is taking place at Harvard University and is
accessible via Zoom

When we imagine things, many of us have the impression that we create
full, rich, vivid scenes. But, we also have the impression of a full,
rich world before us in perception, and decades of cognitive science
have proven us wrong. I’ll examine how recent work shows that when
we imagine, we may only be creating partial scenes, leaving parts of
the scene uncommitted, with much of the work of the imagination done
by rough-and-ready representations.

—

Tomer Ullman is a cognitive scientist interested in common-sense
reasoning, and building computational models for explaining high-level
cognitive processes and the acquisition of new knowledge by children
and adults. In particular, he is focused on how children and adults
come to form intuitive theories of agents and objects, and providing
both a functional and algorithmic account of how these theories are
learned. Such an account would go a long way towards explaining the

events.description:
Speaker: IPPOKRATIS PANDIS, Distinguished Engineer, Databricks

Talk Title: Lakebases, Lakehouses, and LTAP: Unifying Transactions and
Analytics on Open Storage

Traditionally, data architectures maintain a strict division between
high-throughput operational databases and large-scale analytical
lakehouses. The general wisdom for organizations seeking low-latency
real-time analytics is to copy data into dedicated serving layers,
which creates data redundancy, stale insights, and fragmented
governance.

In this talk, we explore how unifying operational and analytical
workloads on open storage eliminates the need to copy data. In the
first part, we present LakehouseRT, an analytical query engine
designed to deliver millisecond-level query latency and high
concurrency directly over open table formats in object stores governed
by a unified catalog. In the second part, we show how Lakebase and its
disaggregated compute and storage OLTP architecture not only provides
best-in-class performance, elasticity, and availability for Postgres
workloads, but also seamlessly enables low-latency analytics directly
on live operational data without compromises.

Ippokratis Pandis is a Distinguished Engineer at Databricks working on

he served as Chief Architect of AWS Analytics and led the development
of Amazon Redshift. Earlier, he contributed to Cloudera Impala and IBM
DB2 BLU. He earned his Ph.D. from Carnegie Mellon University, where in
the dungeons of Wean and Hamerschlag Halls, he worked on multicore
transaction processing. He has authored numerous research papers and
served the database community as General Chair of SIGMOD 2023 and

events.description:
Speaker: DAVID BLEI, William B. Ransford Professor of Statistics and
Computer Science, Departments of Statistics and Computer Science,
Columbia University

Talk Title: A Fresh Look at Empirical Bayes

Empirical Bayes improves simultaneous inference by learning from
related data. In this talk, I will present three recent directions in
empirical Bayes. First, I will discuss an empirical Bayes approach to
combining randomized experiments and observational studies, where
calibration studies make it possible to learn the distribution of
observational bias and use observational data in a principled way.
Second, I will discuss empirical Bayes for implicit likelihoods, where
the model is available only through a simulator, and show how
simulation-based inference can be used to produce empirical Bayes
estimates without evaluating a density. Third, I will discuss a
general method based on probabilistic symmetries, which extends
empirical Bayes beyond exchangeable settings to structured problems
such as arrays, graphs, conditional data, and spatial models. These
three ideas illustrate new roles for empirical Bayes in modern
statistics and machine learning.

This is joint work with Diana Cai, Don Green, Sebastian Salazar,
Xinwei Shen, Eli Weinstein, Bohan Wu, Cheng Zhang.

—

David Blei is the William B. Ransford Professor of Statistics and
Computer Science at Columbia University. He studies probabilistic
machine learning and Bayesian statistics, including theory,
algorithms, and application. David has received several awards for his
research, including the ACM Prize in Computing (2013), a Guggenheim
fellowship (2017), a Simons Investigator Award (2019), the AAAI John
McCarthy award (2024), and the ACM/AAAI Allan Newell Award (2024). He
was the co-editor-in-chief of the Journal of Machine Learning Research

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Zikun Li
events.description:
Speaker: ZIKUN LI, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: OpWeave: Flexible Operator Disaggregation for
Heterogeneous LLM Serving

LLM serving systems increasingly disaggregate inference into
finer-grained stages, with recent approaches separating attention from
FFN or MoE execution during decode. This operator-level disaggregated
serving (ODS) can improve hardware matching and enable independent
scaling, particularly across heterogeneous devices. However, existing
systems fix operator boundaries and lack a unified characterization of
when disaggregation reduces serving cost.

In this talk we present OpWeave, an end-to-end framework for
heterogeneous ODS. OpWeave provides an analytical cost model that
bounds the gains of homogeneous and heterogeneous ODS over colocated
serving. It jointly optimizes operator partitioning and deployment
configuration through a regularity-aware planner that keeps the search
tractable even for hybrid-attention models. A vLLM-based runtime
executes the synthesized plans with flexible operator stages across
heterogeneous device groups. In our evaluation, OpWeave reduces
serving cost by up to 1.78× on homogeneous and 1.89× on
heterogeneous GPU clusters relative to the best feasible baseline,
while meeting latency SLOs.

events.description:
Speaker: ALEXANDER POLYANSKII, Assistant Professor, Department of
Mathematics, Emory University

Talk Title: Tight colorful no-dimensional Tverberg theorem

In this talk, I will discuss a tight colorful dimension-free Tverberg
theorem. If P1,…,k are finite disjoint sets of n points in a
Euclidean space, then our result guarantees a partition of the union
P1∪⋯∪Pk into n rainbow sets of size k such that a single ball
intersects the convex hull of every set. The radius of this ball
depends only on the number of color classes, the number of rainbow
sets, and the largest diameter of a color class --- not on the
dimension of the ambient space. Moreover, the resulting bound is best
possible.

The key tool is a Pythagorean-type subadditivity property of the
Chebyshev radius, which is of independent interest. Given sequences X
= (x1,…,xn) and Y = (y1,…,yn) of points in a Euclidean space,
contained in balls of radii RX and RY, respectively, one can
re-enumerate Y so that the pointwise-sum sequence Z = X + Y is
contained in a ball of radius satisfying R2/Z ≤ R2/X + R2/Y.

This is joint work with Polina Barabanshchikova and Grigory Ivanov.

events.title: Statistics and Data Science Seminar - Andrej Risteski
events.description:
Speaker: ANDREJ RISTESKI, Associate Professor, Machine Learning
Department, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Inference-Time Algorithms: A Theoretical Lens on
Tractability and Error Propagation

Modern AI systems are increasingly built by placing trained models
inside larger computational loops. Inference-time algorithms are a
basic instance of this idea: they use one or more trained models at
test time to incorporate new information, exploit pretrained models as
priors, and trade computational effort for accuracy, sample quality,
or control. Examples include generator-verifier search for reasoning,
diffusion models for solving inverse problems, and reward-guided
generation. Theoretically, this revisits a classical question from
optimization and theoretical computer science: what can be done with
access to an oracle? Here, however, the oracles are new and
non-standard: they model the capabilities of large pretrained models,
making them powerful, but also imperfect because they are learned.
This combination leads to new questions about algorithm design and
error propagation.

This talk studies two central aspects of this paradigm: computational
efficiency and error propagation. The first vignette considers
generator-verifier systems, and shows how stochastic backtracking can
trade additional computation for accuracy, giving a principled version
of test-time scaling even with imperfect learned oracles. The second
vignette studies diffusion steering: when can we efficiently bias a
pretrained diffusion model toward higher-reward samples while staying
close to the original model? We show that tractability depends
strongly on both the reward structure and the alignment objective, and
that simple primitives—such as sampling from linear tilts—can be
surprisingly useful for handling richer reward classes

Based on arxiv.org/abs/2510.03149, arxiv.org/abs/2602.16570,
arxiv.org/abs/2605.11361.

—

Andrej Risteski is an Associate Professor at the Machine Learning
Department in Carnegie Mellon University. Prior to that, he was a
Norbert Wiener Research Fellow jointly in the Applied Math department
and IDSS at MIT. He received his PhD in the Computer Science
Department at Princeton University.

His research interests lie in the intersection of machine learning,
statistics, and theoretical computer science, spanning topics like
generative models, algorithmic tools for learning and inference,
representation and self-supervised learning, out-of-distribution
generalization and applications of deep learning to scientific
domains. The broad goal of his research is principled and mathematical
understanding of statistical and algorithmic problems arising in
modern machine learning paradigms.

Speaker: SARAH CEN, Assistant Professor, Department of Electrical and

Talk Title: The AI Supply Chain: Relationships, Dependencies, and
Vulnerabilities in the AI Industry

The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems,
particularly general-purpose models, has spawned a complex,
interdependent ecosystem of organizations that produce, deploy, and
maintain AI systems. We refer to this network of dependencies as the
AI supply chain. In this talk, we will discuss the origins and
implications of the AI supply chain, as well as recent projects on (1)
mapping the supply chain and its dependencies, (2) tracking how
properties in the AI supply chain are propagated, and (3) exploring
the legal ramifications of the AI supply chain

learning, statistics, economics, law, and public policy. Her recent
work includes projects on AI audits, AI supply chains, social media
regulation, algorithmic fairness, causalinference under network
interference, individual rights in the age of AI, and procedural due
process for AI-driven decisions. She was previously an HAI
postdoctoral researcher at Stanford, jointly affiliated with Stanford
Law School’s RegLab and the Department of Computer Science, working

Cen earned her Ph.D. in electrical engineering and computer science at

autonomous vehicles; and a BSE in mechanical engineering at Princeton

Talk Title: Text-based Tactile Graphics Generation for the Visually
Impaired

Tactile graphics help blind and low-vision (BLV) people access
non-textual information, but creating customized graphics remains
difficult and time-consuming. We present the first generative system
that produces fabrication-ready 2.5D tactile graphics directly from
natural-language prompts. The system integrates global relief
geometry, tactile surface textures, and standard-compliant braille

automatic generation and interactive texture control. In-person
studies with BLV and blindfolded sighted participants using physically
printed outputs show consistent preference for our results over
existing baselines. By extending generative graphics from visual
images to touchable objects, this work explores how generative AI can
make accessible content creation more scalable and personalizable.

events.title: Machine Learning Ph.D. Thesis Proposal - Jacob Springer
events.description:
Speaker: JACOB SPRINGER, Ph.D. Student, Machine Learning Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Learning for Adaptation

Language models must learn from new data while preserving the
capabilities and variety of behavior that make them useful. However,
fine-tuning can lead to catastrophic forgetting, reduce semantic
diversity, and cause learned behavior to generalize beyond its
training context in undesirable directions. This thesis studies how to
train models for future adaptation, with three objectives: mitigating
catastrophic forgetting, preserving semantic diversity, and making
generalization of learned behavior possible to understand, predict,
and control.

We approach these objectives through optimization and data design
during upstream training, including pretraining and mid-training. From
an optimization perspective, we study how training methods and
hyperparameters influence the ability to learn new tasks while
preserving prior capabilities. From a data perspective, we study how
the order and structure of training data can make capabilities more
robust and retain variety in model completions. We evaluate these
approaches through both preservation and learning, with the goal of
developing models that can adapt to new objectives without giving up
useful properties of their previous training.

We further study how learned behavior appears across different types
of prompts and completions, with the goal of understanding where
changes induced by fine-tuning will generalize and how this transfer
can be controlled. Our proposed work will connect this question to
robustness by testing whether upstream optimization and data order can
shape how different context types respond to later updates. The goal
is desirable selective transfer: new behavior should generalize where
it is useful, while other behavior remains stable. Across these
directions, we aim to guide the development of base models that retain
useful capabilities and semantic diversity while allowing adaptation
whose effects we can understand and control.

Graham Neubig

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Runming Li
events.description:
Speaker: RUNMING LI, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science Department,
Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Directed proof-relevant logical relations in simplicial
HoTT

Intrinsically-typed presentations of type theory often use equality
types in the meta-language to represent object-language judgmental
equality. In such equational syntax, proof-relevant logical relations
define computability predicates on judgmental equivalence classes of
types and terms. This approach, however, does not directly account for
reduction, which is directed and plays a central role in many
logical-relations arguments.

This work develops a directed version of proof-relevant logical
relations in simplicial homotopy type theory, a directed variant of
homotopy type theory, where reductions are internalized as inequality
types. We construct object syntax as a directed quotient inductive
type. The central observation is that contravariant families in
simplicial type theory provide exactly the proof-relevant form of
closure under expansion for logical relations: computability evidence
can be transported backward along reductions, with the required
functoriality and universal property built in.

Using this observation, we construct a unary logical relations model
with contravariant computability predicates and prove directed Boolean
canonicity: every closed Boolean term reduces to either true or false.
We then extend the construction to dependent types and universes,
where a comonadic flat modality provides the discreteness needed for
type conversion and universe predicates. Finally, we adapt the method
to binary logical relations, separating vertical reduction from
horizontal parametricity and obtaining a proof-relevant account of
representation independence.

events.description:
Talk Title: Peer Review Processes

Topic

Peer review at major research journals now involves hundreds of
submissions per month, and the case for automated reviewer assignment
is clear. What is less clear is how to do it well: unlike conference
assignment, which can be solved offline once all submissions are in,
journal assignment must be done online: each paper assigned
immediately upon arrival, from a pool of reviewers who may become
unavailable for weeks once assigned.

We study this as an instance of online task assignment with reusable
resources: tasks arrive over time, each must be immediately assigned
to k of R available resources, and each assigned resource is busy for
d subsequent timesteps. This model captures peer review, healthcare
scheduling, ridesharing, and emergency dispatch. I will present
restless-bandit based policies and upper bounds. I will also discuss a
closed-form Whittle index policy for automated reviewer assignment and
insights from evaluation on a four-year trace of submissions to TMLR.

Led by students of all levels, these sessions offer a casual forum to
discuss AI-related research while exploring cross-cutting connections
between various disciplines in artificial intelligence. All students
welcome!

Talk Title: Compiling Coinductive Logic Programs to Concurrent
Processes

In this talk we present two calculi for describing concurrently
running processes: CoLF logic programs and the semi-axiomatic sequent
calculus (SAX).

Focusing on the first-order fragment of CoLF, we show how CoLF logic
programs can be compiled into SAX processes. The main idea is to treat
logic variables as communication channels shared between processes,
allowing different parts of a logic program to run in parallel without
backtracking.

events.title: Machine Learning / Artificial Intelligence Seminar - Mahsa Bastankhah
events.description:
Speaker: MAHSA BASTANKHAH, Ph.D. Student, Department of Electrical and
Computer Engineering, Princeton University

Talk Title: Learning abstract representations of the world through
control

Supervised learning has achieved tremendous success in extracting
patterns from large datasets. However, it remains unclear whether the
same models and data can help solve novel tasks in data-scarce
regimes, where massive datasets cannot be collected, and intelligent
data collection through interaction with the environment (i.e., RL) is
itself a big part of the problem. Efficient data collection requires
the agent to learn an abstract representation of the environment that
does not attend to every detail, but instead captures the core factors
governing the dynamics. Otherwise, the real world is so complex that
no agent can model it (the only computer that can model it is the real
world itself). In this work, we argue that representation learning
should be intertwined with learning to control the environment through
interaction. We show that empowerment –the channel capacity between
an agent’s actions and future states– that has been historically
used for diverse behavior learning in RL, is a principled objective
for learning these representations. Maximizing this mutual information
requires the agent to discover different axes of controllability in
the environment. Our main contribution is to show that empowerment
agents learn two distinct and complementary representations of the
state (forward and backward representations), both centered on control
and both discarding control-irrelevant factors, and that these
representations substantially improve performance in complex
environments with high-dimensional distractors. Overall, our work
establishes empowerment as a principled objective for learning
intrinsic representations of an MDP that are independent of any
particular dataset or downstream task, and are centered on
control—the defining aspect that distinguishes reinforcement
learning from supervised learning.

—

Mahsa Bastankhah is a fourth-year PhD student at Princeton. She is
advised by Prof. Benjamin Eysenbach. Her work is focused on
exploration and skill learning in unsupervised RL. She is interested
in emergent exploration and understanding how agents learn to do
complex tasks without hand-designed curricula and what the key
ingredients of such exploration are. She is also interested in
abstract representation learning and understanding the interplay
between representation learning and exploration in high-dimensional
environments.

events.title: CyLab Seminar - Rolfe Schmidt
events.description:
Speaker: ROLFE SCHMIDT, Research Engineer, Signal Messenger

Talk Title: Signal is More Than the Signal Protocol: A Tour of
Vulnerabilities the Proofs Missed

The Signal Protocol is among the most heavily analyzed cryptographic
protocols ever deployed: pen-and-paper proofs, symbolic models, and
machine-checked computational proofs all attest to its security. Those
results are real. Nevertheless, over the years we have found — and
fixed — vulnerabilities in Signal that degraded the security of real
conversations.

This talk surveys a few of them, ranging from the core protocol
implementation to product features layered well above it. For each, I
answer the obvious question: what did the proofs actually cover, and
why did the deployed system fall outside that coverage? These were not
errors in the analysis. They were gaps between the mathematical
abstractions and the engineering ones.

To put those cases in context, I show a bird's-eye view of Signal's
codebase: how small a fraction is the protocol proper, and how much of
the rest determines the security users actually experience. I close
with how I think the research community and industry can narrow the
gap, and how advances in formal verification are letting us analyze
the code that ships.

—

Rolfe Schmidt is a Research Engineer at Signal Messenger, where he
works to bridge academic research with Signal's engineering and
security needs. He co-designed the PQXDH key agreement protocol and
the SPQR post-quantum ratchet, and has worked on Signal's ORAM-backed
contact discovery, Secure Value Recovery, and anonymous credential
systems. He collaborates widely on formal analysis of deployed
protocols.

→ The CyLab Seminars are only open to CyLab Partnersand current CMU
faculty, staff and students.

In Person and Zoom Participation. See announcement.

events.title: Doctoral Speaking Skills Talk - Keerthana Gurushankar
events.description:
Speaker: KEERTHANA GURUSHANKAR, Ph.D. Student, Computer Science
Department, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: Maximizing Match Quality in Online Skill-based Routing

When a customer calls, which agent should answer? When a new paper
arrives, which reviewers should we assign it to? When an emergency
occurs, which responders should we send? We study these as the problem
of maximizing match quality in online skill-based routing.

We develop a simple index policy, LAG, that assigns tasks to resources
not just based on instantaneous match quality, but also on the
opportunity cost of consuming scarce resources. We prove that LAG is
fluid-optimal when task arrival rates and the number of servers scale
proportionally. We demonstrate its effectiveness on peer-review and
call-center instances, where LAG achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound
and substantially outperforms greedy assignment.

In-person and Zoom

Presented as part of the AI-SDM Seminar Series

Presented in Partial Fulfillment of the CSD Speaking Skills
Requirement

events.description:
Speaker: TOM M. MITCHELL, SCS Founders University Professor, Machine
Learning Department, School of Computer Science, and, Block Center for
Technology and Society, Carnegie Mellon University

Talk Title: The History of Machine Learning: How Did We Get Here?

Machine learning is the key technology underlying today's amazing
artificial intelligence systems.

How did we get to today's technology which now supports a trillion
dollar AI industry? What were the key scientific breakthroughs? What
were the surprises and dead-ends along the way, as seen by the
researchers who created them? Who were the personalities involved, and
what were they thinking at the time? What should we learn from all
this?

—

Tom M. Mitchell is the Founders University Professor at Carnegie
Mellon University, where he founded the world's first Machine Learning
Department, and served as Interim Dean of the School of Computer
Science (2018-2019). Beginning with his 1979 Ph.D. research he has
worked in machine learning and AI, and he remains optimistic about its
future. In 2010 Mitchell was elected to the U.S. National Academy of
Engineering \"For pioneering contributions and leadership in the
methods and applications of machine learning.\" Mitchell is also a
member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and a Fellow and
Past President of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial
Intelligence (AAAI).

This talk will explore the history of machine learning based on
personal experience of the speaker, augmented by video interviews with
a dozen pioneering researchers in the field.

events.title: AI-SDM Seminar Series: Tom Costello
events.description:
Correcting Inaccurate Beliefs Using Human-AI Dialogues

Join us for our biweekly seminar series! Lunch is provided for in-person attendees. Please complete the RSVP form to help us with logistics.

Abstract
Dialogues with large language models can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories, a class of beliefs often thought to be resistant to evidence. Further, in field experiments, AI replies on Truth Social and Bluesky reduce later conspiratorial posting. This cuts both ways. When the same models are told to argue that a conspiracy is true, they are about as persuasive as when they argue it is false. In this talk I’ll discuss a set of studies on why these conversations work and what that implies. Finally, I’ll describe a new approach extending this research to climate skepticism. An AI-driven cognitive interview first maps the beliefs underlying a person’s view, and tailored arguments then target those beliefs. This approach outperforms the most effective human-written climate messages, and the advantage persists weeks later. I’ll close by discussing what these results imply for designing the AI systems people increasingly turn to for information.

Speaker Bio

Thomas Costello is an Assistant Professor in Social and Decision Sciences at Carnegie Mellon University. He also holds appointments as Affiliated Faculty at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and is a Research Affiliate at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. His research integrates psychology, political science, and human-computer interaction to examine where our viewpoints come from, how they differ from person to person, and why they change. He also studies the sweeping impacts of artificial intelligence on these belief- and society-related processes.

events.title: AI-SDM Student Brainstorming Session
events.description:
Led by: AI-SDM Meta AI for Good team

During major natural disasters, emergency responders are often faced with severe information overload and conflicting data. Serving as a key partner during these events, NSF AI-SDM creates outputs that incorporate Meta’s restricted-access datasets alongside open-source AI models to deliver clear, standardized data products that prioritize actionable insights.

Led by students of all levels, these sessions offer a casual forum to discuss AI-related research while exploring cross-cutting connections between various disciplines in artificial intelligence. All students welcome!

Students meet regularly to participate in informal discussion sessions that delve into cutting-edge AI topics. These discussions are a breeding ground for collaboration, innovative thinking, and problem-solving from the ground up. They provide a stress-free forum for exchanging ideas, brainstorming new approaches to challenges, and fostering lasting connections within the AI-SDM community in an environment distinct from a traditional seminar. Lunch is provided for in-person attendees! Please complete the RSVP form below to help us with logistics.

events.description: On March 22, Hindus celebrate Holi, which is known as the Festival of Colors, Festival of Spring, and the Festival of Love. It marks the arrival of spring, the divine love of Radha Krishna, and the victory of good over evil with a celebration of color and maybe attendance at their temple. CMU usually has its own celebration of Holi on April 18, the Sunday of Carnival weekend.

events.title: X in the Loop Webinar Series
events.description:
X in the Loop is an interdisciplinary webinar series that questions what it means for humans to remain “in control” of AI. By replacing “human” with the open variable “X,” the series explores who holds power in AI systems, whose perspectives are included and what other species, cultures and ways of knowing might belong in the loop.

Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: ​Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

The seminar series’ second installment will be a talk called “Challenges and Opportunities to Ensure Critical Components and Dynamics in Operational Energy Systems” with Greg Shannon, Ph.D., a laboratory fellow and chief cybersecurity scientist at Idaho National Laboratory.

events.title: CMU/Pitt Colloquium: Dan Baxter (Fermilab)
events.description:
Speaker: Daniel Baxter (Fermilab)

Topic: Harnessing Quantum Sensors to Search for Dark Matter

Abstract: The CosmiQuantum group at Fermilab is at the center of understanding the relationship between particle impacts in quantum processors and qubit errors. This research hopes to enable high-fidelity quantum computation by resolving the issue of phonon-mediated correlated errors following cosmic ray impacts in a superconducting qubit chip. Additionally, this challenge for quantum computing presents a unique opportunity for fundamental science, as the same errors that follow a particle impact can be used to search for low-energy signatures of new physics originating from dark matter or neutrino impacts. At Fermilab, we have two world-class underground facilities which are already being used to study this problem: NEXUS and QUIET. I will present results from operating superconducting qubits in each of these facilities, and the potential implications towards utilizing qubits as sensors of new physics.

events.title: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)
events.description:
Speaker: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)

Topic: Arch and Scaffold: Jordan’s statistical transformation theory and von Neumann’s Hilbert space formalism

Abstract: In early 1927, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, independently of one another, published their versions of a general formalism tying the various forms of the new quantum theory together and giving the theory’s statistical interpretation in full generality. This formalism has come to be known as the Dirac-Jordan (statistical) transformation theory. A few months later, in response to these publications, John von Neumann published his Hilbert space formalism for quantum mechanics. The relation between these two formalisms can be captured in terms of a metaphor for theory change in which one theory serves as the scaffold for the arch of another theory. What is unclear in this case is which formalism serves as the scaffold and which one as the arch. Did von Neumann build an arch on the scaffold built by Jordan? Or did von Neumann build a scaffold to prevent the arch built by Jordan from collapsing? Either way, the arch-and-scaffold metaphor is a promising alternative to Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm shifts for understanding theory change.

Note: Based on joint work with Anthony Duncan (University of Pittsburgh)

Meeting ID: 978 4615 2917.

Passcode: 299792

events.title: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Christina Marchetti (UCSB)
events.description:
Active Matter: The Physics of Self-Organization

Birds flock, bees swarm and fish school. These are just some of the remarkable examples of collective behavior found in nature. Physicists have been able to capture some of this behavior by modeling organisms as ``flying spins’’ that align with their neighbors according to simple but noisy rules. Successes like these have spawned a field devoted to the physics of active matter – matter made not of atom and molecules but of entities that consume energy to generate their own motion and forces. Through interactions, collectives of such active particles organize in emergent structures on scales much larger than that of the individuals. Living systems are the paradigm of such behavior, but same behavior has also been mimicked in the lab through the engineering a variety of ``active particles’’ that self-assemble to form smart materials.

In this lecture I will introduce the field of active matter and highlight ongoing efforts by physicists, biologists, engineers and mathematicians to model the complex behavior of these systems, with the goal of identifying universal principles. I will specifically focus on two examples of active behavior. The first highlights how active particles bypass the laws of equilibrium thermodynamics and spontaneously aggregate in the absence of any attractive interactions. The second describes the interplay of flow and topological defects in controlling dynamics and structure of active phases with liquid crystalline order, with relevance from materials science to biology.

Meeting ID: 978 4615 2917.

events.title: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen
events.description:
LCAL’s Informal Conversations on Research (ICOR) Series provides a welcoming forum for faculty and graduate students to share and discuss their most recent research in an engaging, accessible format.

Translingual Borders: Refugee Testimony and the Politics of Translation

Isabelle Chen, assistant professor of global French studies, will challenge the assumption that translation is a liberatory practice — one that enables people to cross linguistic, cultural and geographic borders — by examining how translation can also reinforce borders, reproduce unequal power dynamics and constrain individual agency.

Focusing on Shumona Sinha’s novel Assommons les pauvres ! (Down with the Poor!), Dr. Chen’s talk explores the experiences of a Bengali interpreter working with asylum seekers in France. She examines how Sinha uses translation both as a literary strategy and a central thematic motif to portray interpretation as a potential barrier to human mobility and freedom.

Drawing on translation theory and recent migration data, Dr. Chen considers what literary representations of translation can reveal about its real-world consequences — and about the roles of multilingualism, interpretation and language in immigration policy and advocacy today.

events.title: X in the Loop Webinar Series
events.description:
X in the Loop is an interdisciplinary webinar series that questions what it means for humans to remain “in control” of AI. By replacing “human” with the open variable “X,” the series explores who holds power in AI systems, whose perspectives are included and what other species, cultures and ways of knowing might belong in the loop.

Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: ​Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: World of Music: Christopher Mark Jones’ “Montréal Encore”
events.description:
Christopher Mark Jones, professor emeritus of French & Francophone studies, returns with a celebration of his French-language album Montréal Encore, premiered with his collaborator Bernard Pozier at City of Asylum in March of 2023.

This concert features selections from that album and mix-ins by Québécois, French Caribbean and Parisian singer-songwriters—the likes of Boris Vian, Michel Rivard, Louis Aragon and Henri Salvador.

Free In-Person Tickets | Free Livestream Tickets

Featured Musicians:

Christopher Mark Jones: vocals, guitar

Brad Yoder: vocal harmonies, guitar, saxophone, glockenspiel

Mark Perna: bass

Eric George: African djembe and hand cymbals

Matt Siegler: piano and accordion

About the Artist:

Christopher Mark Jones draws from folk, country, blues, jazz and R&B sources to stage his literate folk-rock meditations. Using diverse points of view to narrate and critique life and love in uncertain times, he invites listeners to think, feel and dance. Recorded and live arrangements leave space for his musical co-conspirators to both express their personalities and honor the host creation. Listeners hear echoes of “Greg Brown’s pacing and a Lyle Lovett attitude” (Ben Shannon), as well as of John Prine, Bruce Coburn and Darrell Scott.

Between careers as a basketball player and French professor, Christopher busked in Paris, toured the UK, Denmark and Holland, and played New England clubs. He now tours and streams solo from Pittsburgh, PA, and plays regionally in formats varying from solo to full band. Looking for the Light (2021) is his sixth recording of original folk/roots songs, while Montréal Encore (2022) is a French-language recording created in collaboration with the poet Bernard Pozier.
