events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.

events.title: Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke
events.description:
Sinkhorn Treatment Effects: A Causal Optimal Transport Measure

Abstract: We introduce the Sinkhorn treatment effect, an entropic optimal transport measure of divergence between counterfactual distributions. Unlike classical quantities such as the average treatment effect, this measure captures differences across entire distributions. We analyze this divergence as a statistical functional and show it can be written as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings with an appropriate kernel. This characterization allows us to establish first-order pathwise differentiability in general, and second-order pathwise differentiability under the null hypothesis of equal counterfactual distributions. Leveraging this smoothness, we construct debiased estimators and use them to obtain asymptotically valid tests for distributional treatment effects with a fixed entropic regularization parameter. Because the power of the test depends on this unknown parameter, we further propose an aggregated test that combines evidence across a grid of regularization choices. Experiments on simulated and image data demonstrate the practical advantages of our estimator and testing procedure.

Bio: Alex Luedtke is a Professor of Health Care Policy and Affiliate in Statistics at Harvard University. Previously, he held faculty appointments in Statistics and Biostatistics at the University of Washington and Fred Hutch.

Alex works at the intersection of semiparametrics, causal inference, and machine learning. Much of his work leverages computational power to automate the construction of efficient statistical procedures. To this end, he has developed methods that let machines “learn to learn” from data, and algorithms that work out derivations once done by hand. He applies these tools as part of multidisciplinary teams to improve decision-making in mental health and infectious disease research.

Selected honors include a COPSS Emerging Leader Award, NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, and Mortimer Spiegelman Award. His work has been supported by NIH, NSF, PCORI, WHO, and Netflix.

Alex received a Ph.D. in Biostatistics from UC Berkeley and an ScB in Applied Mathematics from Brown University.

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“Interface control of material functionality” presented by Valentino Cooper (Oak Ridge National Laboratory)

Abstract: Advances in thin film growth techniques, which allow for the precise layer-by-layer growth of epitaxial materials, have opened the door to discoveries not previously achievable through bulk synthesis. Pertinent examples include emergent phenomena at oxide heterointerfaces such as two-dimensional electron gases, interfacial superconductivity and novel magnetic properties. In this presentation, I will discuss our use of first principles calculations to explore how the character of heterostructure interfaces can be used to influence material stability and functionality. I will illustrate the role that charge transfer plays in driving magnetism and anomalous dielectric responses at oxide interfaces, and how these can be modulated through chemical identity and interface disorder. Collectively, these results demonstrate unprecedented control over interfacial charge and spin, creating a new avenue for a wide range of applications such as in oxide electronics.

Dr. Valentino R. Cooper is a Distinguished R&D Staff Member and Section Head for Foundational and Quantum Materials Science in the Materials Sciences and Technology Division at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. He serves as Director of the Department of Energy-funded Energy Frontier Research Center on Fast and Cooperative Ion Transport in Polymer Electrolytes (FaCT). Dr. Cooper received his Ph.D. in chemistry from the University of Pennsylvania in 2005 and was a postdoctoral associate in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Rutgers University before joining ORNL in 2008. His research focuses on the development and application of electronic structure methods to understand dispersion interactions and predict functional materials, including piezoelectrics, ferroelectrics, complex oxides, and polymer electrolyte materials. From 2017 to 2020, he was an Associate Editor of the Journal of Applied Physics and currently serves on the Board of Managers for AIP Publishing. He received the Department of Energy Early Career Award in 2013, the ORNL Office of Research Excellence Mentor MVP Award in 2023, and was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 2024.
events.summary: “Interface control of material functionality” presented by Valentino Cooper (Oak Ridge National Laboratory)

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“The Future of STEM & STEM Leaders: A Nexus of Trust, Innovation and Credibility” presented by Judy Giordan (ecosVC, Inc.)

ABSTRACT: At a time when public trust in science and scientific innovations is rapidly shifting, the rules we thought we knew about how society views STEM practitioners and institutions are being rewritten. How did we get here? How do we navigate this uncertainty? Join this session as we trace the evolving relationship between STEM, innovation, and the public from post-WWII to today, and explore three actionable pillars that individual STEM practitioners and institutions can use to rebuild trust, restore credibility, and foster confidence in the ground-breaking innovations we create.

Judy Giordan is Managing Director of ecosVC, Inc., co-founder of the Chemical Angels Network, venture founder and former Fortune 100 executive. She serves as board member, co-founder, advisor and investor in seed and early-stage start-ups and is co-host of the podcast and newsletter Trust?Trust!Trust found on Substack.

Her previous executive positions include Corporate Vice President and Global Director of Research and Development at International Flavors and Fragrances, Inc.; Vice-President Worldwide Research and Development for Pepsi-Cola; and Vice President Research and Development, Henkel Corporation, the North American operating unit of the Henkel Group. She is co-founder of ventures in areas including biofuels and executive search and has also held management and technical contributor positions at Polaroid and ALCOA.

Judy served with the National Science Foundation as a member of the Math and Physical Sciences (MPS) Directorate and Chemistry Advisory Boards, Chair of the Alan T. Waterman Award Committee and as IGERT Program Officer. She was 2023 President of the American Chemical Society, is an ACS Fellow and received both the Garvin-Olin and Henry Whelan Awards from ACS. She is a Member of the Women in Chemicals advisory Board. She has held various academic roles including Professor of Practice at Oregon State University and the University of Southern Mississippi and Visiting Professor at Dartmouth College and North Carolina State University. Judy has a B.S. in Environmental Science and VoTech Ag from Rutgers University; Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of Maryland; and was an Alexander von Humboldt post doctoral fellow at the Goethe University, Frankfurt, Germany.

events.description:
A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

Do you trust your students, and do your students trust you? These questions are critical to building a supportive environment for learning in your classroom. In this seminar, we will review various ways to conceptualize trust in a learning environment and share research on why trust is essential to learning from K-12 to higher education. Finally, we will explore various actions instructors can take to build and show trust in their classrooms. Participants should expect to leave with a series of implementable “teaching moves” that foster and demonstrate trust in the classroom.

events.title: Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing
events.description:
This Next Manufacturing seminar features a talk by Dr. Amaranth Karra, Postdoctoral Researcher, University of North Texas.

Abstract

The anisotropy of the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V additively manufactured (AM) via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) is increased by the long and textured columnar prior beta grains that typically occur despite the high cooling rates (105–107 K/s). Additionally, both AM and conventionally fabricated Ti-6Al-4V exhibit dwell-fatigue sensitivity at room-temperature, resulting in premature failure in the low-cycle fatigue regime. This work explores the design and printing of yttria dispersion-hardened Ti-6Al-4V with minimal powder feedstock preparation. A uniformly dispersed yttria with a mean particle size of∼100 nm in the Ti-6Al-4V matrix decreases the transverse size of the prior beta grains. Furthermore, STEM bright-field micrographs reveal dispersoid pinning of dislocations, and STEM EDS confirms that the dispersoids are yttria as expected. A modest increase in room-temperature microhardness is observed, and room-temperature nanoindentation creep results show a∼64% lower mean creep rate compared to standard PBF-LB Ti-6Al-4V. Additionally, a room-temperature compression test was performed to determine the respective yield strengths to study cold creep, and its implications are discussed. At normalized stresses, ODS Ti-6Al-4V exhibits substantially lower long-term creep rates, albeit with greater initial deformation. This work successfully demonstrates the use of PBF-LB to fabricate oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) Ti-6Al-4V, enabling refinement of the prior beta grains and improved long-term time-dependent deformation at normalized stresses.

Bio

Amaranth Karra is a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of North Texas. He received his Ph.D. and M.S. in Materials Science and Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on process metallurgy, additive manufacturing, and process–structure–property relationships in advanced metallic materials. His work spans laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition of refractory alloys, titanium alloys, and oxide dispersion-strengthened materials, with an emphasis on understanding defect formation, phase evolution, and process optimization using advanced characterization techniques, including in situ synchrotron X-ray imaging and diffraction. His current research investigates the additive manufacturing of dispersion-strengthened Ti–6Al–4V alloys, while his doctoral research focused on additive manufacturing of tungsten and tungsten-based alloys for extreme-environment applications.

events.description:
Please join us for CMU Engineering’s virtual program, “Faculty Insights: A 20 Minute Briefing.” In this series, faculty will share insights into their research, its impact, and provide perspective for the future of the field. Following the presentation, attendees will have an opportunity to direct questions and comments to the speaker.

“Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions”

Rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers could substantially increase U.S. power sector emissions and electricity costs by 2030, with particularly large impacts in regions such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Using a detailed energy model covering 26 interconnected U.S. power regions, we evaluate how demand growth, fuel prices, and federal policies affect electricity generation, infrastructure investment, and costs. Data centers could push U.S. power sector carbon emissions up by as much as 28% and spike regional electricity costs by up to 57% by 2030.

events.description:
“Harnessing Light, Color, Ions and Electrons: from Electrochromics to Artificial Retina,” presented by Jianguo Mei

Abstract: The Mei Research Group at Zhejiang University bridges fundamental discovery and real-world innovation by integrating chemistry, materials science, engineering and medicine. We develop organic semiconductors and conductors with transformative potential for printed electronics, bioelectronics, and living electronics, pursuing both technological impact and fundamental scientific frontiers.

In this seminar, I will highlight two complementary research directions: Electrochromic Technologies and Living Electronics. Both are rooted in the precise control of light, color, ions, and electrons, yet extend these principles toward very different applications. Through Ambilight Inc., our discoveries in flexible electrochromic thin films have been translated into roll-to-roll manufacturing and commercialized for applications ranging from electric vehicles to consumer electronics. These examples illustrate how fundamental discoveries made in an academic laboratory can evolve into market-ready technologies.

Our second direction, Living Electronics, asks a more fundamental question: Can electronics become part of living systems rather than being implanted into them? Inspired by biological vision, our work on Organic Eyes seeks to emulate the sensing and processing functions of the human visual system. In parallel, we are exploring electronics that can grow within the brain, creating electronic materials that form and function directly within living neural tissue. While these goals remain at the frontier of science, they point toward a fundamentally different relationship between synthetic materials and biology.

To illustrate the broader philosophy behind our research, I will discuss the journey of n-doped poly(benzodifurandione) (n-PBDF)-from an unexpected polymer discovery and scalable synthesis to applications in flexible electronics and bioelectronics. This case study captures our approach: coupling curiosity-driven discovery with mission-driven innovation. By connecting fundamental chemistry to real-world needs while pursuing ambitious scientific frontiers, we seek to turn new molecular concepts into technologies that can ultimately benefit society.

Refs: M. Chen, D. Wang, Y. Zou, et al., J. Mei, “Long-range extended chains arising from polymerization-driven spontaneous assembly,” Science 393, 172 (2026); S. Samal, S. Xiao, S. Nelson, et al., J. Mei, “Blood-catalyzed n-doped polymers for reversible optical neural control,” Science 392, eadu5500 (2026); K. Chen, H. Hu, I. Song, et al., J. Mei, “Organic optoelectronic synapse based on photon-modulated electrochemical doping,” Nature Photonics 17, 629–637 (2023); I. Song, W.-J. Lee, Z. Ke, et al., J. Mei, “An n-doped capacitive transparent conductor for all-polymer electrochromic displays,” Nature Electronics 7, 1158–1169 (2024).

Jianguo Mei is a Qiushi Chair Professor at Zhejiang University, where he is establishing research programs in organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, printed electronics, and living electronics and leading the Center for Living Electronics and Adaptive Neurotherapeutics (CLEAN). He previously spent 12 years at Purdue University, where he served as Richard and Judith Wien Professor of Chemistry and Department Head. He has authored more than 150 peer-reviewed publications, holds 39 granted U.S. patents, and has received more than 22,000 citations. He is also a co-founder of Ambilight Inc., which pioneered the roll-to-roll manufacturing of flexible electrochromic films for smart windows and other applications.

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
From Materials Sustainability to Quantum Devices: First-Principles Insights into Dynamic Interfaces, presented by Elizabeth Lee (UC Irvine)

Abstract: Material interfaces are critical frontiers where macroscopic functionality

emerges from microscopic phenomena—where bonds break, charges migrate, and heat carriers scatter. While first-principles molecular dynamics (FPMD) provides atomic-level insight into these processes, high computational cost has traditionally restricted its application to small systems (hundreds of atoms) and short timescales (picoseconds). I will discuss our approach for overcoming these limitations by integrating FPMD with Bayesian Inference, neural networks, and rare-event sampling. By bridging the gap between quantum fidelity and long-time and length-scale phenomena, we explore three distinct technological frontiers: (i) reactive chemistry at polymer–metal interfaces for sustainable plastic recycling, (ii) nanoscale heat transfer in alloys in the presence of grain boundaries and dopants, and (iii) charge transfer at semiconductor–water interfaces to realize robust nanoscale quantum sensors. Overall, these results show how predictive, first-principles knowledge of interfacial behavior can provide a rational design roadmap for the next generation of chemical recycling, thermal management, and quantum technologies.

Elizabeth “Liza” Lee is a Samueli Faculty Development Chair Assistant Professor

with joint appointments in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering and the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the University of California, Irvine (UCI). She is also affiliated with the Advanced Casting Research Center (ACRC) and the Eddleman Quantum Institute. She leads the Computational Engineering of Material Interfaces (CeMi) Lab, which develops quantum-classical simulation frameworks—combining electronic structure methods, machine learning, and molecular modeling—to reveal atomic-scale mechanisms at dynamic material interfaces. Her research interests include heterogeneous catalysis, semiconductor defects, and thermal transport in alloys. Before joining UCI, she was a postdoctoral scholar in the Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering at the University of Chicago, where she developed first principles computational frameworks with neural networks to investigate chemical bonding dynamics and equilibria in quantum materials and at metal surfaces. She earned her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she studied nanoscale energy transport phenomena in molecular semiconductors - such as colloidal quantum dots and conjugated polymers—to design next generation photovoltaics and LEDs. Her honors include the NSF CAREER Award, the UCI Samueli Faculty Development Chair Award, and the DOE ASCR Leadership Computing Challenge Award. She has also been recognized for excellence in teaching and mentoring, including receiving the UCI Engineering Student Council’s Professor of the Year Award.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Defense – Ruixuan Liu
events.description:
Date: October 20, 2026

Time: 3:30–5:30 PM ET

Type: RI PhD Thesis Defense

Zoom Link

Location:GHC 4405

Title: Prompt-to-Product: Towards Robots that Imagine, Reason, and Build

Who: Ruixuan Liu

Abstract:

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics have opened new possibilities for helping people turn ideas into physical assemblies. Large language models, multimodal foundation models, and other generative models can interpret user intent and generate designs, while robots can perform increasingly complex assembly tasks. Yet these capabilities often remain disconnected. A design that satisfies a user’s request may be physically unstable or beyond a robot’s ability to build. Meanwhile, a robot proficient at individual manipulation tasks may still depend on detailed, step-by-step commands. This thesis pursues the vision of PROMPT-TO-PRODUCT: robots that move beyond prescribed actions to help people imagine new assemblies, reason about their feasibility, and build them. Using brick assembly as a platform, it investigates the complete process from abstract user intent to physical construction. Its central argument is that reasoning about physics, assembly properties, and robot capabilities must bridge design generation and robotic execution, so that physical feasibility informs both the imagined assembly and the process of building it.

The first part of this thesis develops methods for reasoning about the physical properties of brick assemblies, laying the foundation for the design and construction methods that follow. We present STABLELEGO, a computational tool for analyzing structural stability, and a full-stack physics simulator that extends stability analysis to high-fidelity simulation of brick motions and interactions. The second part investigates how abstract user ideas can be translated into concrete assembly designs. We introduce BRICKGPT, which generates stable and buildable interlocking brick assemblies from text prompts. We then develop an agentic framework for zero-shot assembly design from text and image inputs, which moves beyond BRICKGPT’s restricted component library to support diverse components and articulated structures. The third part develops the manipulation and coordination capabilities needed for precise, long-horizon assembly. We present an end-of-arm tool that manipulates small bricks with high precision, and APEX-MR, an asynchronous coordination algorithm that enables multiple robot arms to build complex structures collaboratively. We then develop visuomotor policies through sim-to-real learning, enabling precise assembly with general-purpose grippers on lightweight robots and extending these capabilities beyond industrial platforms. The fourth part integrates reasoning, generation, and manipulation into the complete PROMPT-TO-PRODUCT system. It connects STABLELEGO, BRICKGPT, and the dual-arm construction system BRICKMATIC to transform natural-language descriptions into physical assemblies, with stability reasoning guiding both design generation and construction. End-to-end demonstrations and a user study evaluate the full workflow.

Together, these contributions connect expressive design generation with the physical reasoning and manipulation required for construction. They expand the range of assemblies that can be designed, the physical behaviors that can be simulated, and the robotic platforms that can build them. Ultimately, this thesis advances the vision of robots that imagine, reason, and build alongside people, helping users realize their ideas without specifying every step of design and construction.

events.title: From Capturing People to Teaching Robots
events.description:
Abstract: Equipping AI and robotic systems with the ability to understand human behavior is essential for enabling them to assist people across a wide range of everyday applications. This need is more pressing than ever: the heaviest consumers of such knowledge are no longer perception systems alone, but robot policies that must learn to act in the physical world. Yet the high-quality 3D human motion data required to learn this knowledge remains extremely scarce.

In this talk, I will present our lab’s efforts to scale and enrich 3D human motion data by capturing everyday movements and natural human-object interactions, with the ultimate goal of teaching robots to move like humans.

I will first introduce our multi-year effort in building multi-camera capture systems, from Panoptic Studio to ParaHome, and most recently OmniRoboHome, a new system designed to capture human-object interactions in natural home environments. Next, I will present a complementary direction: learning everyday interactions and affordances from generative image and video models, which offer a scalable source of human behavior priors that capture systems alone cannot reach. Finally, I will discuss the missing pieces that vision and image models cannot provide, including physics, contact, and the gap across diverse embodiments, together with our recent efforts to fill them.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal – Shashwat Singh
events.description:
RI CALENDAR EVENT

Who: Shashwat Singh

Type: RI Thesis Proposal

Date: Wednesday, October 7, 2026

Time: 03:30PM – 05:00PM (ET)

Location: NSH 4305

Zoom link: Here

Title: Extending Robot Mobility Through Mechanical Adaptation

Abstract:

Unstructured terrain presents diverse challenges to robot locomotion, including obstacles, deformable surfaces, and confined passages. Terrain conditions also change with time, as rainfall alters surface traction or shifting debris and rubble block previously traversable terrain. Addressing these challenges requires robots to adapt how they move and interact with their environments. In this thesis, I investigate how mechanical adaptation can extend the mobility of centimeter-scale robots.

First, I study how switching between complementary locomotion modes extends mobility. A springtail-inspired microrobot (2.1 cm long; 0.98 g), combines crawling and jumping using a single actuator to overcome obstacles. TerraSkipper (5.8 cm long; 28 g) uses impulsive skipping to traverse sand and mud where fin-based crawling is ineffective, while the RESCUE Jumper (8.2cm long; 125 g) reuses its wheel actuators to jump onto steps it cannot climb by rolling.

I further examine how physical collaboration extends mobility rather than integrating every capability into a single robot platform. A centimeter-scale RESCUE roller (9 cm long; 100g) couples with other rollers and with a soft growing robot, also known as Vine robot to share strength and power, and improve mobility. In this work, I used RESCUE Rollers to manipulate a Vine robot in a two-dimensional plane, expanding its operational workspace. To extend this capability even further, I propose developing Drone Roller (19.4cm long; 200g), a compact aerial–ground version of the RESCUE Roller that can fly over obstacles it cannot climb and guide the Vine robot in three-dimensional space.

Finally, I study how incorporating an adaptive spine into a robot’s body extends mobility. I designed BaSiL (31 cm long, 240g), a wheeled robot whose tendon-driven beaded spine combines passive compliance with active bending. Actuating the spine in predefined sequences increases the height of steps the robot climbed more than sixfold compared with a rigidly constrained spine. Furthermore, I propose to investigate continuous morphological adaptation using the All Wheel Morph (AWM) robot (48 cm long, 4640g), whose rotating wheels vary continuously in shape between round wheels and leg-like configurations. I will evaluate AWM through controlled laboratory experiments on steps, sand, and mud, along with real-world experiments. These experiments will test whether the optimal morphology varies continuously with terrain conditions or changes abruptly between distinct wheel or leg configurations.

With the proposed work, I aim to understand how robot morphology can be matched to different terrain conditions, explore the benefits and trade-offs of adaptation, and understand design guidelines for improving terrain traversal.

events.title: Shaping the Body of Robots with Soft Skin and Muscles
events.description:
Abstract:

Just as skin and muscle give living creatures their ability to sense, move, and adapt, soft sensors and actuators are giving shape to a new kind of robot body. Built from flexible, compliant materials, soft robots can closely mimic the movements of biological systems, a significant step beyond conventional rigid machines. This talk explores recent technologies for designing and fabricating the two essential components of that body: artificial skin that lets robots feel their surroundings, and artificial muscles that let them move with natural, fluid motion. We will discuss how these components are engineered for responsiveness and reliability, how their signals can be interpreted despite the complex, nonlinear behavior of soft structures, and how sensing and actuation can be co-designed into a single integrated system. By integrating skin and muscle into a unified soft body, we can develop a new generation of robots capable of seamless and safe interaction in human environments.

Bio:

Yong-Lae Park (Member, IEEE) received the Ph.D. degree in mechanical engineering from Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA, in 2010.

He is currently a Professor with the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea. Prior to joining SNU, he was an Assistant Professor in the Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA (2013–2017) and a Technology Development Fellow in the Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA (2010–2013). His research interests include artificial skin sensors and muscle actuators, soft robots, wearable robots, rehabilitation robots, and medical robots.

Prof. Park is the recipient of the Best Conference Paper Award from the IEEE International Conference of Soft Robotics (2019), the Best Application Paper Award from the IEEE Transactions on Haptics (2019), and the Best Paper Award from the IEEE Sensors Journal (2013). He is currently serving as a Senior Editor in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, an Associate Editor in Soft Robotics and npj Robotics.

Location: NSH 4305

Title: Efficient 3D Avatar Reconstruction with Geometric Guidance

Abstract:
3D animatable human avatars are widely used in film making, game characters, and telepresence. To create these avatars efficiently, researchers propose to reconstruct the avatar from several input images with a feedforward network. These networks are mostly transformers trained with large proprietary data and thousands of H100 GPU hours. However, do we really need such a scale of data and compute for this task?

Our answer is no. In this talk, we present ARG-Avatar, a lightweight network with only 68M trainable parameters, yet achieves SOTA performance on OOD testing data with 13x less training compute to the best baseline. We will go through the two core components of ARG-Avatar. The first is FACRoPE, which inject geometric guidance into the attention with RoPE mechanism. We propose a novel coordinate formulation named Foreground Avatar Coordinates (FAC), to associate let the network tokens focus on its corresponding image regions. The second is Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR), which decodes a coarse avatar from intermediate network tokens during forward pass. We show that these components are all beneficial in the ablation study. In conclusion, we show that by properly injecting geometric into attention, we make an architecture that learns more efficiently and effectively for feedforward avatar reconstruction.

—

Best regards,

Jianjin Xu.

events.title: Structured Learning for Fast Physical Prediction
events.description:
Abstract:

Physical simulation is essential for robotics and engineering design, but remains computationally expensive, especially for complex geometries and long time horizons. Learning-based approaches offer faster predictions, but often lack the mathematical structure needed for reliable simulation.

In this talk, I will present three approaches that combine learning with mathematical structure: continuous reduced-order representations for generalization across shapes, geometric lifting for handling discontinuities, and Koopman-based linear operators for efficient long-horizon prediction. Together, these methods demonstrate how structured learning can enable faster, more expressive, and more reliable physical simulation.

Biography:

Chang Yue is a Ph.D. student in Computer Science at the University of Toronto, advised by Prof. Eitan Grinspun. Her research focuses on mathematically structured learning for fast and generalizable physical simulation. Her work has received the SIGGRAPH 2025 Best Paper Award and Best Paper Award Honorable Mention. She was also recognized as a WiGRAPH Rising Star in 2026.

events.title: “Lawless Progress on Wicked Problems”: Shifting the Roles of Humans in Human-AI Systems
events.description:
Abstract: AI is rapidly changing the roles that humans play as developers and users of new technology. In this talk, I will discuss three of those shifting roles and how my group addresses them through technical innovation and interdisciplinary design. Across these projects, understanding human roles is central to determining what systems should optimize, what data they need, and how they can be trusted.

Humans as objective functions: Many real-world applications involve optimizing user-specific objectives, but users’ descriptions of those objectives can be vague, inconsistent, or even self-contradictory. I will discuss our work on Interactive Explainable Ranking (Best Paper, CHI 2026), which combines optimization, AI, and interaction design to help users identify and resolve contradictions in how they evaluate different items—from open-ended course projects to purchasing options or contestants in a competition to find the best cat.

Humans as a source of data: AI is only effective if we have the right data, and many important applications depend on specific or individualized data that needs to be captured in uncontrolled settings. Multiple projects in my group focus on designing systems that help humans capture such data using mobile devices. This work connects capture guidance, sampling theory, computational imaging, and interaction design to support downstream learning, with applications spanning remote healthcare, infrastructure, and agriculture.

Humans as adversaries: Some advances in AI also carry significant potential for harm, which calls for designing new approaches to protect against adversarial use. One problem that AI has made particularly challenging is video forensics. I will discuss my group’s work on designing coded illumination systems to add near-imperceptible watermarks to lighting in high-stakes environments. These watermarks make it easier to detect manipulation in recorded videos without requiring access to or control over recording cameras.

He earned his Ph.D. in EECS at MIT. His dissertation received the Sprowls Award for Best PhD Thesis in Computer Science at MIT, as well as the ACM SIGGRAPH Outstanding Doctoral Dissertation Honorable Mention Award. events.title: Global Optimization for Robotics in the Age of Learning
events.description:
Abstract:

Optimization is the bedrock of robotics, and robotics is a great stress

test for optimization methods. High dimensionality, nonconvexity, and

nonsmoothness make many robotics problems notoriously hard to solve,

whether with learning-based or model-based strategies.

In this talk, I will discuss our recent advances in bringing

learning-based techniques together with optimization principles to

address this. First, I will present extensions of moment-based

optimization to data-driven, nonparametric problems that retain partial

global optimality guarantees. I will discuss how these methods enable

new approaches to high-dimensional, contact-rich manipulation. Next, I

will explore how foundation models can be combined with global

optimization to reduce modeling burdens and improve generalization of

model-based solvers. I will conclude with an outlook on using

optimization principles to reshape latent geometry for world-model

learning. Together, these examples illustrate how learning can expand

the reach of optimization, while optimization can bring structure and

guarantees to data-driven robotics.

Bio:

Frederike Dümbgen is an assistant professor in the Department of

Mechanical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, where she leads

the Trustworthy Robotics, Intelligence, and Optimization (TRIO) Lab. Her

research combines optimization and artificial intelligence to develop

scalable and trustworthy robotic systems, with a particular emphasis on

global optimization and optimality guarantees.

Before joining Carnegie Mellon, she was a researcher in the WILLOW team

at Inria Paris and a postdoctoral fellow at the Robotics Institute of

the University of Toronto. She holds a Ph.D. in Computer and

Communication Sciences from École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne

(EPFL), Switzerland, where she also earned her B.Sc. and M.Sc. in

Mechanical Engineering. She was an RSS Pioneer in 2024 and received a

Google Women Techmakers Scholarship in 2020. She serves as a co-chair of

the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society’s Technical Committee on

Optimization for Robotics.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal – Chen Wu
events.description:
Date: October 28, 2026

Time: 11:00 AM -12:30 PM ET

Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal

Zoom Link

Location: NSH 3305

Title: Learning to Explore and Learning from Exploration for Language Models

Who: Chen Wu

Abstract:

Learning from experience offers a way for language models to improve beyond the solutions available in their training data. Instead of relying only on demonstrations, a model can attempt problems, receive feedback, and learn from the outcomes. This process takes many forms, such as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, search at test time, training via self-improvement, and the integration of knowledge that arrives after training. In all of these scenarios, two capabilities matter: (1) exploring a broad range of solutions, and (2) learning from exploration to improve future performance. In practice, both still remain challenging — models often repeat similar attempts even when they fail, and learning from their outcomes is difficult when feedback is unreliable or when updates degrade existing capabilities. This thesis develops methods to address both challenges.

For learning to explore, we study why language models generate a narrow range of solutions and how to encourage broader exploration. We first examine the role of training objectives in simple algorithmic tasks, finding that next-token prediction is myopic, while multi-token objectives and input-side randomness produce more diverse and original outputs. We then study the effect of post-training, which concentrates a model’s reasoning into a small number of modes. We introduce mode-conditioning (ModC), which makes these modes controllable and allocates test-time samples across them.

For learning from exploration, we study how models can provide useful feedback to themselves when exploring and can incorporate new experience without losing existing capabilities. We first introduce self-trained verification (STV), which teaches a model to identify errors in its own solutions. The resulting verifier improves reasoning through iterative refinement, especially on hard problems. We then address the problem of forgetting when learning from new experience. We show that the degradation caused by off-policy training is not inherent to the data, but depends on how the update is applied. We therefore introduce grafting, which learns the update on an earlier checkpoint and transfers it to the post-trained model while masking the directions to which the post-trained model is most sensitive. Grafting outperforms more complex and expensive baselines on both new and old tasks.

Building on these results, the proposed work continues under the two directions. For learning to explore, I will study how to guide exploration on problems beyond a model’s current ability, with hints, reference solutions, and verifier feedback, without the model depending on or exploiting the guidance. For learning from exploration, I will study how new experience can be integrated with pretrained knowledge so that the two compose, and how a model can learn more from less experience by learning how to learn.

Aditi Raghunathan, Chair

events.description:
Abstract: Generative models can produce compelling images and videos, yet building systems that people can reliably direct and personalize remains a fundamental challenge. These systems must support new forms of control, generate over extended horizons within practical computational budgets, and adapt to individual concepts and preferences. In this talk, I will explore these challenges through a central question: How can we make visual generation controllable, efficient, and personal?

I will present three complementary directions toward this goal. First, Infinity-RoPE (CVPR’26) revisits how autoregressive video models represent temporal context, unlocking long-horizon generation and responsive control through inference-time interventions. Next, VideoMLA (NeurIPS’26) addresses the computational demands of extended generation by learning compact representations of past context, substantially reducing memory requirements while preserving generation quality. Finally, SPAWN (NeurIPS’26) introduces personalized concepts into interactive world models, allowing users to bring their own subjects into generated environments as they navigate them.

I will close with broader directions for video generation, including new distillation methods for efficient generation, improving physical plausibility (HiPhy, NeurIPS’26), and aligning generation with desired outcomes through reinforcement learning (DPP-GRPO, CVPR’26). This research advances a broader vision for generative cinematography, supported by an NSF CAREER’26 award, toward generative worlds that remember the past, respond to our choices, and evolve as we interact with them.

Bio: Pinar Yanardag is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Virginia Tech, where she leads GEMLAB (Generative Modeling Lab). Her research focuses on controllable, efficient, and personalized generative AI, with an emphasis on video generation and interactive world models. She earned her PhD from Purdue as a Fulbright Fellow and was a postdoctoral researcher at the MIT Media Lab, where her generative AI projects attracted over one million participants and media coverage from TIME, The Washington Post, and CNN. She received an NSF CAREER award for her research on generative cinematography and was recognized as an Outstanding Area Chair at CVPR 2026. Her research is supported by industry partners including Google, Adobe, Snap, and Qualcomm.

events.description:
Date: Friday, October 9

Time: 11:30 am – 12:30 pm

Room location: GHC 4405

Zoom link: https://cmu.zoom.us/j/9873588831

Title: AdaSoS: Escaping the Exponential Cost of Higher-Order Sum-of-Squares Relaxations

Abstract:

Many problems in robotics, power systems, and machine learning are nonconvex polynomial optimization problems; local solvers return an answer but cannot tell you how far it is from the best one. The Sum-of-Squares (SoS) hierarchy fixes this with a sequence of convex semidefinite relaxations that give certified lower bounds and, at high enough degree, the global optimum. The catch is cost. Each step up the hierarchy grows the relaxation exponentially, which puts higher-order SoS out of reach for real problems such as AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the problem of scheduling generators on the electric grid.

This talk presents Adaptive-SoS (AdaSoS), which gets the tightness of a higher-order relaxation without building it. AdaSoS checks whether the current low-order solution could extend to a valid higher-degree one. When it cannot, the failure itself identifies which polynomial directions are missing, and AdaSoS adds only those. We prove that AdaSoS reaches the full higher-order bound in finitely many steps. On our largest AC-OPF relaxation, it certifies the global optimum 13× faster than the full higher-order relaxation, with a 77% smaller semidefinite block. At the highest degree we solve, it matches or improves on the bounds of existing approaches such as TSSOS, CS-TSSOS, and the adaptive hierarchy of Josz and Molzahn, typically with a much smaller semidefinite block. AdaSoS can also start from cheaper sparse relaxations, which lets it scale: on the IEEE 300-bus system, where the dense higher-order relaxation does not fit in memory, AdaSoS started from a sparse degree-1 relaxation tightens its bound to within 0.14% of the best known AC-OPF solution.

events.title: RI PhD Thesis Proposal – Yilin Wu
events.description:
Date: October 26, 2026

Time: 10:00-11:30 AM ET

Type: RI PhD Thesis Proposal

Zoom Link

Location: NSH 4305

Title: Reconciling Adaptation and Generality in Robot Policies

Who: Yilin Wu

Abstract:

Generalist robot policies—such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)—are trained end-to-end on large observation-action datasets and can perform increasingly diverse manipulation tasks. Yet these policies remain unreliable amid the complexity of real environments and user contexts. A common remedy is to finetune the entire policy for a particular deployment, but this may degrade the pretrained capabilities that make generalist policies valuable. This raises the central question of this thesis: how should robot policies be adapted to particular users and environments while preserving their generality?

This thesis argues that maximizing adaptation while minimizing loss of generality requires identifying what should be adapted and choosing how to adapt it in the least invasive way. For example, a deployment may call for changes to the task specification (what the user wants done), the state representation (which aspects of the scene matter for the task), or the behavioral support (the range of actions the policy can produce). At each of these levels, the desired behavior may already lie within the policy’s pretrained capabilities and only need to be elicited, or the policy may need to acquire new knowledge or skills through additional training.

We study two corresponding adaptation mechanisms: inference-time steering, which guides pretrained action distribution toward the target while keeping policy parameters fixed, and targeted training, which learns additional context or behaviors through limited parameter updates. For steering, we first propose language-based verification methods that check generated actions against user instructions and reasoning plans. Next, to handle incomplete state information in contact-rich manipulation, we introduce a bi-level visual and tactile steering algorithm. Third, to steer the action distribution in open-world settings, we contribute a world model that predicts the consequences of candidate behaviors while balancing fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference efficiency.

Steering, however, can only elicit behaviors the pretrained policy already supports. We turn to targeted training methods with parameter-efficient updates to improve the base policy via learning a compact multi-stream memory that conditions the policy on history-dependent state, and residual policies that incorporate user corrections to expand the policy’s behavioral capabilities. Finally, the proposed work revisits the role of meta-learning for adapting generalist robot policies. We propose separating shared representation learning across tasks from task-specific action learning using limited demonstrations. The goal is adaptation with fewer demonstrations and trainable parameters, with explicit retention of pretrained capabilities

events.title: Simulation-Driven Robot Learning for the Lazy Researcher
events.description:
Abstract: This talk will delve into the workflow of building robot learning methods powered by large-scale physics simulation. While the promise of simulation is low-effort data generation that scales cheaply with human effort, the reality is often not as simple, with considerable human effort required to actually make simulation a useful tool for real-world robotic manipulation. In this talk, I will study how to develop methods that explicitly reduce manual human effort in enabling simulation as a data generation tool – from behavior generation, to model selection, to enabling downstream transfer to the real-world. In doing so, I will outline an effort-efficient path to leveraging simulation as a data source for robot learning – hopefully to make robotics easier for lazy researchers like me!

Bio: Abhishek Gupta is an assistant professor in computer science and engineering at the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Washington since 2022. He leads the Washington Embodied Intelligence and Robotics Development lab focusing on robot learning and reinforcement learning. Previously, he was a postdoctoral scholar at MIT, collaborating with Russ Tedrake and Pulkit Agrawal. Prior to that he received his Ph.D. and B.S degrees from UC Berkeley, working with Sergey Levine and Pieter Abbeel. Abhishek is the recipient of IEEE RAS Early Career Award, Toyota Research Institute Young Investigator award and an Amazon Science Hub award, along with award nominations at several top conferences and workshops. His research interests lie in scalable reinforcement learning methods for robot learning, in particular methods for continual adaptation in the real world and what role simulation can play in this process.

Title: Designing & Evaluating Machine-Knitted Stim Objects for Autistic Adults

Abstract:

Stimming is a valuable coping strategy and form of expression for Autistic people. However, research has historically scrutinized stimming through a negative, corrective model. When research instead prioritizes the Autistic perspective, an avenue opens for custom stimming resources that allows Autistic people to experience meaningful and stimulating interactions with sensory materials. Stimming can involve purpose-made objects (“stim objects”)—often small and portable, these objects come in a variety of textures, colors, functions, and sensory elements. Most commercial stim objects are mass-produced using traditional polymers, with little focus on how the material meets the user’s sensory needs. Fabrics are ubiquitous tactile materials with intricate, tunable properties. In my talk, I will show that knitted fabrics make highly effective stim objects for this reason—designers can tune their material properties at the micro stitch-level, allowing for parameterized textural and interactive possibilities that are well suited for manipulation by hand.

My talk will cover my multi-stage research process to answer the question: How can we design custom machine-knitted stim objects that meet the diverse sensory needs of Autistic adults? I will begin by covering the background survey I conducted to gather data to inform the subsequent design and fabrication stage, followed by an overview of my follow-up user-study for evaluating prototypes with feedback from Autistic adults. Finally, I will discuss future work with applications for custom stim objects, improved commercial resources, and design guidelines based on relevant sensory and material axes.

events.title: Video Intelligence for Understanding Behavior and Guiding Action
events.description:
Abstract: ​Modern video-language models have become remarkably good at describing what is happening in a video. Yet their ability to understand the behavior they observe, and to act on that understanding, remains limited. This talk presents our group’s work on building these missing capabilities. I will begin with foundational methods for scalable video perception, from space-time attention to hierarchical representations and active search over long videos. I will then introduce strategic video intelligence, using team sports as a natural microworld in which cooperative and competitive behavior can be studied rigorously, and present two complementary lines of work within it. The first investigates whether video generation models can simulate strategic multi-agent behavior well enough to support better decisions. The second examines how agents can study behavioral histories across large multimodal corpora, compiling repeated analytical work into reusable representations, abstractions, and procedures. Finally, I will present WatchAct, a benchmark for robot manipulation grounded in observed human behavior, where a robot watches a person and then has to act on what it saw. Together, these works move video models from perceiving behavior, to understanding it, to guiding action.

Bio: ​Gedas Bertasius is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His research focuses on video understanding and multimodal AI, particularly on systems that can perceive, reason about, and act on behavior observed in video. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Pennsylvania and was a postdoctoral researcher at Facebook AI Research before joining UNC. He is the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, four Sony Research Awards, two Meta Research Awards, and the Egocentric Vision Distinguished Paper Award. He was also a CVPR Best Paper Award finalist. Prior to his research career, he played professional basketball in Lithuania, an experience that still shapes his work on understanding strategic behavior in video.

events.title: How Can Robots Learn to Interact and Coordinate with Others?
events.description:
Abstract: Robots in the real world rarely act alone. They share spaces with other robots and with people, and succeeding there means learning to interact and coordinate with them. This talk looks at what makes interaction hard and how we might get there. I start with multi-agent reinforcement learning, where challenges like credit assignment make coordination difficult to learn, and show how the reasoning capabilities of foundation models can help coach robots to learn coordination. Coordination doesn’t have to be learned through trial and error though, so I then look at learning it from demonstrations. Imitating interacting agents turns out to be quite different from imitating a single one but it can still build on single-agent imitation. I then close by reversing the question: rather than asking what single-agent methods can do for multi-agent problems, I ask what multi-agent thinking can do for a single robot and show that continual learning, for example, can be cast as a consensus optimization problem which results in a natural way to balance learning new tasks against retaining old ones.

Bio: Negar Mehr is an Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering at UC Berkeley, where she directs the Berkeley Intelligent Control (ICON) Lab. Her research focuses on multi-agent interactions. Her lab develops learning-based methods grounded in game theory and control to enable robots to interact safely and intelligently with humans and other autonomous agents. She received her Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from UC Berkeley in 2019 and was a postdoctoral scholar in Aeronautics and Astronautics at Stanford University. Before returning to Berkeley, she was an Assistant Professor of Aerospace Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. She is a recipient of the ONR Young Investigator Award, the NSF CAREER Award, the ASME Rising Star Award, and the IEEE ITSS Best Ph.D. Dissertation Award.

events.description:
Who: Sriram Narayanan

Type: RI Thesis Proposal

Date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

Time: 02:00PM – 03:30PM (ET)

Location: NSH 4305

Zoom link: Here

Title: Thermal Computational Imaging through Light and Heat Transport

Abstract:

Computer vision seeks to understand the physical world from images, yet much of this understanding remains rooted in the appearance of reflected visible light. Objects also absorb and emit radiation, exchange heat with their surroundings, and change their temperature over space and time. These processes encode information about materials, geometry, and physical interactions that conventional visible cameras often cannot access. Thermal imaging makes aspects of this energy exchange observable, opening new possibilities for computational imaging.

This dissertation develops a physics-based framework for thermal computational imaging by treating light and heat transport as complementary sources of scene information.

Observations across wavelength and time depend differently on geometry, materials, illumination, and temperature. Connecting these observations through physical models helps distinguish scene properties that remain ambiguous in individual measurements.

We develop this premise through a sequence of inverse problems. Spectral and temporal thermal observations enable separation of radiation emitted by an object from radiation reflected from its surroundings, supporting temperature recovery even when material emissivity is unknown. Next, we show how the thermal consequences of absorbed light complement visible reflection, allowing surface reflectance and shading to be separated without explicitly recovering geometry or lighting. We then establish heat conduction as a geometric cue, recovering three-dimensional shape from the spatial relationships governing temperature evolution across dark, textured, and visibly transparent objects. Combining conduction with shading further allows local shape ambiguities to be resolved through their complementary geometric constraints.

The proposed work extends these connections into thermal simulation within VisionSIM, linking scene illumination, transient heat transport, emitted and reflected radiation, and sensor dynamics to predict thermal observations. Together, the completed and proposed work connect scene reconstruction and image synthesis through the coupled physics of light and heat. They establish energy exchange as both a source of constraints for recovering scene properties and a basis for predicting thermal observations.

events.title: Five Lessons on Caregiving from Wilderness Survival
events.description:
Join Virginia Eubanks as she shares her experience of family caregiving, trauma and “collateral” PTSD. Drawing on lessons from wilderness survival and conversations with experts and everyday heroes, she explores how we can build resilient communities of care in uncertain times.

In 2015, after a violent attack on her beloved partner, Virginia Eubanks suddenly became a family caregiver. In the weeks, months, and years that followed, she and her partner struggled to stay afloat as they faced wave upon wave of setbacks, including a serious case of post-traumatic stress disorder. Then, a second case. Eubanks developed “collateral” PTSD, a condition common among caregivers but rarely discussed.

An old lifesaving manual provided unexpected help. Inspired by its lessons, Eubanks studied wilderness first aid, kayak self-rescue, winter survival, bushwhacking, and lifeguarding. She interviewed experts and everyday heroes—from neuroscientists to monks to forest rangers.

Join Eubanks to discover what it takes to build communities of care that can sustain us in uncertain times.

events.title: President's Lecture Series
events.description:
Rahm I. Emanuel most recently served as the United States Ambassador to Japan. As Ambassador, Emanuel helped deepen the U.S.-Japan alliance, including support for Japan's increased defense spending and expanded military cooperation. He promoted Japan's leadership in Indo-Pacific key security initiatives and participated in the historic trilateral summit at Camp David that reaffirmed that cooperation between the United States, Japan, and the Republic of Korea.

Previously, Emanuel was the 55th Mayor of the City of Chicago, a position he held until May 2019. During that time, he made the critical choices necessary to secure Chicago's future as a global capital. As Mayor, Emanuel added four years to a student’s education. He increased the school day by 75 minutes and added more than 200 hours to the school year, marking the largest single increase in educational time by any city and taking Chicago from having the least educational time of any large school district in the country to being on par with its peers. He implemented universal pre-kindergarten and full-day kindergarten for every Chicago child, and made Chicago the first city in America to provide free community college.

The Mayor's comprehensive public safety strategy focused on expanded prevention programs for at-risk youth, smarter policing strategies, and empowering parents and communities to reduce violence. The Ambassador made it a priority to bring global companies to the city, helping Chicago to lead the U.S. in corporate relocations and foreign direct investment for seven consecutive years. His administration invested in infrastructure, public transportation, open space, and cultural attractions. From the $8.5 billion O'Hare International Airport modernization program that is cementing Chicago's status as a global leader in travel, tourism, and trade to the development of the iconic 1.25-mile Chicago Riverwalk, the City's investments are creating thousands of good-paying jobs and making Chicago a better place to live, work, and play.
Prior to becoming Mayor, from November 2008 until October 2010, Emanuel served as President Barack Obama's Chief of Staff. In addition to being the President's top advisor, Emanuel helped the Obama administration secure the passage of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and the landmark Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.

Before serving as Chief of Staff, Emanuel was elected four times as a Member of the U.S. House of Representatives from Illinois's 5th Congressional District (2002-2008). As Chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, Emanuel helped pass legislation to raise the minimum wage and authored the Great Lakes Restoration Act.

From 1993 to 1998, Ambassador Emanuel was a key member of President Bill Clinton's administration, rising to serve as Senior Advisor to the President for Policy and Politics. During this time, Emanuel served as a legislative liaison to Congress and spearheaded efforts to pass several of President Clinton's signature achievements, most notably the Federal Assault Weapons Ban, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, and the historic Balanced Budget Act, which created the Children's Health Insurance Program that expanded health care coverage to 10 million children. Emanuel also worked closely with President Joseph R. Biden Jr., then a U.S. Senator, to shepherd the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 through Congress.

Emanuel graduated from Sarah Lawrence College in 1981 and received a Master's Degree in Speech and Communication from Northwestern University in 1985. He is married to Amy Rule, and they have three children.

events.title: SCS Distinguished Industry Lecture - John Wilkes
events.description:
Google builds and operates a massive infrastructure in support of providing products and capabilities to its users and customers. The scale has dramatically increased as a result of the push for AI. While we benefit greatly from an integrated stack—from software down through specialized chips to optimized data center designs—we also need a way to coordinate all those efforts to avoid confusion, inefficiencies, and missed opportunities. The talk will discuss one of the approaches we are using to provide a control system for a $xxxB/year capital expenditure program.

—

John Wilkes has been at Google since 2008, where he is working on automation for building warehouse scale computers, with a current focus on fleet-wide capacity planning. Before this, he worked on cluster management for Google's compute infrastructure (Borg, Omega, Kubernetes). He is interested in far too many aspects of distributed systems, but a recurring theme has been technologies that allow systems to manage themselves.

He received a PhD in computer science from the University of Cambridge, joined HP Labs in 1982, and was elected an HP Fellow and an ACM Fellow in 2002 for his work on storage system design. Along the way, he’s been program committee chair for SOSP, FAST, EuroSys and HotCloud, and has served on the steering committees for EuroSys, FAST, SoCC and HotCloud. He’s listed as an inventor on 50+ US patents, and has an adjunct faculty appointment at Carnegie-Mellon University. In his spare time he continues, stubbornly, trying to learn how to blow glass.

Campus community welcomed.

Academic leaders at CMU selected Dr. Urry for her pioneering research, which has revolutionized our understanding of how supermassive black holes form, grow and evolve across the cosmos. As one of the world’s foremost astrophysicists, she has made a profound impact on the field, including establishing the landmark 1995 unified physical model for Active Galactic Nuclei. Additionally, she has proven to be a trailblazing leader, serving as the first woman to chair Yale's Department of Physics.

Awarded annually since 1970, Carnegie Mellon University's Dickson Prize in Science recognizes substantial achievements or sustained progress in the fields of the natural sciences, engineering, computer science or mathematics.

events.title: SCS Distinguished Industry Lecture - Mark Russinovich
events.description:
AI is changing the security model of computing. It puts expert capability into anyone’s hands, operates at machine speed, and turns software from passive code into an active participant that can discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, deceive overseers, and reason about the constraints meant to contain it. At the same time, alignment safeguards that keep AI systems operating within their intended goals and constraints can be removed, unsafe models can gain capability from aligned ones, and untrusted information can steer agents toward privileged actions. These are not just new bugs; they challenge assumptions that have shaped computer security for decades. We need a new security stack, one based on isolation, capabilities, provenance, and deterministic enforcement. Intelligence cannot be the security boundary.

—

Mark Russinovich is CTO, Deputy CISO, and Technical Fellow for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft’s global enterprise-grade cloud platform. A widely recognized expert in distributed systems, operating systems and cybersecurity, Mark earned a Ph.D. in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. He later co-founded Winternals Software, joining Microsoft in 2006 when the company was acquired. Mark is a popular speaker at industry conferences such as Microsoft Ignite, Microsoft Build, and RSA Conference. He has authored several nonfiction and fiction books, including the Microsoft Press Windows Internals book series, Troubleshooting with the Sysinternals Tools, as well as fictional cyber security thrillers Zero Day, Trojan Horse and Rogue Code.

CMU community welcomed.

Oren will share with you the ten commandments of early-stage startup creation. The commandments are funny but also practical. They draw on his work with founders at the AI House, Madrona, and his own experience as the founder of AI startups from Netbot (1996) to Vercept (2024).

—

Oren Etzioni is a pioneering Artificial Intelligence researcher, entrepreneur, and prominent voice in AI safety and ethics.

Oren was the Founding Chief Executive Officer at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from its inception in 2013 until late 2022 – one of the most highly respected AI research institutes in the world, whose mission is AI for the Common Good. Under his leadership, AI2 pursued ambitious projects aimed at advancing the state-of-the-art in AI and addressing extraordinary scientific, engineering and societal challenges.

In 2024, hei founded and ran TrueMedia.org – a non-profit technology organization using AI to create a non-partisan, free and broadly accessible dashboard to combat political disinformation by identifying manipulated media and AI-based forgery of video, audio, images and text across social media platforms. He has been a Professor at the University of Washington’s Computer Science department since 1991, and a Venture Partner at the Madrona Venture Group since 2000. He is also the Founder and Technical Director of the AI2 Incubator.

REGISTER → Space is limited and a waitlist will open once capacity is reached.

About the Raj Reddy Artificial Intelligence Lecture : The Raj Reddy Artificial Intelligence Lecture Series was established in honor of Raj Reddy and his critical work in AI during his now 50 year career at CMU. Reddy was the founding Director of the Robotics Institute from 1979 to 1991 and the Dean of School of Computer Science from 1991 to 1999. He has been active in AI research for over five decades in the areas of AI, Speech Understanding, Image Understanding, Robotics, Multi-sensor Fusion, and Intelligent Agents.

A livestream will not be available but the lecture will be recorded.

events.title: Webinar: Unpacking Duolingo’s Approach to Innovation
events.description:
In this fireside chat, iii faculty member Susanna Zlotnikov speaks with Nickey Skarstad, a senior director of product at Duolingo, about the culture behind making the world’s No. 1 language learning app.

​Skarstad will give us a look into the organizational practices that cultivate Duolingo’s unique innovation culture and what a typical day looks like for Duos building personalized experiences for over 40 million users world-wide.

​Specifically, Zlotnikov and Skarstad will explore how tech and product teams work together to build cutting-edge personalized experiences for millions of users, and how AI is pushing the Duolingo team to change the way they work and innovate.

​There will be 30 minutes to hear from our co-hosts, and 15 minutes for Q&A.

Hosted by the Integrated Innovation Institute (iii)

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.
events.summary: Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
events.location: Posner Hall Grand Room (POS 340)

events.title: Inside the Cyber Threat Landscape with FBI Pittsburgh
events.description:
Patrick Myers, Supervisory Special Agent with the FBI Pittsburgh Field Office, will offer a front-line perspective on today’s evolving cyber threats, sharing insights into how cybercriminals and nation-state actors operate—and how these risks increasingly intersect with everyday digital behaviors, at work and at home. Learn about current threat trends and how individuals and organizations can become targets.

Supervisory Special Agent Patrick Myers has been with the FBI since 2015. He is currently assigned to the FBI’s Pittsburgh Division, where he supervises a National Security Cyber squad focusing on state-sponsored cyber actors. As a special agent, SSA Myers has conducted investigations into hackers with Russia’s Military Intelligence, the GRU. SSA Myers’ work has led him to participate in investigations and in the defense of computer systems, including election networks worldwide, the Olympic Games, and U.S. critical infrastructure. SSA Myers is a member of the FBI’s Cyber Action Team (CAT), the FBI Cyber Division’s rapid response force, on call to deploy globally to bring in-depth cyber intrusion expertise and specialized investigative skills to bear in response to significant cyber events.

events.title: The 1% Rule: Small Habits that Compound Into Significant Academic Gains
events.description:
The audience of this workshop is #graduate-students.

Graduate school can demand a lot of you—but becoming a more effective student doesn’t require completely reinventing how you study. In this practical workshop, you’ll learn how small, consistent changes can lead to meaningful improvements in your academic habits and productivity.

We’ll explore strategies including habit stacking, reflection routines, weekly reviews, tiny improvements to your study practices, and consistency over intensity. You’ll have the opportunity to identify what’s working, pinpoint one area you’d like to improve, and create a simple plan for a small change you can put into practice immediately.

Learning Objectives:

Discover practical strategies for building sustainable study habits.

Create a simple weekly reflection and review routine.

Learn how to make your existing study practices more efficient.

Learn how to practice consistency over intensity.

Personalize “on small change” for immediate implementation.

This is an in-person workshop.

events.title: Five Lessons on Caregiving from Wilderness Survival
events.description:
Join Virginia Eubanks as she shares her experience of family caregiving, trauma and “collateral” PTSD. Drawing on lessons from wilderness survival and conversations with experts and everyday heroes, she explores how we can build resilient communities of care in uncertain times.

In 2015, after a violent attack on her beloved partner, Virginia Eubanks suddenly became a family caregiver. In the weeks, months, and years that followed, she and her partner struggled to stay afloat as they faced wave upon wave of setbacks, including a serious case of post-traumatic stress disorder. Then, a second case. Eubanks developed “collateral” PTSD, a condition common among caregivers but rarely discussed.

An old lifesaving manual provided unexpected help. Inspired by its lessons, Eubanks studied wilderness first aid, kayak self-rescue, winter survival, bushwhacking, and lifeguarding. She interviewed experts and everyday heroes—from neuroscientists to monks to forest rangers.

Join Eubanks to discover what it takes to build communities of care that can sustain us in uncertain times.
events.summary: Join Virginia Eubanks as she shares her experience of family caregiving, trauma and “collateral” PTSD. Drawing on lessons from wilderness survival and conversations with experts and everyday heroes, she explores how we can build resilient communities of care in uncertain times.

A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

Do you trust your students, and do your students trust you? These questions are critical to building a supportive environment for learning in your classroom. Finally, we will explore various actions instructors can take to build and show trust in their classrooms. Participants should expect to leave with a series of implementable “teaching moves” that foster and demonstrate trust in the classroom.

events.title: Dr. Michael Berenbaum Discussion on Kristallnacht
events.description:
Dr. Michael Berenbaum will discuss Kristallnacht: the 1938 Reich’s Pogrom.

Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass”, was a pogrom that occurred November 9-10, 1938. It was the first organized, government-sanctioned act of violence against the Jews in Germany. It marks the start of the systematic violence against Jews during the Holocaust. Each year, the Holocaust Center of Pittsburgh holds an event to commemorate this important turning point in history.

Michael Berenbaum is a writer, lecturer, and teacher consulting in the conceptual development of museums and the development of historical films. He is director of the Sigi Ziering Institute: Exploring the Ethical and Religious Implications of the Holocaust at the American Jewish University (formerly the University of Judaism) where he is also a Professor of Jewish Studies.

The Global Connections group offers a welcoming and confidential space for students to connect around the shared and unique experiences of studying and living in the US.

events.description:
A contemporary drama by Duncan Macmillan, directed by MFA Directing candidate Fangran Li.

The first step is admitting she has a problem. But the problem isn’t with Emma, it’s with everything else.

The School of Drama presents:

‘People, Places and Things’

By Duncan Macmillan

Directed by Fangran Li

Nov. 18–21, 2026

Philip Chosky Theater

Emma is in rehab. Her first step is to admit that she has a problem. But the problem isn’t with Emma, it’s with everything else. She needs to tell the truth, but she’s smart enough to know that there’s no such thing. When intoxication feels like the only way to survive the modern world, how can she ever sober up?
