events.title: World of Music: Christopher Mark Jones’ “Montréal Encore”
events.description:
Christopher Mark Jones, professor emeritus of French & Francophone studies, returns with a celebration of his French-language album Montréal Encore, premiered with his collaborator Bernard Pozier at City of Asylum in March of 2023.

This concert features selections from that album and mix-ins by Québécois, French Caribbean and Parisian singer-songwriters—the likes of Boris Vian, Michel Rivard, Louis Aragon and Henri Salvador.

Free In-Person Tickets | Free Livestream Tickets

Featured Musicians:

Christopher Mark Jones: vocals, guitar

Brad Yoder: vocal harmonies, guitar, saxophone, glockenspiel

Mark Perna: bass

Eric George: African djembe and hand cymbals

Matt Siegler: piano and accordion

About the Artist:

Christopher Mark Jones draws from folk, country, blues, jazz and R&B sources to stage his literate folk-rock meditations. Using diverse points of view to narrate and critique life and love in uncertain times, he invites listeners to think, feel and dance. Recorded and live arrangements leave space for his musical co-conspirators to both express their personalities and honor the host creation. Listeners hear echoes of “Greg Brown’s pacing and a Lyle Lovett attitude” (Ben Shannon), as well as of John Prine, Bruce Coburn and Darrell Scott.

Between careers as a basketball player and French professor, Christopher busked in Paris, toured the UK, Denmark and Holland, and played New England clubs. He now tours and streams solo from Pittsburgh, PA, and plays regionally in formats varying from solo to full band. Looking for the Light (2021) is his sixth recording of original folk/roots songs, while Montréal Encore (2022) is a French-language recording created in collaboration with the poet Bernard Pozier.

About Your Visit:

The in-house restaurant, Cucina Alfabeto, is open for dinner from 5 to 10 p.m. Please visit OpenTable or call 412-435-1111 to make a reservation.
events.summary: Christopher Mark Jones, professor emeritus of French & Francophone studies, returns with a celebration of his French-language album Montréal Encore, premiered with his collaborator Bernard Pozier at City of Asylum in March of 2023.

events.title: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen
events.description:
LCAL’s Informal Conversations on Research (ICOR) Series provides a welcoming forum for faculty and graduate students to share and discuss their most recent research in an engaging, accessible format.

Translingual Borders: Refugee Testimony and the Politics of Translation

Isabelle Chen, assistant professor of global French studies, will challenge the assumption that translation is a liberatory practice — one that enables people to cross linguistic, cultural and geographic borders — by examining how translation can also reinforce borders, reproduce unequal power dynamics and constrain individual agency.

Focusing on Shumona Sinha’s novel Assommons les pauvres ! (Down with the Poor!), Dr. Chen’s talk explores the experiences of a Bengali interpreter working with asylum seekers in France. She examines how Sinha uses translation both as a literary strategy and a central thematic motif to portray interpretation as a potential barrier to human mobility and freedom.

Drawing on translation theory and recent migration data, Dr. Chen considers what literary representations of translation can reveal about its real-world consequences — and about the roles of multilingualism, interpretation and language in immigration policy and advocacy today.
events.summary: LCAL’s Informal Conversations on Research (ICOR) Series provides a welcoming forum for faculty and graduate students to share and discuss their most recent research in an engaging, accessible format.

events.title: X in the Loop Webinar Series
events.description:
X in the Loop is an interdisciplinary webinar series that questions what it means for humans to remain “in control” of AI. By replacing “human” with the open variable “X,” the series explores who holds power in AI systems, whose perspectives are included and what other species, cultures and ways of knowing might belong in the loop.

Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: ​Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.
events.summary: Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

events.title: Ostatni Etap: The Last Stage
events.description:
Restored Version of the 1948 film, often described as the “Mother of all Holocaust Films.”

Director Wanda Jakubowska survived Auschwitz. She set and filmed the movie in Auschwitz and used survivors and locals in the cast. This film influenced a generation of filmmakers but then was forgotten, and surviving negatives began to decay.

This restoration from 2020 makes the film available for new generations. The pandemic limited its distribution, but now we are welcoming you to join us for the Pittsburgh premiere.

Sponsors: European Studies Center, Holocaust Center of Pittsburgh, The Polish Cultural Council– Pittsburgh,The CMU Jack Buncher Chair in Jewish Studies, University Center for International Studies

events.title: Faculty Insights with Joe DeCarolis
events.description:
Please join us for CMU Engineering’s virtual program, “Faculty Insights: A 20 Minute Briefing.” In this series, faculty will share insights into their research, its impact, and provide perspective for the future of the field. Following the presentation, attendees will have an opportunity to direct questions and comments to the speaker.

“Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions”

Rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers could substantially increase U.S. power sector emissions and electricity costs by 2030, with particularly large impacts in regions such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Using a detailed energy model covering 26 interconnected U.S. power regions, we evaluate how demand growth, fuel prices, and federal policies affect electricity generation, infrastructure investment, and costs. Data centers could push U.S. power sector carbon emissions up by as much as 28% and spike regional electricity costs by up to 57% by 2030.

events.title: EPP Seminar: Sonia Mangones — Transportation, Air Pollution, and Inequalities: Evidence from Bogotá, Colombia
events.description:
Environmental justice research often examines the burden of pollution in relation to the population’s socioeconomic vulnerability. Climate justice research examines differential responsibility, asking who emits and who ultimately carries the burden they create. Urban mobility justice research rarely combines these two questions empirically, even though mobility is where they intersect most directly, since travel generates emissions and also shapes where resulting pollution concentrations fall across the city. This talk presents findings from an empirical study of Bogotá, Colombia, that measures both sides of this relationship at the level of city blocks, combining residential pollution concentration (NO2 and PM2.5) with a block-level proxy for travel-emission responsibility built from official mobility and emissions data. Two findings challenge a simple story in which the poor pollute least and suffer most. First, pollution concentration does not increase monotonically with deprivation; it peaks at intermediate socioeconomic levels. Second, emission responsibility does decline cleanly with vulnerability, but the resulting imbalance, where responsibility is low and pollution concentration is high, concentrates in population segments that can only be identified by combining policy instruments that separately inform socioeconomic vulnerability and the spatial distribution of the imbalance. I discuss what this means for the mobility justice conversation and the implications for transportation and environmental policy.

Speaker BIo:

Sonia Cecilia Mangones Matos is an Associate Professor at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, where she directs the Translogyt Research Group. Her work lies at the intersection of transportation engineering, urban sustainability, environmental impacts of transportation, road safety, and public policy. Her research combines quantitative methods, data analytics, and interdisciplinary approaches to examine sustainable urban mobility, transportation-related air pollution, emissions, and the implications of transportation systems for public health and urban equity.

Sonia holds a Ph.D. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University and an M.Sc. in Transportation Engineering from Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Her international academic experience includes research stays at CNRS in Toulouse and the LIVE Laboratory at the University of Strasbourg in France, as well as a research visit to Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile. She is Co-Chair of the Sustainable Transport Committee of the Pan-American Society of Transportation Research (PANAMSTR) and actively contributes to the World Conference on Transport Research, Community Modeling and Analysis System (CMAS) South America, and the Transportation Research Board in the US. She has led and collaborated on research projects with public institutions in Colombia, including the Ministry of Transport and the National Road Safety Agency. Her recent work has received broader recognition, including the 2025 L’Oréal–UNESCO “For Women in Science” Regional Award for her work on AI-enabled sustainable urban mobility and the 2025 Afro-Colombian of the Year Award in the Science and Technology category, recognizing her contributions to science and applied research in Colombia.

She is currently a Fulbright Visiting Scholar in Carnegie Mellon University’s Department of Engineering and Public Policy, where her project develops a justice-based framework integrating mobility, emissions, and pollution concentration and examines how complex technical evidence can be translated into actionable policy.

events.title: Departmental Seminar: Dr. Iain Cheeseman
events.description:
Research Area: analyzing the process by which cells duplicate, focusing on how the molecular machinery that segregates the chromosomes is rewired across diverse physiological contexts.

Guest Speaker: Iain Cheeseman, PhD

Professor of Biology at MIT

Core Member, Whitehead Institute

Title: “Unlocking the Hidden Proteome”

Our lab is fascinated by the molecular machinery that directs core cellular processes, and in particular how these processes are modulated and rewired across different physiological contexts. Our work has focused on the proteins that direct chromosome segregation and cell division, including the macromolecular kinetochore structure that mediates chromosome-microtubule interactions. Although cell division is an essential cellular process, this machinery is remarkably flexible in its composition and properties, which can vary dramatically between species and are even modulated within the same organism — over the cell cycle, during development, and across diverse physiological situations. To define the basis by which the kinetochore and other core cellular structures are rewired to adapt to diverse situations and functional requirements, we are currently investigating diverse transcriptional, translational, and post-translational mechanisms that act to generate proteomic variability both within individual cells and across tissues, cell state, development, and disease.

Student Invited Seminar Speaker
events.summary: Research Area: analyzing the process by which cells duplicate, focusing on how the molecular machinery that segregates the chromosomes is rewired across diverse physiological contexts.

Title: Driving Measurable Value Through Owner Focused Innovation

Abstract:

Digital transformation in the built environment is increasingly defined not by technology adoption alone, but by the ability to demonstrate measurable value. AI, openBIM, VDC, digital twins, Lean practices, and performance metrics are becoming more closely connected as organizations seek better project, asset, and business outcomes.

Drawing on more than 30 years of experience in openBIM and digital innovation, including owner-focused initiatives across 30 countries, Dr. Calvin Kam will explore how governments, owners, and industry organizations can translate emerging technologies, open standards, and mandates into practical implementation strategies and measurable results.

Building on his work as Founder and CEO of Strategic Building Innovation, his work with buildingSMART International on Global openBIM Mandates and openBIM Business Value, and research associated with Stanford University’s Center for Integrated Facility Engineering (CIFE), the presentation will examine how frameworks such as the VDC Scorecard can help organizations connect information requirements, quality controls, technology adoption, KPIs, and performance with broader business value.

Looking forward, the session will explore how AI, openBIM, and VDC can increasingly enable digital twins, GIS, IoT, sustainability, and decarbonization - creating a stronger foundation for informed decision-making, smarter mandates, and improved whole-lifecycle performance across the built environment.

Bio:

Dr. Calvin Kam is Founder & CEO of Strategic Building Innovation and Strategic Green Innovation — the “GPS Navigator” for any enterprise charting a course for construction innovation while optimizing the value of built assets. Dr. Kam serves as the Chapter President of buildingSMART Chapter in the United States and an Executive of buildingSMART International’s Compliance Program. He received his Doctor of Philosophy degree from Stanford University in Design/Construction Integration and Construction Engineering & Management.

As an Adjunct Professor at Stanford University’s Center for Integrated Facility Engineering (CIFE) and a Co-Founder of GSA’s National BIM Program, Dr. Kam advises built asset owners globally on strategic innovation, including customized AI applications and digitalized construction management leveraging openBIM/GIS global standards. Dr. Kam has advised public agencies in APEC, Finland, Hong Kong China, Norway, UAE, U.K., U.S., and Singapore on AI, digitalization, innovation, open standards, productivity, value chain, and management science.

Elevated as a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects as well as buildingSMART International, Dr. Kam has given keynotes and lectures in over 30 countries and has been published in industry handbooks, APEC official publications, journals, and conference papers. He has been recognized through ENR’s “20 Under 40” and BD+C’s “40 Under 40” awards, and honored with fellowships by ASCE, SOM, and Stanford University.

Hosted by Professor Pingbo Tang

events.title: Academic Cultures in Conversation: Teaching, Learning and Higher Education Across Different Educational Contexts
events.description:
Join faculty, students and Russian scholars in exile from Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Pittsburgh and the Russian Academic Renewal and Exchange Program (U.S.-RAR) for a roundtable discussion on teaching, learning and higher education across academic cultures.

How do academic cultures shape the ways we teach, learn and engage with challenging ideas?

Participants will share perspectives on innovations in teaching and learning, the growing role of generative AI in education, academic freedom and the discussion of sensitive topics in the classroom and evolving expectations of students and instructors. The conversation will also examine how institutional policies, political and social developments and educational traditions influence academic experiences, particularly for international students, faculty and scholars working in exile.

By bringing together voices from different disciplines, institutions and educational contexts, the roundtable aims to foster dialogue, exchange ideas and reflect on the challenges and opportunities shaping higher education today.

Participants

Andreea Deciu Ritivoi — English, Carnegie Mellon University

Svitlana Maksymenko — Economics, University of Pittsburgh

Stuart McAdams — Undergraduate Student, Political Science/Russian/ROTC, University of Pittsburgh

Stephen Sudia — Ph.D. Student, Rhetoric, Carnegie Mellon University

Elizaveta Volkovskaia — Ph.D. Student, Slavic Languages and Literatures, University of Pittsburgh

Fellows of the Russian Academic Renewal and Exchange Program (U.S.-RAR)

Moderator: Olga Klimova, Department of Languages, Cultures & Applied Linguistics, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: Seminar: Designing & Printing Dispersion Strengthened Ti-6Al-4V via Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing
events.description:
This Next Manufacturing seminar features a talk by Dr. Amaranth Karra, Postdoctoral Researcher, University of North Texas.

Abstract

The anisotropy of the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V additively manufactured (AM) via laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) is increased by the long and textured columnar prior beta grains that typically occur despite the high cooling rates (105–107 K/s). Additionally, both AM and conventionally fabricated Ti-6Al-4V exhibit dwell-fatigue sensitivity at room-temperature, resulting in premature failure in the low-cycle fatigue regime. This work explores the design and printing of yttria dispersion-hardened Ti-6Al-4V with minimal powder feedstock preparation. A uniformly dispersed yttria with a mean particle size of∼100 nm in the Ti-6Al-4V matrix decreases the transverse size of the prior beta grains. Furthermore, STEM bright-field micrographs reveal dispersoid pinning of dislocations, and STEM EDS confirms that the dispersoids are yttria as expected. A modest increase in room-temperature microhardness is observed, and room-temperature nanoindentation creep results show a∼64% lower mean creep rate compared to standard PBF-LB Ti-6Al-4V. Additionally, a room-temperature compression test was performed to determine the respective yield strengths to study cold creep, and its implications are discussed. At normalized stresses, ODS Ti-6Al-4V exhibits substantially lower long-term creep rates, albeit with greater initial deformation. This work successfully demonstrates the use of PBF-LB to fabricate oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) Ti-6Al-4V, enabling refinement of the prior beta grains and improved long-term time-dependent deformation at normalized stresses.

Bio

Amaranth Karra is a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of North Texas. He received his Ph.D. and M.S. in Materials Science and Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on process metallurgy, additive manufacturing, and process–structure–property relationships in advanced metallic materials. His work spans laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition of refractory alloys, titanium alloys, and oxide dispersion-strengthened materials, with an emphasis on understanding defect formation, phase evolution, and process optimization using advanced characterization techniques, including in situ synchrotron X-ray imaging and diffraction. His current research investigates the additive manufacturing of dispersion-strengthened Ti–6Al–4V alloys, while his doctoral research focused on additive manufacturing of tungsten and tungsten-based alloys for extreme-environment applications.

events.title: Pitt/CMU AstroLunch: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)
events.description:
Speaker: Sumit Sarbadhicary (Johns Hopkins)

Topic: Where do stars explode in the ISM? A new constraint on stellar feedback models

Abstract: In this talk, I will present the first set of direct observational constraints on where stars explode in the interstellar medium (ISM) from high-resolution surveys of nearby galaxies with JWST, HST, VLA, ALMA and VLT/MUSE. Explosions of stars, i.e. supernovae (SNe) are the main regulators of star-formation in galaxies. They achieve this most directly by launching winds, which remove cold star-forming gas from the ISM, and creating pressure in the ISM by supplying heat, turbulence and cosmic rays. The efficiency of these processes depend sensitively on the environments where SNe occur, particularly the correlation between SNe and dense gas clouds. While there is evidence of SN shocks interacting with molecular clouds, the ionizing radiation and stellar winds from massive stars can quickly unbind and disperse dense clouds before SNe occur. How these different feedback channels limit star-formation in molecular clouds and launch winds is one of the biggest open questions in galaxy evolution. I will discuss how we can address this topic with the novel method of observations of evolved massive stars and supernova remnants in the Local Volume, supplied by high-resolution multiwavelength surveys like PHANGS, LGLBS and SDSS. I will also show preliminary comparisons with hydrodynamical simulations of galaxies to show how these observations can serve as valuable checks on the underlying stellar feedback models.

events.title: CEE Department Seminar: Burcin Becerik-Gerber
events.description:
The CEE department seminar series presents lectures from a diverse range of professors, industry leaders, and alumni, and covers topics discussed throughout CEE’s four core research areas. All members of the CMU community are welcome to attend CEE department seminars.

From Sensing to Adaptation: Human-Centered Intelligence in the Built Environment

The built environment is increasingly able to sense, learn, and respond, creating new opportunities to rethink how we design, construct, operate, and experience buildings and infrastructure. This talk presents our research toward human-centered intelligent built environments, from multimodal sensing and modeling of human experiences and interactions with buildings to AI-enabled simulation of human behavior and emergency response, adaptive building systems, and human–robot interaction and teleoperation in construction. Across these applications, a common question drives our work: how can we move beyond systems that simply collect data or automate predefined tasks toward environments and machines that understand context, anticipate human needs, and adapt their behavior accordingly? I will discuss recent advances and remaining challenges in creating built environments in which people, machines, and physical spaces can increasingly sense, learn from, and adapt to one another.

Bio: Dr. Burcin Becerik-Gerber is a Professor and Chair of the Sonny Astani Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Southern California and the Founder and Director of the USC Center for Intelligent Environments (CENTIENTS). Her research focuses on advanced sensing, data science, and artificial intelligence to support the design, construction, and operation of human-centered, adaptive buildings and infrastructure systems. She pioneered the field of Human-Building Interaction (HBI), which examines how human experience and behavior interact with intelligent, engineered systems in the built environment. Dr. Becerik-Gerber has authored over 200 peer-reviewed publications and has led more than $15 million in sponsored research funded by agencies including the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Transportation. Her work has received numerous honors, including MIT Technology Review TR35, the FIATECH Celebration of Engineering and Technology Innovation Award, ASCE’s Computing in Civil Engineering Award, the ASCE Henry L. Michel Award for Industry Advancement of Research, and the ASCE Peurifoy Construction Research Award. She is a member of the National Academy of Construction and serves on the National Academies Board on Infrastructure and the Constructed Environment.

events.title: Student Recital: Ziyu Cai
events.description:
Ziyu Cai, piano

Program

J.S. Bach – French Suite No. 5 in G Major, BWV 816

Ludwig van Beethoven – Piano Sonata No.2 in A Major, Op. 2 No. 2

Robert Schumann – Piano Sonata No.1 in F-sharp minor, Op.11

Cost: Free and open to the public, no tickets required.

Ziyu Cai is currently a piano performance student in the Advanced Music Studies program at Carnegie Mellon University, where he studies under Professor Sergey Schepkin. He previously earned a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence from Peking University and a Master of Science in Music Technology from Carnegie Mellon University.

Originally active as a pop musician, Ziyu discovered his love for classical music during his undergraduate years at Peking University. As president of PKU Piano, he soon became an active performer in the university’s classical music community. He made his concerto debut with the Peking University Symphony Orchestra, performing Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2 as the orchestra’s first piano soloist in recent years. He also presented a recital at Peking University Hall, featuring Chopin’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in collaboration with the Peking University String Quartet.

Ziyu has won numerous prizes in piano competitions. Over the past season, he won the Wenzhou Piano Competition, performing Beethoven Piano Concerto No. 3 with the Wenzhou Symphony Orchestra, as well as the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh Concerto Competition, performing Schumann Piano Concerto with the Chamber Orchestra of Pittsburgh. He was also named the winner of the All University Orchestra Concerto Competition and is scheduled to perform Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with the orchestra in spring 2027.

Ziyu has previously studied with Luz Manriquez and Frederic Chiu at Carnegie Mellon University. Alongside his piano studies, he works as a research assistant with Professor Roger Dannenberg, focusing on score-following research.
events.summary: Ziyu Cai, piano

events.title: Rare Books & Ancestral Machines: The Inaugural Exhibition of the Posner Center for Special Collections
events.description:
This exhibition inaugurates University Libraries’ newly renovated Posner Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning.

The Posner Center is a cabinet of rarities and technological marvels: paper-and-string cipher machines, centuries-old books, cogwheel computers and 19th century “digital” images. Part museum and part laboratory, it is a site for discovery, research, and innovation with the materials of the past.

Rare Books & Ancestral Machines features more than 30 books and objects from the Posner Center’s holdings. Many of these materials are on view for the first time. The exhibition inaugurates the newly renovated Center, surveying its collections and tracing more than four centuries of scientific inquiry and learning. Organized into five thematic sections — mechanical computing, robotics, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and scholarly method — the exhibit explores the histories of these disciplines, uncovering abandoned prototypes and long-forgotten technologies.

What will you discover?

Exhibit Hours

During the summer, the Posner Center operates by appointment only. Contact Sam Lemley to make an appointment to visit the exhibit.

Public open hours will resume the first full week of the fall 2026 semester as follows:

Monday, closed

Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. (Reading Room & Exhibitions)

Thursday, 3-7 p.m. (Exhibitions only)

Learn more about University Libraries Special Collections.

events.title: Department Colloquium: Dr. David Badre
events.description:
Title: The organization of neural representations for control

Abstract: Cognitive control allows us to think and behave flexibly based on our context and goals. Most theories of cognitive control propose a control representation that enables the same input to produce different outputs contingent on contextual factors. However, the computational features of these control representations that enable this flexible mapping remain unknown. In this talk, I will focus on the geometry of neural control representations that enable cognitive control. I will present evidence from fMRI and EEG showing how these representations are organized and change as a function of different task structures, over the course of a trial, and over the course of practice; and I will discuss how these changes relate to efficient behavioral control.

Takes place in rm 336B in Baker Hall. Zoom link available if you are not able to make it in person.

events.title: Kearra Amaya Gopee: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

REGISTER HERE

Join us for an evening with artist Kearra Amaya Gopee as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the works featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

About the Artist

Kearra Amaya Gopee (born 1994, Miami, FL, raised in Carapichaima, Kairi (Trinidad and Tobago); lives on Lenape land in New York) is an anti-disciplinary artist and facilitator. Using video, sculpture, sound, and writing, they identify both violence and time as primary conditions that undergird the anti-Black world in which they work. Gopee has shown work at documenta 15, Kassel, Germany (2022), and The Kitchen, among other international film venues. They have participated in residencies at Skowhegan, the International Studio and Curatorial Program, Headlands Center for the Arts, and NLS Kingston. They have been awarded fellowships at MacDowell, the Leslie Lohman Museum, Queer|Art, and the Global Fund for Women. In 2024, Gopee was an Elaine G. Weitzen Fellow at the Whitney Museum Independent Study Program. They have lectured at Emory University, Rutgers University, and the Caltech-Huntington Program in Visual Culture. In 2025, Gopee was an artist in residence at MASS MoCA. They hold an MFA from University of California, Los Angeles, with a concentration in interdisciplinary studio and a BFA in photography and imaging from New York University.

Finding the Carnegie Museum of Art Theater

The theater is located on the ground floor of the Carnegie Museum of Art. From the main entrance of the museum, head down the stairs to the right of the reception desk and the theater will be at the end of the corridor. If you are entering from the parking lot at the rear of the museum, the theatre will be immediately to your right.

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.
events.summary: Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

events.title: Inside the Cyber Threat Landscape with FBI Pittsburgh
events.description:
Patrick Myers, Supervisory Special Agent with the FBI Pittsburgh Field Office, will offer a front-line perspective on today’s evolving cyber threats, sharing insights into how cybercriminals and nation-state actors operate—and how these risks increasingly intersect with everyday digital behaviors, at work and at home. Learn about current threat trends and how individuals and organizations can become targets.

Supervisory Special Agent Patrick Myers has been with the FBI since 2015. He is currently assigned to the FBI’s Pittsburgh Division, where he supervises a National Security Cyber squad focusing on state-sponsored cyber actors. As a special agent, SSA Myers has conducted investigations into hackers with Russia’s Military Intelligence, the GRU. SSA Myers’ work has led him to participate in investigations and in the defense of computer systems, including election networks worldwide, the Olympic Games, and U.S. critical infrastructure. SSA Myers is a member of the FBI’s Cyber Action Team (CAT), the FBI Cyber Division’s rapid response force, on call to deploy globally to bring in-depth cyber intrusion expertise and specialized investigative skills to bear in response to significant cyber events.

The Global Connections group offers a welcoming and confidential space for students to connect around the shared and unique experiences of studying and living in the US.

This group provides an opportunity to explore challenges such as adjusting to the new culture, navigating language or communication differences, managing academic expectations, coping with homesickness, isolation, or visa-related stress, and balancing family and cultural values with life at CMU. events.description:
Global Entrepreneurship Week (GEW) is a global movement that celebrates and supports entrepreneurship by creating opportunities for people to learn, connect, share ideas, and take action. At Carnegie Mellon University Africa (CMU-Africa), GEW provides an opportunity to bring together students, founders, alumni, industry, investors, ecosystem partners, and the wider university community around entrepreneurship, innovation, and technology. Through the Innovation Hub, CMU-Africa supports students and entrepreneurs through business incubation, mentorship, technical talent, industry connections, and opportunities to develop and test solutions to real-world challenges. GEW 2026 will build on these efforts by creating a week that brings the CMU-Africa entrepreneurship community together to explore ideas, build capabilities, connect with opportunities, and showcase what is being created.

This year’s theme “Entrepreneurs Thrive Here” reflects CMU-Africa’s ambition to create an environment where students and founders can explore entrepreneurship, develop their ideas, access the resources and networks they need, and turn ideas into meaningful solutions. It recognises that entrepreneurs thrive when they have access not only to knowledge and technology, but also to people, mentorship, opportunities, and a supportive community.

events.title: Ghostly Preferences: When Coherence Requires a Strict Preference Among Equivalent Random Variables
events.description:
Join the Philosophy Department for our annual Halloween talk! We will be handing out candy and while costumes are not required, they are welcome!

Presenter: Teddy Seidenfeld

Abstract: When utilities for outcomes are bounded, or when all variables are simple, it is required by (canoncial) expected utility to have preferences defined over probability distributions or lotteries over outcomes. That is, under such circumstances two random variables with a common probability distribution over outcomes – equivalent random variables – must occupy the same place in an agent’s preference ordering over lotteries. For example, with outcomes determined by a flip of a fair coin (i.e, where the probability of landing heads = the probability of landing tails = 1/2), winning $1 if heads and losing $1 if tails is equally preferred to losing $1 if heads and winning $1 if tails. Also, then one is indifferent between trading one of these lotteries for the other.
events.summary: Join the Philosophy Department for our annual Halloween talk! We will be handing out candy and while costumes are not required, they are welcome!

events.title: Teaching Inclusively: Creating Trust in the Classroom
events.description:
A seminar for graduate students and postdocs hosted by the Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence & Educational Innovation

Do you trust your students, and do your students trust you? These questions are critical to building a supportive environment for learning in your classroom. In this seminar, we will review various ways to conceptualize trust in a learning environment and share research on why trust is essential to learning from K-12 to higher education. Finally, we will explore various actions instructors can take to build and show trust in their classrooms. Participants should expect to leave with a series of implementable “teaching moves” that foster and demonstrate trust in the classroom.

In this fireside chat, iii faculty member Susanna Zlotnikov speaks with Nickey Skarstad, a senior director of product at Duolingo, about the culture behind making the world’s No. 1 language learning app.

​Skarstad will give us a look into the organizational practices that cultivate Duolingo’s unique innovation culture and what a typical day looks like for Duos building personalized experiences for over 40 million users world-wide.

​Specifically, Zlotnikov and Skarstad will explore how tech and product teams work together to build cutting-edge personalized experiences for millions of users, and how AI is pushing the Duolingo team to change the way they work and innovate.

​There will be 30 minutes to hear from our co-hosts, and 15 minutes for Q&A.

Hosted by the Integrated Innovation Institute (iii)

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
From Materials Sustainability to Quantum Devices: First-Principles Insights into Dynamic Interfaces, presented by Elizabeth Lee (UC Irvine)

Abstract: Material interfaces are critical frontiers where macroscopic functionality

emerges from microscopic phenomena—where bonds break, charges migrate, and heat carriers scatter. While first-principles molecular dynamics (FPMD) provides atomic-level insight into these processes, high computational cost has traditionally restricted its application to small systems (hundreds of atoms) and short timescales (picoseconds). I will discuss our approach for overcoming these limitations by integrating FPMD with Bayesian Inference, neural networks, and rare-event sampling. By bridging the gap between quantum fidelity and long-time and length-scale phenomena, we explore three distinct technological frontiers: (i) reactive chemistry at polymer–metal interfaces for sustainable plastic recycling, (ii) nanoscale heat transfer in alloys in the presence of grain boundaries and dopants, and (iii) charge transfer at semiconductor–water interfaces to realize robust nanoscale quantum sensors. Overall, these results show how predictive, first-principles knowledge of interfacial behavior can provide a rational design roadmap for the next generation of chemical recycling, thermal management, and quantum technologies.

Elizabeth “Liza” Lee is a Samueli Faculty Development Chair Assistant Professor

with joint appointments in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering and the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the University of California, Irvine (UCI). She is also affiliated with the Advanced Casting Research Center (ACRC) and the Eddleman Quantum Institute. She leads the Computational Engineering of Material Interfaces (CeMi) Lab, which develops quantum-classical simulation frameworks—combining electronic structure methods, machine learning, and molecular modeling—to reveal atomic-scale mechanisms at dynamic material interfaces. Her research interests include heterogeneous catalysis, semiconductor defects, and thermal transport in alloys. Before joining UCI, she was a postdoctoral scholar in the Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering at the University of Chicago, where she developed first principles computational frameworks with neural networks to investigate chemical bonding dynamics and equilibria in quantum materials and at metal surfaces. She earned her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she studied nanoscale energy transport phenomena in molecular semiconductors - such as colloidal quantum dots and conjugated polymers—to design next generation photovoltaics and LEDs. Her honors include the NSF CAREER Award, the UCI Samueli Faculty Development Chair Award, and the DOE ASCR Leadership Computing Challenge Award. She has also been recognized for excellence in teaching and mentoring, including receiving the UCI Engineering Student Council’s Professor of the Year Award.

events.title: CNA seminar: Melanie Rupflin (University of Oxford)
events.description:
Please note the unusual time.

Quantitative estimates for almost harmonic maps

Abstract: A fundamental question in the analysis of variational problems is whether functions that almost minimise a given energy, or almost solve its Euler-Lagrange equations, provide good approximations of true minimisers or critical points. In practice, one would like to understand this question not only at a qualitative level, but to obtain precise quantitative control on the distance of almost solutions to exact solutions in terms of the size of the error.

A major challenge in such a quantitative analysis of geometric variational problems is that the classical approach breaks down in the presence of singularities or changes of topology.

In this talk, we will discuss these issues for the Dirichlet energy of maps from surfaces into Riemannian manifolds for which the concentration of energy on small domains leads to a loss of compactness and the formation of a so-called bubble tree.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.description:
The audience of this workshop is #graduate-students.

Graduate school can demand a lot of you—but becoming a more effective student doesn’t require completely reinventing how you study. In this practical workshop, you’ll learn how small, consistent changes can lead to meaningful improvements in your academic habits and productivity.

We’ll explore strategies including habit stacking, reflection routines, weekly reviews, tiny improvements to your study practices, and consistency over intensity. You’ll have the opportunity to identify what’s working, pinpoint one area you’d like to improve, and create a simple plan for a small change you can put into practice immediately.

Learning Objectives:

Discover practical strategies for building sustainable study habits.

Create a simple weekly reflection and review routine.

Learn how to make your existing study practices more efficient.

Learn how to practice consistency over intensity.

Personalize “on small change” for immediate implementation.

This is an in-person workshop.

events.description:
This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

events.title: CMU/Pitt Colloquium: Dan Baxter (Fermilab)
events.description:
Speaker: Daniel Baxter (Fermilab)

Topic: Harnessing Quantum Sensors to Search for Dark Matter

Abstract: The CosmiQuantum group at Fermilab is at the center of understanding the relationship between particle impacts in quantum processors and qubit errors. This research hopes to enable high-fidelity quantum computation by resolving the issue of phonon-mediated correlated errors following cosmic ray impacts in a superconducting qubit chip. Additionally, this challenge for quantum computing presents a unique opportunity for fundamental science, as the same errors that follow a particle impact can be used to search for low-energy signatures of new physics originating from dark matter or neutrino impacts. At Fermilab, we have two world-class underground facilities which are already being used to study this problem: NEXUS and QUIET. I will present results from operating superconducting qubits in each of these facilities, and the potential implications towards utilizing qubits as sensors of new physics.

Meeting ID: 964 3585 2486

Passcode: 172095

events.title: Five Lessons on Caregiving from Wilderness Survival
events.description:
Join Virginia Eubanks as she shares her experience of family caregiving, trauma and “collateral” PTSD. Drawing on lessons from wilderness survival and conversations with experts and everyday heroes, she explores how we can build resilient communities of care in uncertain times.

In 2015, after a violent attack on her beloved partner, Virginia Eubanks suddenly became a family caregiver. In the weeks, months, and years that followed, she and her partner struggled to stay afloat as they faced wave upon wave of setbacks, including a serious case of post-traumatic stress disorder. Then, a second case. Eubanks developed “collateral” PTSD, a condition common among caregivers but rarely discussed.

An old lifesaving manual provided unexpected help. Inspired by its lessons, Eubanks studied wilderness first aid, kayak self-rescue, winter survival, bushwhacking, and lifeguarding. She interviewed experts and everyday heroes—from neuroscientists to monks to forest rangers.

Join Eubanks to discover what it takes to build communities of care that can sustain us in uncertain times.
events.summary: Join Virginia Eubanks as she shares her experience of family caregiving, trauma and “collateral” PTSD. Drawing on lessons from wilderness survival and conversations with experts and everyday heroes, she explores how we can build resilient communities of care in uncertain times.

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“The Future of STEM & STEM Leaders: A Nexus of Trust, Innovation and Credibility” presented by Judy Giordan (ecosVC, Inc.)

ABSTRACT: At a time when public trust in science and scientific innovations is rapidly shifting, the rules we thought we knew about how society views STEM practitioners and institutions are being rewritten. How did we get here? How do we navigate this uncertainty? Join this session as we trace the evolving relationship between STEM, innovation, and the public from post-WWII to today, and explore three actionable pillars that individual STEM practitioners and institutions can use to rebuild trust, restore credibility, and foster confidence in the ground-breaking innovations we create.

Judy Giordan is Managing Director of ecosVC, Inc., co-founder of the Chemical Angels Network, venture founder and former Fortune 100 executive. She serves as board member, co-founder, advisor and investor in seed and early-stage start-ups and is co-host of the podcast and newsletter Trust?Trust!Trust found on Substack.

Her previous executive positions include Corporate Vice President and Global Director of Research and Development at International Flavors and Fragrances, Inc.; Vice-President Worldwide Research and Development for Pepsi-Cola; and Vice President Research and Development, Henkel Corporation, the North American operating unit of the Henkel Group. She is co-founder of ventures in areas including biofuels and executive search and has also held management and technical contributor positions at Polaroid and ALCOA.

Judy served with the National Science Foundation as a member of the Math and Physical Sciences (MPS) Directorate and Chemistry Advisory Boards, Chair of the Alan T. Waterman Award Committee and as IGERT Program Officer. She was 2023 President of the American Chemical Society, is an ACS Fellow and received both the Garvin-Olin and Henry Whelan Awards from ACS. She is a Member of the Women in Chemicals advisory Board. She has held various academic roles including Professor of Practice at Oregon State University and the University of Southern Mississippi and Visiting Professor at Dartmouth College and North Carolina State University. Judy has a B.S. in Environmental Science and VoTech Ag from Rutgers University; Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of Maryland; and was an Alexander von Humboldt post doctoral fellow at the Goethe University, Frankfurt, Germany.
events.summary: “The Future of STEM & STEM Leaders: A Nexus of Trust, Innovation and Credibility” presented by Judy Giordan (ecosVC, Inc.)

events.title: Kwanzaa Ends
events.description: An African-American and Pan-African holiday celebrating family, community, and culture, Kwanzaa is a secular observance with some religious participation. Each day of Kwanzaa celebrates one of the Nguzo Saba, or the seven life principle in the language, Kiswahili. They are honored with candle-lighting each day of the season: umoja (unity), kujichagulia (self-determination), ujima (collective work and responsibility), ujamaa (cooperative economics), nia (purpose), kuumba (creativity), and imani (faith). Symbols include crops. Kwanzaa began on December 26.

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: Halloween at Heinz Hall
events.description:
On Halloween, the Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic will perform a free concert for the Pittsburgh community at Heinz Hall. This 80-minute program, designed for families and audience members of all ages will be led by Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

The Halloween-themed event includes spooky standards like Modest Mussorgsky’s Night on Bald Mountain (conducted by CMU Philharmonic Associate Conductor, John William Brink) and Paul Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. The concert will also feature wizard of the keyboard, Tino Cardenes (current Music and Technology student of the School of Music and winner of the Philharmonic Soloist Competition, undergraduate division) performing Nikolai Kapustin’s jazzy Piano Concerto No. 2. The heart of the program is Manuel de Falla’s magical El Amor Brujo, which includes the famous “Ritual Fire Dance.” This performance will feature recent graduate of the School of Music, mezzo-soprano Isabelle Hoyou. Kids are encouraged to come in costume and arrive early for pre-concert fun in the lobby.

Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Jacob Joyce, guest conductor

John William Brink, associate conductor

Featured Artists:

Isabelle Hoyou, mezzo-soprano

Tino Cardenes, piano

Program:

Modest Mussorgsky – Night on Bald Mountain

Manuel de Falla – El Amor Brujo

Nikolai Kapustin – Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 14

Paul Dukas – The Sorcerer’s Apprentice

Cost:

FREE and open to the public. Tickets required.
events.summary: On Halloween, the Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic will perform a free concert for the Pittsburgh community at Heinz Hall. This 80-minute program, designed for families and audience members of all ages will be led by Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce.

events.title: Carnegie Mellon Philharmonic: A Night of Italian Opera
events.description:
Daniel Nesta Curtis, Director of Orchestral Studies

Crystal Manich, Interim Director of Opera Studies

Matthew Kereama, director

On April 14th at Carnegie Music Hall, the philharmonic will team up with the School of Music’s opera department to present a gala-style concert of Italian opera. Conducted by Director of Orchestral Studies, Daniel Nesta Curtis, and directed by Matthew Kereama, the program will feature vocalists from the School of Music in select arias, ensembles, and scenes from famous operas. The first half will feature music from Gioachino Rossini’s Il Barbiere di Siviglia and L’Italiana in Algeri along with Gaetano Donizetti’s Don Pasquale and Lucia di Lammermoor. The second half will feature a condensed, 1-hour version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Boheme, focused on the opera’s 4 main characters.

Program:

Gioachino Rossini – Excerpts from Il Barbiere di Siviglia Overture

Gioachino Rossini – Act I Finale from L’italiana in Algeri

Gaetano Donizetti – Act III Duet: “Tornami a dir che m’ami” from Don Pasquale

Gaetano Donizetti – Excerpts from Lucia di Lammermoor

Giacomo Puccini – “BoheMedley”

Cost:

$10 Regular Admission

$5 Senior Citizen (65+) Admission

All students, along with CMU/Pitt faculty and staff, are free w/ valid ID

events.title: Student Recital: Jason Wells
events.description:
“What do you NOT play?” is a quote said by those who’ve seen enough of J Wells to fully discover his obsession with orchestral winds and double reeds. J Wells proves that lifelong musicians do not have to start early. After taking up a hobby in the flute and soprano saxophone at age 17, he settled on the oboe and bassoon, having now played for four and three years respectively.

J Wells originally came to CMU for composition, but after experiencing the joys of performing in CMU’s All University Orchestra (AUO) and learning the bassoon within the Kiltie Band, decided to switch to a “Student Defined Major” encompassing the music education certification and the study of both double reeds. J Wells is director of the AUO Flute Choir and has a passion for working with ensembles. He also loves to double multiple woodwinds in the pit orchestra for student-run musicals and playing in the school’s bagpipe band.

Having grown up in Hong Kong, J Wells plans to return there after graduating to teach K-12 music and private double reed lessons.

Jason Wells, oboe

BASEPLATE and Velum Fermentation are teaming up for a hands-on LEGO® building night for all ages. Build alongside fellow LEGO fans, explore your creativity with loose bricks, and create a custom model designed by BASEPLATE exclusively for Brick & Brew to take home.

BASEPLATE is a playful learning ecosystem for the Entertainment Technology Center (ETC) at Carnegie Mellon University. BASEPLATE champions brick-based experiences that are joyful, iterative, socially interactive, actively engaging, and meaningful.

Your $25 ticket includes:

Welcome drink: One drink voucher to get the evening started (cash bar thereafter).

Exclusive take-home model: Build a custom, limited-edition model designed by BASEPLATE exclusively for Brick & Brew, using LEGO® bricks.

Free-build zone: Explore your creativity with loose LEGO bricks and build whatever inspires you.

Whether you’re an AFOL (Adult Fan of LEGO), a casual builder, or simply looking for a creative night out, Brick & Brew is an invitation to play, connect, and make something of your own.

Brick & Brew is open to all ages, and every attendee needs a ticket. Guests under 18 must be accompanied by an adult. Alcohol is for guests 21+ with a valid photo ID; younger guests can use their drink voucher for a non-alcoholic option. To request a refund or transfer, contact Jillian Conrad (jconrad2@andrew.cmu.edu) by Nov. 10. Take-home models are not shipped or held for no-shows. Please drink responsibly and plan a safe ride home.

events.title: Ostatni Etap: The Last Stage
events.description:
Restored Version of the 1948 film, often described as the “Mother of all Holocaust Films.”

Director Wanda Jakubowska survived Auschwitz. She set and filmed the movie in Auschwitz and used survivors and locals in the cast. This film influenced a generation of filmmakers but then was forgotten, and surviving negatives began to decay.

This restoration from 2020 makes the film available for new generations. The pandemic limited its distribution, but now we are welcoming you to join us for the Pittsburgh premiere.

Sponsors: European Studies Center, Holocaust Center of Pittsburgh, The Polish Cultural Council– Pittsburgh,The CMU Jack Buncher Chair in Jewish Studies, University Center for International Studies

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.
events.summary: Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

events.title: Jonathan González: Visiting Artist Lecture
events.description:
Co-presented by Carnegie Museum of Art and the CMU School of Art

REGISTER HERE

Join us for an evening with artist Jonathan González as they share an in-depth look at their practice and the work featured in If the word we: 59th Carnegie International. Lectures are free and open to the public.

The Strikebreakers

The Strikebreakers is a new site-specific, four-hour performance conceived for the Grand Staircase of Carnegie Museum of Art. Performed by five dancers over five consecutive days, the work unfolds as a slow transformation of bodies, relationships, and collective attention, using the museum’s architecture as both stage and collaborator.

Drawing its title from the complicated history of labor, industry, and Western Pennsylvania, The Strikebreakers does not seek to reenact a historical event. Instead, it approaches the figure of the worker as a choreographic proposition: a body shaped by repetition, endurance, care, fatigue, solidarity, and the continual negotiation between individual agency and collective responsibility. Historical archives surrounding labor movements and Black social life circulate throughout the work not as illustrations, but as conditions that quietly inform its movement, rhythm, and atmosphere.

The performance is less concerned with representing history than with asking how history continues to move through bodies in the present. The title also resonates with the legacy of the 1892 Homestead Strike and the histories of labor surrounding Andrew Carnegie’s industrial empire, while opening the work toward broader questions of collective action and social choreography.

About the Artist

Jonathan González (b. 1988, Queens, NY; lives in New York, NY) is an interdisciplinary artist whose work spans choreography, sound, image, writing, video, and collective practice. Their artistic research engages themes of memory, Black geographies, and African diasporic temporalities, often through site-specific and durational performance. By combining movement, sound, and image, González creates works that explore embodiment as both a record of history and a rehearsal for the future. González has presented work nationally at major institutions, including Spectral Dances (American Academy of Arts and Letters, 2024), a durational performance and sonic installation, and perejil (Crystal Bridges Museum of Art / The Momentary, 2022), a performance and video installation presented in the exhibition Entre / Between. Their writing extends their choreographic and visual investigations, with a forthcoming book, Ways to Move: Black Insurgent Grammars, to be published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2025. González is the recipient of major awards, including the Herb Alpert Award in the Arts (Dance, 2024), the MAP Fund (2024), and the Foundation for Contemporary Arts Grants to Artists (Performance Art / Theater, 2019). Their practice foregrounds hybridity and collaboration, positioning collective action as both an artistic method and a social intervention.

Finding Kresge Theatre

Kresge Theatre is located in the College of Fine Arts building on the south end of CMU’s campus (near the Hunt Library). To find the theatre, enter the College of Fine Arts building from the west (main) entrance closest to the College of Fine Arts Lawn. Street parking is available along Frew and Tech streets or in CMU’s East Campus Garage.

events.title: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress
events.description:
This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

events.title: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)
events.description:
Speaker: Michel Janssen (University of Minnesota)

Topic: Arch and Scaffold: Jordan’s statistical transformation theory and von Neumann’s Hilbert space formalism

Abstract: In early 1927, Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, independently of one another, published their versions of a general formalism tying the various forms of the new quantum theory together and giving the theory’s statistical interpretation in full generality. This formalism has come to be known as the Dirac-Jordan (statistical) transformation theory. A few months later, in response to these publications, John von Neumann published his Hilbert space formalism for quantum mechanics. The relation between these two formalisms can be captured in terms of a metaphor for theory change in which one theory serves as the scaffold for the arch of another theory. What is unclear in this case is which formalism serves as the scaffold and which one as the arch. Did von Neumann build an arch on the scaffold built by Jordan? Or did von Neumann build a scaffold to prevent the arch built by Jordan from collapsing? Either way, the arch-and-scaffold metaphor is a promising alternative to Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm shifts for understanding theory change.

Note: Based on joint work with Anthony Duncan (University of Pittsburgh)

Meeting ID: 978 4615 2917.

Passcode: 299792

events.description:
In this installment of the CyLab Seminar Series, Praneeth Vepakomma of MIT will share his latest research.

Speaker:
Praneeth Vepakomma

Visiting Professor

MIT

Talk Title:
Talk title coming soon

Abstract:
Abstract coming soon

Bio:
Praneeth Vepakomma is currently a Visiting Assistant Professor at MIT in IDSS and is an Assistant Professor at MBZUAI. He previously obtained his PhD at MIT in and works on trustworthy/responsible computation that includes a sub-focus on distributed (resource-efficient) and private computation in statistics, ML and data science at large. He has extensive industrial experience across Meta, Apple, Amazon, Motorola Solutions, Corning and several startups. His research focuses on developing algorithms for distributed computation in statistics & machine learning under constraints of privacy, & efficiency.

He won the Meta PhD research fellowship in Applied Statistics, two SERC Scholarships (for Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing) from MIT’s Schwarzman college of computing. He co-founded a research based non-profit (Integrity Distributed) that won the Financial Times Digital Innovation Award. He won a Best Student Paper Award at FL-IJCAI, a Baidu Best Paper Award at NeurIPS-SpicyFL and a Best Paper Runner Up Award at FG-2021. His technical work is inspired by foundations of non-asymptotic statistics, randomized algorithms, learning augmented algorithms, combinatorics, and at times just by systems design. Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass”, was a pogrom that occurred November 9-10, 1938. It was the first organized, government-sanctioned act of violence against the Jews in Germany. It marks the start of the systematic violence against Jews during the Holocaust. Each year, the Holocaust Center of Pittsburgh holds an event to commemorate this important turning point in history.

Michael Berenbaum is a writer, lecturer, and teacher consulting in the conceptual development of museums and the development of historical films. He is director of the Sigi Ziering Institute: Exploring the Ethical and Religious Implications of the Holocaust at the American Jewish University (formerly the University of Judaism) where he is also a Professor of Jewish Studies.

events.title: Chemistry Seminar: Anindita Das, Southern Methodist University
events.description:
Anindita Das
Southern Methodist University

Tuning Atomically Precise Materials for Sustainable Chemistry

Host: Stefan Bernhard

Friday, October 30th, 2026

12:30 p.m.

Mellon Institute Conference Room 348

Abstract: With the advent of nanotechnology in the mid-1980s, nanomaterials have attracted tremendous interest due to their unique properties which make them suitable for diverse applications. However, the inherent polydispersity of conventional nanoparticles has precluded an atomic-level understanding of their structure-property relationships. This, in turn, has greatly hampered the complete realization of their target functional properties in real-world applications. This talk will focus on leveraging the principles of synthetic organic and inorganic chemistry to engineer multifunctional atomically precise materials for applications in catalysis, water harvesting, and iodine capture. Specifically, we will discuss two classes of materials, (1) molecularly pure, ligand-protected coinage metal clusters, and (2) covalent organic frameworks (COFs), which are atomically precise tunable materials with extraordinary porosity and crystallinity. Overall, these efforts aim to establish design rules for making functional heterogeneous nanomaterials with known structure-property-function relationships.

Bio: Anindita (Dia) Das obtained her Ph.D. with Prof. Rongchao Jin at Carnegie Mellon University, where her research focused on the synthesis and single-crystal growth of atomically precise gold nanoparticles to gain in-depth understanding of catalytic mechanisms. Prior to this, she earned B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees at Osmania University, India and the University of Pune, India respectively. Following her PhD., Dia carried out postdoctoral research with Prof. Chad Mirkin at Northwestern University, where her work centered on the development of spherical nucleic acids based on atomically precise gold nanoclusters for applications in colloidal crystal engineering. Dia started her independent lab in the Chemistry Department at Southern Methodist University in Fall 2020.
events.summary: Tuning Atomically Precise Materials for Sustainable Chemistry

events.title: ACO Seminar: Veit Elser (Cornell University)
events.description:
Speaker: Veit Elser, Cornell University

A greedy method for solving even hard problems

Abstract: Greed is a great instinct for solving problems. Its geometrical analog is a projection. Say your problem has many variables. It’s always possible to let them live in a continuous space, and define solutions to your problem as some subset in that space. A projection is the greedy operation of moving an arbitrary point to the set as efficiently as possible — by the least Euclidean distance. For many kinds of sets, even discrete and other highly non-convex ones, the projection computations are easy. Of course we know that cannot be the case when the task at hand is truly hard. Fortunately, even hard problems can be formulated as finding a point in the intersection of two sets, where projecting to each set individually is easy. This talk describes a general method that uses two easy projections, iteratively, to solve hard problems. After some history I will go over several examples, including sudoku, square packing, and data clustering. Problem requests will be considered if received (at ve10@cornell.edu) at least one week before the talk.

events.title: Formalization for Physics at ICARM
events.description:
https://icarm.io/events/2026/formalization-for-physics/

The Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM) at Carnegie Mellon is hosting a meeting, Formalization for Physics, organized by Sergey Cherkis, Michael Douglas, James Halverson, and Xi Yin on November 4-6. Local faculty and students are welcome to attend. Please register using the link below; you can join the participants’ discussion channel on the ICARM Zulip.

Register: https://icarm.io/join/0btzmSk86L5VdlJqNmQ7m1B6CQP6TKZ-7e1Vr-ZGYcw/

Zulip: https://icarm.zulipchat.com/join/pueyd62pbxstlmc43qeojl7q/

Description: Formal methods are becoming increasingly relevant to physics, not only as tools for checking completed arguments but also as instruments for clarifying definitions, exposing hidden assumptions, and organizing large bodies of technical knowledge. This workshop will bring together theoretical physicists, mathematical physicists, mathematicians, and proof-assistant practitioners to identify where machine-checked reasoning can be genuinely useful for physics research.

The proposal is not that formalization should replace physical intuition. The more realistic and scientifically useful goal is to understand how formalization can make precise which parts of an argument are rigorous, which parts depend on explicit mathematical assumptions, and which parts remain heuristic. This is especially relevant in theoretical and mathematical physics, where important arguments often involve several layers of definitions, conventions, and intermediate structures.

The timing is favorable because several communities are now converging. Proof assistants such as Lean, Coq, Isabelle, and Agda have reached the point where substantial parts of modern mathematics can be formalized. AI-assisted theorem proving and code generation are rapidly changing the cost profile of formalization. Physicists have recently completed several medium-size formalizations in quantum theory, on topics ranging from quantum information theory to constructive quantum field theory, and are starting to encounter the issues of coordination and organization which arose and were addressed in earlier large-scale projects.

events.title: Fall Seminar - Alex Luedtke
events.description:
Sinkhorn Treatment Effects: A Causal Optimal Transport Measure

Abstract: We introduce the Sinkhorn treatment effect, an entropic optimal transport measure of divergence between counterfactual distributions. Unlike classical quantities such as the average treatment effect, this measure captures differences across entire distributions. We analyze this divergence as a statistical functional and show it can be written as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings with an appropriate kernel. This characterization allows us to establish first-order pathwise differentiability in general, and second-order pathwise differentiability under the null hypothesis of equal counterfactual distributions. Leveraging this smoothness, we construct debiased estimators and use them to obtain asymptotically valid tests for distributional treatment effects with a fixed entropic regularization parameter. Because the power of the test depends on this unknown parameter, we further propose an aggregated test that combines evidence across a grid of regularization choices. Experiments on simulated and image data demonstrate the practical advantages of our estimator and testing procedure.

Bio: Alex Luedtke is a Professor of Health Care Policy and Affiliate in Statistics at Harvard University. Previously, he held faculty appointments in Statistics and Biostatistics at the University of Washington and Fred Hutch.

Alex works at the intersection of semiparametrics, causal inference, and machine learning. Much of his work leverages computational power to automate the construction of efficient statistical procedures. To this end, he has developed methods that let machines “learn to learn” from data, and algorithms that work out derivations once done by hand. He applies these tools as part of multidisciplinary teams to improve decision-making in mental health and infectious disease research.

Selected honors include a COPSS Emerging Leader Award, NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, and Mortimer Spiegelman Award. His work has been supported by NIH, NSF, PCORI, WHO, and Netflix.

Alex received a Ph.D. in Biostatistics from UC Berkeley and an ScB in Applied Mathematics from Brown University.

Abstract

Cognitive control allows us to think and behave flexibly based on our context and goals. Most theories of cognitive control propose a control representation that enables the same input to produce different outputs contingent on contextual factors. However, the computational features of these control representations that enable this flexible mapping remain unknown. In this talk, I will focus on the geometry of neural control representations that enable cognitive control. I will present evidence from fMRI and EEG showing how these representations are organized and change as a function of different task structures, over the course of a trial, and over the course of practice; and I will discuss how these changes relate to efficient behavioral control.
