events.title: Formalization for Physics at ICARM
events.description:
https://icarm.io/events/2026/formalization-for-physics/

The Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics (ICARM) at Carnegie Mellon is hosting a meeting, Formalization for Physics, organized by Sergey Cherkis, Michael Douglas, James Halverson, and Xi Yin on November 4-6. Local faculty and students are welcome to attend. Please register using the link below; you can join the participants’ discussion channel on the ICARM Zulip.

Register: https://icarm.io/join/0btzmSk86L5VdlJqNmQ7m1B6CQP6TKZ-7e1Vr-ZGYcw/

Zulip: https://icarm.zulipchat.com/join/pueyd62pbxstlmc43qeojl7q/

Description: Formal methods are becoming increasingly relevant to physics, not only as tools for checking completed arguments but also as instruments for clarifying definitions, exposing hidden assumptions, and organizing large bodies of technical knowledge. This workshop will bring together theoretical physicists, mathematical physicists, mathematicians, and proof-assistant practitioners to identify where machine-checked reasoning can be genuinely useful for physics research.

The proposal is not that formalization should replace physical intuition. The more realistic and scientifically useful goal is to understand how formalization can make precise which parts of an argument are rigorous, which parts depend on explicit mathematical assumptions, and which parts remain heuristic. This is especially relevant in theoretical and mathematical physics, where important arguments often involve several layers of definitions, conventions, and intermediate structures.

The timing is favorable because several communities are now converging. Proof assistants such as Lean, Coq, Isabelle, and Agda have reached the point where substantial parts of modern mathematics can be formalized. AI-assisted theorem proving and code generation are rapidly changing the cost profile of formalization. Physicists have recently completed several medium-size formalizations in quantum theory, on topics ranging from quantum information theory to constructive quantum field theory, and are starting to encounter the issues of coordination and organization which arose and were addressed in earlier large-scale projects.

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“Harnessing Light, Color, Ions and Electrons: from Electrochromics to Artificial Retina,” presented by Jianguo Mei

Abstract: The Mei Research Group at Zhejiang University bridges fundamental discovery and real-world innovation by integrating chemistry, materials science, engineering and medicine. We develop organic semiconductors and conductors with transformative potential for printed electronics, bioelectronics, and living electronics, pursuing both technological impact and fundamental scientific frontiers.

In this seminar, I will highlight two complementary research directions: Electrochromic Technologies and Living Electronics. Both are rooted in the precise control of light, color, ions, and electrons, yet extend these principles toward very different applications. Through Ambilight Inc., our discoveries in flexible electrochromic thin films have been translated into roll-to-roll manufacturing and commercialized for applications ranging from electric vehicles to consumer electronics. These examples illustrate how fundamental discoveries made in an academic laboratory can evolve into market-ready technologies.

Our second direction, Living Electronics, asks a more fundamental question: Can electronics become part of living systems rather than being implanted into them? Inspired by biological vision, our work on Organic Eyes seeks to emulate the sensing and processing functions of the human visual system. In parallel, we are exploring electronics that can grow within the brain, creating electronic materials that form and function directly within living neural tissue. While these goals remain at the frontier of science, they point toward a fundamentally different relationship between synthetic materials and biology.

To illustrate the broader philosophy behind our research, I will discuss the journey of n-doped poly(benzodifurandione) (n-PBDF)-from an unexpected polymer discovery and scalable synthesis to applications in flexible electronics and bioelectronics. This case study captures our approach: coupling curiosity-driven discovery with mission-driven innovation. By connecting fundamental chemistry to real-world needs while pursuing ambitious scientific frontiers, we seek to turn new molecular concepts into technologies that can ultimately benefit society.

Refs: M. Chen, D. Wang, Y. Zou, et al., J. Mei, “Long-range extended chains arising from polymerization-driven spontaneous assembly,” Science 393, 172 (2026); S. Samal, S. Xiao, S. Nelson, et al., J. Mei, “Blood-catalyzed n-doped polymers for reversible optical neural control,” Science 392, eadu5500 (2026); K. Chen, H. Hu, I. Song, et al., J. Mei, “Organic optoelectronic synapse based on photon-modulated electrochemical doping,” Nature Photonics 17, 629–637 (2023); I. Song, W.-J. Lee, Z. Ke, et al., J. Mei, “An n-doped capacitive transparent conductor for all-polymer electrochromic displays,” Nature Electronics 7, 1158–1169 (2024).

Jianguo Mei is a Qiushi Chair Professor at Zhejiang University, where he is establishing research programs in organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, printed electronics, and living electronics and leading the Center for Living Electronics and Adaptive Neurotherapeutics (CLEAN). He previously spent 12 years at Purdue University, where he served as Richard and Judith Wien Professor of Chemistry and Department Head. He has authored more than 150 peer-reviewed publications, holds 39 granted U.S. patents, and has received more than 22,000 citations. He is also a co-founder of Ambilight Inc., which pioneered the roll-to-roll manufacturing of flexible electrochromic films for smart windows and other applications.

events.title: CMU Theory Seminar: Rich Holman
events.description:
Speaker: Rich Holman

Title: Tensor Catalyzed Scalar Decoherence in Inflation

Abstract. We provide the first complete calculation of the leading contribution to the decoherence of primordial fluctuations in the scalar part of the metric fluctuations within simplest, single-clock, inflationary models, assuming decoherence comes from gravitational interactions with an environment made up of the other, unmeasured, short-wavelength scalar and tensor modes.

We include the contributions from all of the contributing interactions at leading order in powers of (H/Mp) and of the slow-roll parameter ϵ. Unlike all extant calculations in the literature we find a result that is not slow-roll suppressed (and so is the same order of magnitude as tensor-mode decoherence). The difference arises because the dominant decoherence comes from interactions that involve both the tensor and scalar environments simultaneously (and so are missed when they are examined separately). We verify that the leading contributions to decoherence are UV finite (as they must be). We confirm that the interactions driving decoherence become time-local and Gaussian in the deep super-Hubble inflationary regime and show how this can be used to reliably compute the evolution of the purity in the late-time regime relevant for observations (where naive perturbation theory is known to break down). The same derivation shows explicitly why the effects that undermine perturbation theory for decoherence do not also undermine the basic inflationary prediction for the amplitude of primordial fluctuations.

events.title: CNA seminar: Amit Acharya (Carnegie Mellon University)
events.description:
An Adaptive Variational Dual Scheme for equation solving

Abstract: I will describe a scheme for converting the question of solving a given system of equations and associated side-conditions into a variational problem whose formal Euler-Lagrange system recovers the given system and side-conditions using a change-of-variables generated by the scheme. The variational principle is convex, and the method uses a string of such convex variational principles to seek a solution of the original question as an interior minimizer of the last variational problem of the string. Weak coercivity of a variational problem in the string endows its minimizer the status of a weaker `variational dual solution’ to the original, possibly non-variational problem. This last point of view is directly related to Y. Brenier’s Hidden Convexity approach to nonlinear PDE.

Due to the inherent convexity of the scheme, it allows for obtaining `unstable’ solutions of the original, primal system of equations in a `stable’ manner. A ChatGPT-enabled exploration of the scheme in the context of approximation of the mixed curvature isometric embedding problem from R^2 to R^3 will be discussed, as well as the problem of finding deformations of a membrane with prescribed principal stretch fields. This last problem is practically important for questions of sensing and actuation.

The event will be available both by Zoom and in Wean Hall 7218.

events.title: EPP Seminar: Sonia Mangones — Transportation, Air Pollution, and Inequalities: Evidence from Bogotá, Colombia
events.description:
Environmental justice research often examines the burden of pollution in relation to the population’s socioeconomic vulnerability. Climate justice research examines differential responsibility, asking who emits and who ultimately carries the burden they create. Urban mobility justice research rarely combines these two questions empirically, even though mobility is where they intersect most directly, since travel generates emissions and also shapes where resulting pollution concentrations fall across the city. This talk presents findings from an empirical study of Bogotá, Colombia, that measures both sides of this relationship at the level of city blocks, combining residential pollution concentration (NO2 and PM2.5) with a block-level proxy for travel-emission responsibility built from official mobility and emissions data. Two findings challenge a simple story in which the poor pollute least and suffer most. First, pollution concentration does not increase monotonically with deprivation; it peaks at intermediate socioeconomic levels. Second, emission responsibility does decline cleanly with vulnerability, but the resulting imbalance, where responsibility is low and pollution concentration is high, concentrates in population segments that can only be identified by combining policy instruments that separately inform socioeconomic vulnerability and the spatial distribution of the imbalance. I discuss what this means for the mobility justice conversation and the implications for transportation and environmental policy.

Speaker BIo:

Sonia Cecilia Mangones Matos is an Associate Professor at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, where she directs the Translogyt Research Group. Her work lies at the intersection of transportation engineering, urban sustainability, environmental impacts of transportation, road safety, and public policy. Her research combines quantitative methods, data analytics, and interdisciplinary approaches to examine sustainable urban mobility, transportation-related air pollution, emissions, and the implications of transportation systems for public health and urban equity.

Sonia holds a Ph.D. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University and an M.Sc. in Transportation Engineering from Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Her international academic experience includes research stays at CNRS in Toulouse and the LIVE Laboratory at the University of Strasbourg in France, as well as a research visit to Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile. She is Co-Chair of the Sustainable Transport Committee of the Pan-American Society of Transportation Research (PANAMSTR) and actively contributes to the World Conference on Transport Research, Community Modeling and Analysis System (CMAS) South America, and the Transportation Research Board in the US. She has led and collaborated on research projects with public institutions in Colombia, including the Ministry of Transport and the National Road Safety Agency. Her recent work has received broader recognition, including the 2025 L’Oréal–UNESCO “For Women in Science” Regional Award for her work on AI-enabled sustainable urban mobility and the 2025 Afro-Colombian of the Year Award in the Science and Technology category, recognizing her contributions to science and applied research in Colombia.

She is currently a Fulbright Visiting Scholar in Carnegie Mellon University’s Department of Engineering and Public Policy, where her project develops a justice-based framework integrating mobility, emissions, and pollution concentration and examines how complex technical evidence can be translated into actionable policy.

Bio:

Andrew Ilyas is an assistant professor at CMU. Previously, he was a Stein Fellow at Stanford Statistics and a Ph.D. student MIT, where he was fortunate to be advised by Costis DaskalakisOpens in new window and Aleksander MadryOpens in new window and supported by an Open Philanthropy AI FellowshipOpens in new window. Ilyas’s goal is to uncover general principles that describe and predict the behavior of ML systems—ideally enabling predictably reliable future systems. He also likes thinking broadly about (human) trust in AI systems.

events.title: CERCA Webinar with Orange Country Water District
events.description:
“Co-creating tomorrow: Community Driven Engineering for a Resilient Future” is a webinar series exploring the critical intersection of community wisdom and engineering expertise in the face of a changing climate. Organized by CERCA, CMU CEE’s Center for Engineering Resilience and Climate Adaptation, this series will foster a deeper understanding of how community engagement can enhance the effectiveness, equity, and sustainability of climate adaptation initiatives.

The Orange County Water District (OCWD) manages the Orange County Groundwater Basin, which provides approximately 85% of the water supply for 2.5 million people. Maintaining a reliable groundwater supply in a highly urbanized coastal basin requires an integrated approach that includes seawater intrusion protection, water reuse, stormwater capture, and managed aquifer recharge (MAR).

Seawater intrusion has been a challenge in the Orange County Groundwater Basin since the 1920s. In response, OCWD constructed the Talbert Seawater Intrusion Barrier in the 1970s, creating a hydraulic barrier to protect the basin from further seawater intrusion. Today, OCWD continues to operate and improve its coastal barriers and is evaluating development of a new barrier in the Sunset Gap to address an additional potential pathway for seawater intrusion. Bill Leever, OCWD Principal Hydrogeologist, will discuss the history, operation, and future of OCWD’s seawater intrusion barrier program.

Adam Hutchinson, OCWD Recharge Planning Manager, will discuss how OCWD uses Forecast-Informed Reservoir Operations (FIRO) and MAR to increase the capture and recharge of stormwater while maintaining flood-risk-management objectives. OCWD operates an extensive recharge system along the Santa Ana River and has worked with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for decades to temporarily store stormwater behind Prado Dam for subsequent release and groundwater recharge.

Together, the presentations will illustrate how a coastal groundwater basin can integrate seawater intrusion protection, flood management, stormwater capture, groundwater recharge, and recycled water as complementary elements of a resilient regional water-supply system.

events.title: Masterclass: Valerie Coleman & Monica Ellis
events.description:
Valerie Coleman, flute

Monica Ellis, bassoon

Valerie Coleman is regarded by many as an iconic artist who continues to pave her own unique path as a composer, GRAMMY®-nominated flutist, and entrepreneur. Highlighted as one of the “Top 35 Women Composers” by The Washington Post, she was named Performance Today’s 2020 Classical Woman of the Year, an honor bestowed to an individual who has made a significant contribution to classical music as a performer, composer or educator. Her works have garnered awards such as the MAPFund, ASCAP Honors Award, Chamber Music America’s Classical Commissioning Program, Herb Alpert Ragdale Residency Award, and nominations from The American Academy of Arts and Letters and United States Artists. Umoja, Anthem for Unity was chosen by Chamber Music America as one of the “Top 101 Great American Ensemble Works” and is now a staple of woodwind literature.

Bassoonist Monica Ellis is a founding member of the Grammy nominated wind quintet, Imani Winds, who in their 23rd season, continue to make ground-breaking art while maintaining a vigorous international touring schedule.

Monica’s strong work ethic was instilled very early on from her mother and father, the late jazz saxophonist, Clarence Oden. As the administrative director & tour manager for Imani Winds, and Co-Artistic Director for the Imani Winds Chamber Music Festival, she maintains a fulfilling leadership role within group.

events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“Cooking, Fishing and Jogging through Phase Space: A Practical Guide to Discovering and Understanding New Materials,” presented by Paul C. Canfield (Iowa State University)

Abstract: The design, discovery, characterization and control of novel materials is perhaps the most important research area for humanity as it moves into the 21rst century. A myriad of societal problems concerning energy, clean water and air, and medicine all need to be solved by the discovery of new compounds with dramatically improved, or even new, properties. The search for such materials requires a blending of skills and mindsets that, traditionally, have been segregated into different academic disciplines: physics, chemistry, metallurgy, materials science. In this colloquium I will outline the basic philosophy and techniques that we use to search for novel materials. These include a combination of intuition, experience, compulsive optimism and a desire to share discovery.[1]

In the second half of the lecture, the specific case of superconductivity will be used as an example of one such search. Over the past couple of decades a growing sense of where and even how to search for new superconductors has been developing, with the recent discoveries of MgB2 and the FeAs based materials providing, at least for me, clear guidance. [2]

[1] Paul C. Canfield, Rep. Prog. Phys. 83 [2020] 016501.

[2]Paul C. Canfield,Nature Materials10[2011] 259.

Paul C. Canfield is an Ames Laboratory Senior Scientist, a Distinguished Professor and the Robert Allen Wright Professor of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa State University.

Canfield’s research interests include the design, discovery, growth and characterization of novel electronic and magnetic compounds - often in single crystal form - and the study of their electrical, magnetic and thermal properties. Over the past three decades, he has helped discover, understand, and optimize materials with ferromagnetic and superconducting states as well as more exotic system that have fragile magnetism that can be manipulated so as to shed light on basic questions addressing the very origins of magnetic behavior.

Canfield has received numerous awards and citations for his work. In 2020 he was elected to be a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2016, he was awarded the James C. McGroddy Prize for New Materials by the American Physical Society (APS). In 2015, he received a Humboldt Research Award. In 2014, he was awarded the David Adler Award in the field of Material Physics by the American Physical Society (APS) and was also placed on the Thomson Reuters’ World’s Most Influential Scientific Minds list. In 2011, Canfield received the Department of Energy Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award.
events.summary: “Cooking, Fishing and Jogging through Phase Space: A Practical Guide to Discovering and Understanding New Materials,” presented by Paul C. Canfield (Iowa State University)

events.title: Supporting Student Well-Being: Faculty Professional Development in Recognizing and Assisting Students in Distress
events.description:
This faculty-designed professional development opportunity serves as a broad overview of how best to aid students at Carnegie Mellon University.

This session combines 30 minutes of asynchronous work in FocusU with a 90-minute, in-person presentation. Upon completing the training, faculty should be able to (1) articulate key findings about the CMU student mental health experience, (2) describe the vital role of faculty in supporting students, (3) identify the appropriate methods to assist students, and (4) describe the available support resources on campus.

Please note that this training is one of three options that faculty can complete to fulfill required training on student mental health and well-being. As part of CMU’s ongoing commitment to student mental health and well-being, all faculty members are expected to complete professional development focused on recognizing and supporting students in distress. Faculty may choose from the three training options listed on the Counseling & Psychological Services website (https://www.cmu.edu/counseling/services/cope.html#trainings). For more information, please refer to Provost Garrett and Dean Casalegno’s message to faculty (https://www.cmu.edu/leadership/the-provost/campus-comms/11-05-25).

“Projected Impacts of Data Centers on U.S. Electricity Costs and Emissions”

Rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers could substantially increase U.S. power sector emissions and electricity costs by 2030, with particularly large impacts in regions such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Using a detailed energy model covering 26 interconnected U.S. power regions, we evaluate how demand growth, fuel prices, and federal policies affect electricity generation, infrastructure investment, and costs. Data centers could push U.S. power sector carbon emissions up by as much as 28% and spike regional electricity costs by up to 57% by 2030.

events.description:
Christopher Mark Jones, professor emeritus of French & Francophone studies, returns with a celebration of his French-language album Montréal Encore, premiered with his collaborator Bernard Pozier at City of Asylum in March of 2023.

This concert features selections from that album and mix-ins by Québécois, French Caribbean and Parisian singer-songwriters—the likes of Boris Vian, Michel Rivard, Louis Aragon and Henri Salvador.

Free In-Person Tickets | Free Livestream Tickets

Featured Musicians:

Christopher Mark Jones: vocals, guitar

Brad Yoder: vocal harmonies, guitar, saxophone, glockenspiel

Mark Perna: bass

Eric George: African djembe and hand cymbals

Matt Siegler: piano and accordion

About the Artist:

Christopher Mark Jones draws from folk, country, blues, jazz and R&B sources to stage his literate folk-rock meditations. Using diverse points of view to narrate and critique life and love in uncertain times, he invites listeners to think, feel and dance. Recorded and live arrangements leave space for his musical co-conspirators to both express their personalities and honor the host creation. Listeners hear echoes of “Greg Brown’s pacing and a Lyle Lovett attitude” (Ben Shannon), as well as of John Prine, Bruce Coburn and Darrell Scott.

Between careers as a basketball player and French professor, Christopher busked in Paris, toured the UK, Denmark and Holland, and played New England clubs. He now tours and streams solo from Pittsburgh, PA, and plays regionally in formats varying from solo to full band. Looking for the Light (2021) is his sixth recording of original folk/roots songs, while Montréal Encore (2022) is a French-language recording created in collaboration with the poet Bernard Pozier.

events.title: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen
events.description:
LCAL’s Informal Conversations on Research (ICOR) Series provides a welcoming forum for faculty and graduate students to share and discuss their most recent research in an engaging, accessible format.

Translingual Borders: Refugee Testimony and the Politics of Translation

Isabelle Chen, assistant professor of global French studies, will challenge the assumption that translation is a liberatory practice — one that enables people to cross linguistic, cultural and geographic borders — by examining how translation can also reinforce borders, reproduce unequal power dynamics and constrain individual agency.

Focusing on Shumona Sinha’s novel Assommons les pauvres ! (Down with the Poor!), Dr. Chen’s talk explores the experiences of a Bengali interpreter working with asylum seekers in France. She examines how Sinha uses translation both as a literary strategy and a central thematic motif to portray interpretation as a potential barrier to human mobility and freedom.

Drawing on translation theory and recent migration data, Dr. Chen considers what literary representations of translation can reveal about its real-world consequences — and about the roles of multilingualism, interpretation and language in immigration policy and advocacy today.

events.title: X in the Loop Webinar Series
events.description:
X in the Loop is an interdisciplinary webinar series that questions what it means for humans to remain “in control” of AI. By replacing “human” with the open variable “X,” the series explores who holds power in AI systems, whose perspectives are included and what other species, cultures and ways of knowing might belong in the loop.

Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: ​Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: Condensed Matter Physics (CMP) Seminar: Yiming Xu (PRX)
events.description:
Title: The Character of PRX: Editorial Insights from the First 15 Years and Beyond

Abstract: PRX is published by the American Physical Society, a nonprofit membership society of scientists. Its mission goal is to select around 250 *landmark* papers a year from all fields of physics and showcase them to a broad and multidisciplinary readership.

After 15 years, one might still wonder exactly what PRX is—or, asked differently, how PRX defines a “landmark” through the peer-review process. As an author or referee, you may be curious about how PRX editors actually select these papers. Furthermore, there is always the fair question: are these selections always accurate?

In this talk, I will discuss how we approach these questions. Many of these questions do not have a black-and-white answer in the case of a single paper. Instead, open-minded, reasoned, and constructive dialogue among authors, editors, and referees is key. Ultimately, we, at PRX, strive to navigate the editorial and peer-review process effectively to ensure that the experience is meaningful, productive, and - at times - even a pleasure for everyone involved.

events.title: Pitt/CMU Colloquium: Christina Marchetti (UCSB)
events.description:
Active Matter: The Physics of Self-Organization

Birds flock, bees swarm and fish school. These are just some of the remarkable examples of collective behavior found in nature. Physicists have been able to capture some of this behavior by modeling organisms as ``flying spins’’ that align with their neighbors according to simple but noisy rules. Successes like these have spawned a field devoted to the physics of active matter – matter made not of atom and molecules but of entities that consume energy to generate their own motion and forces. Through interactions, collectives of such active particles organize in emergent structures on scales much larger than that of the individuals. Living systems are the paradigm of such behavior, but same behavior has also been mimicked in the lab through the engineering a variety of ``active particles’’ that self-assemble to form smart materials.

In this lecture I will introduce the field of active matter and highlight ongoing efforts by physicists, biologists, engineers and mathematicians to model the complex behavior of these systems, with the goal of identifying universal principles. I will specifically focus on two examples of active behavior. The first highlights how active particles bypass the laws of equilibrium thermodynamics and spontaneously aggregate in the absence of any attractive interactions. The second describes the interplay of flow and topological defects in controlling dynamics and structure of active phases with liquid crystalline order, with relevance from materials science to biology.

events.title: CMU Theory Seminar: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)
events.description:
Speaker: Thomas Colas (Cambridge)

Title: Exploring non-equilibrium universality with Schwinger–Keldysh effective field theories

Abstract: Dissipation and noise arise throughout physics, from condensed matter to cosmology, whenever observable degrees of freedom interact with a medium. The Schwinger–Keldysh formalism provides a systematic framework for describing such dynamics. Building on techniques developed in fluctuating hydrodynamics, I will discuss how symmetry, locality and unitarity constrain the allowed interactions. I will then explain how dissipation and noise modify the EFT power counting compared with vacuum quantum field theory. Using a scalar theory with a Kardar–Parisi–Zhang interaction, I will finally explore the emergence of a non-equilibrium universality class and discuss whether cosmological expansion in de Sitter spacetime can make this new dynamical regime accessible in three spatial dimension.

events.title: CNA seminar: Alpar Meszaros (Durham University)
events.description:
Equilibria and quantitative convergence for Mean Field Games of Controls

Abstract: We study equilibria in large-population stochastic differential games with interactions through both states and controls, within the framework of Mean Field Games. Focusing on general nonseparable Hamiltonians under displacement monotonicity assumptions, we investigate the existence, uniqueness, and quantitative convergence of different notions of Nash equilibria, including open-loop, closed-loop, and distributed equilibria.

A central challenge in this setting is the analysis of nontrivial consistency relations on the space of probability measures, whose structure depends on the equilibrium concept. We discuss how a careful study of these relations, combined with suitable a priori estimates, yields well-posedness and quantitative convergence results as the number of players tends to infinity. The results cover both stochastic and deterministic models, including some settings with common noise. The talk will be based on two recent works in collaboration with J. events.title: Graduate Student Seminar
events.description:
“Interface control of material functionality” presented by Valentino Cooper (Oak Ridge National Laboratory)

Abstract: Advances in thin film growth techniques, which allow for the precise layer-by-layer growth of epitaxial materials, have opened the door to discoveries not previously achievable through bulk synthesis. Pertinent examples include emergent phenomena at oxide heterointerfaces such as two-dimensional electron gases, interfacial superconductivity and novel magnetic properties. In this presentation, I will discuss our use of first principles calculations to explore how the character of heterostructure interfaces can be used to influence material stability and functionality. I will illustrate the role that charge transfer plays in driving magnetism and anomalous dielectric responses at oxide interfaces, and how these can be modulated through chemical identity and interface disorder. Collectively, these results demonstrate unprecedented control over interfacial charge and spin, creating a new avenue for a wide range of applications such as in oxide electronics.

Dr. Valentino R. Cooper is a Distinguished R&D Staff Member and Section Head for Foundational and Quantum Materials Science in the Materials Sciences and Technology Division at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. He serves as Director of the Department of Energy-funded Energy Frontier Research Center on Fast and Cooperative Ion Transport in Polymer Electrolytes (FaCT). Dr. Cooper received his Ph.D. in chemistry from the University of Pennsylvania in 2005 and was a postdoctoral associate in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Rutgers University before joining ORNL in 2008. His research focuses on the development and application of electronic structure methods to understand dispersion interactions and predict functional materials, including piezoelectrics, ferroelectrics, complex oxides, and polymer electrolyte materials. From 2017 to 2020, he was an Associate Editor of the Journal of Applied Physics and currently serves on the Board of Managers for AIP Publishing. He received the Department of Energy Early Career Award in 2013, the ORNL Office of Research Excellence Mentor MVP Award in 2023, and was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society in 2024.

events.title: Open Source in Energy Access Symposium (OSEAS)
events.description:
The Open Source in Energy Access Symposium (OSEAS) is the first global event dedicated to harnessing Open Source technologies to accelerate universal energy access. Co-organized by EnAccess and WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, OSEAS has quickly become a flagship global gathering for open innovation in the energy sector.

The first edition took place in 2024 in Abuja, Nigeria, marking a groundbreaking moment in uniting global stakeholders.

The second edition, hosted in 2025 in Nairobi, Kenya, which drew even greater momentum.

Due to overwhelming demand from participants and partners, OSEAS is now set to become an annual event. The third edition will take place on October 26-27, 2026 in Kigali, Rwanda.

OSEAS 2026 will once again unite global policymakers, entrepreneurs, industry leaders, tech innovators and the Open Source Community to explore challenges, seize opportunities and create synergies. Based on your valued feedback, we’ve enhanced this year’s program with:

Expanded working group sessions

Dedicated poster exhibition space

Product fair

A donor roundtable

An improved hackathon experience

Site visit

Open Source technology and tools have been transforming the Energy Access landscape - enhancing interoperability, boosting cost efficiency, and ensuring high quality. However, it’s only recently that their full potential has started to shine through. By accelerating collaboration and dialogue, OSEAS 2025 aims to push us closer to universal energy access.

Global Entrepreneurship Week (GEW) is a global movement that celebrates and supports entrepreneurship by creating opportunities for people to learn, connect, share ideas, and take action. At Carnegie Mellon University Africa (CMU-Africa), GEW provides an opportunity to bring together students, founders, alumni, industry, investors, ecosystem partners, and the wider university community around entrepreneurship, innovation, and technology. Through the Innovation Hub, CMU-Africa supports students and entrepreneurs through business incubation, mentorship, technical talent, industry connections, and opportunities to develop and test solutions to real-world challenges. GEW 2026 will build on these efforts by creating a week that brings the CMU-Africa entrepreneurship community together to explore ideas, build capabilities, connect with opportunities, and showcase what is being created.

This year’s theme “Entrepreneurs Thrive Here” reflects CMU-Africa’s ambition to create an environment where students and founders can explore entrepreneurship, develop their ideas, access the resources and networks they need, and turn ideas into meaningful solutions. It recognises that entrepreneurs thrive when they have access not only to knowledge and technology, but also to people, mentorship, opportunities, and a supportive community.

events.title: CNBC Writing Group
events.description:
CNBC Writing Group
Tuesdays, 10-12pm
Contact: Andrew Papale (papalea@pitt.edu)
Location is typically Zoom: https://pitt.zoom.us/j/93000073719
Meeting ID: 930 0007 3719
Passcode: 3141

Description: Two hour block dedicated to writing papers, grants, reviews, etc. We use the Pomodoro system of 25 min blocks with 5 min breaks in between to chitchat.
There’s a group of ~10 people who attend semi-regularly. On any given week, it’s typical to have 3-5 people. It’s used for accountability and setting aside a dedicated chunk of time for writing (although some people use it for analysis or whatever else they may need to focus on). events.description:
Admiral Rachel Levine has spent her career on the distance between the care people need and the care they receive. She trained as a pediatrician and specialized in adolescent medicine. She served as Pennsylvania's Physician General and then Secretary of Health. She was confirmed as the 17th Assistant Secretary for Health at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, where she led the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps.

Her remarks will explore how health systems can better serve LGBTQIA+ patients, and what meaningful equity looks like in everyday practice. She will also address how these pressures show up outside of healthcare settings, including on college campuses.

The evening opens with brief remarks from Admiral Levine, followed by a moderated discussion and audience questions.

This event is offered alongside the Combating Hate Series from the Office of the Vice Provost for Community, Culture and Engagement.

events.title: Biophilic Design Club - intro meeting
events.description:
My name is Sola Nishimura. I am founding a club called "Biophilic Design Club".

Join the first intro meeting on October 1st 5:30pm @ Posner 152.

I believe this climate crisis, at its core, is a cultural problem layered underneath an economic one. People don't love nature enough, desire a change, or know that a better life could exist, which is being fueled by the lack of financial investments into sustainable solutions. So then, what if we can make nature and sustainability something so visually and emotionally irresistible, yet something that can be so effortlessly AND practically be integrated into the daily texture of our life, so that they can begin to HOPE, and DESIRE these changes? Then, using the concept of "demand-driven market creation" (the idea that the market doesn't just satisfy pre-existing wants, it can be reshaped by creating new wants, which then drive supply side investment"), can we somehow convince society that sustainable products/solutions can very well be economically sound?

These are some activities I am thinking of for this club:
- Creating Nature Booth @ Carnival: walls covered in grass, moss, vines. Solar panels and wind turbine on the roof.
- Green fashion @ Lunar Gala?
- Starting a Green Cafe?
- Monthly "Nature time" at Schenley Park: We bring music, free tea, bubbles, blankets to lay on, drawing materials, balloons, sports activities, peace, rest, and joy
- Increase social media presence
- Creating short film about "Biophilia" and what we do as a club
- Make music that matches our vibe
- Compete in business cases
- Talk to our Government
---

events.title: ICOR Series with Isabelle Chen
events.description:
LCAL’s Informal Conversations on Research (ICOR) Series provides a welcoming forum for faculty and graduate students to share and discuss their most recent research in an engaging, accessible format.

Translingual Borders: Refugee Testimony and the Politics of Translation

Isabelle Chen, assistant professor of global French studies, will challenge the assumption that translation is a liberatory practice — one that enables people to cross linguistic, cultural and geographic borders — by examining how translation can also reinforce borders, reproduce unequal power dynamics and constrain individual agency.

Focusing on Shumona Sinha’s novel Assommons les pauvres ! (Down with the Poor!), Dr. Chen’s talk explores the experiences of a Bengali interpreter working with asylum seekers in France. She examines how Sinha uses translation both as a literary strategy and a central thematic motif to portray interpretation as a potential barrier to human mobility and freedom.

Drawing on translation theory and recent migration data, Dr. Chen considers what literary representations of translation can reveal about its real-world consequences — and about the roles of multilingualism, interpretation and language in immigration policy and advocacy today.

events.title: X in the Loop Webinar Series
events.description:
X in the Loop is an interdisciplinary webinar series that questions what it means for humans to remain “in control” of AI. By replacing “human” with the open variable “X,” the series explores who holds power in AI systems, whose perspectives are included and what other species, cultures and ways of knowing might belong in the loop.

Through perspectives from Carnegie Mellon University faculty and industry leaders, the rotating series examines how generative AI is reshaping data and prediction, AI literacy, immersive media and games, film and authorship and workforce development. No technical background is required. Each session is 60 minutes on Zoom, including time for audience questions.

Topic: Patterns, Predictions and the Power of Data: An Introduction to Data Science and Machine Learning

Every data project begins with a human question. This session shows how observations become datasets, how datasets reveal patterns, and how machine-learning models turn those patterns into classifications or predictions — and why correlation is not explanation. Examples draw from markets, public life, media, sport or biological systems. No prior programming or computer-science background is assumed.

Speaker: ​Raja Sooriamurthi — Teaching Professor, Information Systems Program, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: World of Music: Christopher Mark Jones’ “Montréal Encore”
events.description:
Christopher Mark Jones, professor emeritus of French & Francophone studies, returns with a celebration of his French-language album Montréal Encore, premiered with his collaborator Bernard Pozier at City of Asylum in March of 2023.

This concert features selections from that album and mix-ins by Québécois, French Caribbean and Parisian singer-songwriters—the likes of Boris Vian, Michel Rivard, Louis Aragon and Henri Salvador.

Free In-Person Tickets | Free Livestream Tickets

Featured Musicians:

Christopher Mark Jones: vocals, guitar

Brad Yoder: vocal harmonies, guitar, saxophone, glockenspiel

Mark Perna: bass

Eric George: African djembe and hand cymbals

Matt Siegler: piano and accordion

About the Artist:

Christopher Mark Jones draws from folk, country, blues, jazz and R&B sources to stage his literate folk-rock meditations. Using diverse points of view to narrate and critique life and love in uncertain times, he invites listeners to think, feel and dance. Recorded and live arrangements leave space for his musical co-conspirators to both express their personalities and honor the host creation. Listeners hear echoes of “Greg Brown’s pacing and a Lyle Lovett attitude” (Ben Shannon), as well as of John Prine, Bruce Coburn and Darrell Scott.

Between careers as a basketball player and French professor, Christopher busked in Paris, toured the UK, Denmark and Holland, and played New England clubs. He now tours and streams solo from Pittsburgh, PA, and plays regionally in formats varying from solo to full band. Looking for the Light (2021) is his sixth recording of original folk/roots songs, while Montréal Encore (2022) is a French-language recording created in collaboration with the poet Bernard Pozier.

About Your Visit:

The in-house restaurant, Cucina Alfabeto, is open for dinner from 5 to 10 p.m. Please visit OpenTable or call 412-435-1111 to make a reservation.

events.title: Academic Cultures in Conversation: Teaching, Learning and Higher Education Across Different Educational Contexts
events.description:
Join faculty, students and Russian scholars in exile from Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Pittsburgh and the Russian Academic Renewal and Exchange Program (U.S.-RAR) for a roundtable discussion on teaching, learning and higher education across academic cultures.

How do academic cultures shape the ways we teach, learn and engage with challenging ideas?

Participants will share perspectives on innovations in teaching and learning, the growing role of generative AI in education, academic freedom and the discussion of sensitive topics in the classroom and evolving expectations of students and instructors. The conversation will also examine how institutional policies, political and social developments and educational traditions influence academic experiences, particularly for international students, faculty and scholars working in exile.

By bringing together voices from different disciplines, institutions and educational contexts, the roundtable aims to foster dialogue, exchange ideas and reflect on the challenges and opportunities shaping higher education today.

Participants

Andreea Deciu Ritivoi — English, Carnegie Mellon University

Svitlana Maksymenko — Economics, University of Pittsburgh

Stuart McAdams — Undergraduate Student, Political Science/Russian/ROTC, University of Pittsburgh

Stephen Sudia — Ph.D. Student, Rhetoric, Carnegie Mellon University

events.title: Becoming Madam Europe: Ursula von der Leyen and the European Union in the Age of Trump
events.description:
Join Joyce Mushaben, Curators’ distinguished professor emerita of political science at the University of Missouri – St. Louis, for an examination of the challenges facing the European Union and the leadership of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The European Union faces a rapidly changing international landscape shaped by security challenges, geopolitical tensions, economic pressures and evolving relationships with global powers. In this lecture, Joyce Mushaben, a leading scholar of German politics, European Union affairs and women’s leadership, examines how Ursula von der Leyen and the European Commission have sought to navigate these challenges.

Drawing on von der Leyen’s tenure as European Commission president since 2019 and her second term, which runs through 2029, Mushaben explores the leadership strategies and political dynamics that have shaped von der Leyen’s influence within Europe and on the world stage.

The lecture will consider what von der Leyen’s leadership reveals about the European Union’s evolving role in world politics — and the opportunities and challenges ahead for Europe in an increasingly complex global environment.

events.title: Chemistry Seminar: Anindita Das, Southern Methodist University
events.description:
Anindita Das
Southern Methodist University

Tuning Atomically Precise Materials for Sustainable Chemistry

Host: Stefan Bernhard

Friday, October 30th, 2026

12:30 p.m.

Mellon Institute Conference Room 348

Abstract: With the advent of nanotechnology in the mid-1980s, nanomaterials have attracted tremendous interest due to their unique properties which make them suitable for diverse applications. However, the inherent polydispersity of conventional nanoparticles has precluded an atomic-level understanding of their structure-property relationships. This, in turn, has greatly hampered the complete realization of their target functional properties in real-world applications. This talk will focus on leveraging the principles of synthetic organic and inorganic chemistry to engineer multifunctional atomically precise materials for applications in catalysis, water harvesting, and iodine capture. Specifically, we will discuss two classes of materials, (1) molecularly pure, ligand-protected coinage metal clusters, and (2) covalent organic frameworks (COFs), which are atomically precise tunable materials with extraordinary porosity and crystallinity. Overall, these efforts aim to establish design rules for making functional heterogeneous nanomaterials with known structure-property-function relationships.

Bio: Anindita (Dia) Das obtained her Ph.D. with Prof. Rongchao Jin at Carnegie Mellon University, where her research focused on the synthesis and single-crystal growth of atomically precise gold nanoparticles to gain in-depth understanding of catalytic mechanisms. Prior to this, she earned B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees at Osmania University, India and the University of Pune, India respectively. Following her PhD., Dia carried out postdoctoral research with Prof. Chad Mirkin at Northwestern University, where her work centered on the development of spherical nucleic acids based on atomically precise gold nanoclusters for applications in colloidal crystal engineering. Dia started her independent lab in the Chemistry Department at Southern Methodist University in Fall 2020.

events.title: Artificial Intelligence and Precision Medicine: From Traditional Machine Learning to AI?
events.description:
Precision medicine has evolved significantly alongside advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence, moving from foundational statistical models to today’s deep-learning-driven and foundation-model diagnostic tools. This talk traces that progression, examining how AI enables large-scale analysis of complex medical data to support more personalized disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Beyond the technical advances, the talk considers the broader implications of this shift—including questions of regulation, interpretability, cost, and responsibility—as AI-based tools move from research settings into everyday clinical practice.
The talk will outline how AI relates to precision medicine, introduce the core concepts underlying AI and machine learning, present how these methods are being applied in real diagnostic and clinical settings, and close with a discussion of their broader impact on health and policy.
